It offers full-service book creation and publishing in paperback, hardback, digital and audiobook formats, along with children's titles, compact Express Books, website design and SEO, and podcast and video production. We are glad to publish the testimony of a woman who went looking for soul food and found Jesus.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The Preface gives two reasons. She wanted to encourage other Christians, and she hoped non-Christians would see that the Jesus of the Bible is real:
"He continues to transform lives today in the most extraordinary ways."
She closes the book the same way she began it, as a testimony:
"I have written this book as a testimony to Christ, who has shown me that He has always been the Lord of my life."

faq.q: What is Forever Changed about?
faq.a: It is Mary Mowoe's account of searching for meaning and finding Jesus. In August 2019, alone on her sofa in Paris, she heard a voice say "I need soul food" and set out to find what it meant. Across thirteen chapters she tells what came before and what came after, including her baptism, her doubts and her new life as a prison chaplain.

faq.q: Is it a true story?
faq.a: Yes. It is a first-person testimony. The Preface says she is no expert on Christianity, only on her own experience.

faq.q: Is it a dramatic conversion story?
faq.a: No, and she says so on purpose. The Preface notes that many people wait for a dramatic encounter before they take Christ seriously, and she writes that she does not believe an extraordinary encounter is necessary, because the real miracle happens when you allow Him into your life.

faq.q: Does the book help answer whether Jesus is real?
faq.a: It is a testimony rather than an argument. Mary writes that she hopes non-Christians will see that the Jesus of the Bible is real, and Chapter 5, The Gospel Made Plain, explains the Bible's message in plain English for readers who have never read it.

faq.q: Does she write about hearing God's voice?
faq.a: Yes. The book opens with the voice she heard three times on her sofa, and Chapter 9, When God Talks, tells other times she believes God spoke to her, including through answered prayer. She also writes about how she knows it is Him.

faq.q: Is it helpful for someone reading the Bible for the first time?
faq.a: It may be. Mary had never been able to read past the first chapter of the Bible, and she tells how she finally started and what landed in her heart. She uses the New International Version throughout.

faq.q: What is The Valley?
faq.a: Chapter 10. It covers the fifteen months, from January 2023 to April 2024, when her mother was seriously ill in Nigeria, and what that time taught her about sacrifice and forgiveness. She read those pages to her mother before publishing them.

faq.q: Does it talk about baptism?
faq.a: Yes. She was baptised on 27 June 2021, fully immersed, after the Covid-19 pandemic delayed it, and she chose to make it a public profession of her faith in front of the people in her life.

faq.q: Does it talk about finding a church?
faq.a: Yes. At first she wanted to live her faith alone at home with YouTube sermons. Chapter 4 tells how she came around to going, and Chapter 11, The Church, covers choosing a church, what to do when something is wrong and her church family.

faq.q: Does it talk about her career in human resources?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 6, Old Profession, covers her thirty-plus years in Human Resources in the UK and France, the stress, being let go, and how she left HR for good in 2024. Chapter 12, New Profession, describes what she does now.

content_note.title: Content note
paras: The book covers her mother's long illness, a job loss, and a young man hurt by someone in a church. It is told gently and with humor.

hero.audience_line: For children ages 3 to 7 and the parents, grandparents, Sunday school teachers and homeschool families who read Bible stories aloud with them, especially any child who feels small or afraid.
hero.tagline: David is ready to face a giant, but first he really has to pee! A funny retelling of David and Goliath from 1 Samuel 17, where a shepherd boy and a great big giant both need a bathroom break, and only one knows his heavenly Father is with him.

audience.headline: A shepherd boy, a giant with a HUGE spear, and two very necessary bathroom breaks.
audience.body: For children ages 3 to 7 and the grown-ups who read to them: parents at bedtime, grandparents sharing Bible stories, Sunday school and children's church teachers, preschool and kindergarten teachers, and homeschool families. Shelly White retells David and Goliath from 1 Samuel 17 with big sound words and two imagined bathroom breaks, one for David behind a bush and one for Goliath behind a great big rock. Under the giggles is the real story: a boy who cared for sheep in danger faces a giant in our heavenly Father's name. A note on subjects: the stone hits the giant's forehead and he falls, THUD!, with dust around his feet. Nothing more is shown, and the soldiers cheer. The bathroom scenes are played for giggles. The author's note says plainly which parts are imagined additions to the Bible story.

quote.text: David was small. Goliath was big. Goliath trusted his spear. David trusted his heavenly Father.
quote.cite: Give Me a Minute, Goliath!, page 53

what_makes.title: What makes this book for little listeners
paras: It gives a big story a small, funny moment every child knows. The author's note says children ages three to seven are discovering how their bodies work, and that giggling about peeing and pooping can be part of that discovery. Then it says what the story is really about: David was not brave because he was big, but because he knew his heavenly Father was with him.
Five things set it apart:
list: It keeps the real story. David brings bread and cheese to his brothers, Saul says he is only a boy, the armor is too heavy, and David picks five smooth stones from the stream. The author's note points to 1 Samuel 17.
It gives the giant a bathroom break too. Even a great big giant needed a little bathroom break, the book says, and the note adds that Goliath had everyday needs, just like us.
It names the Father. The note says the retelling uses “our heavenly Father” to help children connect the God of David's story with the Father Jesus reveals.
It says what is imagined. The bathroom breaks, some dialogue and David's whispered thank-you are imagined additions, and the note says so.
It has a seek-and-find. A sheep is hidden in every scene, and a Where's the Sheep? key at the back lists every spread from pages 4-5 to 52-53.

sections.h2: For bedtime and family read-aloud
paras: The pages are built for a reading voice: STOMP! STOMP! CLANK!, CLUNK! CLANK!, WHIRR! WHIRR! WHOOSH! and a long Pssssssssssssssss! for the giant. Children can count the stones with you, one, two, three, four, FIVE, and call out “Give me a minute, Goliath!” with David.

sections.h2: For Sunday school and children's church
paras: The beats of 1 Samuel 17 are all here: the army camp, the giant's challenge, frightened soldiers, Saul's armor, the lion and the bear, the five stones, the sling and David's words, “I come in our heavenly Father's name.” The two bathroom breaks give the room a laugh before the big moment.

sections.h2: For children who feel small or afraid
paras: The book opens with Joshua 1:9 from the Father's Heart Bible, “Be strong and courageous. Do not fear or be discouraged, for I, your Father, am with you wherever you go.” The note ends with the point for every small listener: when children feel small or afraid, they can remember that the Father is with them too.

sections.h2: For families who want to say thank you
paras: After the soldiers cheer, David looks up at the sky and whispers a thank-you. It is an imagined line, the note says, and it gives children simple words to borrow: “You were with me all along.”

details.Title: Give Me a Minute, Goliath!
details.Subtitle: A Funny Bible Story with Potty Humor for Kids
details.Author: Shelly White
details.Series: Big Bible Stories, Little Bathroom Breaks
details.Binding: Paperback (perfect bound, matte) and hardback (case laminate, matte)

paras: Nobody wants to fight the giant. Nobody at all. King Saul tells David he is only a boy, but David has cared for sheep in danger, and he answers:
“Our heavenly Father was with me when a lion and a bear came. He will be with me when I face this giant, too.”

Saul's helmet and armor go CLUNK! CLANK!, and David cannot move in them. Off they come. David takes his staff, his shepherd's bag and his sling, and then his knees squeeze together. He calls across to the giant that he needs a minute, hurries behind a bush, and comes back saying “That feels better!” Then he picks five smooth stones from the stream.

Goliath laughs at the boy with a stick. David holds his sling and says that he comes in our heavenly Father's name. Round and round goes the sling, WHIRR! WHIRR! WHOOSH!, and one stone flies straight to the giant's forehead. Down goes Goliath. The soldiers cheer, and David whispers his thanks to the Father who was with him all along.

author.bio: Shelly White believes childhood is synonymous with laughter, a gift our heavenly Father has given each of us. With a degree in early childhood education and years of teaching young children, she knows little ones learn best through stories, play and fun. Her grand littles' giggles and endless conversations about pee and poop inspired her first book, about Zacchaeus and how meeting Jesus changed his life. Through her Big Bible Stories, Little Bathroom Breaks series, she hopes children discover that their heavenly Father loves them and delights in their life and laughter.

The book quotes the Father's Heart Bible, our translation, and we are glad to bring David's courage to young children with a laugh.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author's bio says her grand littles' giggles and endless conversations about pee and poop started this series. Her note on this book says what she wants a small child to hold on to:
“David was not brave because he was big. He was brave because he knew his heavenly Father was with him.”
“When children feel small or afraid, they can remember that the Father is with them too.”

faq.q: What is Give Me a Minute, Goliath! about?
faq.a: It is a funny picture book retelling of David and Goliath. David brings food to his brothers, sees the giant, refuses Saul's armor and gets ready to fight, but first he has to pee. Then Goliath has to go too. When they meet, one smooth stone brings the giant down.

faq.q: Where is the story of David and Goliath in the Bible?
faq.a: In 1 Samuel 17. The author's note gives that reference and says the bathroom breaks, some dialogue and David's whispered thank-you are imagined additions.

faq.q: Does it teach children about courage?
faq.a: Yes. The book opens with Joshua 1:9, “Be strong and courageous,” and the author's note says David was not brave because he was big, but because he knew his heavenly Father was with him.

faq.q: Is it a book about facing giants?
faq.a: Yes, in a child-sized way. David is small and Goliath is big, and the note tells children that when they feel small or afraid, they can remember that the Father is with them too.

faq.q: Does it teach trusting God?
faq.a: Yes. The last page sets it side by side: “Goliath trusted his spear. David trusted his heavenly Father.” Earlier David tells Saul that our heavenly Father was with him when a lion and a bear came.

faq.q: Is it a potty training book?
faq.a: No. It does not teach toilet steps. It uses bathroom humor that children ages 3 to 7 already enjoy to bring them into a Bible story, and the author's note explains why.

faq.q: What age is it for?
faq.a: Ages 3 to 7, as a read-aloud picture book. Most pages carry two to four short lines and a sound word.

faq.q: Is there a seek-and-find in the book?
faq.a: Yes. A sheep is hidden in every scene, and the Where's the Sheep? page at the back lists every spread from pages 4-5 to 52-53.

faq.q: Is it part of a series of Bible stories for kids?
faq.a: Yes. It belongs to Big Bible Stories, Little Bathroom Breaks, and the More from Shelly page at the back shows the four books. They are, in order: Zacchaeus Has to Pee!; Noah, What's That Smell?; Give Me a Minute, Goliath!; and Hold It, Daniel! Each one retells a real Bible story with one imagined bathroom break and its own seek-and-find.

hero.audience_line: For children ages 5 to 8, for families who read aloud together, and for grandparents who want to tell children where the family came from.
hero.tagline: From a little village in Greece to grocery store shelves in America: a picture book, based on a true story, about a girl who dreamed of becoming a chef and never gave up.

audience.headline: A poor girl from a small Greek village says she will become a chef. Some people laugh. She decides to keep believing.
audience.body: For children ages 5 to 8, for families who read aloud together, and for grandparents who want to tell children where the family came from. Tyler Stavlas tells the true story of his Greek grandmother, YiaYia Voula: a cook who moves to America without speaking the language, hears no from job after job, raises three children on her own and trusts God until her tzatziki reaches the grocery store. A note on subjects: it is a short picture book with a hopeful ending. Along the way Voula lives through poverty, nights with no place to call home, three jobs at once and an illness so serious that she falls into a coma. The book tells it simply, and her family prays at her side. If a child in your care has lived through illness or loss at home, it is a good one to read together and leave room for questions.

quote.text: “I’ll keep believing. I won’t give up on my dreams!”
quote.cite: YiaYia Voula's Big Dream, Voula after the others laugh at her

what_makes.title: What makes this book for children who dream big
paras: It is the story of a real person, told by her grandson. From the first page a child knows that Voula is real and that her dream came true. The book is about everything that happened in between.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is a true story. The subtitle says so, and the first page tells how to say the name, YAH-yah VOO-lah, and that it means Grandma Voula.
It shows rejection honestly. In America, Voula tried and tried, and job after job said no, until a resort hired her as a chef.

Faith is there in the hardest moments. Voula prays when the family moves, her faith gives her strength through three jobs, and the family keeps praying while she is sick. Faith is not an add-on at the end; it is what holds the family together.
It is written to be read aloud. The sentences are short, and nearly every page ends with something Voula does: she takes a deep breath, studies, tries again, smiles, keeps going.

It ends with two questions for the child, "What is your dream?" and "What can you accomplish if you never give up?" Then a page tells what became of the family brand, YiaYia Voula's Foods, which the book says launched in 2024 and is now in over 300 stores.

sections.h2: For families looking for picture books with values
paras: If you want a short book about hard work, family and faith that still reads like a story, this is one. It has a real heroine, and each page moves her life one step forward.

sections.h2: For grandparents and grandchildren
paras: The book was born in a kitchen, between a grandson and his grandmother. If you are a grandparent, read it and then tell your grandchild about your own beginnings. The question at the end is made for that: what is your dream?

sections.h2: For teachers and libraries
paras: It is a short classroom read with a clear story, a heroine who gets up after every no, and a question to talk about. The About the Author page says a copy is being donated to every public library in his county.

sections.h2: For children who have a dream and are afraid of being laughed at
paras: Voula's first hard moment is not the language or money. It is other people laughing at her when she is a girl. The book shows what she does: she cries, walks away, takes a deep breath and decides to keep going. It is a short scene a child recognizes right away.

blocks.text: The book opens with a wish for whoever reads it:

paras: you can trust God, keep dreaming, and never give up.

blocks.text: That line comes right after the book explains the name YiaYia Voula, and it returns at the end. The story begins:

paras: In a little village in Greece, lived a young girl named Voula with a very big dream.

blocks.text: On the next page, she says out loud what she wants to be:

paras: One day, I will become a chef, and all my recipes will be shared around the world!

details.Title: YiaYia Voula's Big Dream
details.Subtitle: A True Story of Never Giving Up
details.Author: Tyler Stavlas

paras: Soon after the story begins, some people hear Voula say she will become a chef, and they laugh: how could a poor girl from a small town ever be a great chef? Tears trickle down her face. Then she walks away, takes a deep breath and makes a choice. It is the choice that carries the rest of the book, and the one a child will remember.

In America, Voula is left to care for her three children on her own. She works three jobs: in a cold fish market, as a waitress and as a chef. The book says her faith in God gave her strength. And it says something more:
"Some nights, Voula and her children didn’t have a place to call home."
But kind hearts opened their doors, and little by little, hope found them again.

stories.h2: From a hospital bed to the grocery store
paras: When Voula becomes very sick, her family stays by her side day after day. Then the book asks the question it leaves hanging: "Would Voula get better?" She opens her eyes, the doctors are amazed and the family thanks God. Then they begin sharing her tzatziki with grocery stores. Some say they have no room. At one, the owner tastes it and exclaims that the sauce must be in all their stores.

author.bio: Tyler Stavlas grew up in the kitchen with his YiaYia, his Greek grandmother, helping her cook and make her famous tzatziki while listening to her stories of the struggles she faced and how she never gave up. He wrote this book to share her message with children everywhere: dream big and never quit. Today he serves as Chief Product Officer of YiaYia Voula's Foods. He founded Hunger for Change, a nonprofit that, the book says, has donated 750 pounds of unsold YiaYia Voula's tzatziki to local food shelters, and he speaks about perseverance, entrepreneurship and servant leadership.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The About the Author page says it in his own words: those kitchen stories stayed with him, and "he wrote this book to share her message with children everywhere: dream big and never quit."
The book closes with the same message in another form:
"YiaYia Voula's greatest gift wasn't just her recipes. It was showing people around the world that even when life gets hard, you can trust God, keep trying, and never give up on your dreams."

faq.q: What is YiaYia Voula's Big Dream about?
faq.a: It is an illustrated picture book, based on a true story, about a girl from a little village in Greece who dreams of becoming a chef. Voula moves to America, faces closed doors, raises three children on her own and keeps believing until her tzatziki sauce reaches the grocery store.

faq.q: Is it a true story?
faq.a: Yes. The subtitle is A True Story of Never Giving Up, and the About the Author page says the story began in the kitchen with the author's YiaYia, his Greek grandmother, and her stories of the struggles she faced.

faq.q: Is it a good picture book to read aloud?
faq.a: Yes. It is short, the sentences are simple, and it ends with a quiet question for the child. It does include a scene of serious illness and a coma, so some parents may prefer to read it in the daytime or with time to talk.

faq.q: Does it teach children to follow their dreams?
faq.a: That is its message. Voula says as a girl that she will become a chef, keeps saying it after people laugh and after job after job says no, and the book ends by asking the reader: "What is your dream?"

faq.q: Is it a story about a grandmother?
faq.a: Yes. YiaYia means grandma, and the book tells the life of the author's grandmother from girlhood in Greece to the success of her tzatziki. It is a natural book for a grandparent and grandchild to share.

faq.q: Does it teach perseverance?
faq.a: Yes, through the story rather than a list of tips. Voula keeps going through people laughing, a new language, rejection, three jobs at once and a serious illness. The last page names the lesson: trust God, keep trying and never give up on your dreams.

faq.q: Does it talk about God?
faq.a: Yes. Voula prays and trusts God to take care of the family when they move to America, her faith gives her strength through three jobs, and her family prays and trusts God while she is sick. It is a Christian story told without preaching.

faq.q: What ages is it for?
faq.a: Children ages 5 to 8, the reading age on the book's Spanish edition record. A younger child can enjoy it read aloud, and an eight-year-old can read it alone.

faq.q: Is there a Spanish edition?
faq.a: Yes. The copyright page lists the Spanish edition, El Gran Sueño de la YiaYia Voula, in paperback, hardback and eBook.

content_note.title: Content note
paras: Voula lives through poverty, nights with no place to call home and an illness that leaves her in a coma. The book tells it simply, her family prays at her side, and the story ends in hope.

hero.audience_line: For Christians in secular jobs who dread Monday morning, for managers and HR professionals who want to keep Jesus at the center of their work, and for small groups that want to talk honestly about faith and work.
hero.tagline: After fifteen years in human resources, John Englehart Jr. names the dread that shows up on Sunday evening and offers a simple, Scripture-rooted way to stay steady at work.

audience.headline: An HR professional who has sat in his car on a Monday morning, praying through tears, writes for every believer who feels Sunday night in the stomach.
audience.body: For Christians who work in secular jobs and feel the pull between providing and trusting, for managers and HR professionals, for anyone who wonders whether ordinary work matters to God, and for small groups and Bible studies. John Englehart Jr. first heard the phrase "Sunday Scaries" at an HR conference and laughed, then realized he knew the feeling well. The book walks through a framework he calls STEADY, one letter per chapter, with stories from the Postal Service and from fifteen years in HR. A note on subjects: the book speaks plainly about anxiety, workplace gossip, burnout, King David's sin with Bathsheba, and the hard choice to leave a job. It says it is not medical, mental health, legal or professional advice, and that names and details in its stories have been changed and some characters are composites.

quote.text: You can work in a secular world without becoming shaped by it.
quote.cite: The Sunday Scaries, Chapter 1: The Sunday Scaries

what_makes.title: What makes this book for Christians in ordinary jobs
paras: The book grew out of a conversation. A friend from church said, "I wish there were more books that encouraged people like us," people who work in secular jobs and try to keep Jesus first. The author's answer was two words: "Challenge accepted." He is careful to say the book is not a guilt trip, a sermon or a promise that work gets easy.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is built on one framework, STEADY. Seek God First; Treat Your Work as Worship; Excel as If Working for the Lord; Add Value Where You Are; Demonstrate Christ Through Good Work; and Yield to Forgiveness, Mercy, and Grace. Chapters 3 through 8 take one letter each.

It is written by someone who sits across the table. The author has worked in HR for fifteen years and started out as a mail carrier, and he tells stories from both, including the ones where he got it wrong.

It uses Bible people who did ordinary work under pressure. Nehemiah served a king who did not share his faith, the apostle John was a fisherman, and the book points out that Jesus Himself was known as "the carpenter."

It does not pretend. A chapter called Unsteady looks at King David's fall and gives a plain tool for mistakes: own it, learn from it, prevent it. It also says that verses about faithfulness at work are "not permission slips for abuse."
It is made for groups. Every chapter ends with discussion questions and space to write, and three short frameworks, STEADY, GRACE and OLP, are collected at the back.

sections.h2: For believers who dread Monday morning
paras: If Sunday nights feel heavy, the author says plainly that this book is for you. He does not promise that you will love your job. He points to something deeper than job satisfaction: "Happiness is temporary and circumstantial. Joy runs deeper and stays steady." A pastor's line gave him a reboot he passes on: God is our eternal source, and our jobs are a temporary resource.

sections.h2: For managers, leaders and HR professionals
paras: The author's note says what years in HR taught him: the way we treat people at work matters, and "Leadership has a human cost." In Chapter 5 he tells how, working in higher education during the pandemic, he replaced annual ratings with a twice-a-year coaching conversation he calls EXCELL. Chapter 7's GRACE framework gives five steps to run through before you speak in a hard conversation, starting with a pause and a short prayer: "Jesus, help me honor you here."

sections.h2: For small groups and Bible studies
paras: Every chapter closes with four or five discussion questions, from when your Sunday Scaries show up to where you are resisting surrender this week. The author hopes the book "keeps going in your small groups, your Bible studies, your conversations over coffee," so that someone who says work is eating them alive is met with prayer and encouragement instead of shallow advice.

sections.h2: For anyone wondering whether to stay or go
paras: Chapter 9 does not tell you to push through no matter what. It says sometimes the most faithful next step is admitting a workplace is shaping you in the wrong direction. It offers questions to ask before God, urges you to bring trusted voices into the decision, and states it simply: "Faithfulness doesn't mean staying trapped."

stories.h2: The mail truck and the Oldsmobile
paras: In Chapter 3, the author is a new mail carrier in Baltimore City in 2000, in the last week of a ninety-day probation where one serious mistake meant you were gone. He misses a house, backs up the truck against the rules, and hits an older woman's car. She gets out, smiles and says, "Oh honey, I'm okay." Her husband had worked for the Post Office, there was no damage, and she drove away. Around that time an aunt had encouraged him to start each morning in prayer, so he prayed on every commute. His lesson is careful:
"Seeking God first doesn't always change the situation, but it changes who we're becoming inside it."

stories.h2: Did God get glory from that?
paras: Chapter 4 tells of a coworker who was like a spiritual mother to him. When he told an off-color joke, she never shamed him. She asked one calm question, and he passes it on as a filter for emails, meetings and hallway talk:
"John, did God get glory from that?"

Then he admits a failure. In a meeting where gossip about two leaders crossed the line, he did not laugh, but he did not speak up either. He writes that silence is sometimes neutral, "but sometimes it becomes agreement."

In Chapter 9, a young, rushing mail carrier fills up his truck, grabs a soda and drives off with the gas hose still attached. He tries to jam it back into the pump, gives up and finishes his route. When his supervisor asks if he knows anything about it, he lies. The supervisor already knows, laughs, and tells him the real problem was the rushing. Then he gives the advice that became the book's tool for mistakes: own it, learn from it, prevent it. The author reports the result:
"I have never driven off with a gas hose again."

author.bio: John Englehart Jr. has worked in human resources for fifteen years, and his byline lists the MDE and SHRM-CP credentials. He began his working life in 2000 as a U.S. mail carrier in Baltimore City. He writes that he is not seminary-trained but "a fellow disciple of Jesus Christ" who has spent years trying to study, love and live the Word, and he calls himself a teacher at heart. He started writing The Sunday Scaries during the holiday season of 2025.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: It started with a friend from church who named a gap: encouragement for believers trying to follow Jesus faithfully in workplaces that do not naturally reinforce faith. In his Author's Note, he adds a second reason. After years in HR, he wanted to say out loud that the way we treat people at work matters. But the book, he writes, has a different aim than challenging leaders:
"My hope is that it shepherds believers."
He closes with a word for the week ahead:
"take a breath, say a prayer, and keep walking with Jesus."

faq.q: What is The Sunday Scaries about?
faq.a: It is a book for Christians who work in secular jobs and feel the dread that shows up as the weekend ends. John Englehart Jr., who has worked in HR for fifteen years, shows how to find peace and purpose at work while keeping Jesus at the center, using a framework he calls STEADY.

faq.q: What is the STEADY framework?
faq.a: They are, in order: Seek God First; Treat Your Work as Worship; Excel as If Working for the Lord; Add Value Where You Are; Demonstrate Christ Through Good Work; and Yield to Forgiveness, Mercy, and Grace. Chapters 3 through 8 take one each, and the framework is summarized again at the back of the book.

faq.q: What Bible verses about work does the book use?
faq.a: Many. Colossians 3:23, "work at it with all your heart, as working for the Lord," sits at the heart of the book, along with 1 Corinthians 10:31 on doing everything for the glory of God, Genesis 22:14 on the Lord who provides, and Proverbs 24:16 on rising again after a fall. Scripture is quoted from the New International Version.

faq.q: Does it help with prayer at work?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 3, Seek God First, tells how the author began praying every morning on his commute, and the GRACE framework for hard conversations starts with a pause and a short prayer before you speak. The book is about putting God first before work starts demanding answers.

faq.q: Is it about identity in Christ?
faq.a: In part. The book says plainly that your job is not the source of your security, your identity, your joy or your worth, and that God is. It calls a job a temporary resource and God our eternal source.

faq.q: Can a small group or a women's Bible study use it?
faq.a: Yes. Every chapter ends with discussion group questions and space to write, and the author hopes the book keeps going in small groups and Bible studies. It is written for men and women alike, not for one group only.

faq.q: Is it a devotional for men?
faq.a: Not a daily devotional. It is ten chapters you can read straight through or one per group meeting. Men will recognize the stories from a man's working life, from a broken lawnmower at fourteen to a mail truck, but it is written for every believer in a secular job.

faq.q: Does the book say to stay in a hard job no matter what?
faq.a: No. Chapter 9 says sometimes the most faithful step is admitting an environment is shaping you in the wrong direction and letting go. It urges you to seek counsel first, and it says faithfulness at work is not permission for abuse, intimidation or unethical pressure.

hero.audience_line: For parents, grandparents and Sunday school teachers who want to read aloud about prayer and faith, and for any child who loves a family dog or is facing a pet's illness or a trip to the vet.
hero.tagline: A boy's sick puppy, a hard visit to the vet and a heartfelt prayer come together in this gentle rhyming picture book about bringing every fear to God.

audience.headline: Co-Co will not touch her eggs, the vet has heavy news, and a boy remembers all the people Jesus healed.
audience.body: For parents and grandparents who want to read aloud with children about prayer, faith and caring for animals; for Sunday school teachers and children's ministry leaders; for a child who loves a family dog or is facing a pet's illness or a trip to the vet; and for families who want to talk about bringing every worry to God. Told in rhyming verse by a boy named Ray, the story follows his little dog Co-Co from a morning when she will not eat, through a quiet drive and an x-ray, to a prayer on the ride home and a morning when she is sitting by the door. A note on subjects: the vet finds a tumor in Co-Co's heart and says he cannot make her well today, and Ray cries on the way home. In the story Co-Co gets well after the family and their church pray. Parents of a child whose own pet did not recover may want to read it first. It is a story about prayer and trust, not veterinary advice.

quote.text: I bowed my head and asked God To make my Co-Co well. I felt such peace and joy inside,
quote.cite: Co-Co AKA The Lazarus Dog, page 26

what_makes.title: What makes this book for families who pray together
paras: It puts a child's real worry in a child's own voice. Ray tells the story himself, from the first sad morning to the last happy one, and every page rhymes, so a young listener can follow along and feel each turn with him.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is told by the boy. Ray notices first that something is wrong, asks to go to the vet, and says out loud that he is nervous and scared.
It shows a grown-up praying. In the car, Mom pats Ray's knee and whispers a short prayer that a child can learn by heart.
It is honest about bad news. The vet listens, takes an x-ray, and says plainly that Co-Co has a tumor in her heart and he cannot make her well today.
It shows where to turn. On the ride home Ray remembers all the people Jesus healed, bows his head and asks God to make Co-Co well, and feels peace and joy inside.
It brings in the church. Mom texts their pastor, and the people at church pray all that day while Co-Co sleeps.

sections.h2: For parents and grandparents reading aloud
paras: Each page is a short rhyming verse of four to twelve lines, easy to read in one breath and easy to pause on. The prayers are written out in full, so a child can say them with you: “Dear God, You made all things. You made sweet Co-Co, too.”

sections.h2: For a child whose pet is sick
paras: Ray's feelings are named one at a time: his heart is full of fear, he is nervous, he cries. The book does not rush past them. It shows a mother who comforts, a vet who is gentle and honest, and a boy who brings what he cannot fix to God.

sections.h2: For Sunday school and children's ministry
paras: The story connects a child's everyday trouble to the healings of Jesus, and it shows prayer in three settings: a mother in the car, a boy in a waiting room and a church praying together. It ends with a shout a class can join: “A-men and A-men!”

paras: Co-Co will not touch her eggs and does not even look at her leash. Ray wants to take her to the vet. Mom thinks she is probably just tired and says to wait another day. The next morning Co-Co is sleeping so soundly it is hard to wake her, and Ray says:
“Co-Co is just not herself. My heart is full of fear.”

Doc gently touches Co-Co's chest, listens to her heart and takes an x-ray. Ray waits and prays again, asking God not to let Co-Co be scared. Then Doc comes out and gently says that she has a tumor in her heart. “I can't make her well today,” he says, with a heavy heart.

On the ride home Ray cries, then remembers all the people Jesus healed. He bows his head and asks God to make Co-Co well, and he feels such peace and joy inside that he tells Mom he has good news: Co-Co is going to be okay. They stop for chicken and rice. Mom texts their pastor, the church prays all day, and at dinner time Co-Co's tail gives a little flick. The next morning she is sitting by the door, a sick dog no more.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author dedicates the book to her brother, “who was known for his love of animals and quiet faith,” and the story carries both: a boy who loves his dog and a faith that turns to prayer when the news is hard. At the turning point, the boy remembers who to ask:
“I remembered all the people That Jesus healed—so many times.”

faq.q: What is Co-Co AKA The Lazarus Dog about?
faq.a: It is a rhyming picture book about a boy named Ray whose little dog Co-Co stops eating. At the vet, an x-ray shows a tumor in her heart. Ray remembers the people Jesus healed and prays for Co-Co, his mother texts their pastor and the church prays, and the next morning Co-Co is well.

faq.q: Is it a prayer for healing book for kids?
faq.a: It is a story about praying for healing, not a collection of prayers. Ray asks God to make Co-Co well and feels peace and joy, and in the story Co-Co gets well. The vet is honest that he cannot make her well that day.

faq.q: Is there a prayer for a sick dog in the book?
faq.a: Yes, three short ones. Mom prays in the car, “Dear God, You made all things. You made sweet Co-Co, too.” Ray prays in the waiting room that Co-Co will not be scared, and on the ride home he asks God to make her well.

faq.q: Does Co-Co get well? Does God heal her?
faq.a: Yes, in the story. After the family and the church pray, Co-Co eats chicken and rice at dinner time, and the next morning she jumps up strong upon her paws, a sick dog no more. The book ends, “Oh, thank You, God!”

faq.q: Why do they give Co-Co chicken and rice?
faq.a: Ray asks to buy chicken to feed her when they get home, and Mom stops at the grocery store for chicken and rice. It is part of the story, not feeding advice.

faq.q: Is it about a dog heart tumor?
faq.a: The vet finds a tumor in Co-Co's heart, and that is the only medical detail in the book. It gives no medical information and no advice about pet illness.

faq.q: Does it show a praying family and church?
faq.a: Yes. Mom prays in the car, Ray prays twice, Mom texts their pastor to pray, and the people at church pray all that day.

faq.q: What age is it for?
faq.a: Ages 4 to 8, as a rhyming read-aloud. It is 38 pages in full color, with one short verse on each story page.

faq.q: Who is the book written in memory of?
faq.a: The author's brother, who, the dedication says, was known for his love of animals and quiet faith.

audience.headline: For the believer whose prayers feel unanswered: thirty-one readings on standing firm, keeping hope and living for what lasts.
audience.body: For believers in a season when heaven seems quiet, readers who feel the pull of anxiety and distraction, parents, and anyone who wants to test what they hear against Scripture. R.S. Smith opens one passage a day, explains it, often looks at a key Greek or Hebrew word, and closes with questions for reflection and a song. The last days of the book face the hardest questions directly: guarding your heart, standing firm when the world is shaking, living with eternal perspective and what to do when God seems silent. This is Book 4 of the Rightly Dividing the Truth series, and every volume stands on its own. Scripture is quoted from the New International Version, with some passages from the Amplified Bible.

quote.text: Yet Scripture assures us that feeling distant from God is not the same as being abandoned by God.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for believers holding on
paras: It opens with a warning and ends with a promise. Day 1 says that "we must learn to test everything against the unchanging Word of God." Day 31 sits with David's cry in Psalm 22, the words Jesus prayed on the cross, and says plainly that faith is not the absence of struggle.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is honest about silence and distance. Day 29, When God Seems Silent, reads Psalm 13 and Habakkuk, and Day 31 reads Psalm 22. Both say God welcomes honest questions.
It speaks to life now. Readings on guarding your heart in an anxious world, standing firm when the world is shaking and living with purpose in a distracted world name the pressures readers feel.
It defends the faith. Day 19, The Case for Christ, points to creation and to discoveries such as the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Tel Dan Stele.
It opens the original languages. Readings explain words such as pistis, faith, leb, the heart, and the Hebrew cry "How long?"
Every day ends with reflection questions and a song, from Stand in the Truth and Faith Unseen to When Heaven Is Silent and When You Feel So Far Away.

sections.h2: For anyone in a season when God seems silent
paras: Day 29 begins with the honest admission that there are times when we pray, cry out and wait with no answer. It reads David's cry of how long in Psalm 13 and Habakkuk's complaint, and says that God's silence is not His absence. Day 31 adds: "Faith is not the absence of struggle; it is continuing to cry out even when answers are delayed."

sections.h2: For believers who want to test what they hear
paras: Day 1, Beware of False Teachers, starts with Jesus' warning in Matthew 7:15 and moves through 2 Peter 2, Galatians 1 and 1 John 4. It notes that false teaching "rarely announces itself with fanfare" and points to the Bereans, who examined the Scriptures every day. Day 23, Straining at a Gnat, turns the same warning on misplaced priorities in our own lives.

sections.h2: For readers living with anxiety and distraction
paras: Day 26 opens Proverbs 4:23, "Above all else, guard your heart," and explains that in Hebrew the heart is the whole inner person. As the reading puts it, "The heart is the control center of our lives." Day 27 is about standing firm when the world is shaking, and Day 28 about living with purpose when everything is designed to distract us.

sections.h2: For parents
paras: Day 15, Training Up a Child, takes Proverbs 22:6 and Deuteronomy 6:6-7 and talks about intentional, personal training that fits each child. Day 14, Sons and Daughters, Friends of God and Jesus, describes the relationship every believer has with the Father and the Son.

paras: The book opens with a warning from Jesus: "Watch out for false prophets. They come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ferocious wolves." The reading explains that false teaching mixes truth with error until believers can no longer tell them apart. Its answer is simple but demanding: know the Word of God so well that counterfeits become obvious, as the Bereans did. The day's song is Stand in the Truth.

This reading does not hurry past the pain. It reads Psalm 13:1-2, where David asks "How long?" four times in two verses, and notes that he is not rebuked for asking. It turns to Habakkuk, who watched evil go unchecked, and to God's answer in Habakkuk 1:5. Its central line is:
"God’s silence is not the absence of God, but often the presence of a deeper work taking place beneath the surface."

stories.h2: Day 31: Holding On When God Feels Far Away
paras: The last day reads Psalm 22, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" and notes that Jesus prayed those words on the cross. It explains the Hebrew word for forsaken and shows how David turns, in the same psalm, from anguish to trust. The reading looks at the cross itself as the ultimate reminder that what looks like abandonment is often redemption in motion. The day's song is When You Feel So Far Away.

author.bio: R.S. Smith is the author of Rightly Dividing the Truth, a series of four devotionals of thirty-one days each, published by Spirit Media Publishing between December 2025 and March 2026. The series takes its name from 2 Timothy 2:15, which the first volume explores on Day 20. In every reading he sets passages from the Old and New Testaments side by side, explains them plainly, and closes the day with a song or poem.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The series is named for 2 Timothy 2:15, rightly dividing the word of truth, which the first volume explores on Day 20. This fourth volume begins where careful reading matters most, with a warning to test every teaching, and ends with readings for those who are holding on.
Its last day gives the reason to keep going:
"Yet Scripture assures us that feeling distant from God is not the same as being abandoned by God."

faq.q: What is Rightly Dividing the Truth: Endurance, Hope, and Eternal Glory?
faq.a: A thirty-one-day Christian devotional by R.S. Smith on enduring faith and lasting hope. Each day opens a passage, often explains a Greek or Hebrew word, and closes with reflection questions and a song. It is Book 4 of a four-volume series.

faq.q: How is each day of this daily devotional laid out?
faq.a: A teaching on one passage with related verses, sometimes a word study, then questions for reflection and a song. Each reading stands on its own.

faq.q: How many books are in the Rightly Dividing the Truth series?
faq.a: Four, each with its own thirty-one days, so you can start with any of them. They are, in order: Foundations of Faith and Prayer; Walking in Christ—Obedience and Transformation; The Cross, The Church, and The Spirit's Power; and Endurance, Hope, and Eternal Glory. This is Book 4.

faq.q: What does the book say faith is?
faq.a: Day 7, What Is Faith?, reads Hebrews 11:1 with the Amplified Bible, explains the Greek word pistis as belief, trust and confidence, and says genuine faith produces visible fruit, quoting James 2:26.

faq.q: What does it say about when God seems silent?
faq.a: Day 29 says God's silence is not His absence, reads David's "How long?" in Psalm 13 and Habakkuk's complaint, and encourages honest prayer and surrendered trust. Day 31 continues with Psalm 22 for seasons when God feels far away.

faq.q: Does it help with anxiety?
faq.a: Day 26, Guarding Your Heart in an Anxious World, is built on Proverbs 4:23, and Day 10, Fear Not, reads Isaiah 41:10 alongside the call to fear the Lord. They are devotional readings, not counseling.

faq.q: Does it talk about living with an eternal perspective?
faq.a: Yes. Day 30 is Living with Eternal Perspective, and Day 24, You Know Not the Day nor the Hour, reads Matthew 24:36 on the return of Christ as a call to watchfulness and holy living, not fear.

faq.q: Does it include a reading on being strong and courageous?
faq.a: Yes. Day 8, Be Strong and Courageous, opens with Joshua 1:9 and ends with a song of the same name.

quote.text: We do not cleanse ourselves to be loved. We are loved—and therefore cleansed.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for believers who want to go deeper
paras: It starts with who Jesus says His followers are. Day 1 opens Matthew 5:13-16, "You are the salt of the earth," and Day 2 picks up the town on a hill that cannot be hidden. The last day ends where Paul did: "For I resolved to know nothing while I was with you except Jesus Christ and him crucified."
Five things set it apart:
list: It keeps the cross at the center. Days on Jesus who lives to intercede, the Lord's Supper, grace that transforms and Christ crucified tie the book together.
It takes the church seriously. Iron Sharpens Iron, Don't Forsake Assembling, Making Disciples, Worship in Spirit and in Truth and Unity in Faith all speak to life together.
It opens the original languages. Readings explain words such as metamorphoo, to be transformed, hagiazo, to sanctify, and krino, to resolve.
Every day ends with a question to carry. All thirty-one readings close with reflection questions, often with one step to take that week.
Every day ends with a song, from Salt and Light and Iron Sharpens Iron to Table of Grace and I Know Nothing but Jesus.

faq.q: What is Rightly Dividing the Truth: The Cross, The Church, and The Spirit's Power?
faq.a: A thirty-one-day Christian devotional by R.S. Smith on the heart of the faith. Each day opens a passage, often explains a Greek or Hebrew word, and closes with reflection questions and a song. It is Book 3 of a four-volume series.

faq.q: How is each day of this daily devotional laid out?
faq.a: A teaching on one passage, with related verses and sometimes a word study, then questions for reflection and often one step for the week, then a song. Each reading stands on its own.

faq.q: How many books are in the Rightly Dividing the Truth series?
faq.a: Four, each with its own thirty-one days, so you can start with any of them. They are, in order: Foundations of Faith and Prayer; Walking in Christ—Obedience and Transformation; The Cross, The Church, and The Spirit's Power; and Endurance, Hope, and Eternal Glory. This is Book 3.

faq.q: What does it say about being salt and light?
faq.a: Days 1 and 2 open Matthew 5:13-16. They describe the believer's influence as salt that preserves and light that cannot be hidden, and ask where your saltiness may have faded and where God has placed you to shine.

faq.q: What does iron sharpens iron mean in this book?
faq.a: Day 4 reads Proverbs 27:17 as a picture of believers growing together through encouragement, honest correction, accountability and gathering, and notes that real sharpening involves friction.

faq.q: Does it cover the Great Commission?
faq.a: Yes. Day 17, Making Disciples: The Great Commission, opens Matthew 28:19-20 and ends with the song Go and Make Disciples.

faq.q: Does it include the parable of the prodigal son?
faq.a: Yes. Day 15, Joyful Celebration: The Prodigal Son's Return, reads Luke 15:11-32 and focuses on the Father's heart and the joy of heaven when the lost are found.

faq.q: Does it teach about the sovereignty of God and the Holy Spirit?
faq.a: Yes. Day 29, Sovereign God, explains that God is supreme in authority and actively ruling over all creation, and Day 10, Transformed by Grace, is about the power of Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit to change us.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for believers who want to walk it out
paras: It begins by slowing down. Day 1 takes Psalm 46:10 and describes stillness as more than the absence of noise: "a deliberate quieting of our hearts and minds." It ends with a challenge for the week ahead, five minutes a day in silence before the Lord, and that pattern carries through the book.
Five things set it apart:
list: Most days ask something of you. Twenty-eight of the thirty-one readings close with reflection questions, many with one specific step to try that week.
Every day ends with a song, from Your Peace Will Guard My Heart and Knowing You, Lord to Victory in Jesus and Go into All the World.
It is about obedience in real life: anxiety, calling, marriage, honoring parents, guarding the mind, the fear of the Lord, repentance and baptism, and sharing the gospel.
It explains words and names. Day 25 walks through the names of God, from Elohim and Yahweh to Jehovah Jireh, El Shaddai and Abba Father, with the passages where each appears.
It is honest about hard things. Day 12 is for when our hearts condemn us, and Day 20 speaks to readers whose relationship with their parents is strained or painful.

sections.h2: For anyone carrying worry
paras: Day 4, Be Anxious for Nothing, does not tell you to ignore what is real. It walks through Philippians 4:6-7 and offers four habits: gratitude, trust in God's timing, community and guarding your thoughts. One line sums it up: "Gratitude is a powerful antidote to anxiety." Then it asks, "What specific worry are you carrying that you need to surrender right now?"

sections.h2: For believers asking what God wants them to do
paras: Day 15, Knowing Your Calling, starts with Jeremiah 29:11 and Ephesians 2:10 and looks at gifts in Romans 12. It says "prayer becomes our compass," that God often uses other believers to confirm a calling, and that seasons of preparation are part of the path. Day 14, You Must Follow Me, breaks down Luke 9:23: deny yourself, take up your cross daily, and follow.

sections.h2: For families and marriages
paras: Day 17, What God Has Joined, reads Matthew 19:6, and Day 20 takes Ephesians 6:2-3, the first commandment with a promise. The reading on parents is gentle with those whose relationships are hard: "We honor our parents not because they are perfect but because we acknowledge the role they played in our lives."

sections.h2: For small groups
paras: The reflection questions at the end of most days are ready-made for a group: when did you last quiet your heart before God, which name of God speaks most to you right now, what worry do you need to surrender. A group can take a day a week, or read a week at a time and talk through the questions together.

stories.h2: Day 1: Be Still and Know I Am God
paras: The book opens in the middle of busyness and anxiety, with Psalm 46:10. Being still, the reading says, takes patience and means letting go of the illusion of control. It closes with three questions and a small, concrete step: five minutes a day in silence before the Lord. The day's song begins, "When the waves rise high around me, And my heart begins to fear."

Philippians 4:6-7 is read slowly, phrase by phrase. The reading calls the command a divine imperative, then gives practical help: give thanks, trust God's timing, share burdens with other believers, and guard your mind with God's Word. It asks you to pray through the passage and name your anxiety. Its closing hope is that God's peace does not depend on our circumstances changing, "but on our trust in the One who never changes."

stories.h2: Day 25: Exploring the Names of God
paras: This day reads like a short Bible study. It names Elohim the Creator, Yahweh the self-existent One, Adonai the Lord and Master, Jehovah Jireh who provides, Jehovah Rapha who heals, El Shaddai the all-sufficient One and more, through Jehovah Shammah, the Lord is there, and Abba, the name Jesus used for His Father. Each comes with the passage where it appears. The day's song is Your Name Reveals Your Glory.

faq.q: Will it help with spiritual growth?
faq.a: That is its aim. The subtitle is Obedience and Transformation, and most days end with questions and a step for the week, from five minutes of stillness to praying through Philippians 4:6-7, so the reading turns into practice.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for believers building on solid ground
paras: It starts at the beginning. Day 1 opens with God telling Moses, "I am who I am," and moves straight to the promise that He hears and answers prayer. From there the book walks through the great themes of the Christian life one day at a time, and closes each day with words you can sing or pray.
Five things set it apart:
list: Every day pairs the two Testaments. Joy in John 15 is read beside Psalm 16 and Psalm 37, the command to love one another beside Leviticus 19, and the new covenant beside the Law it fulfills.
Every day ends with a titled song or poem, from Faithful Prayer and Sail On to Word of Truth and Truth in Love, and some add a written prayer.
It covers the foundations in order you can follow: faith, joy, love, hope, the Holy Spirit, prayer, righteousness, the new covenant, assurance of salvation and freedom in Christ.
It teaches how to read the Bible well. Day 20, the title reading, gives practical steps for rightly dividing the word of truth, from beginning with prayer to letting Scripture interpret Scripture.
It is short enough for one sitting a day. Thirty-one readings make a month, and each one stands on its own.

sections.h2: For believers who want a daily quiet time
paras: One day, one truth. A reading takes a few minutes, and the song or poem at the end gives you something to carry into the day. Day 18 invites the weary to take Christ's yoke, and is honest that "Christ's promise of rest is not a guarantee of a trouble-free existence" but an assurance of peace in Him.

sections.h2: For anyone who wants to pray with more confidence
paras: Prayer runs through the whole book. Day 1 calls it our direct line to God, Day 7 is titled Pray with Faith and Act with Confidence, and Day 8 shows how faith and action belong together, from James 2 to Hebrews 11. The closing day returns to prayer before hard conversations, asking for the Holy Spirit's wisdom before we speak.

sections.h2: For parents, mentors and leaders
paras: Day 9, The Shepherd's Heart, applies the parable of the lost sheep to everyone in your care: children, students, colleagues, friends and the people you lead. It asks you to notice who is struggling, "The one lagging behind. The one who has separated from the group."

sections.h2: For small groups and Bible studies

stories.h2: Day 2: Sailing with God or Man
paras: Day 2 begins with a memory from the author's own life. He remembers sailing with a group of friends on the open sea, which felt exhilarating and a bit daunting, like life itself. From there he asks whether we are sailing with God or following the ways of the world, with Proverbs 3:5-6, the calling of the fishermen in Matthew 4 and the fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5.
"Trusting in God is like having a skilled navigator guide our ship."

The shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to find one lost sheep becomes a pattern for every relationship. The reading says the shepherd does not scold the sheep when it is found, but rejoices and carries it home. It asks us to watch for small signs of struggle in the people around us: a change in tone, a forced smile, sudden withdrawal. The closing song is Shepherd's Heart.

The title reading opens 2 Timothy 2:15 and explains what it means to handle God's Word well: careful interpretation and application, context, the intended audience and the whole story of the Bible. It then gives practical steps: begin with prayer, explore the historical and cultural context, study with other believers, and apply what you learn.
"Allow the Bible to be its best interpreter."

faq.q: What is Rightly Dividing the Truth: Foundations of Faith and Prayer?
faq.a: A thirty-one-day Christian devotional by R.S. Smith. Each day takes one biblical truth, ties Old and New Testament passages together, and ends with a titled song or poem. It is Book 1 of a four-volume series.

faq.q: How is each day of this daily devotional laid out?
faq.a: A short teaching opens a passage of Scripture, brings in related verses from both Testaments, applies them to everyday life and closes with a song or poem. Some days also include a written prayer. Each reading stands on its own.

faq.q: Does it teach how to pray?
faq.a: It teaches by example and by Scripture. Day 1 calls prayer our direct line of communication with God, Day 7 is about praying with faith and acting with confidence, and the book returns to prayer on day after day. It is a devotional, not a step-by-step prayer manual.

faq.q: Does it include Christian poems or songs?
faq.a: Yes. Every day closes with a titled song or poem, such as Faithful Prayer, Anchor of Hope, Rest in Me and Truth in Love.

faq.q: How many books are in the Rightly Dividing the Truth series?

faq.q: What does rightly dividing the word of truth mean?
faq.a: Day 20 explains it from 2 Timothy 2:15: reading the Bible with care, understanding its context, audience and whole story, and letting Scripture interpret Scripture, so that what we learn changes how we live.

faq.q: Is it a devotional for women or for men?
faq.a: Both. Nothing in it is written for one group only. The readings speak to every believer, and Day 9 speaks to anyone who cares for others, including parents, teachers, mentors and leaders.

audience.body: For Christian women who are asking what their calling is, for women's ministries and small groups that want a brief Scripture-based study with room to write, and for anyone starting a season of fasting and prayer or looking for an accountability partner. Terri Williams writes as one woman speaking to another. She opens with a letter: hold on to God's unchanging hand, keep your eyes on Jesus, and silence the noise of social media so you can hear Him. The chapters are a page or two each, and most end with a question and a journal page. A note on subjects: the book speaks plainly about temptation, toxic people and late nights, and it treats prayer as spiritual warfare. It is a devotional journal, not a long Bible study or a counseling book.

quote.text: Let this be a challenge to take back our rightful place in prayer.
quote.cite: Become, Letter to the Women

what_makes.title: What makes this book for women who want to walk in their purpose
paras: The book begins with questions many women carry quietly: "Who are you called to? What is your purpose? Do you have a calling?" Then it hands the reader a page and asks her to answer them before God. Every chapter is short enough to read in a few minutes and pointed enough to stay with you all day.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is a journal as much as a book. Ten chapters are followed by a page headed My Journal, and most ask something direct: name the boundaries you need, write down your God-given talent, write down what you have not given up to God.
Most chapters start from Scripture. The King James references sit under the chapter title, from Proverbs 18:16 to Ephesians 6.
It is plain about boundaries. One chapter is a list: have an accountability partner, limit time around toxic people, avoid too many late-night hangouts.
It treats prayer as a fight. Put Your Boots On! and Stay Dressed call women to get up early, pray, and put on the armor of God before their natural clothes.
It ends with a recap of ten reminders and a word for the valleys of life, when it is low, dry and lonely, and the reminder that God says, I am with you.

sections.h2: For women asking what their purpose is
paras: If you are not sure what God has called you to do, the book starts right there. It asks whether you are satisfied with where you are and confident in who you are, and then points you to prayer, fasting and asking God for direction. Give It A Tap reminds you that your gift will make room for you.

sections.h2: For women's groups and prayer partners
paras: The Sisterhood chapter says "We are to be helpers of one another," and asks each reader to send an encouraging text or make a call to a sister who needs it. The chapters are short enough to cover one a week, and the journal questions give a group something real to share.

sections.h2: For a season of fasting and prayer
paras: Go Hungry is about denying the flesh and seeking God's face so you see less of yourself and more of Christ. The book puts it simply: "Self-care is great, but soul-care is rewarding." It works well beside a short fast or a set time of prayer.

sections.h2: For anyone walking through a valley
paras: The recap speaks to the low places, when you may feel forgotten and have no one to turn to. It answers with the word of God: "He will never leave us nor forsake us." Then it tells the reader to wipe her tears, gather her strength and move forward.

stories.h2: The gym and the faith muscle
paras: Get Fit starts with a picture everyone knows: we go to the gym, work out, try all types of diets, all to fix up the outer appearance. Then it turns: "However, it's what's on the inside that counts." Exercising your muscles will not help when you need faith to believe God for something. The book's line is short:
"Faith pushes you to trust God when you can't trace Him."
The chapter ends by asking what you are trusting God for in this season of your life.

Put Your Boots On! opens with "it's time for war," and then makes clear the fight is not with your hands. It is in prayer. When the attacks come and you do not know what to say, the answer is one word: pray. The author tells readers to get up in the wee hours, before starting the day, and set the atmosphere. Then she asks a hard question:
"Have you given God a TOTAL yes?"
The journal page that follows asks you to write down what you have not yet given up to God.

Near the end, the book compares life to hills and valleys. On the mountain top you stand firm like a champion. In the valley it is low, dry, lonely and sometimes dark, and you may call out, "Helloooooo, is anyone there?" The answer comes from the word of God: on the mountain top or low in the valley, God says, I am with you.
"It doesn't matter how you got here, you are here now!"

She is a proud member of Unity in Christ Deliverance Ministries, and she closes her book with a word to all the women around the world: fight on.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The letter that opens the book says why it was written. The author wants to encourage at least one woman to hold on to God's unchanging hand, and she believes women have a part to play in prayer for their families and their nation:
"The nation, this world, and our children are in trouble."
Her closing note names what she hopes her readers will become:
"A watchman on the wall in prayer. A prayer warrior in battle. A soldier in the army of the Lord."

faq.q: What is Become about?
faq.a: It is a short devotional journal by Terri Williams for Christian women who want to start walking in the purpose God placed on their lives. In thirteen brief parts it covers sisterhood, using your gifts, red flags and healthy boundaries, fasting, faith, prayer and the armor of God, and most chapters end with a journal page.

faq.q: Does the book teach the armor of God?
faq.a: Yes. Stay Dressed, based on Ephesians 6:13-18, tells women to put on their spiritual armor before their natural clothes: the helmet of salvation, the belt of truth, feet shod with the gospel of peace, the shield of faith and the sword, which is the word of God.

faq.q: Does it talk about spiritual warfare and prayer?
faq.a: Yes. Red Flags says the enemy is sneaky and that we must stay prayed up. Put Your Boots On! says the fight is in prayer, not with your hands, and tells readers to command their day to line up with the word of God. It is a short call to prayer, not a book of written-out prayers.

faq.q: Is there a chapter on sisterhood in Christ?
faq.a: Yes. Sisterhood, based on 1 Thessalonians 5:11, says we are to be helpers of one another and that our efforts should uplift, empower and strengthen other women. It asks each reader to reach out to a sister with a text, a post or a phone call.

faq.q: What does it say about healthy boundaries?
faq.a: It says creating boundaries will save you from a lot of heartbreak and headaches. The Create Healthy Boundaries page lists a few: have an accountability partner, limit time around toxic people and avoid too many late-night hangouts. Then it asks you to name the boundaries you need.

faq.q: Does it cover fasting and praying?
faq.a: Yes. Go Hungry, based on Matthew 26:41 and Jude 1:20, calls readers to fast, pray and seek God's face so they see less of themselves and more of Christ. It is one short chapter, not a full guide to fasting.

faq.q: Does it talk about walking by faith?
faq.a: Yes. Get Fit asks readers to exercise their faith, not just their muscles. It says having faith means to keep working toward what you believe God for, even when you cannot see beyond the clouds.

faq.q: Does it include declarations?
faq.a: Yes. Stay Dressed tells the reader to decree and declare a thing, and gives two from Scripture: this is the day that the Lord has made, and no weapon formed against me shall prosper. Then it asks for your own declaration today.

faq.q: Is it a devotional journal for women, and which Bible does it use?
faq.a: Yes to both questions it is usually asked. It is written to women, and ten chapters are followed by a My Journal page for writing. All Scripture quotations are from the King James Version.

hero.audience_line: For young adults and men who want true, first-person stories of God's protection and calling, believers learning to discern the unseen world, and readers drawn to short testimonies with a lesson after each one.
hero.tagline: At twenty-three, David Barnes heard a voice call his name and left home with a book bag, his granny's Bible and $300. Thirteen short true stories follow, each closed by a Thought on faith, wisdom and spiritual warfare.

audience.headline: A young man follows God's voice out of his mother's house and into a winter on the streets of North Carolina, where the spiritual world stops being an idea.
audience.body: For young adults and men who want honest stories of faith from someone their age, believers who want to learn spiritual discernment and prayer for protection, and readers who like short chapters they can finish in one sitting. David Barnes tells what happened after he obeyed: a night in a tunnel slide on the coldest night in Raleigh, a breakfast from a police officer, a job managing a burger restaurant, and a growing sense that he was being watched. Each of the thirteen parts ends with a Thought, a short teaching or prayer. A note on subjects: the book is written for adults and older teens. It describes homelessness, demonic encounters and fear, and a planned robbery from the author's teenage years, and the dialogue includes a racial slur and other strong language.

quote.text: Sometimes it’s not about what you’re doing- but where God places you.
quote.cite: The Seed of David, Part 1: The Command

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers who want to see the unseen
paras: The book opens with a voice. "David," it called, and he knew a choice had to be made: stay comfortable at his mom's house or step into the unknown. On the last bus of the night, a stranger hands him a map of the tribes of Israel, and he turns to see two smiles that freeze his heart. From there the stories never stop asking what is happening just behind ordinary life.
Five things set it apart:
list: Every story is the author's own. The thirteen parts follow one season of his life in Raleigh, Louisburg and Wake Forest, North Carolina, told in the first person with real places and plain details, from a $1.25 honey bun to a dead mouse left at a back door.

Every story is followed by a Thought. Some teach, such as the difference between knowledge, understanding and wisdom, or between creating and making. Two are prayers of David, and one lists Hebrew and Greek words from Abba to Teshuvah.
It teaches discernment by example. Part 4 stops to define the word, and the later parts show the author learning to notice, test and pray about what he sees.
It is practical about protection. He remembers his dad, mom and granny anointing him with oil before school, and in a restaurant kitchen he uses olive oil soap and prays in the name of Jesus.
It ends with Scripture. A stranger tells him to read Psalm 5, and the final Thought prints the whole psalm.

sections.h2: For young men finding their way
paras: The author is twenty-three when the book begins, sleeping outside, working, and trying to do the right thing with no one watching. He is honest that he was not always that person. Part 11, The Old Me, goes back to a seventeen-year-old tempted by a $3,000 cut from a robbery. Thought 11 answers with a lesson on self-worth: "If you don't know who you are, someone else will define it for you."

sections.h2: For believers learning spiritual discernment
paras: The book does not explain the spiritual world from a distance. It describes moments: a hotel parking lot that empties in two minutes after he opens his Bible, two motorcyclists who make the same strange gesture, and customers who seem to share a hidden language. Thought 4 puts the lesson simply: "Everything is about perception."

sections.h2: For anyone who prays for protection
paras: When he feels targeted, the author prays out loud and asks that the moment be recorded in heaven. Thought 9 calls the third watch of the night a time to declare divine protection, break every chain and contend in prayer, and it is careful to say no single verse names those hours. The book closes with Psalm 5, a prayer for protection from enemies.

sections.h2: For readers who like short true stories
paras: Each part is only a few pages, and many end on a turn that pulls you into the next. The book can be read in an evening, or one part and one Thought at a time. The story continues in The Seed of David: Book Two.

details.Subtitle: Thoughts from Spiritual Realm Encounters Here on Earth
details.Author: David Barnes

paras: In Part 2, the news calls it the coldest night in Raleigh. Three months into his decision, the author has a job but nowhere to live, and he has asked the voice what to do with no answer. He sleeps balled up in the elbow of a tunnel slide in a park. In the night, he writes, his body slept but his spirit was awake, and a warmth held him:
"The hug of my God."

In the morning, Part 3, he opens his Bible to Psalm 30:5, joy comes in the morning. Then a police car speeds across the park toward him, and the officer holds out a Hardee's bag with two bacon, egg and cheese and a bottle of water. "We are not all bad," he says, and drives off.

In Part 4, the author is staying at a rundown hotel on the bad side of town, where the parking lot is full of drug deals, men led to rooms and children on bikes. An impression stops him: "Stop. What do you see?" Then, "Open the book and watch." Doubting, he digs his Bible out of his book bag and opens it. In about two minutes the lot is empty.
"I sat in silence—shaken, but certain: I had seen reverence."

For days, cars have parked and pointed at him wherever he goes, in what he comes to see as shifts. In Part 13, during a rain at the park, a short older man with an umbrella does something new. He walks over and sits down. "We know you see us," he says, and warns that many do not like that he can see. Before he leaves, he says two more things:
"Guard your mind."
"Read Psalm 5. You’re going to need it."

author.bio: David Barnes tells his own story in The Seed of David: hearing God's voice at twenty-three, leaving his mother's home with his granny's Bible, sleeping outside through a Raleigh winter, and managing a burger restaurant in Louisburg, North Carolina, while learning to discern the spiritual world. He grew up in a family where his dad, his mom and his granny anointed him with oil and prayed over him before school. His story continues in The Seed of David: Book Two.
