why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The book begins with obedience. The author wanted to ignore the voice and deny the feeling, but he could not: "I heard instructions from God." The stories that follow are what he saw once he said yes, and the Thoughts are what he learned.
His prayer in Thought 5 says what he hopes the book will do:
"Let my content save a life, Change a heart, Save a family."
And the second Thought, titled Seed Two, says why it matters for the reader: "I could be so much more. And you could too."

faq.q: What is The Seed of David about?
faq.a: It is a short book of true stories by David Barnes about a season when he followed God's voice out of his mother's home at twenty-three, lived without a home through a North Carolina winter, and began to discern spiritual activity around him. Each of the thirteen parts ends with a Thought, a short teaching or prayer.

faq.q: Is it a true story about angels and demons?
faq.a: It is the author's first-person account of what he experienced. He describes a voice in the night, two smiles he calls demonic, strangers who seem to watch him in shifts, and a man in the rain who tells him to read Psalm 5. He tells what he saw and felt, and lets the reader weigh it.

faq.q: Is it a book about spiritual warfare?
faq.a: Yes, in story form. The author prays out loud when he feels targeted, uses anointing as an act of faith, and in Thought 9 describes the third watch of the night as a time to contend in prayer and pull down strongholds, quoting 2 Corinthians 10:4.

faq.q: Does it include prayers for protection?
faq.a: Yes. Part 6 gives the prayer he spoke after washing his face with olive oil soap: "In the name of Jesus, I am protected." Thoughts 5 and 6 are written prayers, and the book ends with the full text of Psalm 5.

faq.q: Does it teach discernment of spirits?
faq.a: By example. Part 4 defines to discern as to perceive, recognize or understand something subtle, and the stories show the author noticing, testing and praying about what he senses. It is a testimony, not a study guide on spiritual gifts.

faq.q: Is it about walking with God day to day?
faq.a: Yes. The stories are about obeying one step at a time with no guarantees, from a bus ride and a train ticket to a job, a car and a park bench. The author writes that God led him every step, and he continued to follow.

faq.q: Is there a Book Two?
faq.a: Yes. The Seed of David: Book Two, Overcoming Fear, Hearing God's Voice, and Living with Kingdom Purpose, continues the series with ten more true stories, each followed by a Thought.

faq.q: Does the book contain strong language?
faq.a: Yes. Some dialogue includes a racial slur and other strong language, and the book describes demonic encounters, homelessness and a planned robbery. It is written for adults and older teens.

hero.audience_line: For children ages 8 to 12 who love horse and animal adventures, and for the parents, grandparents and teachers who read with them about bullying, forgiveness and loyal friendship.
hero.tagline: A white foal is mocked for the two humps on her back, until she learns they are wings and must fly across a vast canyon to find water for the herd that shunned her.

audience.headline: A chapter-book adventure about a horse who is different, the friend who believes in her and the courage to answer a call no one else can.
audience.body: For readers about eight to twelve who love horses, made-up worlds and funny creatures, and for any child who has felt left out. In the prairies of what used to be called Colorado, a foal named Singer is born with a coat as white as snow. Then two humps grow on her back, the herd turns on her, and only her mother, the wise old king Goldie and a spirited colt named Pinto stand by her. When the stream runs low, Singer is the only one who can fly across the canyon to look for water. On the other side are the herblers and spudgetts of Guttentosh, with their own words, deals and laws. A note on subjects: the herd's bullying is shown plainly, and the last chapters center on a woach spar, a fight to the death between two spudgetts, which ends with no one killed. Singer prays to the spirits of the wind. There is some bathroom humor, and a glossary at the back explains the invented words.

quote.text: Never let them steal your song. Especially the way you sing it,
quote.cite: Singer's Amazing Journey, Chapter 3: A Horse of a Different Color (Goldie to Snowflake)

what_makes.title: What makes this book for young readers who feel different
paras: The book's prelude says it is the story of a special animal "with a heartfelt message that the authors hope you will pass on for generations to come." That message is simple: look past the outside. Singer is laughed at, pushed in the mud and called a freak, and she answers with courage and kindness.
Five things set it apart:
list: Its hero is the one everyone picks on. Singer's humps, and later the black streaks that appear on her coat, make the herd shun her, and the book shows how much that hurts.
It shows bullies changing. Tia apologizes after Singer helps her, and Holly, one of the worst, turns out to be Singer's own sister and asks to be forgiven.
Friendship carries the story. Pinto never cares what Singer looks like. He tells her she will fly long before she believes it herself.
It opens into a whole new world. Across the canyon live the herblers and the spudgetts, with spider-silk clothes, tarnelion ducks, flergensmertz berries and a glossary of their words.
Singer's coat tells her story. A new color appears after each big moment: black after the shame, blue after her flight, brown and purple after she faces the black zaxolts and the égatignals.

sections.h2: For any child who has felt left out
paras: When the yearlings sing a mean song about her, Singer asks her mother what is wrong with her. Her mother's answer is that she is special. Later Singer says what the whole book is about: "I just don't know why horses can't just look past what's on the outside and look a little deeper to what's on the inside."

sections.h2: For kids who love horses and animal adventures
paras: There is a herd with a wise old king, a race to the mountains, a cave full of strange paintings, a leap off a canyon edge and a lush land of waterfalls on the other side. The chapters are short, and many end with something new about to happen.

sections.h2: For families talking about bullying and forgiveness
paras: The book does not stop at the hurt. Goldie tells Snowflake that hatred will "wrap itself around your heart and squeeze all the love out of it," and Singer forgives the horses who were cruel to her. Each scene gives parents and teachers an easy place to ask, what would you have done?

sections.h2: For readers who love invented worlds and words
paras: Guttentosh has its own language. A squimtat is a young one, a sesobeam is a year, a zarn is about a mile and a nuttletut is a predicament. The glossary at the back explains them all, from bleminzotch to zootsnap.

details.Subtitle: Part I: The Woach Spar
details.Author: Russell Smith

paras: A palomino named Tia shoves Singer into a deep mud hole while the herd laughs. The next day Tia charges again, trips on a rock and twists her hoof. Singer runs for Goldie and then helps Tia home. Tia asks why, and Singer answers:
"I didn't want you to feel the embarrassment I felt when no one helped me when I was sprawling in the mud,"
Tia's reply is short: "I'm very sorry I bullied you."

Goldie asks Singer to fly across the canyon to find water before the herd sets out. She is terrified, until Pinto reminds her that the true meaning of bravery is a filly who was picked on and overcame it. At sunrise she spreads her wings to the sun, runs at the edge and leaps, praying,
"Spirits of the wind, I give myself to you now."
An updraft lifts her higher, and on the other side she finds water enough for a thousand horses.

In Guttentosh, Spudgett Jones and young Petus must meet in a woach spar, a fight to the death. Singer cannot bear to lose either friend, so she prays for both. As the fight ends, a twister crosses the lake, passes over Petus and stops in front of Singer. When it is over, both fighters are alive, and Spudgett Wugen declares,
"Never, in all of woach spar history, have both fighters survived."

author.bio: Russell Smith is the author of Singer's Amazing Journey. He dedicates the book to his mother, who taught him about guardian angels, and to his children, writing that without their imaginative minds this story would never have been written.

why.title: Why this story is told
paras: The dedication says the story came from family: a mother who told stories and children with imaginative minds. Inside the book, the reason is spoken by Singer's friends. Goldie tells her:
"There is nothing like having a true friend who will stand beside you your whole life"
And Pinto shows what that looks like from the first chapter to the last, because he could look past what all the others could not and see her beauty within.

faq.q: What is Singer's Amazing Journey about?
faq.a: It is a chapter book about a flying horse. Singer is born with two humps on her back, the herd shuns her, and she learns the humps are wings. When the stream runs dry she flies across a canyon to find water, and her journey leads her to the land of Guttentosh and, she hopes, one day to her father.

faq.q: How does Singer get her wings?
faq.a: She is born with two knots above her shoulders that grow into humps, and then into full wings with gleaming white feathers. Her mother tells her the secret: her father is special, and the humps will be wings one day. Pinto helps her practice in the mountains.

faq.q: Is it a Pegasus story?
faq.a: Not exactly. It is a winged horse story of its own, and the book never uses the name Pegasus. Singer is a prairie horse whose father comes from a faraway place, and the book is more about being different than about myth.

faq.q: Does Singer reach the Mystic Forest?
faq.a: Not in this book. Her father told her mother he comes from the Mystic Forest and that Singer would learn to fly before she could journey to see him. This is Part I, and it ends as the rain dancers ask the spirits of the rain to let them teach Singer the way to the Mystic Forest.

faq.q: Is it a coming of age story?
faq.a: Yes. Singer begins as a frightened foal who weeps alone after the herd laughs at her and ends as a young horse who has saved her herd and two friends. Her mother watches her become, in the book's words, a living legend.

faq.q: What does it say about mothers and daughters?
faq.a: Snowflake stands by Singer when almost no one else will, answers her hardest questions gently and sings her a song of pride before the flight. The book also lets Snowflake struggle, and Goldie has to remind her to forgive the horses who hurt her daughter.

faq.q: What age is it for, and is any of it scary?
faq.a: It is written for readers about 8 to 12. The bullying is plain, the égatignals are described as dangerous creatures, and the closing chapters build to a woach spar, a fight to the death that ends with both fighters alive. Nothing is graphic.

faq.q: Is it a Christian book?
faq.a: It is not a Bible story. Goldie speaks of the great horse spirits, and Singer prays to the spirits of the wind. Its themes are kindness, forgiveness, courage and loyal friendship.

hero.audience_line: For readers who feel overwhelmed or stressed, small groups and Bible studies exploring thankfulness, and anyone ready to make gratitude a daily practice rather than a once-a-year holiday.
hero.tagline: A short, Scripture-rooted book on how giving thanks, practiced daily and on purpose, changes the way we face hardship, from Paul and Silas in prison to a small plane caught in a storm.

audience.headline: A pastor's short book on one idea he says the Holy Spirit gave him: giving thanks is a weapon against discouragement.
audience.body: For readers who feel worn down by hard seasons, for small groups and Bible studies that want to talk about thankfulness, and for anyone who wants gratitude to be a habit and not only a holiday. Lance Bane grew up in a non-religious home and placed his hope in Jesus in his late teens. Years later, in prayer, he sensed the Holy Spirit tell him that giving thanks would be a special weapon. This book unpacks that word through Bible stories, his own experiences as a pastor, husband and father, and a few findings from neuroscience and psychology. A note on subjects: the introduction mentions hard moments from the author's childhood in one or two lines, and the book touches on grief, anxiety and spiritual warfare. It is a short book of encouragement and teaching, not counseling or medical advice.

quote.text: Gratitude is not just seasonal but a daily discipline.
quote.cite: The Gratitude Effect, Introduction: Thanksgiving and the Gratitude Effect

what_makes.title: What makes this book for anyone who wants a grateful heart
paras: The book treats gratitude as a choice, not a mood. In the author's words, "Gratitude is not passive, it's proactive." Each section shows one way giving thanks changes a life: with God, in our well-being, in our relationships and in our character.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is built on Bible stories. Paul and Silas sing in a Philippian prison, Jesus gives thanks at the tomb of Lazarus and over five loaves and two fish, and King Jehoshaphat sends singers ahead of his army.
It uses a pilot's principle: attitude determines altitude. The nose of a plane decides whether it climbs or falls, and the book says gratitude works the same way on our outlook.
It puts Scripture beside research. The author draws on Jim Wilder and Michel Hendricks's The Other Half of Church and on studies of gratitude and well-being, with endnotes for each section.

It is about people as much as feelings. Section 3 walks through Paul's letters, where his thanks for others is always tied to something specific, and asks who has blessed you and how you can tell them.

It ends with something to do. Practice Gratitude gives simple steps: an index card of things you are thankful for, thirty seconds of thanks before you get out of bed, and a morning, midday and evening rhythm.

sections.h2: For anyone in a hard season
paras: Loss, money trouble, strained relationships and health crises come to everyone, and the book starts there. It does not tell you to pretend things are fine. It says, "We are not ignoring difficulties. We look for His goodness, and gratitude helps us see." For days when even that is hard, it offers three small steps, beginning with thanking God for His presence even if you do not feel it.

sections.h2: For small groups and Bible studies
paras: The book is short and each section is built around Scripture, with questions along the way: How might your life change if you began to see gratitude as your first line of defense? Who has blessed you, and how can you express your gratitude to them? It works well for a few weeks of group discussion, especially around Thanksgiving.

sections.h2: For readers curious about gratitude, the mind and the body
paras: Section 2 brings in neuroscience and psychology alongside the Bible. The author writes that "Scripture and science affirm that practicing gratitude can rewire our brains, break cycles of negativity, and enhance our overall well-being." He calls gratitude "a spiritual reset button" for minds that race with worry.

sections.h2: For marriages, families and friendships
paras: Some of the warmest pages are about home. The author tells how a simple daily smile from his wife changed how he felt when he came through the door, and what he tells young couples in premarital counseling: marriages end because "a thousand little things lead to one big thing." Small, daily thanks is his answer.

paras: The author was asked to lead a Celebration of Life service in New England and flew there on a small private plane, heading in the direction a storm had just passed. The sky went dark and the plane bounced like a pinball. He writes that he was sure he would crash in the North Atlantic. When they landed, the co-pilot's windshield was shattered where a chunk of ice had hit it.
"I've never been more grateful to have my feet on solid ground."
He thanked the pilots, his fellow passengers and Almighty God, and says that when you face a scary situation, gratitude becomes the most natural response.

For many years the author's mother-in-law, in her eighties, lived with him and his wife. She wanted the heat at seventy degrees or more, even in summer; the rest of the family thought the house was an oven. From that small household battle he draws a picture of how people give thanks differently:
"Gratitude is a thermostat that can be set to what you need."
So, he says, do not judge the person whose gratitude seems too loud, or the one who seems too quiet.

At his teenage son's eye appointment, the author agreed to have his own eyes checked, sure he did not need it. He read the letters and felt good about his youthful eyes. Then the doctor switched lenses, and he said out loud, "Oh wow! That's much clearer!" He has worn glasses ever since. The point is that you may see many good things already, but things get much clearer when you look through the gratitude lens.

author.bio: Lance Bane is a Christian author, speaker and spiritual leader passionate about helping people encounter the love of Jesus Christ. A devoted husband, father of three and proud grandfather, he finds his greatest joy in his relationship with King Jesus and his family. He believes every challenge is an opportunity to grow, learn and serve others, and he often echoes the words of Mark Twain: "The two most important days in your life are the day you are born, and the day you find out why."

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The book grew out of one moment in prayer. In Final Thoughts, the author writes that many years after the warm Thanksgivings of his childhood, the Holy Spirit revealed something that has helped him for decades:
"Giving thanks will be a special weapon against discouragement, disillusionment, and challenges."
He believes it was not meant for him alone:
"This revelation wasn't meant for me alone. Scripture calls us all to cultivate gratitude."

faq.q: What is The Gratitude Effect about?
faq.a: It is a short book of biblical encouragement by Lance Bane on how thanksgiving, practiced daily and on purpose, changes the way we face hardship. It shows four ways gratitude works. They are, in order: it enriches our relationship with God; it improves our well-being; it enhances our relationships; and it shapes our character.

faq.q: What does it say about Paul and Silas?
faq.a: It opens Section 1 with them. In Acts 16 they are beaten and jailed in Philippi, and instead of despairing they pray and sing hymns. The prison's foundations shake and their chains fall off. The book calls it a prime example of thanksgiving as spiritual warfare, and says gratitude unlocks doors, literally and figuratively.

faq.q: What Scripture on being thankful does it use?
faq.a: Many passages, mostly from the NIV. Among them are 1 Thessalonians 5:18, give thanks in all circumstances; Psalm 100:4, enter his gates with thanksgiving; Philippians 4:6-7, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God; and Paul's thanks for others in Philippians, Romans and 1 Corinthians.

faq.q: Does it help you count your blessings every day?
faq.a: Yes. Practice Gratitude suggests a card listing things you are grateful for, thirty seconds of thanks before you leave bed, naming three things each morning, a five-minute midday check-in and writing down moments of gratitude before sleep.

faq.q: Does it talk about renewing your mind?
faq.a: Yes. Section 2, Your Mindset Matters, says gratitude shifts our perspective from scarcity to abundance and from frustration to hope. It calls gratitude a spiritual reset button and says it reminds us of God's truth, which renews our minds.

faq.q: Does it help with trusting God in hard times?
faq.a: That is its main subject. The book describes giving thanks as a faith declaration that says, God, I trust You, right now, even here. It points to Joseph, who kept a heart of gratitude and trust through betrayal and prison.

faq.q: Is it a book of prayers of thanks?
faq.a: No. It is a short teaching book, not a prayer collection. It does look closely at one prayer of thanks, Jesus's words at the tomb of Lazarus, Father, thank you for hearing me, and it suggests starting your prayers for others by thanking God for them.

faq.q: Does it treat worship and thanksgiving as spiritual warfare?
faq.a: Yes. It says gratitude is one of the weapons available to us, and it uses Jehoshaphat's army in 2 Chronicles 20, where singers went ahead giving thanks and Israel won without a battle. In the book's words, gratitude was their weapon, and worship won the war.

faq.q: How does the book suggest building a grateful heart?
faq.a: Start small and keep at it. The author dares readers to practice daily gratitude for two weeks and see whether their attitude lifts, and he suggests a gratitude journal, a weekly family time to share what you are thankful for, and a heartfelt note to someone who has blessed you.

hero.audience_line: For middle grade readers who love pirates, treasure hunts, magical creatures and a loyal dog, and for families and grandparents looking for an adventure to share.
hero.tagline: A pirate's magic book, five fearsome Guardians and a ten-year-old boy who sets out with his dog to finish what his family started generations ago.

audience.headline: A middle grade fantasy adventure about a boy, his dog and the grandfather whose secret he inherits.
audience.body: For readers around eight to twelve who like their stories full of action, riddles and strange creatures, and for parents, grandparents and teachers looking for a chapter book to read together. It begins with a pirate legend, Captain Smoke and her golden book, and then jumps to the present day, where ten-year-old Tri and his dog Rayna explore the woods behind his house. After Grandpa Troy dies, Tri receives a letter that sends him into the hidden lands inside The Golden Atlas, where every Guardian has a different kind of test: a maze of water walls, a memory game, a swimming race, a climb above lava. A note on subjects: the opening chapter has a sea battle in which sailors are shot and drown, and Captain Smoke goes down with her ship. Tri grieves his grandfather, and the last chapter brings them together for one minute to say goodbye. The peril is adventure-story peril, with nothing graphic.

quote.text: To go forward, sometimes you must go back.
quote.cite: The Golden Atlas, Chapter 4 (a saying of Grandpa Troy's that Tri remembers in the maze)

what_makes.title: What makes this book for young readers who love adventure
paras: It opens like a pirate tale. Captain Smoke is so mean that "To say this pirate was mean is like saying a hurricane is a little windy," and yet she wears pink, sparkly shoes. From there the story becomes a quest with clear rules, real choices and a heart at its center: a boy who wants to make his grandfather proud.
Five things set it apart:
list: It has rules a reader can follow. Tri must defeat each Guardian with his own skill, he may take the treasure and go home or leave it and press on, and he gets only one failure for the whole journey.
Every land is different. Rainbow-striped Zynx in a land of wrong colors, burrowing Lorpians in the Sandlands, a sea with one small island, volcanoes and lava, and finally the Octodragon's hill.

The challenges reward thinking. Tri solves riddles, finds a hidden phrase, matches sixty cards from memory and plays a song on a rainbow of light, using things he learned from his mother and his grandfather.
A dog goes too. Rayna sniffs out the path, rides a giant frog-turtle across a river and wears her own lava-proof boots. The Dreamy, who has never seen a dog, calls her a dog creature.
It is about family. A secret passes from father to son, and then from grandfather to grandson, and the last wish is not for treasure.

sections.h2: For readers who love pirates and treasure
paras: The first chapter is a full pirate story: a captain with C.S. branded on her cheek, a Navy trap set in thick fog, a cannon battle and a sinking ship. A boy on her crew named Trintin grabs the golden book from a floating trunk as he is pulled from the water, and the treasure hunt begins.

sections.h2: For kids who love puzzles, riddles and games
paras: Each Guardian sets tests instead of simply fighting. The Zyng's Maze Squared has walls of water and a riddle, "I can save and I can destroy," that Tri has to answer. The Scormodo sets a memory game, a ball-and-box game and a choice of four doors. Readers can try to solve them before Tri does.

sections.h2: For families, grandparents and read-aloud time
paras: Eight chapters, plenty of dialogue and a dog who barks her agreement make it easy to read aloud a chapter at a time. Grandpa Troy's letter, printed in full in Chapter 2, is a natural place to talk about family stories and the things grandparents pass on.

sections.h2: For a child who misses a grandparent
paras: Tri is devastated when his grandfather dies, and the whole quest is done in his honor. When he finally gets his wish, he asks only to say goodbye. His grandfather tells him, "no matter how hard life may get, I will always be with you." It is a gentle way into a hard subject.

paras: Grandpa Troy's letter says the book is hidden in the place he loved more than any other, and Tri knows where that is. In his grandfather's living room hangs a picture he has seen a thousand times: a forest path, a gate and a creature like a dragon mixed with an octopus. This time he notices a small taped rip in the top corner. Behind it is a button the same color as the wall. He presses it, the picture turns all the way around, and there sits The Golden Atlas, shining like a new gold coin. Tri holds it close and says:
"This is for you, Grandpa. I miss you and will always love you."

At the end of the Zyng's maze, a wall of water blocks the way and twenty-three streams of colored light appear. Rayna is no help, since she is color blind. Tri touches the green one, his favorite color, and it makes a sound. Then blue, then red. It is a rainbow piano. He hated piano lessons, but his mom told him to keep trying. Then he remembers her singing to him when he was small, and he plays and sings "Row, row, row your boat" until the wall sinks into the ground.
When the last Guardian falls, the Dreamy reminds Tri that he has earned one wish. He does not ask for more treasure. He says,
"I'd like to say goodbye to my Grandpa."

The Dreamy can give him only one minute. His grandfather tells him how proud he is, and Tri tells him he did all of it for him. Then Tri goes home, hugs his parents, and when his mom offers him an exciting story at bedtime, he says he has had enough excitement for today.

author.bio: Matthew Rathbun is the author of The Golden Atlas, a middle grade fantasy adventure about a ten-year-old boy, his dog and a pirate's magic book, published by Spirit Media Publishing in 2025. He writes a story of a secret passed from grandfather to grandson, and of a boy who learns never to give up.

We are glad to publish an adventure for young readers about courage, family and a love that outlasts loss.

why.title: Why this story is told
paras: At its heart, The Golden Atlas is about what one generation leaves to the next. Grandpa Troy writes to Tri that the book has been "our family's biggest secret and greatest failure," and that he believes Tri is the one to finish it. Tri carries that trust through every land. When the Dreamy congratulates him on his tenacious spirit, Tri explains where it came from:
"Well, my Grandpa taught me to never give up and always give my all, so that's what I always do."
The book's last line leaves the door open:
"This was the story of Tri and The Golden Atlas … but perhaps it was only the beginning."

faq.q: What is The Golden Atlas about?
faq.a: It is a middle grade fantasy book by Matthew Rathbun. A pirate named Captain Smoke hides her treasure inside a magic golden book, guarded by creatures she has a Dreamy create. Generations later, ten-year-old Tri inherits the book from his grandfather and, with his dog Rayna, enters its hidden lands to try to defeat all five Guardians.

faq.q: What age is it for?
faq.a: It is written for readers about 8 to 12. Younger children can enjoy it read aloud. Its hero, Tri, is ten years old.

faq.q: Is it a chapter book?
faq.a: Yes. It has eight chapters in 116 pages, told in plain, lively prose with a lot of dialogue. Most chapters are one land and one Guardian, which makes them easy stopping points.

faq.q: Is it a good read aloud for families?
faq.a: Yes. The short scenes, the riddles readers can try to solve, Rayna's barks and Grandpa Troy's letter all work well out loud, and the ending gives families something to talk about.

faq.q: Who are the five Guardians?
faq.a: They are, in order: the Zyng, king of the rainbow-striped Zynx; the Scormodo, part komodo dragon and part scorpion; the Dolphican, part dolphin and part pelican with wings; the Rambear, with a bear's body and a ram's horns; and the Octodragon, a fire-breathing dragon with eight octopus arms.

faq.q: Does it help children who have lost a grandparent?
faq.a: It can. Tri's grandfather dies early in the story, Tri is very sad, and the whole quest is done to honor him. The last chapter gives them one minute to say goodbye. It is an adventure first, not a book about grief, but it handles the loss gently.

faq.q: Is it scary or violent?
faq.a: It has adventure-story danger. The first chapter includes a cannon battle in which sailors are shot or drown, and later Tri faces fire, lava and the Octodragon. Nothing is described in a graphic way, and Tri and Rayna come through safely.

audience.headline: Light on the first day, rest on the seventh: the creation story from Genesis 1, one bright spread at a time, in two languages.
audience.body: For babies, toddlers and preschoolers and the parents, grandparents and Sunday school teachers who read to them, in English, in Spanish or in both. Each day of creation gets its own spread, with a short English line on one side, the Spanish on the other, and labels that name what God made in both languages: sky and cielo, sun and sol, whale and ballena, lion and león, man and hombre, woman and mujer. Jeci Ware, a mother of four, wrote it to help moms teach their children God's Word. It is a first-words picture book, not a full Bible storybook; it covers Genesis 1 only.

quote.text: “He looked over all he had made and he saw that it was very good.”
quote.cite: The Creation of the World, Day Six

what_makes.title: What makes this book for little ones learning two languages
paras: The book opens with a line in both languages: the story of creation based on the book of Genesis 1. From there, each day turns the page on something new, and every new thing has a name a child can point to and say twice.
Five things set it apart:
list: It follows Genesis 1 in order. Light, sky, land and sea, plants, the sun, moon and stars, fish and birds, animals, man and woman, and rest on the seventh day.
Every line is in English and Spanish. The English text sits on one page and the Spanish on the facing page, so a parent can read either one, or both.
It is a first-words book too. Picture labels name 35 things in both languages, from vegetation and vegetación to the bald eagle and águila calva.
The animals are many and friendly. A whale, a shark and a seahorse; a hummingbird, an owl and a dove; a goat, a cow and a pig; a frog, a zebra, a giraffe and an elephant.
It is short and simple. One or two sentences per page, made for a baby on a lap or a toddler who wants to turn the pages.

sections.h2: For bilingual and Spanish-speaking families
paras: Read it in the language your family speaks at home, then in the other. The labels let a child hear sun and sol, horse and caballo, man and hombre on the same page.

sections.h2: For parents of babies and toddlers
paras: The pages are bright and the words are few. It works as a first Bible story: a child learns that God made the light, the animals and people, and that He saw it was very good.

sections.h2: For Sunday school and preschool teachers
paras: Each day of creation is its own spread, which makes it easy to teach one day at a time and point to what God made. A class can name the animals in both languages.

sections.h2: For grandparents
paras: A grandparent who speaks Spanish and a grandchild learning English, or the other way around, can read the same story together, each from their own side of the page.

details.Title: The Creation of the World
details.Subtitle: La Creación del Mundo
details.Author: Jeci Ware

paras: The first spread is black, with one bright star of light in the middle. On the English side: God created the light, called it day, and called the darkness night. On the Spanish side, the same words: "Llamó a la luz día y a la oscuridad llamó noche." It is a simple way to show a small child what the first day looked like.

On the fifth day God fills the waters with fish and the earth with birds. A whale, a shark and a seahorse swim across one spread. On the next, a hummingbird, a sparrow, a blue jay, a bald eagle, a dove and an owl each wear their name twice: owl and búho, dove and paloma.

Day Six is the busiest day: livestock, creeping things, wild animals from the alligator to the giraffe, and last of all a man and a woman, labeled man and hombre, woman and mujer. Then God looks at everything He has made. In Spanish:
"Miró todo lo que había hecho y vio que era muy bueno."

author.bio: Jeci Ware is a mother of four who writes bilingual books for children. Her author note on the back page says she has a heart for integrating faith and learning, a lifelong passion for God's Word and a deep commitment to nurturing young minds, and that what began as a personal practice grew into a mission to create content that educates and inspires little learners.

faq.q: What is The Creation of the World?
faq.a: It is a 34-page full-color baby and toddler book that tells the seven days of creation from Genesis 1 in English and Spanish, with picture labels in both languages. It is a first-words book as much as a story.

faq.q: Is it based on Genesis 1?
faq.a: Yes. The book says so on its opening page: the story of creation based on the book of Genesis 1. It follows the days in order, from light on the first day to rest on the seventh.

faq.q: Is it a bilingual book for preschool and toddlers?
faq.a: Yes. Every line appears in English and in Spanish on facing pages, and 35 labels name what God made in both languages. Its reading age is 0 to 5.

faq.q: Can it help with raising bilingual children?
faq.a: It can be one tool. A parent can read the English, the Spanish or both, and point to labels like sun and sol or horse and caballo. It does not teach grammar; it gives words and a story in both languages.

faq.q: Does it show the animals God made?
faq.a: Yes. Day Five shows a whale, a shark, a seahorse and birds such as the hummingbird, bald eagle, dove and owl. Day Six shows livestock like the goat, cow, horse, pig, hen and sheep, and wild animals like the alligator, frog, zebra, giraffe, lion, elephant and gorilla, each labeled in both languages.

faq.q: Is it one of the good Bible stories for preschoolers?
faq.a: It tells one Bible story, creation, in a way a preschooler can follow: one day per spread and one or two sentences per page. It does not include other Bible stories.

faq.q: Can we use it as a baby devotional?
faq.a: Not exactly. It has no prayers or devotional notes. It is a short Bible story to read aloud, and many parents will use it to start talking with a little one about the God who made everything.

faq.q: Is it a Spanish children's Bible?
faq.a: No. It retells Genesis 1 only, in both English and Spanish. The Spanish is a parallel telling of the same story, not a Bible translation.

hero.audience_line: For dads raising daughters, and for the girls, about ages 6 to 12, who read it with them: thirty short lessons to share, one day at a time.
hero.tagline: A devotional a father and daughter read together: who God is, who she is in Him, and honest talks about growing up, written by a dad of four daughters.

audience.headline: A dad of four girls writes thirty lessons a father can read with his daughter, with street tacos, a coronation ceremony and a dance along the way.
audience.body: For dads raising daughters, and for the girls, about ages 6 to 12, who read it with them; also for stepfathers, grandfathers and men's groups who want to lead girls toward their Heavenly Father. Freddie Prado walks a father and daughter through three parts: who God is, from creation to the Holy Spirit; who she is in Him; and honest talks about responsibility, money, forgiveness, beauty, crushes, dating, marriage and safe sharing. Every lesson ends with a Daily Declaration, a prayer to say together and a Make a Memory Together activity. Between the lessons, Just for Dads pages speak father to father. A note on subjects: the lessons are written for children and kept gentle. The Just for Dads pages are written for adults and are candid; one tells of the author's recovery from pornography and sexual addiction, and others touch on father wounds and his own mistakes.

quote.text: “There once was a daughter, created in the image of the Father.”
quote.cite: Daughters of the King, the opening epigraph

what_makes.title: What makes this book for dads and daughters
paras: Lesson 1 starts with mac 'n' cheese and street tacos. No one knows a dish better than the chef who made it, the author says, and God is the chef who made you. That is the tone of the whole book: playful, Scripture-based and made to be read out loud by a dad.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is built in three parts. Part One, Who is God?, covers creation, the Trinity, the fall, the promised hero, Jesus and the Holy Spirit. Part Two, Who Am I?, builds a girl's identity. Part Three, Just Us, opens honest talks.
Every lesson ends the same way. A Daily Declaration that begins "I am God’s daughter. I am a daughter of the King," a prayer to say together and an activity to make a memory.

The activities are real memories. Draw each other as a team of detectives for the fridge, plan a daddy-daughter date, take a silly selfie, hold a Coronation Day with a crown and a sword, and end with a father-daughter dance.
It speaks to dads too. Nine Just for Dads pages are father to father, about surrender, false beliefs about God, breaking family patterns and being honest about struggles.
It does not dodge growing up. Part Three talks about money, forgiveness, beauty, crushes, dating, marriage, and a promise that in our family, we share the weird things.

sections.h2: For girl dads
paras: If you want to lead your daughter in faith but are not sure where to start, the book hands you the words. Each lesson is a few pages, written to be read aloud, with a declaration, a prayer and an activity already planned.

sections.h2: For daughters ages 6 to 12
paras: The lessons are funny and short, full of snacks, detectives, princesses and Disneyland lines. Part Two tells her who she is: God's daughter, made very good, strong and able, one of a kind, and free to not be perfect.

sections.h2: For dads who did not have a good model
paras: The author writes that every one of us carries some hurt from an imperfect earthly father, and that the pattern can change. His Just for Dads pages tell how his own family line turned when his dad followed Jesus.

sections.h2: For churches and men's groups
paras: The book can carry a fathers' group through thirty weeks or thirty days. The Just for Dads pages give men something to talk about, and the lessons give them something to do at home.

paras: Ask God what His heart is for your daughter and together let’s lead our girls toward their Heavenly Father.

paras: I am God’s daughter. I am a daughter of the King. He created me and says that I am very good. He knows me best.

blocks.text: The last lesson, Let's Dance, sends every dad and daughter off with this:

paras: Daughters, you are a daughter of the King forever. Dads, you are sons of the Most High God.

details.Subtitle: A Devotional for Dads and Their Daughters
details.Author: Freddie Prado

paras: In the first Just for Dads page, the author remembers the Sunday he grabbed his guitar and, for the first time ever, the keys to his dad's white Chevy pickup. On the highway he felt free and in charge. He compares it to free will: God handed us the keys. Then he admits that taking the wheel of his own life led to a lot of wreckage, and asks dads to put God back in His rightful place.

In Breaking the Pattern, he notices that Abraham, Isaac and Jacob repeat the same lie down three generations. Then he tells his own story: he grew up hearing about the harm his grandfather did, until his dad decided to follow Jesus when the author was about four.
"And in that very moment, the trajectory of our entire family line changed."

Lesson 14 is a ceremony. Dad and daughter mark a pathway with toys or flower petals, she puts on her favorite dress and a crown, royal music plays, and Dad finds something to use as a sword. Then he reads a short script that declares her royalty in the Kingdom of God: strong, brave, beautiful and created to make a difference.

author.bio: Freddie Prado is a dad of four daughters. The book prints no biography, but he writes plainly about himself in it: his dad came to faith when he was about four, which he says turned his family line around, and in the Just for Dads pages he shares his own mistakes and his recovery through counseling, The Genesis Process and Celebrate Recovery. He writes that his greatest desire is to be a protector and to live in a way that honors God, his wife and his family.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: It began as a letter. In A Note to My Girls, the author writes to his own daughters that he is far from perfect, but that they have a Father in heaven who never messes up:
"For the rest of my life, I will do my best to teach you about our heavenly Father, who created you and has amazing plans for your lives."
The book closes with the words he gives every dad who finishes it:
"God is writing a story with your life. One step at a time."

faq.q: What is Daughters of the King about?
faq.a: It is a devotional for a father and daughter to read together, built to grow the father-daughter relationship around God's Word. Over thirty short lessons they learn who God is, who she is in Him, and how to talk honestly about growing up. Every lesson ends with a declaration, a prayer and an activity.

faq.q: Is it a good devotional for girl dads?
faq.a: That is who it is written for. The author is a dad of four daughters, and each lesson is written so a dad can read it aloud. The Just for Dads pages speak to fathers directly.

faq.q: Does it teach my daughter her identity in Christ?
faq.a: Yes. That is Part Two, Who Am I? Its lessons are, in order: I Am God's Daughter; I Was Made Very Good; I Was Created to Make a Difference; Coronation Day; I Am Not Perfect, and That's Perfectly Okay; I am Strong and Able; I am One of a Kind; My Words Matter; I am Honest, Even When it Hurts; and I am Prophetic.

faq.q: Can our family use it as a devotional?
faq.a: It is written for a dad and his daughter or daughters, but the lessons are short and read aloud, so a family can share them. Each one ends with a Daily Declaration, a prayer to say together and an activity.

faq.q: Does it include a father-daughter dance?
faq.a: Yes. Lesson 30, Let's Dance, closes the book. Dad and daughter choose a special Father-Daughter song together, put on their best outfits, clear some space and dance.

faq.q: What does Part Three talk about?
faq.a: Part Three, Just Us, opens honest conversations. Its lessons are, in order: Responsibility; Money; Our family; Forgiveness; Beauty; Boys (Crushes); Boys (Dating); Boys (Marriage); Something Weird (Safe Sharing); and Let's Dance. On dating, the rule is simple: whenever your mom and dad say it's okay.

faq.q: Is there anything in it for dads on godly fatherhood?
faq.a: Yes. Nine Just for Dads pages speak father to father about surrendering control to God, false beliefs about God, being filled with the Holy Spirit, breaking family patterns and being honest about struggles. They are written for adults, and one tells candidly of the author's recovery from pornography and sexual addiction.

faq.q: What ages is it for?
faq.a: Girls about 6 to 12, read together with Dad, according to the book's record. The humor and activities suit younger girls, and Part Three's talks suit girls nearing their teens.

faq.q: Which Bible translation does it use?
faq.a: It quotes the New Living Translation and the New International Version, marked NLT and NIV.

faq.q: Is it a good Father's Day gift?
faq.a: The book does not mention Father's Day. It is a book a dad uses with his daughter over thirty lessons, with a page for him to write her a note first, so it works best for a dad who wants to start that habit.

content_note.title: Content note
paras: The lessons are written for children. The Just for Dads pages are written for adults and are candid; one tells of the author's recovery from pornography and sexual addiction.

hero.audience_line: For young children learning to trust Jesus, parents reading aloud at bedtime, grandparents sharing faith with grandchildren, Sunday school teachers, children's ministry leaders and Christian homeschool families.
hero.tagline: A little lamb says yes when the Shepherd asks it to follow Him, and on the long road through desert, battle, storm and night it learns a new name for Him at every turn.

audience.headline: One little lamb leaves the green pasture to follow the Shepherd, and finds Him faithful through it all.
audience.body: For young children learning to trust Jesus, parents reading aloud at bedtime, grandparents sharing faith with grandchildren, Sunday school teachers and children's ministry leaders, Christian homeschool families, kids learning the names of God, and children facing fear or loneliness. Dana House tells the story in the little lamb's own voice, in rhyming lines that run like a poem across each page. The lamb expects green meadows and gets a dry desert, a battlefield, crashing waves and a long dark night, and at each one the Shepherd gives it a name to call Him by. A note on subjects: the lamb is frightened in places, cries out in battle, feels alone in the dark and feels ashamed of its tarnished coat. Each fear is met by the Shepherd, and nothing in the book is graphic. The text is longer than most picture books, a full paragraph on each story page, so it suits a child who can sit for a read-aloud.

quote.text: I needed Him to be many different things to me; each time I found Him to be exactly what I needed Him to be.
quote.cite: Jesus Had a Little Lamb, page 31

what_makes.title: What makes this book for children learning to trust Jesus
paras: It turns the names of God into a story a child can walk through. The little lamb does not learn them from a list. It learns each one in the moment it needs Him: El Shaddai on the battlefield, Jehovah Shalom on the quiet shore, Emmanuel in the dark.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is told by the lamb. The voice is a child's voice, glad to be chosen, puzzled by the desert, scared of the waves and honest about wanting the easy road.
It names who the Shepherd is. Six names of God appear in the story, each tied to one hard place on the road.
It brings in Bible stories. The Shepherd tells the lamb about Abraham and the ram in the thicket, and reminds it of Peter on the waves.
It does not pretend the road is easy. The lamb admits it thought it was chosen for a perfect place, and the book answers that the Shepherd was faithful through it all.
It ends by sending the reader out. The last pages ask children to help a lamb who has wandered from the fold find the Shepherd, and close with Matthew 16:25.

sections.h2: For bedtime and family read-aloud
paras: Each story page is one rhyming paragraph, so a single spread makes a natural stopping place. The questions the lamb asks are the ones children ask: “Have you left me here alone? Do you not love me anymore?” Reading it slowly gives room to talk about each answer.

sections.h2: For Sunday school and children's ministry
paras: The book gives a teacher six names of God in story order, each with a picture and a reason: the Almighty when the battle is too big, peace on the shore, God with us in the dark, the God who is present even when unseen, the one who heals, and the God of eternity. Abraham, Peter and Matthew 16:25 are already woven in.

sections.h2: For children facing fear or loneliness
paras: The lamb is afraid of the waves, sure it will not stand in battle and convinced it has been left alone at night. Each time the Shepherd answers. In the dark He says, “just call me Emmanuel, for with you I'll always be.” Even when the lamb cannot feel Him, the book says, He was present there with me.

sections.h2: For grandparents and families sharing faith
paras: The story is about saying yes to the Shepherd and leaving the familiar pasture behind, and about finding out who He is along the way. It gives a grown-up words for their own story: “Now I know my Shepherd in many new ways.”

paras: “Little lamb, if you lift your head up high and stop holding it so low, you'll smell the rose of Sharon and lilies in the valley below.”

paras: He just quietly spoke, “Call me Jehovah Rapha. I am the one who heals.”

paras: As the journey starts, the lamb asks where they will live. The Shepherd only says, “The Lord will provide,” and tells it about Abraham, who placed his son on the altar and believed God would spare or raise him. A ram was in the thicket, and the voice of God called. The lamb does not know the way, but it has been told who will provide.
At the great waters the Shepherd walks on the waves and bids the lamb come, but it is afraid it will drown. He reminds it of Peter, whom Jesus took by the hand and stood upon his feet, and promises:
“Stick with me, little lamb, even when the waves are at their peak. I will walk you through them, if only Me you'll seek.”

Near the end the lamb is bruised and battered, sure its scars will never be gone. Its beautiful white coat is tarnished, it blames itself for not following close, and it thinks the Shepherd must be ashamed. It asks, “Oh precious Shepherd, can you love me still?” The answer is a name: Jehovah Rapha, the one who heals.

author.bio: Dana House wrote the poem behind Jesus Had a Little Lamb in 2001, as her small-town community was reeling from the loss of a 17-year-old in an accident. In the dedication she honors a great-uncle who encouraged her to pursue publishing her writings, and thanks her parents for raising her to be unafraid to follow God's call wherever He asked her to go. More than twenty years later, the poem became this picture book. Dana House is also the author of I Missed You While You Were Sleeping.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The dedication says the poem was written in 2001, as the author's small-town community was reeling from the loss of a young man of 17. It became a story about a Shepherd who is faithful in the desert, the storm and the night. The lamb says what it learned:
“I learned that my Shepherd was faithful to be with me through it all.”
And the last pages pass that on to the reader:
“Help them find the Shepherd, He'll lead them the right way.”

faq.q: What is Jesus Had a Little Lamb about?
faq.a: It is a rhyming Christian picture book about a little lamb that says yes when the Shepherd asks it to follow Him. The road leads through a desert, a battlefield, great waters and a dark night, and at each place the Shepherd tells the lamb a new name to call Him by.

faq.q: Is it a book about the Good Shepherd?
faq.a: Yes. The Shepherd leads the little lamb the whole way, carries it when it is too weak to walk and comes to its rescue every time He hears its cry. The book does not use the words Good Shepherd, but He is the Shepherd who is faithful through it all.

faq.q: Which names of God are in the book?
faq.a: They are, in order: El Shaddai; Jehovah Shalom; Emmanuel; Jehovah Shammah; Jehovah Rapha; and El Olam. Each one comes at a different place on the lamb's road, from the battlefield to the promise of living forever.

faq.q: What does Jehovah Rapha mean in the story?
faq.a: When the lamb is bruised, ashamed and afraid the Shepherd cannot love it still, He quietly says, “Call me Jehovah Rapha. I am the one who heals.”

faq.q: What does Jehovah Shalom mean in the story?
faq.a: On the quiet shore after the storm, the Shepherd holds the lamb to His chest and says that only He can be its peace: “just call me Jehovah Shalom.”

faq.q: Does it mention Jehovah Jireh?
faq.a: Not by that name. The Shepherd tells the lamb “The Lord will provide” and tells the story of Abraham and the ram in the thicket, but the name Jehovah Jireh does not appear.

faq.q: Does it help children trust in God?
faq.a: That is the heart of it. The lamb learns that the Shepherd was faithful through it all, that He was present even when it could not feel Him, and that each time He was exactly what it needed Him to be.

faq.q: Is it a Christian poem?
faq.a: Yes. The dedication calls it a poem, written in 2001, and the whole book is told in rhyming lines, one paragraph to a page.

hero.eyebrow: By Mario Tubiolo & Craig Tubiolo · Ages 4–8
hero.audience_line: For children ages 4 to 8 and the parents, grandparents and teachers who read aloud with them, especially little animal lovers learning to share and to forgive.
hero.tagline: A curious boy can talk to the squirrel in his backyard. He talks his mom into giving up her almonds, the squirrel runs off with the whole jar, and the boy has to decide whether to forgive his friend.

audience.headline: A boy shares his mom's almonds with his squirrel friend, and the squirrel runs up a tree with the whole jar.
audience.body: For children ages 4 to 8 and the parents, grandparents and teachers who read aloud with them. Mario names every animal he meets, from the butterflies in the garden to the deer in the yard, but a light-brown squirrel named Jimmy is special: Mario can talk to him. When Jimmy says he is hungry, Mario begs his mom for one almond, then two, then enough for Jimmy's family, until she hands him the whole jar. Then Jimmy grabs it and scurries up the tree. It is a short, gentle story about friendship, sharing and forgiving a friend who makes a mistake, with four reflection questions at the end.

quote.text: “It’s okay, Jimmy. I forgive you.”
quote.cite: Mario and the Squirrel Named Jimmy, Mario after Jimmy brings the almonds back

what_makes.title: What makes this book for little animal lovers
paras: Mario does not just name the squirrel in his yard; he can talk to him. That small bit of magic turns a simple backyard day into a lesson a young child can feel: wanting to share, being let down by a friend, and choosing to forgive.
Five things set it apart:
list: A boy who loves every creature. Mario's love for animals, big and small, reminds his mom of St. Francis of Assisi, the saint known for his connection with nature.
A bargain children will recognize. Mario asks for one almond, then two, then more for Jimmy's family, and his mom finally says yes to the whole jar.
A friend who makes a mistake. Jimmy takes more than he should, and Mario thinks he has lost both the almonds and the friendship.
A friend who says sorry. From the treetop, Jimmy sees Mario's tears, brings the jar back and drops it at his feet with remorseful eyes.
Questions to talk about. Four reflection questions at the end ask children why forgiveness matters, how it feels to be forgiven, and how holding onto anger can hurt a friendship.

sections.h2: For bedtime read-alouds
paras: It is short enough for one sitting and ends at sunset with two friends sharing almonds in the grass. A good last story of the day.

sections.h2: For children learning to share
paras: Mario wants to share something that is not his, and he keeps asking until he gets it. Then he learns how it feels when someone takes too much. It gives a parent an easy way to talk about sharing from both sides.

sections.h2: For teachers and social emotional learning
paras: The reflection questions at the back are ready for a class discussion about forgiveness, mistakes and anger. The story models a clear sequence: a wrong, a sorry and a choice to forgive.

sections.h2: For children who love animals
paras: Butterflies, deer, chipmunks and a talking squirrel fill the backyard, and Mario's yard stays a safe place for creatures of all kinds even though a grumpy neighbor does not like animals.

details.Title: Mario and the Squirrel Named Jimmy
details.Author: Mario Tubiolo & Craig Tubiolo

paras: Jimmy whispers that he is hungry, and Mario runs to his mom with a fistful of almonds. She says just one. Then, seeing his face, two. Then Mario has an idea: "Jimmy has a family, Mom." With a deep sigh she gives in, hands him the whole jar and reminds him to put on his shoes. He does not listen.

Mario dashes out barefoot and reaches out with the jar. Jimmy grabs it in his tiny paws and scurries up the tree as fast as his legs can carry him. "Jimmy, no!" Mario shouts. Tears well up in his eyes. He thinks he has lost not only his mom's almonds but also his friend.

From the treetop, Jimmy sees Mario crying and feels terrible. He hurries down with the jar in his mouth and drops it at Mario's feet, as if to say he is sorry. Mario wipes his eyes, gives Jimmy a few almonds from his hand and forgives him. They sit together in the grass, and Jimmy's mother watches proudly from the tree, just like Mario's mom from the kitchen window.

author.bio: Mario Tubiolo and Craig Tubiolo wrote Mario and the Squirrel Named Jimmy together. The book prints no biography of either author. Its story follows a boy named Mario who loves animals so much that he names every one he meets, and it closes with four reflection questions about forgiveness.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The book says its purpose in its last page of story. Even though Jimmy took more than he should have, Mario's choice to forgive him "showed that true friendship needs understanding and compassion."
Then it hands the lesson to the reader with its first reflection question:
"Why is it important to forgive others, even when they make mistakes?"

faq.q: What is Mario and the Squirrel Named Jimmy about?
faq.a: It is a 34-page full-color picture book about a curious boy who can talk to a squirrel in his backyard. He talks his mom into giving him her whole jar of almonds to share, the squirrel runs off with it, and Mario has to decide whether to forgive his friend.

faq.q: Is it a good bedtime story for kids?
faq.a: Yes. It is short, gentle and ends at sunset with two friends sharing almonds in the grass. The reflection questions can wait for another day if it is late.

faq.q: Is it a book about forgiveness?
faq.a: Yes, that is its center. Jimmy takes the whole jar, sees Mario's tears and brings it back, and Mario tells him he forgives him. The last page says true friendship is about learning to forgive and growing stronger together.

faq.q: Is it a book about friendship?
faq.a: Yes. Mario and Jimmy talk every morning, and the story tests the friendship when Jimmy makes a mistake. By the end, Mario knows the friendship is stronger than ever.

faq.q: Does it teach children about sharing?
faq.a: Yes. Mario wants to share his mom's almonds, asks for one, then two, then the whole jar for Jimmy's family, and then learns how it feels when a friend takes more than he should.

faq.q: What ages is it for?
faq.a: Children ages 4 to 8, read aloud, according to the book's record. The sentences are simple enough for an early reader to try alone.

faq.q: Does the squirrel really talk?
faq.a: Only Mario can hear him. The book calls it a magical connection that nobody else seems to notice, and his mom tells him squirrels don't talk. Children can decide for themselves.

faq.q: Can teachers use it for social emotional learning?
faq.a: Yes. Four reflection questions at the end ask why forgiveness matters, how it feels to be forgiven, whether the child has ever forgiven someone when it was hard, and how holding onto anger can affect friendships.

faq.q: Is it a faith-based book?
faq.a: Some of it. Mario's love for animals reminds his mom of St. Francis of Assisi, and the story teaches forgiveness, but it has no Bible verses or prayers. It is a gentle values story more than a Bible story.

hero.audience_line: For Christians preparing their hearts for Christmas, small groups and families reading the Christmas story together, and anyone who wants to know who the wise men were and why they came.
hero.tagline: Six short readings on Matthew 2 that follow the wise men from the east to the newborn King, and show how God guided, protected and delivered His Son in a dark world.

audience.headline: Every December, plastic wise men stand beside the manger. This short book reads the chapter they come from and finds a story far bigger than the lawn scene.
audience.body: For Christians preparing for Christmas, small groups and families who want a short devotional to share, and readers curious about the wise men, King Herod and the prophecies behind Matthew 2. Adam Dixon walks through the chapter in six readings. Each opens with the Bible passage itself, then sets it against the history of the time: four hundred years with no prophet in Judah, Greece fallen to Rome, a growing expectation of the Messiah, and a king who thought he was a god. Each reading closes with a few questions or short points to take into your own life. A note on subjects: the fourth reading describes Herod's killing of the boys of Bethlehem, as Matthew records it, and the cruelty of his reign. It is written for adults and older readers.

quote.text: “Following God is a journey that leads to significant impact.”
quote.cite: Light the Way, Reading 1: The Earnest Witness

what_makes.title: What makes this book a Christmas devotional with depth
paras: It starts on a front lawn. Adam Dixon notes that some pastors and theologians move the wise men across the yard in nativity scenes, because they arrived long after the shepherds. Then he says the story is worth leaning into, because “it is much deeper, far more dramatic, and much more miraculous than we know.”
Five things set it apart:
list: It stays in one chapter. All six readings come from Matthew 2, ending with Isaiah 9, so you see the whole story the nativity scene leaves out.
Every reading opens with Scripture. The passage is printed in full (ESV) at the top of each reading before any comment on it.
It brings in the history. Roman roads and armies, Herod's thirty-five-year reign, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures, and the historian Josephus on how Herod died.

It connects the prophecies. Numbers 24, Micah 5:2, Isaiah 60, Jeremiah's voice in Ramah, the prophet's “Out of Egypt I called my son” and Isaiah's branch from the stump of Jesse all come into the story.
It ends with you. Most readings close with questions or short points, such as what God has done to protect and deliver you, and what He might be doing right now behind the scenes.

sections.h2: For Christians preparing for Christmas
paras: The book is short enough to read in one sitting, or one reading a night across a week of December evenings. It closes with Isaiah 9 and a plain call to remember Jesus at Christmas: Gift, Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace and eternal King.

sections.h2: For small groups and Bible studies
paras: Each reading prints its passage, explains it, and ends with questions such as “How has God used your simple faith as a testimony to others?” That gives a group a text, a teaching and a discussion in a few pages.

sections.h2: For readers curious about the wise men and Herod
paras: Who were the magi, where did they come from, and why were they openly seeking a Jewish king? The book takes up those questions, and paints Herod the Great as unstable, insecure and murderous, set against a Messiah born in Bethlehem and raised in Nazareth.

sections.h2: For anyone walking through a dark season
paras: The book's picture is light in thick darkness. Herod ruled, Rome pressed down, and no prophet had spoken in centuries. “But some wise men had seen a star.” Its message is that God was working the whole time, and still is.

whats_inside: Six readings that walk through Matthew 2 in order, from the magi's arrival in Jerusalem to the family's return to Nazareth
The full Bible passage (ESV) printed at the start of every reading, with Isaiah 9 for the last one
History from the time of Jesus' birth: Rome's empire and roads, Herod's reign and death, and the four hundred years with no prophet
Prophecies from Numbers, Micah, 2 Samuel, Isaiah and Jeremiah, and the Hebrew word behind “Nazarene”
Reflection questions and short lists to apply each reading, ending with seven names and truths about Jesus from Isaiah 9

paras: The magi were wealthy, influential men from the east. The book notes some scholars say there may have been as many as a hundred of them, arriving by camel after several hundred miles. They went all over Jerusalem asking where the newborn King of the Jews was, until Herod himself had to consult the priests and scribes. Their simple faith became a testimony to the leaders and the capital city.
“Following God is a journey that leads to significant impact.”

stories.h2: The gifts that paid for an escape
paras: The magi came to worship. They found the child, bowed, and opened their treasures: gold, frankincense and myrrh. Then, warned in a dream, they went home another way. The book points out what they could not have known: those gifts gave Joseph and Mary the resources to travel. When an angel warned Joseph in a dream, the family left immediately and went 225 miles to the southwest, to Egypt.
“They had no idea God was using them to save his life.”

stories.h2: A king in silver, a King in the backwoods
paras: The fifth reading contrasts two kings. Herod, the book says, stood to speak at Caesarea in an outfit covered with polished silver plates, timed so the sun would reflect off him onto the crowd, and was struck with pain and died. Jesus grew up in Nazareth, a town the book calls the backwoods of the backwoods.
“So it was in this backwoods of backwoods where the King of the Universe landed.”

author.bio: Adam Dixon wrote Light the Way, six readings on Matthew 2 published by Spirit Media Publishing in 2024. In it he reads the Christmas story alongside Roman and Jewish history, the Old Testament prophets and the Hebrew and Greek words behind the text, and closes each reading with questions for the reader's own walk with God.

We are glad to publish a short Christmas book that points readers to the King the wise men came to worship.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The book wants readers to see the familiar Christmas story with fresh eyes. In the third reading Adam writes that the way God worked in Matthew 2 stuns him:
“He led them through a star, then a dream. Most importantly, He introduced them to His Son. He was working the whole time.”
Its last line is the reason it was written:
“This Christmas, remember Jesus and all that He brings.”

faq.q: What is Light the Way about?
faq.a: It is a short Christian devotional on Matthew 2, the Christmas story of the wise men. In six readings Adam Dixon follows the magi to Jerusalem and Bethlehem, Herod's plot, the escape to Egypt, the killing of Bethlehem's boys and the family's return to Nazareth, then closes with Isaiah 9.

faq.q: Is it a Christmas devotional for adults?
faq.a: Yes. It is written for adults and older readers. It deals with history, prophecy and the cruelty of Herod's reign, including the slaughter of the innocents, so it is not a children's Christmas book.

faq.q: What does it teach about the Gospel of Matthew?
faq.a: It covers one chapter of the book of Matthew, chapter 2, verse by verse. It explains how Matthew contrasts a worldly king of the Jews, Herod the Great, with Jesus Christ, and how Matthew links the events to the prophets.

faq.q: What are the six readings?
faq.a: They are, in order: The Earnest Witness; Consulting the Scholars; The Gifts and Escape; Slaughter of the Innocents; A Backwater Town; and Who is this King?

faq.q: Can it be used as a Matthew Bible study or small group study?
faq.a: Yes. Each reading prints its passage in full, explains it and ends with questions or short points to discuss. It is brief, so a group could take one reading a week or several in one meeting.

faq.q: Can families read it together at Christmas?
faq.a: It works for families with teenagers and adults. The readings are short and close with questions to talk about, but the fourth reading tells of Herod's killing of young boys, so parents of small children may want to read it first.

faq.q: Who were the wise men, according to the book?
faq.a: The book says the Greek word is magi: wealthy, influential men from the east who followed a star, and who seem to have known a messianic passage from Numbers 24. It calls the star a supernatural event, not a comet or supernova.

hero.eyebrow: By Gene Tahyi, PRS, CDCA · Foreword by Kamala Tahyi, MS, LPC
hero.audience_line: For churches starting a recovery ministry, the leaders and volunteers who run it, and the people they serve who struggle with drugs, alcohol or anger.
hero.tagline: An eight-week, Scripture-based program a church can use to welcome people who struggle with drugs, alcohol and anger, and lead them from recovery to restoration in Christ.

audience.headline: A leader's guide for churches that want to open their doors to people in recovery, and offer them more than recovery.
audience.body: For pastors, ministry leaders and volunteers who want to start or strengthen a recovery class, and for the people that class is for: anyone who struggles with drugs, alcohol or anger, and the families who love them. Gene Tahyi lays out eight lessons, each built on a Bible passage, with reflection questions and talking points for the leader. The lessons can be taught in any order, people can join any week, and graduates receive a certificate of completion. The book respects the Alcoholics Anonymous 12 steps and says it is not trying to rewrite them; it aims to bring God into people's recovery. A note on what is included: this is the Leader's Edition. Each class pairs the lesson with a fifteen- to twenty-minute video that is not part of the book, and the lesson pages give the passage reference, questions and talking points rather than a full script.

quote.text: “God wants more than recovery for His people; He wants restoration.”
quote.cite: Recovery and Restoration, Introduction: Leader’s Edition

what_makes.title: What makes this book a recovery program a church can actually run
paras: The introduction is plain about the problem. People and their families often say they want “the old” person back. The book answers that the old person found drugs, alcohol or anger a sufficient way to cope, and that “The restored person in Christ has new needs and coping skills.”
Five things set it apart:
list: It is built for church. The book recommends holding the class an hour before the service, inviting participants to stay for church (never required), and having church members sit in to connect with them.
It is flexible. There are eight lessons, they can be taught in any order, participants can join any week, and anyone can stay longer than eight weeks.
Every lesson starts with a Bible story. Naaman, Jonah, the rich young man, David and Bathsheba, Peter and Judas, and Nehemiah rebuilding the wall.
It meets people where they are. It names steps 1, 2 and 3 of the 12 steps in the first lesson, and asks questions like “Have you ever attempted to ask a ‘power greater than you’ to help you?”
It equips leaders with lived experience. An appendix shows how to shape and share a recovery testimony, so a leader who has walked this road can tell their story well.

sections.h2: For churches starting a recovery ministry
paras: The introduction gives the practical frame: a sign-in sheet, a short welcome and explanation, a video, discussion, and ending about ten minutes before church starts. Its goal is to meet new people and reach them with the Gospel, offering the safety and acceptance many wounded people need first.

sections.h2: For recovery leaders and volunteers
paras: Each lesson gives you the Bible passage, reflection questions and talking points. Some come with notes for the leader, such as letting people answer questions about forgiveness “without judgment, correction, and preaching.”

sections.h2: For people struggling with drugs, alcohol or anger
paras: The lessons ask honest questions: when life became unmanageable, where pride kept you from help, what your red flags are, and what boundaries could lessen the power of the barriers to your restoration. The foreword calls the removal of shame the best healing balm for addiction.

sections.h2: For families of loved ones in addiction
paras: The book speaks to the hope families carry, and reframes it. Instead of wishing for the old person back, it points to a restored person in Christ, with new needs and new ways to cope.

stories.h2: Addressing Pride: the combination lock and Naaman
paras: The second lesson takes 2 Kings 5:9–14, where the army commander Naaman is told to wash in the Jordan to be healed and at first refuses. The questions turn the story toward the participant: where pride has kept you from getting what you need, and how open you are to direction from others. The talking point is simple:
“Being willing to do the work it takes to change.”

The third lesson reads Jonah, from the storm to the belly of the fish to God's second call. It asks what kind of water people draw from you, and where you would land if you were given a second chance:
“If you were a well, what type of drink would someone get from you?”

The sixth lesson reads the story of David and Bathsheba in 2 Samuel 11 and talks openly about relapse: recognizing the signs, naming your own red flags (pulling away from family, not praying consistently, not going to church, not talking to your sponsor), and what forgiveness looks like, both given and received. The leader is asked to let people answer “without judgment, correction, and preaching.”

author.bio: Gene Tahyi, PRS, CDCA, wrote Recovery and Restoration as a Leader's Edition for churches that want to reach people who struggle with drugs, alcohol and anger. The book draws on the 12 steps and on peer-support guidance for telling a recovery story, and it encourages leaders with lived experience to share their own story of restoration.
