It offers full-service book creation and publishing in paperback, hardback, digital and audiobook formats, along with children's titles, compact Express Books, website design and SEO, and podcast and video production. We are glad to publish a guide that helps churches welcome people in recovery and walk with them toward restoration.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The introduction says it directly:
“The goal of Recovery and Restoration is to meet new people and reach them with the Gospel of Jesus Christ.”
It also says what the church brings that a program alone cannot:
“Still, many wounded people need safety and acceptance to begin a relationship with Jesus. You, the church, can provide these elements.”

faq.q: What is Recovery and Restoration?
faq.a: It is an eight-week Christian recovery program for churches, written as a Leader's Edition. Each lesson pairs a Bible passage with reflection questions and talking points, for people who struggle with drugs, alcohol or anger.

faq.q: How can a church use it to start a recovery ministry?
faq.a: The book recommends holding the class an hour before church, with a sign-in sheet, a welcome, a fifteen- to twenty-minute video and discussion, ending about ten minutes before the service. Participants are invited, not required, to stay for church, and church members are encouraged to sit in.

faq.q: Is it a 12 step program?
faq.a: Not exactly. The first lesson hands out steps 1, 2 and 3 of the Alcoholics Anonymous 12 steps, and the book says it is not here to rewrite them. Its aim is to connect with the recovery community and help people bring God into their recovery.

faq.q: What are the eight lessons?
faq.a: They are, in order: Beginning Steps; Addressing Pride (Combination Lock and Naaman); Wells and Whales; Choices; Change; Failure is Not Final; Balance; and Rebuild. They can be taught in any order.

faq.q: Does it address relapse?
faq.a: Yes. Failure is Not Final, built on David and Bathsheba, covers recognizing relapse, naming your red flags and receiving forgiveness. Balance, built on Peter and Judas, asks what you can learn from your mistakes and how self-care keeps you in balance.

faq.q: Does it help with anger?
faq.a: Yes. Anger is named alongside drugs and alcohol throughout, starting with step 1 on the handout. The Change lesson uses Ephesians 4:23–32, and the questions ask how irritation can help you and why change is hard.

faq.q: Does it show how to share your testimony?
faq.a: Yes. The appendix lists seven things to include in a recovery story, from early signs of a problem and your lowest point to what helped, who helped, and what you do to stay well. The introduction encourages leaders with lived experience to practice a short testimony.

faq.q: Can someone in recovery use it on their own?
faq.a: It is written for a leader running a class, and each lesson is a guide for discussion rather than a full reading. A person in recovery will get the most from it in a group, though the foreword and questions can be read alone.

hero.audience_line: For stroke survivors and anyone in physical rehabilitation, people facing a sudden diagnosis or a long recovery, the families and caregivers beside them, and nurses and healthcare workers who care for the sick.
hero.tagline: Thirty-one daily devotions from a registered nurse's own stroke recovery, each pairing a true moment from rehab with Scripture, a prayer and space to reflect.

audience.headline: A registered nurse of more than twenty years becomes the patient after a sudden stroke, and writes down what rehab taught her about God.
audience.body: For stroke survivors, people in physical or occupational therapy, anyone facing illness or a hard season of healing, and the families, caregivers, chaplains and church care teams who walk beside them. Triffina Brown had been a nurse for over twenty years when a sudden stroke put her in the hospital and then into the long work of rehab: relearning to walk, using a walker, a wheelchair and a gait belt, and fighting fear for her future and her children. Each of the 31 short devotions starts with one real moment from that recovery, opens a Bible verse, closes with a prayer, and leaves room to write how you were encouraged. A note on subjects: the book speaks honestly about paralysis on one side of the body, falls, headaches, loneliness, grief and worry about insurance and money. It is gentle and hopeful, written for adults, and it treats medicine and faith as partners.

quote.text: “I discovered that healing is more than just physical; it’s emotional and spiritual too.”
quote.cite: Healing with Hope, Author’s Note

what_makes.title: What makes this devotional for people who are healing
paras: On Day 2, Triffina loses her balance during a therapy session and starts to fall. Her physical therapist reaches out with lightning-fast reflexes and catches her before she hits the ground. That moment becomes the book's pattern: a real scene from rehab, then a truth from Scripture. “Just like my physical therapist caught me when I was falling, God catches us in our moments of weakness.”
Five things set it apart:
list: It is written from the hospital bed and the therapy gym. The lessons come from her neuro psychotherapist, her physical and occupational therapists, the rehab nutrition team and the tools of recovery.
It is written by a nurse. She knows the care team from both sides, and Day 20 honors everyone from the doctors and nurses to the people who clean the floors.
Every day follows one simple shape: a short reflection, a Bible verse, a prayer, and the question “How were you encouraged today?” with space to write.
It welcomes medicine as God's gift. Day 27 tells of headaches after the stroke and the medication that brought relief, and calls God the ultimate healer working through medical professionals.
It ends with a Scripture Index that groups every verse by need: Trust, Healing, Restoration, Provision, Strength, Guidance, Patience & Peace, Assurance and Faith.

sections.h2: For stroke survivors and people in rehab
paras: If you are relearning to walk, counting small gains or comparing yourself with the patient in the next bed, you will find your days here. Her therapist told her the smallest amount of daily work adds up over time, and the book turns lessons like that, and like slowing down, conserving energy and building core strength, into lessons for faith.

sections.h2: For caregivers and families
paras: The book shows what the patient is carrying: fear of the unknown, loneliness even with people around, and worry about who would care for her teenage daughters. Day 11 is about learning to accept help, and Day 26 about the gait belt that kept her safe and let her helpers guide her with confidence.

sections.h2: For nurses and healthcare workers
paras: A nurse who became a patient writes a thank-you to the whole team. Day 20, The Healing Hands of Compassion, calls healthcare workers the hands and feet of God and prays for their strength, wisdom and compassion.

sections.h2: For anyone in a hard season
paras: Not every reader has had a stroke. The days on fear, waiting, worry, loneliness and starting over speak to any long road. The Author's Note says these devotions “deliver hope, reminding us that even in the darkest moments, there is light to be found.”

details.Title: Healing with Hope
details.Subtitle: Encouragement From One Who Walked the Path
details.Author: Triffina Brown

paras: Every therapy session was a struggle to regain strength and mobility. One day she pushed herself to the limit, lost her balance and began to fall, and her physical therapist caught her before she hit the ground. Day 2 sets that beside Paul's words that God's power is made perfect in weakness:
“Just like my physical therapist caught me when I was falling, God catches us in our moments of weakness.”

In rehab, the nutrition team put a Bible verse on her meal tray every day. Those verses became, in her words, a beacon of hope. Day 8 builds on Psalm 119:105, “Your word is a lamp for my feet, a light on my path,” and on the idea that Scripture feeds a person the way a meal does.

Four days after the stroke, her left leg had shown no sign of motion for days. Then her physical therapist felt something: a flicker of muscle activity, not seen but palpable. Day 17 calls it a glimmer of possibility and ties it to Jesus' words about faith as small as a mustard seed.
“Just a trace of movement during my immobility became a symbol of hope and progress”

author.bio: Triffina Brown has been a Registered Nurse for over twenty years. Life took an unexpected turn when she had a sudden stroke, which carried her into hospital care, medical interventions and physical rehabilitation. Through her recovery she found a new purpose: to share her experiences, struggles and triumphs with others facing their own battles with illness and recovery. She lives with her daughters in Orlando, Florida.

It offers full-service book creation and publishing in paperback, hardback, digital and audiobook formats, along with children's titles, compact Express Books, website design and SEO, and podcast and video production. We are glad to publish a nurse's daily encouragement for everyone walking the long road of healing.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: About the Author says the stroke gave Triffina a new calling: to share what she went through with others who are facing illness and recovery. The Author's Note invites the reader in:
“In Healing with Hope, I invite you to walk with me through one of the most challenging seasons of my life—stroke recovery.”
The last devotion says what she hopes the reader finds, that God's work goes beyond the body:
“He brought about a newness that extended to every aspect of my being.”

faq.q: What is Healing with Hope about?
faq.a: It is a 31-day Christian devotional by Triffina Brown, a registered nurse who had a sudden stroke. Each daily devotion takes one true moment from her hospital stay and rehab, connects it to a Bible verse, and closes with a prayer and space to reflect.

faq.q: Is it a devotional for people facing illness?
faq.a: Yes. It was written for anyone facing their own battle with illness and recovery, not only stroke survivors. It speaks to fear, weakness, loneliness, waiting and worry, and it encourages trust in God alongside good medical care.

faq.q: Does it include Bible verses for healing and comfort?
faq.a: Yes. Every devotion is built on Scripture, such as Isaiah 53:5, Isaiah 40:31, Isaiah 41:10, Psalm 119:105 and 2 Corinthians 12:9–10. The Scripture Index at the back gathers the verses under Trust, Healing, Restoration, Provision, Strength, Guidance, Patience & Peace, Assurance and Faith.

faq.q: Does it include prayers for healing?
faq.a: Yes. Every one of the 31 days ends with a written prayer. Many ask for strength, peace and healing for the reader, and several pray for others who are sick and for the healthcare professionals caring for them.

faq.q: Can it be used as a prayer journal?
faq.a: Partly. Each day ends with the question “How were you encouraged today?” and space to write, and there are Notes pages through the book. It is a devotional first, with room to journal.

faq.q: Does it help with trusting God in hard times?
faq.a: Yes. Day 1 is Finding Refuge in God: Trusting Him in Times Of Trouble, Day 10 is Why? Trusting God in the Midst of Trials, and Day 28 is about letting go of worry and trusting God's provision. Day 10 suggests asking what you have learned instead of why it happened.

faq.q: Is it a good get-well gift?
faq.a: It was made to be given. The front of the book has a To and From page, the devotions are short enough for a hospital or rehab day, and the author writes as someone who has been the patient.

faq.q: Who is the author?
faq.a: Triffina Brown has been a Registered Nurse for over twenty years. After her stroke she went through hospital care and physical rehabilitation, and she wrote this book to share her struggles and triumphs with others. She lives in Orlando, Florida.

faq.q: Is it helpful for caregivers and healthcare workers?
faq.a: Yes. It shows recovery from the patient's side, which can help caregivers understand what their loved one is feeling. Day 20, The Healing Hands of Compassion, honors nurses, doctors, therapists and support staff and prays for them.

hero.audience_line: For children ages 4 to 8, kids moving to a new home or welcoming a new neighbor, English speakers learning Spanish, bilingual families, and the teachers and parents who read aloud with them.
hero.tagline: He speaks English. She speaks Spanish. With a stack of picture cards and a little courage, two new neighbors build a friendship one word at a time.

audience.headline: His best friend just moved away. She just moved to America. Neither knows what to say.
audience.body: For children ages 4 to 8; kids moving to a new home or welcoming a new neighbor; children learning English and children learning Spanish; bilingual families, Spanish immersion and ESL classrooms, and homeschool Spanish learners; and parents and grandparents reading aloud. Suzanne Gose tells the story of Flip, who watches his best friend's moving truck drive away, and Felipa, who is moving to America from a country that feels worlds away. When they meet, they just stare at each other. Flip's answer is a stack of word cards, a trip to the library and a lot of practice. The story mixes English and Spanish in the speech bubbles, and a glossary at the back gives every Spanish word with its meaning and how to say it. A note on subjects: it is a gentle story about shyness and friendship, with nothing frightening in it.

quote.text: Do you wonder if you can be friends with someone very different from you, even from a different country where they don't speak your language that well yet? Try!
quote.cite: Flip and Felipa, page 57

what_makes.title: What makes this book for children making a new friend
paras: It shows both sides of a move. Flip is the one left behind, and Felipa is the one arriving, and on facing pages they ask the same question in two languages: who will my new friend be?
Five things set it apart:
list: It is truly bilingual. Felipa and her mom speak Spanish, Flip speaks English, and the speech bubbles carry both, so the reader hears the language gap the children feel.
It shows how to reach across. Flip asks his mom for cards to write his new words on, studies them at the library and at home, and practices with his little brother.
It is honest about being scared. At the store Felipa thinks about speaking English but is too scared, and her mom tells her she will have to start speaking it more.
It ends with both children learning. Flip learns Spanish and Felipa practices her English with confidence, playing in the tree house almost daily.
It teaches the words. A glossary at the back lists every Spanish word in the story, with the English meaning and a sounds-like guide.

sections.h2: For kids moving to a new home or welcoming a new neighbor
paras: The book starts with two moving trucks, one leaving and one arriving. It gives a child words for both feelings: the sadness of watching a best friend go and the nervous wondering about who will move in next door.

sections.h2: For English speakers learning Spanish
paras: Flip learns the way a child can: one card at a time, el árbol, la casa, jugar, sounding words out loud and checking with Felipa's mom. A reader who knows no Spanish can follow along, and the author's note says the glossary at the back covers every word.

sections.h2: For children learning English
paras: Felipa understands a lot of English but is afraid to speak it. Her mom reminds her she practiced a lot last year, and Felipa decides to speak more English. A child in the same spot will see that speaking up a little at a time counts.

sections.h2: For classrooms and bilingual families
paras: The story works in an ESL, immersion or homeschool Spanish setting and at home. The closing page asks the reader a question to talk about, and the author's note suggests a library visit like Flip's to find a Dr. Seuss book in English and Spanish.

details.Author: Suzanne Gose
details.Language: English, with Spanish dialogue and a Spanish-English glossary

paras: The moving truck pulls up, and the moms find out each has an 8-year-old. Flip comes out holding his younger brother Benji's hand, and the two children just stare at each other. Then they learn each other's names, Felipa and Flip, and the two of them see it at once:
“We're like twins! ¡Somos como gemelos!”
At the store, Flip's and Felipa's moms pull their carts up and chat. Felipa thinks about speaking in English, but is too scared. Back home Flip tells his little brother what the problem is:
“Okay Benji, we HAVE to learn Spanish. Spanish is what is keeping us out of our tree house!”

Flip asks for cards to write his new words on, studies them at the library and practices at home. Then he rings the bell and asks Felipa's mom to help him sound out the words. When Felipa comes to the door, he quickly flips through his picture cards and asks, in Spanish, if they can play in the tree house. Felipa says yes.

author.bio: Suzanne Gose wrote Flip and Felipa. In the dedication she thanks her very best friend and husband of 27 years for sticking with her and “learning my language,” and says the book never would have existed without him. Her author's note invites readers who loved the way Flip learned Spanish to learn the same words with the See it and Say it Flip Flop Spanish Set.

paras: The dedication says the book grew out of the author's own home, where someone stuck with her and learned her language. The last page passes that on to the reader:
“Try! You may be surprised to find out you're almost GEMELOS!”

faq.q: What is Flip and Felipa about?
faq.a: It is a picture book about making friends across a language gap. Flip's best friend moves away, and Felipa moves in next door from a country that feels worlds away. She speaks Spanish and he speaks English, so Flip learns her words with picture cards until they can play together in the tree house.

faq.q: Is it a bilingual Spanish-English book?
faq.a: Yes. The story is told in English, Felipa and her mom speak Spanish in the speech bubbles, and Flip speaks more and more Spanish as he learns. A glossary at the back translates every Spanish word.

faq.q: Is it good for families raising bilingual children?
faq.a: It shows two children each learning the other's language, one English speaker and one Spanish speaker. The author's note says a reader who does not know enough Spanish can use the glossary, which gives each word's meaning and a sounds-like guide.

faq.q: Can ESL teachers use it?
faq.a: Yes. Felipa understands a lot of English but is scared to speak it, and the story shows her practicing until she speaks with confidence. The mix of English and Spanish suits ESL and immersion classrooms.

faq.q: Is it one of the friendship books for kids?
faq.a: Yes. Friendship is the whole story: losing a best friend to a move, wondering who will be next, and finding a new friend who turns out to be almost a twin.

faq.q: Is it a story about an immigrant family?
faq.a: Felipa and her mom are moving to America from a country that feels worlds away. The book does not name the country, and its focus is the two children's friendship rather than the family's move.

faq.q: What age is it for, and does it read aloud well?
faq.a: Ages 4 to 8. It reads aloud well for kindergarten and early grades, with short narration and speech bubbles, and the glossary helps a grown-up say the Spanish words.

hero.audience_line: For readers of Christian memoir, women carrying shame or hurt from the past, believers walking through a hard marriage or divorce, and anyone learning to trust God again.
hero.tagline: In 2001 Melissa Curtin prayed, “Lord, do whatever it takes for me to walk close to You.” This is the honest, funny story of how He answered, through devastation and into delight.

audience.headline: A woman who wanted more of God prays a dangerous prayer, and spends the next twenty years finding out what it meant.
audience.body: For Christian women and men who love an honest testimony, survivors of abuse, believers in a painful marriage or facing divorce, singles longing for marriage, and anyone who has felt that God owed them something better. Melissa Curtin tells her story in short chapters, most opening with Scripture: a college relationship that left her with shame, depression and doubts about her identity; a careful courtship and a marriage that grew harder for nearly two decades; a separation she did not want to make, made for her emotional safety; and the new life God built afterward, with a home of her own, new friendships and the freedom to trust Him. She writes with humor, she calls the Holy Spirit the Little Voice, and she is plain that she has no formal theological training. A note on subjects: the book is for adults. It speaks honestly about sexual abuse by a college teammate, questions about sexual identity, depression, an emotionally difficult marriage, separation and divorce, the grief of not having children, and a broken engagement. It does not give graphic detail, and the Epilogue explains how she came to see separation biblically.

quote.text: “Lord, do whatever it takes for me to walk close to You.”
quote.cite: Whatever it Takes, Chapter 1: How This Whole Thing Started

what_makes.title: What makes this memoir different
paras: The book begins with the author admitting she does not feel like writing a single word. She has made excuses for years, but she still feels compelled to share what she has been learning in twenty-plus years of walking with Christ. That honesty runs through every page.
Five things set it apart:
list: It follows one prayer. Every part of the story traces back to what she asked in 2001, and in Part Two she realizes that her circumstances not changing were part of the answer.
It is built from short, titled chapters, most opening with a Bible verse. Many were written in the moment, in the season she describes, so you can read one at a time.
It is funny. A chapter called Cows in Spandex, a mariachi band in the middle of a crisis, and an obnoxiously large bed all carry real lessons.
It is honest about what did not get fixed. She stayed in a hard marriage for years, prayed for relief, and writes about grief, childlessness and a broken engagement without tying a neat bow on them.
It points you to help. The Epilogue tells how a pastor walked her through Scripture on separation and urges readers not to go it alone, and a closing list shares the books that helped her most.

sections.h2: For readers of Christian memoir and testimony
paras: This is a true story told by a woman with a Young Life background, a college softball scholarship and a corporate job, not a pastor or theologian. She tells it as if over coffee, and she hopes it encourages believers to keep going and invites others to meet Jesus.

sections.h2: For women carrying shame from the past
paras: The first chapter tells how an abusive relationship in college left her afraid that if anyone found out, they would judge her, and convinced that she had ruined her chances of being blessed. The turning point came when a ministry director heard her story, did not flinch, and said God could use it.

sections.h2: For anyone in a hard marriage or walking through divorce
paras: The book holds two things together: her conviction that God intends marriage to be permanent, and her pastor's teaching that separation can bring safety, boundaries and clarity. She writes about the cost, the grief and the support she needed, and she urges readers to find at least one mature believer to walk with them.

sections.h2: For people pleasers and anyone learning to trust God
paras: She calls herself a recovering people pleaser, and the book shows the price of fearing people more than God. Its steady message, heard in her lowest season, is the one she sensed from the Lord: “Sweetheart, no matter what, trust Me.”

paras: I am a completely different and changed woman, who walks closely with Jesus.

details.Title: Whatever it Takes
details.Subtitle: A Journey from Devastation to Delight
details.Author: Melissa Curtin
details.Binding: Paperback (perfect bound, matte laminate) and hardback (case laminate)

paras: Days after she left home for her own emotional safety, Melissa still meant to keep a promise: to build a wedding arbor for a friend. She had no tools, no money she could count on and no good wood, so at her parents' house she asked God for some. About an hour later her stepmother mentioned that the previous owner had left lumber in the attic. It was cedar and hickory. A friend at church then found her a truck, and the drive to the wedding was only fifteen minutes.
“For me, this chain of events showed the great love of God for me as His daughter.”

On December 3, 2021, she learned that her divorce was final. She felt relief, grief and shame at the new label. Later that same day a friend asked whether anyone had room for her mother and nine-month-old niece, who needed a place for a couple of weeks. Melissa's house was half renovated and her fridge had died, but she said yes. They shared cozy fires, and the baby left a trail behind her.
“And for weeks, and maybe months later, I’d find a stray Cheerio under a couch or on the floor, and it just made me remember God’s kindness in sending them to comfort me when I needed it most.”

After she called off an engagement, dividing what they had bought for a shared future left her owning a king-size mattress she did not want. She argued with Jesus about how ridiculous it was. Days later an old friend, her Young Life leader from high school, asked to stay the night with her boys, and suddenly there were beds for everyone. Then Melissa built a headboard, footboard and drawers from cherry, oak, walnut, cedar, pine and poplar.
“And, now every time I look at my bed, I love it and think how wonderful a gift Jesus gave me in my obnoxiously large bed.”

author.bio: Melissa Curtin never imagined herself as a writer, but a professor who insisted on active verbs helped her find her knack for putting words together. She became a follower of Jesus in 1993 as a high school junior through Young Life, played catcher on a softball scholarship at a small college in North Carolina, worked with student-athletes at North Carolina State and volunteered with Athletes in Action. She loves to build things, from furniture for her home to sentences for her book, and she enjoys the outdoors and DIY projects, except painting trim. Her dream, if Jesus allows it, is to write and speak, helping free more captives from believing that past pains and failures can only lead to dashed dreams.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The opening pages say she wrote it out of obedience, believing God uses the comfort we receive in our struggles to comfort others. In the last chapters she says friends who read it all told her to publish, and she hopes God will use it to plant seeds and encourage others to keep going. Her closing line sums up the whole story:
“And walking closely with Him is worth whatever it takes.”

faq.q: What is Whatever it Takes about?
faq.a: It is a Christian memoir by Melissa Curtin. It begins with a prayer she prayed in 2001, “Lord, do whatever it takes for me to walk close to You,” and follows how God answered it over about twenty years: through shame from her past, a long and painful marriage, separation and divorce, and into healing and freedom.

faq.q: Is it a true story?
faq.a: Yes. It is her own testimony, much of it written as it happened over about ten years. It is organized in three parts. They are, in order: Disillusionment, Despair and Demolition; Rebuilding, Restoring and Rekindling Affection; and Abiding, Healing and Walking in Freedom.

faq.q: Does it help with overcoming shame from the past?
faq.a: Yes. She tells how an abusive relationship in college left her with shame, depression and fear of being found out, and how God began to lift that, starting with a ministry leader who heard her story and said God could use it. She does not give graphic detail.

faq.q: Does it talk about people pleasing and approval addiction?
faq.a: Yes. She calls herself a people pleaser to her core, names her approval addiction, and in a chapter called People Pleasing Has Consequences she tells how fearing people more than God nearly led her into a second marriage that would have been wrong for her.

faq.q: Does the book address divorce?
faq.a: Yes. She stayed in a hard marriage for many years and believes God intends marriage to be permanent. She separated for her emotional safety, and the divorce was final in December 2021. The Epilogue explains how her pastor showed her from Scripture that separation is not sin and can bring safety, boundaries and clarity.

faq.q: What does it say about Christian dating and courtship?
faq.a: Part One describes her courtship in detail: choosing active time together over movies, and agreeing not to say “I love you” or kiss until they were engaged. Later chapters tell of dating again after divorce, the value of premarital counseling, and calling off an engagement.

faq.q: Does it speak to depression and faith?
faq.a: Yes. She writes openly about seasons of severe depression, feeling betrayed by man and God, and how God met her there. Part Two opens with Psalm 34:18: “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit.”

faq.q: Will it help me trust God in hard times?
faq.a: That is its main message. In her lowest season she sensed the Lord say, “Sweetheart, no matter what, trust Me.” The book follows how that trust grew through moves, money worries and loss, often through small, specific answers to prayer.

faq.q: Is it a book about spiritual growth?
faq.a: Yes. It is about growing closer to Jesus through hard things. She writes that she is not the same woman who started writing ten years earlier, and that she would not be without the painful experiences He walked her through.

hero.eyebrow: By Wendy Reardon · Opening note by Karen Holl
hero.audience_line: For families who read aloud at bedtime or in family devotions, for grandparents who share their faith with grandchildren, and for Sunday school teachers and homeschool families.
hero.tagline: Six read-aloud stories about Mary, John and their parents: a lost teenager, a homeless man on a corner, a line of ants, a toddler crying in the woods and a father who loses his job, and what God's Word says about each.

audience.headline: Two children pray through the night for a lost teenager, and at first light she knocks on their door.
audience.body: For families who read aloud at bedtime or in family devotions, for grandparents who share their faith with grandchildren, and for Sunday school teachers and homeschool families. Mary and John ask the questions children really ask: Can we use our words the way Jesus did? Should we give money to a homeless man? Why did the ants keep walking toward danger? Why would God let Daddy lose his job? Mama and Daddy answer with Scripture and prayer. A note on subjects: the stories include a teenager lost in the mountains overnight, a friend's grandmother who may not live and a grandfather's death remembered, a lost toddler whose mother was hurt, a visit to a homeless shelter, and a father fired for praying with a client. In one story a boy hits a tree in anger until his hand bleeds. Each is told gently and ends in prayer and hope.

quote.text: “I didn’t know God listened to children like that.”
quote.cite: The Blessing Trail 2, Follow the Light

what_makes.title: What makes this book for families who want to talk about God at home
paras: Each story starts with something that happens to a family: a knock at the door, a man on a street corner, a child crying in the woods. Then Mama and Daddy open the Bible.
Five things set it apart:
list: The stories begin in ordinary life. A trip to the lake, a pretend castle in the pine woods and a quiet dinner after a hard day at work are where the questions come from.
The children's questions are honest. John asks whether God used magic to make the world. Mary asks, "What if I need my coat?" when Daddy reads that we should give more than we are asked for.
Scripture is read in the moment. Proverbs 15:4, Matthew 18:20, Matthew 5:42, Isaiah 55:8-9, James 1:5, Matthew 25:40 and Hebrews 13:2 are among the verses the family opens.
Prayer changes the story. The children pray for a lost teenager and she finds their house; the family prays for Daddy and a stranger knocks on the door with a job.

It deals with real feelings. Mary cries over an ant on her shoe, John is so angry at Daddy's boss that he hurts his hand, and Daddy admits he felt the same way, then shows a better way to think about it.

sections.h2: For parents who want a bedtime or devotion story
paras: Each story is short enough for one sitting, and most end at bedtime or around the dinner table. The family conversations give you words to use, and the verses are there to read together.

sections.h2: For grandparents
paras: These began as stories the author told her own children and now tells her grandchildren. They are easy to read aloud and easy to talk about afterward.

sections.h2: For Sunday school teachers and homeschool families
paras: The six stories cover the words we use, prayer, giving, God's wisdom, kindness to strangers and trusting God when bad things happen. Each one is tied to Bible verses a class can look up.

sections.h2: For children going through something hard
paras: A sick grandparent, a lost child, a parent out of work: the stories let Mary and John feel sad, scared or angry out loud, and then let Mama and Daddy show them how to bring it to God.

details.Subtitle: God's Blessings Along The Way
details.Author: Wendy Reardon

paras: A teenager driving home over the mountains takes a logging road for fun, and her car dies. Daddy joins the search, but night falls with no sign of her. That night Mary and John cannot sleep, and they kneel at the hall window to pray that God will lead her to their house. At first light there is a pounding on the door. She tells them she prayed too, and then saw a light in the dark woods that glowed like nothing she had seen, and followed it.

Playing in their pretend castle in the pines, John hears a child crying. The children fetch Mama first, and they find a toddler with a bright pink bow sitting alone in the deep woods. The family names her Gracie, because Mama said it was by grace they found her. When the girl's father comes to say thank you, he asks whether they knew her name really is Gracie. Mary says:
"This is one of those times where God made something good come out of something bad."

Daddy prays with a client at work, and his boss fires him for it. John is furious. The family prays, and Daddy reads his Bible for weeks. Then a lost stranger knocks to ask for directions. He owns a business, has been looking for an honest man and has an opening. The whole office comes out to meet Daddy on the day he is offered the job. Mary decides it was almost fun, "like a great adventure."

author.bio: Wendy Reardon writes The Blessing Trail books, read-aloud stories about two children, Mary and John, and their Mama and Daddy; this is the second. The book prints no biography of her. Its opening note says she "shares the stories she has told her children and now grandchildren," and that her stories share words from Scripture and prayers that give children a model to follow.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The opening note says where the stories come from:
"Wendy Reardon shares the stories she has told her children and now grandchildren."

It says each one gives children a situation they might meet themselves, and that the Scripture and prayers in them provide models "for our children and ourselves, guiding us into appropriate reassurances for our daily lives."

faq.q: What is The Blessing Trail 2?
faq.a: It is an 84-page full-color book of six Bible-based stories for children about Mary, John and their parents, each with verses and a family talk. They are, in order: God's Words; Follow the Light; Helping the Homeless; The Lake Trip; The Child in the Woods; and The Great Adventure.

faq.q: Is it a book of bedtime Bible stories?
faq.a: It works well at bedtime. Each story is short enough for one evening, and several end with the children in bed thinking over what Daddy said, or with the family talking before the lights go out.

faq.q: Can we use it for family devotions?
faq.a: Yes. The family talks through each story at supper, at bedtime or during devotions, reads verses such as Proverbs 15:4, Matthew 5:42, Isaiah 55:8-9, James 1:5 and Matthew 25:40, and prays together.

faq.q: Does it show children that God answers prayer?
faq.a: Yes. In Follow the Light, the children pray that a lost teenager will find their house, and at first light she does. In The Great Adventure, the family prays after Daddy loses his job, and a stranger comes to the door with a new one. Daddy also tells them that God does not always perform miracles.

faq.q: Does it teach children to pray for others?
faq.a: Yes. The children pray for the lost teenager, Mama prays for a toddler they find in the woods, Daddy prays with people at a homeless shelter, and the whole family prays for Daddy before his interview.

faq.q: Does it help children when a parent loses a job?
faq.a: That is the subject of The Great Adventure. Daddy is fired for praying with a client, John is angry, and Daddy admits he felt the same. He then tells the children that God has things under control and that they can think of hard times like a great adventure God is planning.

faq.q: Does it talk about death and grief?
faq.a: Some of it. In The Lake Trip, Mary's friend's grandmother is very sick, and Daddy tells how he was sad and also joyful when his own grandfather died, because the family believed he was with God in heaven. Daddy reads Isaiah 55:8-9 about God's ways being higher than ours.

faq.q: Do I need to read the books in order?
faq.a: No. Each story stands alone. The same family appears in The Blessing Trail 3, with a different set of stories.

content_note.title: Content note
paras: The stories include a teenager lost overnight, a very sick grandmother and a grandfather's death remembered, a lost toddler whose mother was hurt, a homeless shelter, and a father fired for praying with a client. In one story a boy hits a tree in anger until his hand bleeds. Each is told gently and ends in prayer and hope.

audience.headline: A party promoter from a town without a stoplight hears a voice call his name, and his life turns around.
audience.body: For readers who have spent years looking for a place to belong, people fighting drink, drugs or other addictions, and Christians who work in music, events or outreach. John A. Wilson, Jr. grew up in a basement room in Stockton, Missouri, left home at seventeen with his things in two trash bags, and built a career booking national country acts into nightclubs. At a Christian concert he agreed to promote in a small-town church, he gave his life to Jesus. A note on content: the book is candid about drinking, drugs, gambling, pornography and a biker crowd, and it mentions thoughts of suicide, all without graphic detail. It includes a prayer of salvation for the reader. It is a personal memoir, not a recovery program.

quote.text: This is who I was. This is what Jesus did for me. This is who I am now.
quote.cite: Honky Tonk Nights to Christian Lights, Introduction

what_makes.title: What makes this book for anyone looking for where they belong
paras: The author is honest about what drove him: "it was the constant search for a sense of belonging that truly consumed me." The bar, the biker crowd and the backstage parties all promised a family. The book tells how he finally found one, and what God did with the skills he learned along the way.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is a true story told plainly. It moves from a childhood in a basement room to a party house, a biker crowd, a failed try at trucking school and a bar job, without dressing any of it up.
It goes behind the scenes of the country music business: booking national acts about every two weeks for four nightclubs, and big shows for a 5,000-seat coliseum.
Its turning point is one night, July 10, 2016: a Christian heavy metal concert in a small-town church, where 23 others raised their hands and the promoter wept in his pastor's arms.
It tells how a dream of a hay field, a 40-foot cross and a baptism pool became a free Christian festival that drew nearly 43,000 people.
It is honest about giving, debt and pride, and it closes with the promise he made to God at a tent revival and how he nearly forgot it.

sections.h2: For anyone who has never felt they belonged
paras: The book returns to belonging again and again: the boy watching the neighbor kids through a basement window, the young man who felt like a third wheel in a friend's family, the bartender whose regulars felt like family. The acceptance he chased in bars, he found on a church softball field, among people who never once judged the life he was living.

sections.h2: For people fighting addiction
paras: He names his struggles plainly: weed, beer and shots, gambling, pornography. He also names the night they lost their hold, and he asks the reader to stop and take stock: "Are there things you have been battling? This could be anything—drugs, alcohol, pornography, whatever…you fill in the blank."

sections.h2: For Christians in music, events and outreach
paras: Much of the book is a promoter's education: venues, artists, ticket sales and the industry's cardinal rule, "never to write an artist a bad check." It shows what changed when he moved from profit-driven shows to free festivals funded by community members, partners and sponsors, and how a church outreach as simple as Sunday night softball opened the door.

sections.h2: For pastors and church members
paras: The foreword, by Pastor Beau Norman, says the way people loved the author and his wife is what drew them to repentance. The book shows the same thing from the other side: a man who expected judgment and found friendship instead, and a pastor who asked, "Why not do a Christian show?"

details.Title: Honky Tonk Nights to Christian Lights
details.Subtitle: The Unforgettable Journey of a Music Promoter's Transformation
details.Author: John A. Wilson, Jr.

paras: As a student in a church discipleship program, he spent a day working at a large arena event. Watching from the nosebleed seats, he closed his eyes and said, "God, if you’re real, prove it to me!" When he opened them, he was beside the main stage, and a man in white told him he would lead thousands upon thousands to the kingdom of God. He brushed it off with excuses, and soon after he was kicked out of the program.

On July 10, 2016, he was in the far back parking lot with his wife, smoking through the concert he had promoted, when he heard a voice call his name. Inside, the lead singer was telling how a man had saved his life after he tried to kill himself, and then named him: "His name is Jesus Christ!"

When 23 others raised their hands, the promoter could not lift his. Then his pastor walked to the back of the room, put an arm around him and said, "Look what you did, John!" He wept, asked forgiveness for his sins and welcomed Jesus into his heart.

About $50,000 short before his second festival, he was more or less yelling at God to release the funds. He writes that he heard, "I will release My money when you release yours!" With only $100 in the bank, he wrote a check for it to his church that Sunday. The next day a bank called and committed $5,000, a Christian college gave $10,000, and a Christian attorney gave over $5,000. By the end of the week the festival was fully funded.

author.bio: John A. Wilson, Jr. is the founder and CEO of Light the Way Ministry, which produces Christian festivals in three states and hosts Christian concerts and tours nearly every month. He grew up in Stockton, Missouri, served as a volunteer firefighter and first responder, and spent years in the country music business with his company Highway Promotions, LLC, booking national acts into nightclubs and a 5,000-seat coliseum. He gave his life to Jesus in 2016, and his heart is now set on seeing tent revivals spread across the country.

publisher.about: Light the Way Ministry is the nonprofit the author founded in 2017 as Light the Lake, in Stockton, Missouri. Its festivals have always been free, funded by community members, partners and sponsors, under the mission of "Taking Church Outside the Walls." This edition is published under the ministry's own imprint.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author writes that even though the book is short, it took him three years to get down on paper, because he had to learn "to embrace the power of my story and to recognize the call I had to share it with you and the world."
He wants readers to know their own story matters too:
"Do not let fear hold you back from sharing the transformative work God has done in your life."

faq.q: What is Honky Tonk Nights to Christian Lights about?
faq.a: It is a Christian memoir by John A. Wilson, Jr., a country music promoter from Stockton, Missouri, who came to faith at a Christian concert he promoted in 2016. It follows him from a hard childhood and years of partying to founding Light the Way Ministry and its Christian festivals.

faq.q: Is it a true redemption story?
faq.a: Yes. It is the author's own story, told in the first person and candid about drink, drugs, gambling and pornography. He offers it as a testimony and gives readers three statements to start their own: This is who I was. This is what Jesus did for me. This is who I am now.

faq.q: Does it include a prayer of salvation?
faq.a: Yes. Near the end of Chapter 6 the author stops the story and invites the reader to read a short prayer out loud, confessing sin and accepting Jesus as Lord and Savior, followed by his own prayer for anyone who has just prayed it. He urges new believers to tell someone and get plugged into a church.

faq.q: Does it talk about addiction and alcohol?
faq.a: Yes, honestly. The author describes years of drinking, drugs and gambling, the cost to his money and his marriage, and the night those things lost their hold. It is a story of what God did in his life, not a recovery program, and it does not offer medical advice.

faq.q: What does it say about tithing and giving?
faq.a: Chapter 8 tells how he and his wife had agreed never to give their money to the church. Short of funds for his second festival, he felt God tell him to give, and he wrote a check for the last $100 in their account. He describes the sponsorships that came that same week and says giving became an integral part of their lives.

faq.q: What is a tent revival?
faq.a: The author asked the same question when a friend called him in 2020. The book describes a revival under a tent on private property during COVID, where nearly 2,500 people gathered and some threw cigarettes, lighters, phones and bags of weed onto the stage. He now hopes to see tent revivals spread across the country.

faq.q: Is the book about Christian concerts and festivals?
faq.a: Yes. It tells how his first Christian concert, Seventh Day Slumber in a Stockton church in 2016, led to the Light the Lake festival in 2017, nearly 23,000 people in 2018, and a move to a field near Springfield, Missouri, where the festival drew nearly 43,000. Later headliners included For King & Country and TobyMac.

faq.q: Is it a good spiritual memoir for a quick read?
faq.a: It is a short, plain-spoken memoir of one man's turnaround, 68 pages in paperback. Readers who want an honest testimony with a music-business setting will find one; readers looking for a theological study will not.

audience.headline: Only God Works in Marathi: the same ten short chapters, from Called to Finished, for readers who think and pray in Marathi.
audience.body: This is the Marathi translation of Only God Works by Kevin White. Its message is the one he says set him free after ten years as a workaholic for God: God has called you to Himself, not to do His work for Him. The book walks through ten words, with Scripture throughout, and shows how rest leads to more fruit, not less. The whole book, including the Scripture passages, is printed in Marathi in Devanagari script. A note on subjects: the author is frank about burnout, illness from overwork and being voted out as a pastor, and one chapter uses the intimacy of a bride and groom as a picture of closeness with God. It is written for adults.

quote.cite: Only God Works (Marathi edition), Introduction

what_makes.title: What makes this edition for Marathi readers
paras: The Marathi edition keeps the book's opening scene. It asks you to imagine the day after you die, in a heaven where nothing was made by human hands, and where people from many nations thank you because God worked through your giving, your mission trips and your prayers. Then it asks who is really doing the work.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is the whole book in Marathi, with the same ten chapters, the conclusion and the author's personal letter.
Its chapter titles still read as one sentence. In Marathi they begin पाचारण केलेले (Called), केवळ (Only), परमेश्वर (God) and कार्य (Work).
It names a half-truth. God has called you, the author writes, and the enemy adds two words: to work.
It comes from a hard story. The author tells of overwork, being dismissed by his church, and a trip to India in 1998 that changed how he lived.
It looks to the finish line. The last chapter is about the 10/40 window and the people who still have little or no access to know about Jesus.

sections.h2: For Marathi-speaking believers who are worn out
paras: Chapter 5, स्वातंत्र्य (Freedom), reads God's promise of rest in Hebrews 4 and Psalm 23 and says that freedom from work means freedom to rest. Resting, the author adds, does not mean being lazy or useless.

sections.h2: For pastors and church leaders
paras: The author writes that many pastors and leaders have left the ministry because of the lie that God called them to work for Him. A pastor or leader who serves in Marathi can hand this edition to the people in their care.

sections.h2: For families and churches who read in more than one language
paras: The Marathi edition follows the English book chapter for chapter, so a family or a small group can read Only God Works side by side in English and in Marathi.

paras: The introduction asks you to imagine heaven. Nothing there was made by human hands. Your yard and the work on your house are not there. Instead, people you have never met, many from other nations, tell you how God worked through your tithes, offerings, mission trips and prayers to bring them to Jesus.
कल्पना करा, हा तुमच्या मृत्यू नंतरचा दिवस आहे.

In Chapter 4 the author tells how, in 1998, God took him to India and showed him Christ followers without basic necessities, most without Bibles, who still passionately pursued God's presence. On the plane home he committed to pursue the presence of God every day for the rest of his life. Chapter 9 tells the harder story around it: a church he built while working up to ninety hours a week, a vote that dismissed him, and a stranger who told him he had not been fired but set free.

Chapter 10, Finished, describes the 10/40 window, the region of North Africa, the Middle East and Asia where most people with little or no access to know about Jesus live, including many in India. It reads Matthew 24:14 as God's finish line and Revelation 7 as a picture of every nation worshiping together, and says only God can finish the work.

author.bio: Kevin White experienced God's call into full-time vocational ministry at seventeen and has served in full-time Christian ministry for nearly forty years. After a decade as what he calls a workaholic for God, he found freedom in Christ and started With Love From Jesus Ministries and Global Hope India. He has been to India more than fifty times, taking 1,000 people on mission trips. He is CEO of Spirit Media and the author of Audacious Generosity, Get to the Point and What's Your Word?

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: Only God Works was the first book the author wrote, twenty-five years before it was published, and he says it was written more for himself than for the world. His personal letter at the end calls the message a matter of life or death for billions of people far from God, and says the revelation that only God works saved his life.
The book's own pages say Spirit Media is committed to sharing the Good News of Jesus in all 195 nations of the world. The Marathi edition carries that message to readers in their own language.

faq.q: What is this book?
faq.a: It is the Marathi edition of Only God Works by Kevin White, printed under the title केवळ परमेश्वर कार्य करीतो. It teaches that God has never called us to work for Him, but to intimacy with Him, and to let Him work in and through us.

faq.q: What are the chapters?
faq.a: They are, in order: Called; Only; God; Work; Freedom; Intimacy; Humility; Gratitude; Fruit; and Finished. An introduction comes first, and a conclusion and a letter from the author close the book. In this edition the chapters are listed by title, without numbers.

faq.q: Does it quote the Bible in Marathi?
faq.a: Yes. The copyright page says the Scripture passages come from the Marathi Bible of the Bible Society of India. It is a book about the Bible's teaching, not a Bible itself.

faq.q: Is it a book about resting in God?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 5, स्वातंत्र्य (Freedom), reads God's promise of rest in Hebrews 4 and says freedom from work means freedom to rest. The author says rest does not mean being useless or lazy.

faq.q: Does it teach intimacy with God?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 6, जवळीक (Intimacy), is about closeness with God, and the book names intimacy, humility and gratitude as the three things God gives us to focus on.

faq.q: What does it say about faith and work?
faq.a: It says the work God wants done is a work only He can do, and that our part is to pursue His presence and follow His instructions. It does not tell readers to stop working or to become lazy.

faq.q: What does it say about bearing fruit?
faq.a: Chapter 9, फळ (Fruit), says only God produces fruit, and that fruit comes from intimacy with God, not from our own striving.

faq.q: Does it talk about the Great Commission?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 10, समाप्ती (Finished), looks at the 10/40 window and the people with little or no access to know about Jesus, and the author's letter invites readers to be part of fulfilling the Great Commission.

hero.audience_line: For Christians who want to love difficult people, believers who want to understand agape, and anyone who has tried to love others in their own strength and found they could not.
hero.tagline: A short, Scripture-rich book on five vital truths about love, and why God's agape love is something you claim by faith, not something you manufacture.

audience.headline: A pastor's short guide to the one kind of love the book says you cannot produce on your own, and how to receive it by faith.
audience.body: For Christians who want to love people they find hard to love, small groups studying 1 Corinthians 13, and believers who have tried to love by resolution and failed. Pastor Alfred Cherubim sets out five vital truths about love, gathers dozens of Bible passages on God's love, and closes with seven characteristics of divine love and a prayer. A note on content: the book is built mostly from Scripture, quoted at length from The Living Bible, the ESV and the NET, with a few short stories of changed lives. Its conclusion speaks plainly about judgment and eternal punishment for those who reject Christ. It is a devotional teaching book, not a counseling guide.

quote.text: Agape love is given because of the character of the person loving rather than because of the worthiness of the object of that love.
quote.cite: LOVE The Greatest Power Ever Known, Introduction

what_makes.title: What makes this book for believers who want to love like Christ
paras: The book starts from a hard admission: you cannot produce God's kind of love by trying harder. "In your own strength, it is not possible to love with God's kind of love." Then it shows where that love comes from and how to receive it.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is built on five vital truths, one chapter each, from God loves you unconditionally to you love by faith.
It explains the three Greek words translated love in English, eros, phileo and agape, and why agape is an act of the will, not an emotion.
It gives practical steps. One is to make a list of the people you find hard to love, perhaps including yourself, and begin to love them by faith.

It tells short stories of changed lives: two law partners who turn from hatred to friendship, a man who stops kicking his dog the night he receives Christ, and a boy in a burn unit who begins to fight for his recovery after a teacher comes to help with his nouns and adverbs.
It gathers Scripture by theme, from God's love for us to what Jesus said about love, and ends with a prayer the reader can make their own.

sections.h2: For Christians who find some people hard to love
paras: The book does not pretend this is easy. It asks you to love by faith every one of your enemies, which it describes as "everyone who angers you, ignores you, bores you or frustrates you." It suggests your boss, a fellow employee, your spouse, your children or your parents might be on that list, and it asks you to pray for each person and expect God to work through you.

sections.h2: For small groups studying 1 Corinthians 13
paras: 1 Corinthians 13 runs through the whole book. It is quoted in the introduction, in the stories and in the steps, and in the closing prayer the reader claims "the 1 Corinthians 13 kind of love" for God, for all people and for themselves. Chapter 6 adds nine reasons the love of God is worth studying, each with its passages, which suits a group that wants to go slowly.

sections.h2: For new believers learning what agape means
paras: If the word agape is new to you, the introduction explains it simply: God's supernatural, unconditional love, shown most clearly in Christ's death on the cross. It is sometimes love in spite of rather than because of, and it is "expressed, not through mere emotions, but as an act of one's will." The book then shows how that love becomes yours when you receive Christ and the Holy Spirit.

sections.h2: For anyone who wants to share their faith
paras: The end of Chapter 5 ties love to evangelism. When you begin to love by faith, the book says, you begin to see other people as God sees them, "as individuals of great worth," as those for whom Christ died. It calls the Great Commission a personal responsibility and privilege that grows out of that love.

paras: Chapter 5 tells of two gifted attorneys in the same firm who had criticized each other for years. One became a Christian and asked his pastor what to do. When the pastor suggested he ask his partner's forgiveness and tell him he loved him, he answered:
"That would be hypocritical. I don't love him. How could I tell him I love him when I don't?"

The pastor explained that each description of love in 1 Corinthians 13 "is not an expression of the emotions, but of the will." The next morning the lawyer walked into his partner's office, asked forgiveness and told him he loved him. His partner asked forgiveness in return, and then asked how he could become a Christian too.

stories.h2: A lesson in nouns and adverbs
paras: A visiting hospital teacher was sent to help a schoolboy in a burn unit with his nouns and adverbs. She went through the lesson and left, feeling little had been accomplished. The next morning the nurse told her the boy's whole attitude had changed and he was fighting back. He explained it himself:
"They wouldn't send a special teacher to work on nouns and adverbs with a dying boy, now, would they?"
The book draws the lesson: "Sometimes we impart hope to others by just showing up with love and compassion."

A homemaker had seen her family through a long cold winter of mumps, measles, a broken nose, three new teeth for the baby and countless other difficulties. On her knees she began to protest, "Oh Lord! I have so much to do!" Then she heard herself say something else:
"Oh Lord! I have so much to love!"
"You will never run out of opportunities to love by faith," the book adds.

He writes as a pastor to believers, and the book closes with a prayer he invites every reader to make their own. He is also the author of Sharing Your Faith and Testimony and The Miracles of Jesus Christ and His Apostles.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The book says people "may give their lives willingly for ones they deem worthy," but Christ's love reaches those least worthy, and that kind of love cannot be produced by resolution. Chapter 6 adds that the love of God is "widely accepted, but wrongly understood."
The conclusion states the purpose plainly:
"God is the One who defines love, not human beings."
It ends with a prayer for the reader: "Lord, you would never have commanded me to love had You not intended to enable me to do so."

faq.q: What is LOVE The Greatest Power Ever Known about?
faq.a: It is a short teaching book by Pastor Alfred Cherubim on God's agape love and how a Christian can love others with it. It rests on five vital truths, gathers Scripture on God's love, and ends with seven characteristics of divine love and a prayer to claim that love by faith.

faq.q: What is agape love?
faq.a: The book says agape is God's love, "the purest, deepest kind of love," expressed not through emotion but as an act of the will. It sets agape beside the two other Greek words translated love in English: eros, which suggests sensual desire, and phileo, the love of friends and relatives.

faq.q: What are the Five Vital Truths About Love?
faq.a: They are, in order: God loves you unconditionally; you are commanded to love others; you are incapable of loving others on your own; you can love others with God's love; and you love by faith. Each has its own chapter.

faq.q: Does it explain 1 Corinthians 13?
faq.a: It quotes 1 Corinthians 13 in The Living Bible early on and returns to it throughout. Its point is that each description of love there, patient, kind, never jealous or envious, is a choice of the will, and that a Christian can claim that kind of love by faith. It is a teaching book, not a verse-by-verse commentary.

faq.q: What does it say about loving your enemies?
faq.a: It quotes Jesus in Matthew 5:43-47 and asks readers to love by faith everyone who angers, ignores, bores or frustrates them. It suggests making a list of people you do not like and praying for each one, and it tells of two attorneys who turned from hatred to friendship.

faq.q: What does it say about loving your neighbor as yourself?
faq.a: Chapter 2, You are Commanded to Love Others, starts with Jesus' answer about the greatest commandment and quotes Romans 13:9-10. The book says that if you love God with all your heart, soul and mind, you will be rightly related to others too, and that you should love your neighbor because your neighbor is made in the image of God.

faq.q: Does it include Bible verses about God's love?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 5 gathers passages under headings such as More of God's Love Scriptures, Love One Another Bible Verses and What Did Jesus Say About Love, and Chapters 6 and 7 add many more. Most are quoted from The Living Bible, the ESV and the NET.

faq.q: Does it talk about perfect love casting out fear?
faq.a: Briefly. It quotes 1 John 4:18, "perfect love drives out fear," and says the dismissal of the fear of condemnation is one of the main works of God's love, because God's judgment fell on Jesus at the cross.

hero.audience_line: For Christians who want to learn positive confession, believers who want their words to line up with Scripture, and anyone tired of negative talk who is ready to speak life.
hero.tagline: A faith teacher's "anytime" class on speaking God's Word out loud: what a positive confession is, why it works, how to wait for the answer, and hundreds of Scripture-based confessions for every circumstance.

audience.headline: A girl who touched the TV screen every Sunday when Oral Roberts said something good would happen that day grew up to teach faith, and this is her class in a book.
audience.body: For Christians learning positive confession, believers who want to speak Scripture aloud, people trying to change negative self-talk, prayer groups and church classes, and new believers growing in faith. Nora Fozard writes the way she teaches: plainly, warmly and with stories from her own life as a pastor's wife. Every chapter pairs Bible verses with first-person confessions, so you can look up the verse and say the confession the same day. The last chapter is a long list of confessions arranged by topic, from Anointing to Work, followed by her own faith quotes. A note on subjects: the book is written from a Spirit-filled, faith-teaching point of view. It includes confessions for health, healing and finances. It also says plainly that "Only God heals. Doctors help," and warns against treating faith like a wish list.

quote.text: “Nobody can change your confession except you.”
quote.cite: The Positive Power of Speaking God’s Word, Chapter 1: The Importance of Words

what_makes.title: What makes this book a class you can take anytime
paras: Nora wrote it because people kept asking her when she would teach on faith again. So the book is built like a class: a short teaching, the verses behind it, and a confession to say out loud before you turn the page.
Five things set it apart:
list: It defines its main idea in one plain sentence. A positive confession is saying out loud that you agree with God about His good plan for your life and His world, always based on Scripture.
Every teaching ends with words to say. Sections close with "I confess" or "Say it now!" and a first-person version of the verse, with the reference so you can check it.
It is honest about the limits. A chapter on confession and possession says that asking for a private jet is not faith but foolishness, and it recalls how "name it and claim it" confused people.

It has a full chapter of confessions by topic. Courage and Success, Fear and Anxiety, Finances, Health and Healing, Peace, Relationships, Wisdom, Work and many more, with sets for husbands, wives and children.
It is personal. Nora tells how she found faith as a teenager, how she grew into being a pastor's wife in her twenties, and how her church was built debt-free when people said it could not be done.

sections.h2: For believers who want to speak God's Word every day
paras: The book asks you to say the confessions out loud, not just think them. Nora's reason is simple: you tell a beautiful person she is beautiful out loud, and you should tell God's truth out loud too. Each chapter gives you something to say today.

sections.h2: For anyone stuck in negative talk
paras: Somebody taught you the way you talk, the book says, whether it was your parents, your friends or a kind grandmother. If you have spent years saying the same negative things, Nora asks you to say God's Word just as many times until it takes root.

sections.h2: For readers waiting on an answer
paras: Two chapters deal with the hardest part: waiting for what you confessed to appear, and working toward it. Faith is not magic, she writes. You plan, you work, and you wait with anticipation, confidence and expectation.

sections.h2: For prayer groups and church classes
paras: The book grew out of years of classes on faith, and it still reads like one. Chapters are short, each has verses to look up, and the confessions by topic make it easy to choose a theme for a group meeting or a week of prayer.

details.Title: The Positive Power of Speaking God’s Word
details.Subtitle: Change Your Mind, Your Life, and Your World with Your Words!
details.Author: Nora Fozard

stories.h2: A hand on the television screen
paras: Nora grew up one of seven children, raised mostly by her mother and grandfather. The family went to church, but she never heard about God's promises there. Then one Sunday morning, as a young teenager, she heard Oral Roberts on television tell viewers to touch the screen if they wanted a miracle:
"Something good is going to happen to you this very day!"
She touched the screen week after week. She did not know she was planting a seed of faith. She just knew it gave her hope, and later she read every one of his books.

When the Fozards were raising their children, they did not have much. People asked how all those kids fit in such a tiny car. Nora and the children would laugh and confess that one day they would have a big car and a house, and they called themselves their family of faith. She told them honestly when there was no money for something, and prayed with them anyway. Years later they had a car so big they called it their 747, and they all rode in it to take their first child to college.

When Nora and her husband began talking about a big new church with a Christian school, people said they were crazy. They needed land and more than a million dollars, and they had agreed the building would be debt-free when they moved in. The bank said it would not happen. They kept confessing and kept working. The church was built, and Nora writes that doctors, teachers, professors, attorneys and even NBA players have come out of that school.
"You can’t just try faith, you have to keep faith."

author.bio: Nora Fozard has taught about faith for many years. She teaches faith and prayer at Mt. Zion Christian Church in Durham, North Carolina, where her husband is the founding pastor, and she has served beside him for some forty years. One of seven children, she first heard that God had something good for her as a teenager watching Oral Roberts on Sunday-morning television. She learned the importance of positive words from faith teachers including Fred Price, Kenneth Hagin, Lester Summerall and Theo Wolmarans. This is her fifth book with Spirit Media.

publisher.about: Spirit Media Publishing is a Christian publishing and marketing company with a vision to reveal our Father's heart to all nations. It offers full-service book creation and publishing in paperback, hardback, digital and audiobook formats, along with children's titles, compact Express Books, website design and SEO, and podcast and video production. We are glad to publish a faith teacher's class on speaking God's Word for every reader who wants to speak life.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: Nora has taught classes on faith for years, and when no class is running, people ask for one. In the acknowledgements she writes what they tell her:
"We need a fresh word. When are you going to teach about faith again?"
The book is her answer, and its goal is that you never stop speaking God's Word. As she puts it at the end of Chapter 2:
"It becomes a lifestyle, and you can’t say negative things any more."

faq.q: What is The Positive Power of Speaking God's Word about?
faq.a: It is a book on positive confession by faith teacher Nora Fozard. It explains why words matter, what a positive confession is and how faith, patience and action bring it to pass. It ends with confessions for every circumstance, each tied to a Bible verse, and a collection of her faith quotes.

faq.q: What is a positive confession?
faq.a: The book defines it as saying out loud that you agree with God about His good plan for your life and His world. Confessions are always based on Scripture. Often you take a verse and say it in the first person, such as turning Romans 8:37 into "I have overwhelming victory through Christ who loves me."

faq.q: Is it the same as the power of positive thinking?
faq.a: No. The book does not ask you to think positive thoughts on your own. It asks you to speak what God's Word already says, and it warns that presumption, speaking from your own ideas instead of the Word, is not faith. Some confessions are about attitude, but every one points back to a verse.

faq.q: Does the book include Bible affirmations I can say daily?
faq.a: Yes, though the book calls them confessions. Chapter 11, Confessions for Every Circumstance, starts with General Confessions for Every Day and then gives first-person statements by topic, from Anointing to Work, each with its Bible reference. Earlier chapters add more, marked "I confess" or "Say it now!"

faq.q: Does it cover who I am in Christ?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 9, God's Truth Will Reprogram Your Heart!, has a list called Who I Am in Christ and another called Who I Am Not in Christ. Examples include "I am a new creature in Christ" and "I am not defeated," each with its verse.

faq.q: Does the book talk about renewing your mind?
faq.a: Yes. The subtitle is Change Your Mind, Your Life, and Your World with Your Words, and Chapter 9 teaches that filling yourself with God's truth will reprogram your heart. Nora says that is what began to happen to her when she first heard God's goodness preached on television.

faq.q: What does it say about waiting on God?
faq.a: Chapter 7, Waiting for the Manifestation, says faith is not magic and you have to be willing to wait. We wait with anticipation, confidence and expectation. Chapter 8 adds that you still plan and work while you wait, and that the answer may look different from what you expected.

faq.q: Are there healing scriptures in the book?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 11 has a Health and Healing section with confessions To Stay Healthy and For Physical Healing, built on verses such as Isaiah 53 and Psalm 103. The author's view is that healing is a gift of God, and she writes that doctors help, so include good food, good counsel, fresh air and exercise. It is a faith book, not medical advice.

hero.audience_line: For Christians in a hard or confusing season, believers waiting on a promise from God, and pastors and small groups studying the wilderness stories of the Old Testament.
hero.tagline: Through the wilderness stories of Israel, Abraham, Jacob and Moses, pastor Chase Gardner shows how God uses our desert seasons to speak to us and prepare us for His promises.

audience.headline: A pastor sits outside a rented RV in Joshua Tree, reading Genesis in the desert, and realizes he is in the kind of place God takes the people He loves.
audience.body: For Christians in a season that makes no sense: a relationship that fell apart, a promotion that went to someone else, a plan that stalled, a long silence from God. Chase Gardner walks through four Old Testament stories, Israel's detour out of Egypt, Abraham's ten silent years, Jacob's night of wrestling and Moses' last sermon in Deuteronomy, and asks what God was doing in each. He writes as a pastor, a former church planter and a father, and he tells his own wilderness seasons along the way, including an adoption from Ethiopia that fell through. The tone is warm and often funny. A note on subjects: the book touches on infertility in the Bible stories, on the grief of a failed adoption and on foster care. It is a short Christian living book of four chapters, not a verse-by-verse commentary, and it has no study questions.

quote.text: “Those desert seasons aren’t always comfortable, but they are always intentional.”
quote.cite: In the Wilderness, the introduction: The Place of Speaking

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people in a desert season
paras: The book starts with a family RV trip through California. The first stop is Joshua Tree, in 104 degree heat, with no cell service. That night Chase reads about Abraham under thousands of stars and sees that Abraham, Hagar, Moses, Elijah, John the Baptist and Jesus all spent long seasons in places like this one. At the end of the trip, asked for his favorite stop, he answers that it is the type of place God takes the people He loves.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is built on one Hebrew word. Midbar, wilderness, shares its root with the word for speaking, so many Hebrews called the wilderness the place of speaking: the noise dies down and it is just you and God.

Each chapter follows one person or people. Israel learns why God chose the long way around. Abraham learns that God keeps both ends of the covenant. Jacob learns that God Himself is the blessing. Moses teaches that God can spread a table in the wilderness.

It gives more than one reason for a hard season. Sometimes God is preparing you, because your capacity has outpaced your character. Sometimes it has very little to do with you, and a watching world is seeing how you suffer.

The author tells his own story honestly: the years before he was allowed to preach, five lonely years as a church planter, and ten years between a failed adoption and the little girl who arrived in a social worker's van.
It is short and easy to read, with humor on most pages, from a Denny's on the road out of Egypt to a nightstand drawer holding five pinecones from the General Sherman tree.

sections.h2: For anyone in a season that makes no sense
paras: The book names the questions people ask in the desert: Did God really intend to lead me here? Did God forget about me? How can any good come from this? Chase says plainly that he has asked them too. His answer is not that the season is easy, but that there is always a reason, and that whatever route God chooses will bring you closer to Him.

sections.h2: For believers waiting on a promise
paras: Abraham waited ten years in silence and fifteen more before Isaac was born. The chapter on him is for anyone who feels they are doing all the work in their relationship with God. It shows God walking alone between the pieces of the covenant, and it ends at the cross as proof that God is a promise keeper.

sections.h2: For pastors, teachers and small groups
paras: Each chapter opens with a passage of Scripture and works through the story with the text in view, from Exodus 13 to Genesis 15, Genesis 32 and Deuteronomy 32. A quartermaster's numbers on feeding Israel in the desert and the Hebrew behind Jacob's name give a teacher plenty to work with. There are four chapters and an introduction, which suits a short series.

sections.h2: For anyone chasing the next thing
paras: The Jacob chapter describes a different kind of wilderness: a wilderness of plenty, where God lets us have what we want so we learn it cannot satisfy. Approval, romance and money all fail Jacob before he wrestles with God and will not let go. Chase writes that the reason the quest feels endless may be that we have been chasing cheap substitutes instead of the real thing.
