details.Title: In The Wilderness
details.Subtitle: How God Uses Our Desert Seasons to Prepare Us for His Promises
details.Author: Chase Gardner

paras: In Chapter 1, Israel walks out of Egypt free, and the main highway to the promised land is right in front of them. God leads them the other way. Exodus gives the reason: if they faced a battle, they might turn back. They were brick makers, not warriors. Chase connects it to his own story. He wanted to preach from his teens, but he was not ready:
“I may have had the capacity to preach, but I didn’t yet have the character to preach.”
God led him into five hard years as a church planter instead. Two years after he handed that church off, God called him to preach.

Abraham leaves home on a promise, walks about 425 miles into a desert that is already owned, survives a famine, a trip to Egypt and a war, and still has no son. For ten years God says nothing. Chase and his wife spent years trying to adopt from Ethiopia, redoing the process three times, until the country closed. When God speaks to Abraham again, He walks alone between the pieces of the covenant. Ten years after their adoption began, a one-year-old girl arrived at the author's home for foster care. His conclusion:
“God fulfilled His promise to my wife and I. He just waited until the time was right.”

Chapter 4 opens with five pinecones from the General Sherman tree. For about a century people kept fire away from the giant sequoias, and hundreds of trees died, because sequoias need fire to open their cones and prepare the soil. Chase turns to Moses, who reminds Israel in Deuteronomy of the bitter water, the empty desert and the rock that gave water. The question the chapter asks is the one from Psalm 78: can God spread a table in the wilderness? The chapter's answer:
“The fire is good. The flames help us flourish.”

author.bio: Chase Gardner is a pastor and preacher from North Carolina. He knew by age twelve that he wanted to preach, earned a degree in Biblical studies at a Christian college and began his ministry as a youth pastor. He later spent five years as a church planter, learning to lead, raise funds, gather a launch team and walk with families through hospital visits, weddings and funerals. Two years after passing off leadership of that church, he was called to preach. He is a husband and a father.

It offers full-service book creation and publishing in paperback, hardback, digital and audiobook formats, along with children's titles, compact Express Books, website design and SEO, and podcast and video production. We are glad to publish a pastor's honest, hopeful book for anyone walking through a desert season.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The book grew out of a night in Joshua Tree and a look back over the author's own life. He saw an irregular pattern of God leading him into wilderness seasons again and again, and he guessed his readers had seen the same. He writes that if we do not prepare our hearts, we go through those seasons grumbling with our heads down:
“And make no mistake, there is always a reason.”

His hope is that the stories of Israel, Abraham, Jacob and Moses will help readers see their own story, so that the next time God leads them somewhere unexpected they are ready to receive what He intends to give them there.

faq.q: What is In the Wilderness about?
faq.a: It is a short Christian living book by pastor Chase Gardner about wilderness seasons: times when life stops making sense and God seems silent. Through the stories of Israel, Abraham, Jacob and Moses, it shows why God leads the people He loves into the desert and what He gives them there.

faq.q: Is it a book about waiting on God and God's timing?
faq.a: Yes. The Abraham chapter is about waiting: ten years of silence after the promise, and fifteen more before Isaac was born. The author pairs it with his own ten-year wait between a failed adoption and the little girl who came to his family through foster care.

faq.q: Does it help with trusting God in hard times?
faq.a: That is its aim. The author says hard seasons are not always comfortable but are always intentional, and he asks readers to stop grumbling through them and look for what God intends to give them. It is encouragement from Scripture, not a counseling or self-help method.

faq.q: What does the book say about God's promises and the covenant with Abraham?
faq.a: It explains the covenant ceremony in Genesis 15, where animals were cut in half and both parties walked between them. Abraham falls asleep, and God walks through alone. The author reads this as God promising to keep both ends of the covenant, and he points to the cross as proof that God is a promise maker and a promise keeper.

faq.q: What does it say about Jacob wrestling with God?
faq.a: The Jacob chapter calls him the heel grabber, a man who spent his life grasping for a blessing through his father's approval, through romance and through money. When God wrestles him in the wilderness and touches his hip, Jacob stops trying to escape and holds on. The lesson the author draws is that God Himself is the blessing.

faq.q: Does the book explain why God allows suffering?
faq.a: Some of it. It does not try to answer every kind of suffering. It gives reasons the Bible shows for wilderness seasons: God may be preparing you, showing His glory to a watching world, correcting a wrong view of Him, or teaching you that nothing else satisfies. The last chapter compares it to the fire that giant sequoias need to grow.

faq.q: Does the author share his own story of adoption and foster care?
faq.a: Yes. He and his wife tried to adopt from Ethiopia and redid the whole process three times before the country was closed to adoptions. Years later they became foster parents, and a one-year-old girl came to live with them in August 2020. At the time of writing, her adoption was a few months from being final.

faq.q: Can it be used for a small group Bible study?
faq.a: It can be read together, but it is not a study guide. There are no discussion questions or leader notes. The four chapters each open with a Scripture passage and work through one Old Testament story, which makes them easy to read and talk about one at a time.

hero.audience_line: For church members and leaders, Christians tired of religious routine, and small groups who want to live out the book of Acts in the church today.
hero.tagline: In a series of warm, direct letters to the church, pastor Chasty Daniels asks whether we have traded a genuine relationship with God for religion, and points back to the book of Acts.

audience.headline: A pastor writes to the church like a friend writing home: “Dear Church People, I think we've missed the mark.”
audience.body: For church members who never miss a Sunday and still feel stuck, for pastors and ministry leaders who want their people to grow, and for small groups reading the book of Acts. Chasty Daniels writes every part of the book as a letter, signed with her first name, and asks whether worldly values and religious routine have crept into the church. She sets six signs of a religious Christian beside the qualities of a spiritual one, then turns to prayer, the dangers of neglecting your spiritual life, the benefits of being genuine and one young man's story. Real stories from church life sit beside Scripture from Acts, the Gospels and the letters to the early believers. A note on subjects: the closing story touches on secret sexual sin and depression, described without detail, and the book mentions some unusual church practices it calls unbiblical. It is a book of encouragement and challenge, not a verse-by-verse commentary on Acts.

quote.text: “Have we allowed worldly values to creep into the pure Kingdom of God?”
quote.cite: Dear Church People, the introduction

what_makes.title: What makes this book for the church today
paras: Every part of the book opens with a postcard page and reads as a letter. Each begins “Dear Church People” and ends with a short sign-off from the author: Cheering you on, Joining you in prayer, Pursuing genuine repentance. The voice is a pastor talking straight to her own congregation, honest about what she sees and hopeful about what can change.
Five things set it apart:
list: It names the problem plainly. Part One lists six ways you might be a religious Christian, from showing up for every program without growing to preaching the gospel while refusing to forgive.

It goes back to the book of Acts. Part Four walks through the early church at prayer: united in Acts 1, at the three o'clock prayer service in Acts 3, shaking the meeting place in Acts 4 and sending out missionaries after fasting in Acts 13.
It starts from four basic truths: Jesus is the heart of our faith, salvation comes through His death and resurrection, obedience is our response to His grace, and believers need each other.

It tells real stories from church life: a new believer whose passion outran a long-time prayer leader, a woman who took her pastor's advice over her own sense of God's leading, and a man who chose a wife by how she dressed.
It ends practically. The last part closes with steps toward repentance: confess, turn away from sin, seek accountability, make restitution and live a life of service.

sections.h2: For church members who feel stuck
paras: The first letter describes the faithful volunteer who is at every event and still is not growing. The author does not mock that person. She says being a religious Christian is not bad in itself, but a faith that is not growing is a red flag, and she shows what a growing faith looks like: love, faith, humility and integrity.

sections.h2: For pastors and church leaders
paras: Several stories are hard on leaders: a prayer leader who grew jealous of a new believer, and a pastor whose advice about marriage ended in divorce. The point is not to distrust pastors. The author writes that respecting your pastor is good, but the Bible is available to everyone, and every believer needs a relationship with God of their own.

sections.h2: For anyone who wants a stronger prayer life
paras: Part Three is the longest in the book. It begins with twelve simple steps for building any habit, then gives six benefits of regular prayer, each with Scripture, from Philippians 4:6-7 to 1 Thessalonians 5:16-18. Part Four shows how prayer ran through the early church in Acts, chapter by chapter.

sections.h2: For small groups and Bible studies
paras: The short letters, the six signs and the six benefits of prayer give a group clear pieces to read and talk through, though the book has no printed discussion questions. The closing story of a young church musician who lost his way and came back makes a good final conversation about pride, hidden sin and the friends who help us return.

Yes, I think we’ve really veered off track.
I don’t know about you, but I’m longing to be a true Christian.
Prayer is our way of talking to God, but it’s not just about saying words.

whats_inside: An introduction, six parts and a conclusion, each written as a letter to the church
Six signs of a religious Christian and four qualities of a spiritual one
Twelve steps for forming a habit and six benefits of regular prayer
Prayer in the book of Acts, from Acts 1 to Acts 16
A closing story with practical steps toward repentance
Scripture from the NIV and NLT, and an About the Author page

details.Title: Dear Church People
details.Subtitle: Living out the Book of Acts in the 21st Century Church
details.Author: Chasty Daniels

paras: In Part One, a young man joins the author's church as a new believer. He studies the Bible, excels in every class and within a few months is organizing large events where people are healed and helped. The leader of his prayer group, who has served for years, grows jealous. The author's point is that time in church is not the same as closeness to God:
“Just because you’ve been serving in the church for years doesn’t automatically mean you’ve got a deep spiritual connection with Him.”

A woman is choosing between two men. After praying, she believes God has shown her which one. Her pastor recommends the wealthier man, and she follows his advice. The marriage struggles and ends in divorce, and she blames the pastor. The author does not tell readers to ignore their pastors. She tells them to know God's Word for themselves:
“The Bible is available to everyone, not just pastors.”

Part Six tells of a young man from a non-religious family who comes to faith through a Christian friend, plays keyboard at church and is accepted to his dream university. Pride creeps in. One Sunday he arrives late to find a young boy at the keyboard for good. Later, serving as a minister, he hides a secret sin, stops praying and sinks into depression, until a friend prays and fasts with him for seven days. The first lesson the author draws:
“It’s essential to keep in mind that we can’t hide anything from God.”

author.bio: Chasty Daniels is a pastor at Rebirth Deliverance Ministries in Smithfield, North Carolina, and a wife and mother of three. Raised in a Christian household, she holds a degree in Mass Communications with a minor in Journalism from Saint Augustine's College in Raleigh and a Master of Arts in Youth Pastoral and Family Counseling Services from Grand Canyon University. She works in clinical research on oncology, hematology and internal medicine trials. In ministry she leads a tutoring program, a Boys Club for African-American young men and the Sticks and Stones ministry, which advocates for students facing bullying. She founded the Empact Youth Coalition for youth pastors and leaders in Central North Carolina and started a Parent University to help parents guide their children in a digital age.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author believes the church has drifted toward rituals and outward righteousness, and that the answer is not a new program but a return to the basics. In the introduction she writes:
“These days, it’s crucial for us to get back to basics, back to the Cross, and dive deep into the timeless truths found in God’s Word.”
She turns to the first church to do it:
“In this book, we’ll explore the stories and principles from the book of Acts and the letters written to the early believers in the Church.”

faq.q: What is Dear Church People about?
faq.a: It is a book of letters from pastor Chasty Daniels to the church. She asks whether believers have traded a genuine relationship with God for religious routine, and she uses the book of Acts and the letters to the early church to show the way back.

faq.q: How does the book use the book of Acts?
faq.a: Acts is the model throughout. The author compares the first-century church with the church today, and in Part Four she walks through prayer in Acts, from the believers united in prayer in Acts 1 to Paul and his companions seeking a place of prayer in Acts 16. The subtitle calls it living out the book of Acts in the 21st century church.

faq.q: What does the author mean by a religious Christian?
faq.a: Someone active in church who is not growing in a real relationship with God. Part One gives six signs. They are, in order: there is no improvement in your spiritual life; you respect your spiritual leader's words more than the Word of God; you take more care dressing your body than your soul; you take church rules more seriously than God's; you give grudgingly; and you do not forgive people, yet you preach the gospel.

faq.q: What does it teach about how to pray and the power of prayer?
faq.a: Part Three, The Habit of Prayer, gives twelve steps for building a habit and six benefits of regular prayer. They are, in order: a deeper relationship with God; an increase of faith and trust in Jesus; peace and comfort in God; a grateful heart; divine direction; and guidance and protection from the devices of evil men. It is encouragement to pray, not a set of written prayers.

faq.q: What are the qualities of a spiritual Christian?
faq.a: Part Two names four. They are, in order: you express genuine love and compassion to others; you have faith in the things of God and do all that He commands; you are humble in all that you do; and you exhibit integrity in all that you do. The section on integrity is the longest, drawing on Titus, James, Paul's letters and Jesus' words about letting your yes be yes.

faq.q: What does the book say about forgiveness?
faq.a: Refusing to forgive is the last of the six signs of a religious Christian. The author calls forgiveness a piece of clothing you cannot leave home without, and points to Jesus' story of the unforgiving servant and His words about forgiving seventy times seven. She also lists forgiveness among the benefits of being genuine.

faq.q: Does it talk about true repentance?
faq.a: Yes. Part Six ends with practical steps toward genuine repentance. They are, in order: confess your sins; turn away from sin; seek accountability; make restitution; and live a life of service. The author writes that real repentance goes beyond apologies and guilt.

faq.q: Is it a book on spiritual growth?
faq.a: Yes. The author writes that being religious is not bad in itself, but a faith that is not growing is a red flag. The book moves from the signs of stalled faith to the qualities, habits and benefits of a growing one.

hero.tagline: A prayer-room handbook from a church that answers calls from people in desperate need: plain guidance and Bible verses for more than fifty of life's hardest problems, answers to common questions about God, and how to start a prayer ministry.

audience.headline: When strangers call a church saying "I'm desperate. I need prayer," the volunteer on the phone needs to know what to say. This book was written for that person.
audience.body: For prayer-ministry and prayer-team volunteers, pastors, deacons and lay counselors, intercessors, and church members who are often the one friends call in a crisis. Nora Fozard draws on years in her church's prayer room. Each topic starts with a short, plain explanation of what callers are going through and what to keep in mind, then gives Bible verses grouped under simple headings such as God is with you or God helps and strengthens us. Most verses are printed in full from the New Living Translation, with others from the Amplified, ESV, NASB and NIV. A note on subjects: the book covers hard topics directly, including abortion, abuse, addiction, suicide and sexual sin, from a traditional, Spirit-filled Christian point of view. It tells volunteers to report suspected abuse, to refer people to professional help, and never to tell anyone to stop taking medication. It is a guide for prayer, not a substitute for professional counseling.

quote.text: “In the prayer room, Jesus is the counselor who can help.”
quote.cite: Scripture References for Effective Counseling, Introduction: Praying with People Who Need Help

what_makes.title: What makes this book a tool for the prayer room
paras: The people who call, the introduction says, are often not churchgoers. They don't know a lot about God. They just know God answers prayer. This book gives the person who answers the phone a place to turn, topic by topic, while the caller is still on the line.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is arranged A to Z. Part 1 runs from Abortion to Worldliness, so you can find Grief, Loneliness, Gambling or Sleep in seconds.
Every topic starts with people, not verses. Short notes describe what callers face, such as a family losing its housing while someone is in prison, or an older adult who feels no one listens anymore.
Verses are grouped under plain statements. Each group opens with a line you could say out loud, such as God is always with you, followed by the Scripture printed in full.
It is practical about limits. Volunteers are told to report suspected abuse, to know when to refer, and to leave medication decisions between a person and their doctor.
It answers the questions seekers ask. Part 2 covers Who Is Jesus?, How Do I Get Saved?, Aren't All Religions the Same? and more, and an appendix shows how to start a prayer ministry.

sections.h2: For prayer-ministry and prayer-team volunteers
paras: The book was written for people who pray with strangers. It reminds you that your job is to pray, not to run a counseling session, and it gives you verses to share so the caller can experience the word of God through you.

sections.h2: For pastors and church leaders
paras: The appendix explains how one church's prayer ministry grew from street teams into a phone room open about twelve hours a day. It lists what makes a good prayer minister: trustworthy, a listener and truthful. It adds a set of do's and don'ts you can use to train a team.

sections.h2: For anyone people call in a crisis
paras: You do not need a title to use it. If friends and family come to you when a marriage breaks, a loved one dies or the money runs out, the topic pages give you something true and kind to say, and a reminder to listen first.

sections.h2: For seekers and new believers
paras: Part 2 speaks to people who are still asking. It explains who Jesus is, why He matters, what faith is and what the Holy Spirit does. It includes a short prayer for anyone who wants to join God's family, and advice on finding a trustworthy pastor and church.

details.Author: Nora Fozard

stories.h2: The call to the prayer line
paras: The introduction describes the people who call Nora's church for prayer. They feel their needs are beyond what they can handle. Many believe in prayer because a grandmother prayed for them, but they feel they cannot reach God themselves. They say:
"You can get a prayer through. I can’t. I don’t know Him."
The volunteers answer that God is a solution to the problem, and that the caller had enough of God in them to call for prayer.

stories.h2: From street teams to a phone room
paras: The appendix tells how the church's prayer ministry grew. It began with street teams asking neighbors if they needed prayer. Over many years it became a telephone room. Before COVID it had eight phones with partitions between them, and volunteers working three-hour shifts from 8 a.m. until 8 or 9 at night. After hours, a message gave callers an emergency number. Nora adds that it helps to have both men and women on the phones, because some callers only want to talk to one or the other.
"It doesn’t matter how large or small your prayer ministry is."

In the Healing and Illness topic, Nora uses the ten men with leprosy in Luke 17. Jesus told them to show themselves to the priests, and they were cleansed as they went. Healing is often a process, she writes. You do what the doctor says, and your faith is in God. When someone asks whether to put off medical care to see if God heals them directly, her answer is no:
"Not to seek help that is available is foolishness, and we don’t want to get into foolishness."

author.bio: Nora Fozard serves in her church's prayer ministry, where volunteers answer calls from people who feel their needs are beyond what they can handle. Her husband is a pastor, and he encouraged her to share in this book the truths she has learned. She relies on the Holy Spirit, whom she calls the One Great Counselor. This book follows her first four books with Spirit Media.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: People call a church for prayer when they have nowhere else to go, and the volunteers who answer need to be ready. Nora wrote down what her prayer room has learned so others can do the same. The introduction says:
"In this book, I’ll show you how to pray with people who have dozens of different kinds of needs."
And it says what matters most:
"Keep asking the Holy Spirit to guide you, and you’ll find what you need to give them."

faq.q: What is Scripture References for Effective Counseling about?
faq.a: It is a Christian handbook for praying with people in crisis, written by Nora Fozard from years in her church's prayer ministry. Part 1 gives plain guidance and Bible verses for more than fifty problems, from Abortion to Worldliness. Part 2 answers common questions about God and faith. An appendix shows how to start a prayer ministry.

faq.q: Is it a biblical counseling book?
faq.a: Some of it. It is a guide for prayer counselors, not a professional counseling manual. The introduction says the prayer team tries to avoid becoming a counseling session, because their purpose is to pray. It also tells volunteers to refer people to professional counselors and other help when they need more than one call can give.

faq.q: Is it organized as Scripture by topic?
faq.a: Yes. Part 1 is arranged alphabetically, with topics such as Anger, Comfort, Divorce, Fear, Forgiveness, Loneliness, Peace, Sleep and Temptation. Under each topic the verses are grouped by short statements, such as God is with you, so you can find the right verse quickly.

faq.q: Does it include Bible verses for anxiety?
faq.a: Yes. There is a topic called Anxiety, Worry, Stress, and related topics on Fear, Peace and Thoughts. Each gives verses printed in full, with notes on listening to the person first.

faq.q: Does it help with grief?
faq.a: Yes. There are topics on Death - Grief and Grief - Loss. The book says grief is not only about death. We also grieve a child's poor choice, a lost job or the future we hoped for. It offers verses on God's plan, His presence and His strength.

faq.q: What does it say about depression and mental illness?
faq.a: It says it is not the prayer counselor's job to give a diagnosis, and that you can pray with and support people while they wait for a diagnosis or treatment. For mental illness it says to keep listening without fear, ask if the person has sought professional help, and never tell someone to stop taking medication.

faq.q: How do you start a prayer ministry, according to the book?
faq.a: The appendix, How to Develop a Prayer Ministry in Your Church, says the shape depends on who is helping and what resources you have. It tells how one church's ministry grew from street teams to a phone room, names three marks of a good prayer minister (trustworthy, a listener and truthful), and lists do's and don'ts, such as don't try to be the preacher.

faq.q: Does the book explain how to be saved?
faq.a: Yes. Part 2 has a section called How Do I Get Saved? It explains that everyone falls short and that the way into God's family is through Jesus. It gives a short prayer to use, and suggests finding a good church as the next step.

faq.q: What does it say about praying for the sick?
faq.a: The Healing and Illness topic teaches that healing is God's will and gives four steps: pray, seek medical help, keep the faith, believe God. It says plainly that a person should not put off medical care to see if God heals them directly. This is the author's faith teaching, not medical advice.

hero.audience_line: For Urdu readers in Pakistan, India and around the world who want to rest in God instead of working for Him, and for pastors, leaders and churches serving Urdu-speaking believers.
hero.tagline: The Urdu edition of Only God Works, printed as صرف خدا کام کرتا ہے. A minister of nearly forty years shows from Scripture that God calls you to Himself, and to rest while He works through you.

audience.headline: Only God Works in Urdu: the same ten short chapters, from Called to Finished, for readers who think and pray in Urdu.
audience.body: This is the Urdu translation of Only God Works by Kevin White. Its message is the one he says set him free after ten years as a workaholic for God: God has called you to Himself, not to do His work for Him. The book walks through ten words, with Scripture throughout, and shows how rest leads to more fruit, not less. The whole book, including the Scripture passages, is printed in Urdu, read from right to left. A note on subjects: the author is frank about burnout, illness from overwork and being voted out as a pastor, and one chapter uses the intimacy of a bride and groom as a picture of closeness with God. It is written for adults.

quote.text: صرف خدا کام کرتا ہے!
quote.cite: Only God Works (Urdu edition), Introduction

what_makes.title: What makes this edition for Urdu readers
paras: The Urdu edition keeps the book's opening scene. It asks you to imagine the day after you die, in a heaven where nothing was made by human hands, and where people from many nations thank you because God worked through your giving, your mission trips and your prayers. Then it asks who is really doing the work.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is the whole book in Urdu, with the same ten chapters, the conclusion and the author's personal letter.
Its chapter titles still read as one sentence. In Urdu they begin کہا جاتا ہے (Called), صرف (Only), خدا (God) and کام (Work).
It names a half-truth. God has called you, the author writes, and the enemy adds two words: to work.
It comes from a hard story. The author tells of overwork, being dismissed by his church, and a trip to India in 1998 that changed how he lived.
It looks to the finish line. The last chapter is about the 10/40 window and the people who still have little or no access to know about Jesus.

sections.h2: For Urdu-speaking believers who are worn out
paras: Chapter 5, آزادی (Freedom), reads God's promise of rest in Hebrews 4 and Psalm 23 and says that freedom from work means freedom to rest. Resting, the author adds, does not mean being lazy or useless.

sections.h2: For pastors and church leaders
paras: The author writes that many pastors and leaders have left the ministry because of the lie that God called them to work for Him. A pastor or leader who serves in Urdu can hand this edition to the people in their care.

sections.h2: For families and churches who read in more than one language
paras: The Urdu edition follows the English book chapter for chapter, so a family or a small group can read Only God Works side by side in English and in Urdu.

sections.h2: For anyone who wants their life to count in eternity

paras: The introduction asks you to imagine heaven. Nothing there was made by human hands. Your yard and the work on your house are not there. Instead, people you have never met, many from other nations, tell you how God worked through your tithes, offerings, mission trips and prayers to bring them to Jesus.
تصور کریں کہ یہ آپ کے مرنے کے بعد کا دن ہے.

In Chapter 4 the author tells how, in 1998, God took him to India and showed him Christ followers without basic necessities, most without Bibles, who still passionately pursued God's presence. On the plane home he committed to pursue the presence of God every day for the rest of his life. Chapter 9 tells the harder story around it: a church he built while working up to ninety hours a week, a vote that dismissed him, and a stranger who told him he had not been fired but set free.

Chapter 10, Finished, describes the 10/40 window, the region of North Africa, the Middle East and Asia where most people with little or no access to know about Jesus live, including many in India. It reads Matthew 24:14 as God's finish line and Revelation 7 as a picture of every nation worshiping together, and says only God can finish the work.

author.bio: Kevin White experienced God's call into full-time vocational ministry at seventeen and has served in full-time Christian ministry for nearly forty years. After a decade as what he calls a workaholic for God, he found freedom in Christ and started With Love From Jesus Ministries and Global Hope India. He has been to India more than fifty times, taking 1,000 people on mission trips. He is CEO of Spirit Media and the author of Audacious Generosity, Get to the Point and What's Your Word?

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: Only God Works was the first book the author wrote, twenty-five years before it was published, and he says it was written more for himself than for the world. His personal letter at the end calls the message a matter of life or death for billions of people far from God, and says the revelation that only God works saved his life.
The book's own pages say Spirit Media is committed to sharing the Good News of Jesus in all 195 nations of the world. The Urdu edition carries that message to readers in their own language.

faq.q: What is this book?
faq.a: It is the Urdu edition of Only God Works by Kevin White, printed under the title صرف خدا کام کرتا ہے. It teaches that God has never called us to work for Him, but to intimacy with Him, and to let Him work in and through us.

faq.q: What are the chapters?
faq.a: They are, in order: Called; Only; God; Work; Freedom; Intimacy; Humility; Gratitude; Fruit; and Finished. An introduction comes first, and a conclusion and a letter from the author close the book.

faq.q: Does it talk about the signs of the end times?
faq.a: Some of it. Chapter 10 has a section on the last days that reads Acts 2 and the prophet Joel, and says the Bible speaks of wars and natural disasters in the last days. Its point is that God's people should welcome Jesus' return with joy, not fear. It is not a book of prophecy charts.

faq.q: Does it speak to the purpose of life?
faq.a: Yes. The introduction says that when your values shift from your work to God's work, you will have greater meaning and purpose for your life.

faq.q: Does it help readers prepare for the life to come?
faq.a: Yes, that is its subtitle's idea: invest now in what will matter then. It asks what you are working on that will not be found in heaven, and invites you to invest your time, talents and treasures in eternity.

faq.q: What does it say about the power of prayer?
faq.a: It quotes Hudson Taylor: when we work, we work; when we pray, God works. The book says real fruit comes when we let God do the work only He can do.

faq.q: Is it a book about resting in God?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 5, آزادی (Freedom), reads God's promise of rest in Hebrews 4 and says freedom from work means freedom to rest. The author says rest does not mean being useless or lazy.

hero.audience_line: For soldiers and service members, military spouses and families, veterans, and anyone facing a long season of distance from the people they love.
hero.tagline: A U.S. Army NCO's day-by-day journal of his first deployment, to Kuwait and Iraq in 2003 and 2004: the heat, the sandstorms, the long phone lines, and the faith and marriage that carried him home.

audience.headline: On April 13, 2003, a soldier and his wife go to one last church service in Lawton, Oklahoma. The next day he lands in Kuwait.
audience.body: For service members heading out or coming home, for spouses and parents waiting on a phone call, for veterans who remember the camps of Kuwait, and for churches that pray for military families. Ronald Bethune kept a journal through his first deployment in support of Operation Iraqi Freedom, and this book is that journal: short, dated entries from Camp Wolf and Camp Virginia to convoys into Iraq and the flight home a year later. He writes about cleaning weapons two or three times a day, waiting hours for a fifteen-minute call, letters that took three weeks to arrive and temperatures that reached 130°F. He also writes about his Bible, his gospel CDs, Sunday services in a tent and a marriage held together across the distance. Photographs from the deployment run through the book, and each part ends with a prayer. A note on subjects: the journal records several deaths, including a friend at home killed by a drunk driver, an NCO lost in a training accident and a truck driver killed in an accident, and it describes poverty seen in Iraq. It is a personal journal of support duty, not a combat history.

quote.text: “However, my faith served as a rock in the middle of all the chaos, giving me courage when things became hard.”
quote.cite: My First Deployment, the introduction

what_makes.title: What makes this book for military families
paras: The first entry is dated April 13, 2003. A soldier and his wife wake early, eat one last breakfast together and go to church, where the pastor prays over them both. That afternoon he reports for roll call and draws his gear. By the next entry he is at Camp Wolf near Kuwait International Airport, a staging area for troops heading north into Iraq.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is a real journal. Every entry has a date and a title, from First Day on April 13, 2003 to Back Home on April 7, 2004, so you live the year one day at a time.

It is honest about the small things that make up a deployment: chow hall menus, laundry in a five-gallon bucket, a stolen Conex, a lost sleeping cot, a 34-inch satellite TV that brought the tent together.

It is also a marriage story. He calls his wife whenever the lines allow, marks their third anniversary in the desert and counts the days the mail takes: fifteen for his first letter home, thirty-six for a package from his mother, fifty for a gift from his church.
Faith runs through the whole year. He reads his Bible in the dim light of the tent, plays gospel CDs, goes to Sunday services and Joy Night, and points a fellow soldier to Psalm 23.
Each of the three parts ends with a prayer for readers and for service members separated from the people they love, built on Psalm 25, Romans 5 and Proverbs 3.

sections.h2: For military spouses and families
paras: The phone calls are the heartbeat of the book. A fifteen-minute limit, lines that took one to two hours, a wife who drifted to sleep mid-call, a small misunderstanding and tears, and finally seeing her face on the internet for the first time in almost a year. Families at home will see what those calls meant on the other end.

sections.h2: For veterans
paras: Camp Doha, Camp Arifjan, Camp Cedar II, Main Supply Route Tampa, Anaconda and the Ur temple all appear here, along with the heat, the fleas and the rain that flooded the relay points. On Veterans Day 2003 the author writes about the importance of camaraderie among veterans and the people who support them.

sections.h2: For churches that support the military

details.Title: My First Deployment
details.Subtitle: Chronicles of a Military Journey
details.Author: Ronald Bethune

paras: On April 27, 2003, a sandstorm turns to rain overnight, knocks over portable restrooms and flattens a tent. The chow hall built for 6,500 is packed with about 10,000 soldiers. Then a fellow soldier tells the author that he has started reading the Bible every day and found a way to relax:
“He said he learned it from me, that reading the Bible does help.”
The author points him to Psalm 23, and the journal prints the whole psalm.

On May 27, 2003, he comes off an hour of trash-burning duty. It is his third wedding anniversary. He writes that they have had ups and downs, but the good has outweighed the hard, and he wishes they could celebrate in person:
“I’m grateful to the Lord for keeping us together this far.”
Dinner takes fifteen minutes, and outside the sand is still blowing.

On April 4, 2004, he learns he is on Chalk #1, the first group to fly back to the United States. Three days later he arrives at his duty station, where his wife is waiting. He writes that all the struggles faded the moment he saw her, and he gives the credit for the year to one source:
“But the Lord was the one in control.”

author.bio: Ronald Bethune served as a noncommissioned officer in the U.S. Army and deployed to Kuwait and Iraq in 2003 and 2004 during Operation Iraqi Freedom, his first deployment. Before he left, he and his wife attended a service at Zoe Christian Center in Lawton, Oklahoma. During the deployment he relied on Bible reading and gospel music, and he encouraged fellow soldiers to find strength in Scripture. He credits God as the source of his strength, grace and wisdom, and his parents with planting the seed of knowledge in his mind. He is a husband and a father of two.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author says the year was harder than he imagined, and that he is not sure how he and his wife would have made it without faith and determination. He shares his journal so that others can see the ups and downs, in the desert and in his own heart:
“I share this to inspire rather than to boast.”
His hope is that readers facing conflict or distance will find a reminder that they can keep going, and that the prayers at the end of each part will draw them closer to God.

faq.q: What is My First Deployment about?
faq.a: It is the journal Ronald Bethune kept during his first deployment as a U.S. Army NCO, from April 2003 to April 2004, in support of Operation Iraqi Freedom. Short dated entries follow his year in Kuwait and Iraq, his marriage across the distance and the faith that kept him steady.

faq.q: Is it a memoir of an Iraq War soldier?
faq.a: Yes, but most of the year is spent in Kuwait, at Camp Wolf, Camp Virginia, Camp Doha and Camp Arifjan, with convoys and duty in Iraq later on. It describes support work, guard duty and the hazards of the road. It is a personal journal, not a combat history.

faq.q: Does the book include prayers for soldiers?
faq.a: Yes. Each part ends with a prayer. The first, built on Psalm 25, prays for service members separated from loved ones. The second rejoices in Romans 5 that trials produce endurance and hope. The third, built on Proverbs 3:5-6, asks God to protect the author, his comrades and his family.

faq.q: What does it show about a long distance marriage during deployment?
faq.a: A great deal. The author calls his wife whenever he can, writes letters, marks their anniversary and her birthday from Kuwait and records the hard moments too, including a misunderstanding with tears. In one email his wife writes that the Holy Spirit has preserved their marriage through the separation.

faq.q: Which Psalms are in the book?
faq.a: Psalm 23 and Psalm 91 are printed in full from the New Living Translation. The author suggests Psalm 23 to a fellow soldier and reflects on Psalm 91 on a hot day in June. Psalm 25 opens the first prayer.

faq.q: Is it a book for veterans and military families?
faq.a: Yes. Veterans will recognize the camps, the heat and the routine, and families will see the year from the soldier's side. The journal includes an entry for Veterans Day 2003, where the author writes about camaraderie among veterans and the support of the people around them.

faq.q: Does the author share his faith with other soldiers?
faq.a: Yes, simply and in daily life. A soldier tells him that reading the Bible every day helped him relax and that he learned it from the author. He takes another soldier to church, talks about Jesus with his NCOIC and prays for a supervisor who did not share his beliefs.

what_makes.title: What makes this edition for Russian readers
paras: The Russian edition keeps the book's opening scene. It asks you to imagine the day after you die, in a heaven where nothing was made by human hands, and where people from many nations thank you because God worked through your giving, your mission trips and your prayers. Then it asks who is really doing the work.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is the whole book in Russian, with the same ten chapters, the conclusion and the author's personal letter.
Its chapter titles still read as one sentence. In Russian they begin Призванный (Called), Лишь (Only), Бог (God) and Работа (Work).
It names a half-truth. God has called you, the author writes, and the enemy adds two words: to work.
It comes from a hard story. The author tells of overwork, being dismissed by his church, and a trip to India in 1998 that changed how he lived.
It looks to the finish line. The last chapter is about the 10/40 window and the people who still have little or no access to know about Jesus.

paras: Chapter 5, Свобода (Freedom), reads God's promise of rest in Hebrews 4 and Psalm 23 and says that freedom from work means freedom to rest. Resting, the author adds, does not mean being lazy or useless.

paras: The introduction asks you to imagine heaven. Nothing there was made by human hands. Your yard and the work on your house are not there. Instead, people you have never met, many from other nations, tell you how God worked through your tithes, offerings, mission trips and prayers to bring them to Jesus.
Представьте, что настал день после вашей смерти.

In Chapter 4 the author tells how, in 1998, God took him to India and showed him Christ followers without basic necessities, most without Bibles, who still passionately pursued God's presence. On the plane home he committed to pursue the presence of God every day for the rest of his life. Chapter 9 tells the harder story around it: a church he built while working up to ninety hours a week, a vote that dismissed him, and a stranger who told him he had not been fired but set free.

Chapter 10, Finished, describes the 10/40 window, the region of North Africa, the Middle East and Asia where most people with little or no access to know about Jesus live, including many in India. It reads Matthew 24:14 as God's finish line and Revelation 7 as a picture of every nation worshiping together, and says only God can finish the work.

author.bio: Kevin White experienced God's call into full-time vocational ministry at seventeen and has served in full-time Christian ministry for nearly forty years. After a decade as what he calls a workaholic for God, he found freedom in Christ and started With Love From Jesus Ministries and Global Hope India. He has been to India more than fifty times, taking 1,000 people on mission trips. He is CEO of Spirit Media and the author of Audacious Generosity, Get to the Point and What's Your Word?

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: Only God Works was the first book the author wrote, twenty-five years before it was published, and he says it was written more for himself than for the world. His personal letter at the end calls the message a matter of life or death for billions of people far from God, and says the revelation that only God works saved his life.

faq.q: What is this book?
faq.a: It is the Russian edition of Only God Works by Kevin White, translated by K. Denisenko and printed under the title Лишь Бог работает. It teaches that God has never called us to work for Him, but to intimacy with Him, and to let Him work in and through us.

faq.q: What are the chapters?
faq.a: They are, in order: Призванный (Called); Лишь (Only); Бог (God); Работа (Work); Свобода (Freedom); Близость (Intimacy); Смирение (Humility); Благодарность (Gratitude); Плоды (Fruit); and Завершение (Finished). An introduction comes first, and a conclusion and a personal letter from the author close the book.

faq.q: Does it talk about the last days?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 10 has a section on the last days that reads Peter's sermon in Acts 2 from the prophet Joel, and says God's people should welcome Jesus' return with joy, not fear.

faq.q: What does it say about eternal life?
faq.a: It quotes John 3:16 and says salvation and eternal life are God's work, not ours: God gave His Son, and we did nothing to earn it. The author then asks why we think God needs our work for everything else.

faq.q: Does it teach gratitude to God?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 8, Благодарность (Gratitude), says gratitude is the key to humility, and that we can give thanks for what God has promised before we see it.

faq.q: Is it a book about resting in God?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 5, Свобода (Freedom), reads God's promise of rest in Hebrews 4 and says freedom from work means freedom to rest. The author says rest does not mean being useless or lazy.

faq.q: Does it teach intimacy with God?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 6, Близость (Intimacy), is about closeness with God, and the book names intimacy, humility and gratitude as the three things God gives us to focus on.

faq.q: What is this book?
faq.a: It is the Spanish edition of Only God Works by Kevin White, printed under the title Sólo Dios trabaja. It teaches that God has never called us to work for Him, but to intimacy with Him, and to let Him work in and through us.

faq.q: What are the chapters?

faq.q: What does it say about the Holy Spirit?

faq.q: Does it speak to the meaning of life?

faq.q: Is it for people facing emotional exhaustion?

faq.q: Is it a book about spiritual growth?

hero.audience_line: For Christians who want to share their faith, believers with a testimony to tell, and anyone who loves true stories of healing and answered prayer.
hero.tagline: A Sri Lankan pastor tells how four healings in his family broke open a hard heart, how God protected his family when their home was burned in the 1983 riots, and why every believer is called to share what God has done.

audience.headline: A pastor who once kept four miracles to himself writes so that you will not keep yours.
audience.body: For Christians who want to share their faith but feel shy about it, new believers, small groups and evangelism teams, and readers who love true stories of healing and protection. Pastor Alfred Cherubim was a churchgoer by tradition and a YMCA leader in Sri Lanka when his wife, in a coma for nearly six months, woke within minutes of an evangelist's prayer. Three more healings followed in his family before he and his wife accepted Jesus at midnight on Christmas Eve 1980. The first part of the book is that story; the rest teaches why, what, how and when to share your faith. A note on content: the testimony describes the 1983 ethnic riots in Sri Lanka, including a mob attack and the burning of the family's home, told without graphic detail. It is one family's testimony and a Bible teaching book, not medical advice.

quote.text: Once we personally meet the Savior, we’re never again the same. We cannot keep it quiet.
quote.cite: Sharing Your Faith and Testimony, Introduction

what_makes.title: What makes this book for believers who want to share their faith
paras: The book opens with a confession. After his wife was healed, the author writes, "I was thrilled by the healing but had no curiosity about the Healer." He compares himself to the nine lepers who never came back to give thanks. The rest of the book is about not making that mistake.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is a true story first. Part 2 begins with the author's testimony: a wife in a coma, his own heart attack, a five-year-old daughter covered in eczema sores and a fifteen-year-old daughter bedridden with rheumatic paralysis, each healed after prayer.

It tells of protection in the 1983 riots: thirteen people hiding in a latched washroom while a mob beat on the door with an iron bar, a wall that fell when the author struck it with his Bible, and a new bamboo ladder no one could explain.
It follows a ministry across continents: a refugee camp, YMCA posts in India, a children's home for fifty-three boys in Trincomalee, preaching trips abroad and a church in Brampton, Canada.
It teaches the why, what, how and when of sharing your faith, with seven reasons from Scripture, rules for sharing and a walk through the heroes of faith in Hebrews 11.
It ends with a prayer to accept your calling and a short hymn whose watchword is EVANGELIZE.

sections.h2: For Christians who feel shy about witnessing
paras: The author knows the feeling. At the healing meeting he sat in the back rows so his church friends would not see him, and when the healed were invited to testify, he walked out and went home. The book's answer is simple: "Evangelism is not a matter of knowing all the answers, nor does it require that we have a sophisticated theological argument."

sections.h2: For anyone with a testimony to tell
paras: The book gives a starting point: "Tell your story. Let others know what your life was like before you found Christ, and the peace and joy you now experience, knowing your sins are forgiven." It calls sharing your relationship with Jesus, with sincerity and conviction, a powerful way to witness.

sections.h2: For evangelism teams, pastors and small groups
paras: The teaching sections are built for study. They give seven reasons to share your faith, from "Because God has commanded us to do so" to "Because Jesus is coming soon," then cover what is to be shared, how to share it, the rules for sharing and when to share. Each point is set beside the Scripture it comes from.

sections.h2: For believers facing hard seasons
paras: The first sermon the author ever preached was on Job, on Sunday, July 24, 1983. The next day the riots began, and by Tuesday his family was in a refugee camp with only their Bibles. There he knelt with his wife and children and quoted the verse he had just preached: "The Lord gave and the Lord has taken away; may the name of the Lord be praised."

paras: At a healing crusade in a school hall, the evangelist described the author's heart attack and even the clothes he was wearing. He stayed in his seat but prayed in his heart, and as the evangelist prayed for the sick, he writes:
"At that moment, I felt an electric shock pass through my entire body, a heaviness lift from my chest, and an overwhelming sense of joy and happiness that I had never experienced before in my life."
When the healed were invited to the stage to testify, he walked out and went home. He writes that he was like one of the nine lepers who received healing and never came back to give thanks.

stories.h2: The washroom door and the wall
paras: On July 25, 1983, the day after his first sermon, riots swept Sri Lanka. Thirteen people, children among them, hid and prayed in a washroom while a mob ransacked the house for nearly two hours and tried to smash the latched door with an iron bar. The door held.

When the house was set on fire, the family was trapped in the courtyard against an eleven-foot wall. The author struck it with the Bible in his hand, declaring, "In the Name of Jesus, I break this wall." He writes that the wall fell to the other side, just above hip level, and they crossed to a neighbor's land.

Before dawn the family needed to climb back over the broken wall to hide on their own land. They found a brand new bamboo ladder by the wall, exactly the right height, that their neighbor did not own.

In the refugee camp the author knelt with his wife and children and made a promise: he would share their testimonies "with tears for His glory wherever I had the opportunity." He began witnessing in the camp itself.

author.bio: Pastor S. Alfred Cherubim was born in Jaffna, Sri Lanka. He worked for the Department of Agriculture and then held national posts in the YMCA in Sri Lanka and India, and he entered full-time ministry in 1990. In Trincomalee he founded a children's home for boys who had lost their parents in the riots, and between 1996 and 2001 he preached in churches in Europe, North America, India and Australia. Today he is the pastor of Redeemer Christ Assembly in Brampton, Canada, which also runs a TV ministry, a newspaper ministry and booklet publishing.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: In a refugee camp in 1983, with only their Bibles left, the author promised God he would share his family's testimonies wherever he had the opportunity. This book keeps that promise. The dedication gives the reason in one line: it is "dedicated to glorify God, for His grace and mercies provided for me to serve Him these 40 long years."
He writes that he hopes the book will
"encourage and strengthen you to become a tool in God’s hands, bringing glory to His Holy name through your life."

faq.q: What is Sharing Your Faith and Testimony about?
faq.a: It is Pastor Alfred Cherubim's testimony of four healings in his family, his family's escape in the 1983 Sri Lanka riots and the ministry that followed, joined to Bible teaching on why, what, how and when to share your faith. The introduction says a testimony is "not just storytelling; it’s a powerful act."

faq.q: How do you share your testimony?
faq.a: The book says to tell your story: what your life was like before you found Christ, and the peace and joy you have now, knowing your sins are forgiven. It asks you to share with sincerity and conviction, to depend on the Holy Spirit, and to give the glory to God, not to yourself.

faq.q: Why should Christians share their faith?
faq.a: The book gives seven reasons. They are, in order: because God has commanded us to do so; because it demonstrates our love for God; because all are lost; because our sharing is God's chosen method to convey His message to all people; because God desires to save all people; because someone once shared his faith with us; and because Jesus is coming soon.

faq.q: What does it say about evangelism and the Great Commission?
faq.a: Part 4 says evangelism is the duty of all Christians and that the Great Commission in Matthew 28:19 is for everyone who follows Jesus. It gives four reasons to share. They are, in order: Christ commands us to do this; the world urgently needs the gospel; the fields are already ripe for harvest; and our own spiritual health.

faq.q: Is the author Sri Lankan?
faq.a: Yes. He was born in Jaffna, Sri Lanka, and served with the YMCA there. His family lost their home in the ethnic riots that began on July 25, 1983. He later served in India and Sri Lanka and now lives in Canada, where he pastors Redeemer Christ Assembly in Brampton.

faq.q: Does the book include miracles of healing?
faq.a: Yes. The author tells of his wife waking from a coma of nearly six months, his own healing after a heart attack, his younger daughter healed of severe eczema within ten days of prayer, and his elder daughter rising from rheumatic paralysis on Christmas Eve. He tells them as testimony, not as medical advice.

faq.q: What is faith, according to the book?
faq.a: It defines faith as "confidence that someone or something is reliable," then walks through the heroes of faith in Hebrews 11. It adds short teaching on justification, purification and sanctification by faith.

faq.q: Is the author a born-again Christian?
faq.a: Yes. He writes that he was a Christian by tradition whose understanding of God was distant, not personal, until December 24, 1980, when he and his wife accepted Jesus as their personal Savior. Three years later, as a born-again Christian, he preached his first sermon.

chips: Mary and John Go to School

audience.headline: Mary prays that the mean boy in her class will break his leg. Daddy has a different idea: an experiment in praying for him.
audience.body: For parents and grandparents who read aloud with children, and for Sunday school and preschool teachers who want Bible lessons tied to everyday life. In the first book of The Blessing Trail, Mary and John learn to pray for a boy who bullies, get lost in the woods following a hurt rabbit, give away their birthday presents after a neighbor's house burns, see what lying does to a friendship and face the dark on a camping trip. In every story Mama and Daddy talk it over and read from the Bible. A note on subjects: one story includes a house fire, with the family safe, and another a lost-in-the-woods scare and a near snake bite. All end well.

quote.text: “God can make good things come out of bad situations.”
quote.cite: The Blessing Trail, The Fire

what_makes.title: What makes this book for families who want faith to feel real to children
paras: Each story begins with something a child could face this week: a first day in a new class, a scary moment outside, a friend who does not tell the truth. Then the family talks and opens the Bible.
Five things set it apart:
list: The children's feelings are honest. Mary is scared to go to class alone, angry enough to pray that a boy breaks his leg, and afraid of the dark at the campsite.
The parents show how to talk about it. Daddy turns praying for a bully into an experiment, and Mama tells Mary how she was afraid of the dark as a child and what helped her.
Scripture is read in the moment. 1 Peter 3:9, Matthew 5:43-45, Acts 20:35, Luke 6:38, Hebrews 13:16, Mark 5:36 and 1 John 4:18 are among the verses the family reads.

The children's choices matter. Mary hands the boy an eraser and picks him for her kickball team. After the fire, Mary and John offer their birthday gifts to the neighbors, and the whole town joins in.
Prayer is part of every story. The children pray when they are lost in the woods, the family prays the fire will be put out, and Mary repeats a memory verse in her tent until she feels safe.

sections.h2: For parents who want bedtime Bible stories
paras: Each story is short enough for one sitting, and most end at bedtime, with the children in bed thinking over what Mama and Daddy said.

details.Title: The Blessing Trail
details.Subtitle: Stories to Warm the Heart
details.Author: Wendy Reardon

paras: A boy in Mary's class pinches her new friend and kicks another child on the playground. At supper, Mary prays that he will break his leg. Daddy reads 1 Peter 3:9 and Matthew 5:43-45, and the family agrees to pray for the boy every night until his heart changes. Mary hands him an eraser and picks him for her kickball team. One day she tells him she is praying for him, and he begins to cry. The next day, he smiles at her.

Watching the sunset, John and Mary spot a limping white rabbit and follow it deep into the woods. They find her three babies under a woodpile, and then realize they are lost in the dark. They pray, and soon see a light coming down the path: their parents. That night Daddy asks what God would have wanted them to do differently, and Mary says they forgot to tell anyone where they were going.

A neighbor's house burns, and the family gets out with nothing. Mary's birthday is twelve days away, and she has an idea: give their birthday gifts to the neighbors. John thinks about it and says, "I will if you will." Relatives tell neighbors, neighbors tell their neighbors, and on Mary's birthday the park fills with people. The family goes home with gifts and more than $10,000. Daddy reads Acts 20:35:
"It is more blessed to give than to receive."

author.bio: Wendy Reardon writes The Blessing Trail books, read-aloud stories about two children, Mary and John, and their Mama and Daddy; this is the first. The book prints no biography of her. The second book's opening note says she shares the stories she has told her children and now her grandchildren.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The stories answer the questions children ask when life surprises them. After the fire, Mama sums up what the whole book is teaching:
"God can make good things come out of bad situations."
And in the last story, Mary learns to hold onto a verse in the dark:
"Don’t be afraid, just believe."

faq.q: What is The Blessing Trail?
faq.a: It is a 73-page full-color book of five Bible-based stories for children about Mary, John and their parents, each with verses and a family talk. They are, in order: Mary and John Go to School; Rabbit in the Woods; The Fire; Mary and John Learn About Lies; and The Camping Trip.

faq.q: Is it a book of bedtime Bible stories?
faq.a: It works well at bedtime. Each story is short enough for one evening, and most end with the children in bed, thinking over what Mama and Daddy said.

faq.q: Does it teach children to love their enemies?
faq.a: Yes. In Mary and John Go to School, Daddy reads Matthew 5:43-45, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, and the family prays every night for a boy who has been hurting other children. Mary shows him small kindnesses until he changes.

faq.q: Does it teach honesty?
faq.a: Yes. In Mary and John Learn About Lies, a boy keeps lying, then yells "Snake!" and no one believes him. Daddy explains why people lie and what consequences are, and Mama says God always forgives if you are really sorry.

faq.q: Does it teach kindness and generosity?
faq.a: Yes. In The Fire, Mary and John give their birthday gifts to a neighbor family who lost everything, their parents give money too, and the whole community joins in. Daddy reads Acts 20:35, Luke 6:38 and Hebrews 13:16 about giving.

faq.q: Does it help children who are afraid of the dark?
faq.a: Yes. On The Camping Trip, Mary is scared when the fire goes out. Mama tells how she was afraid of the dark as a child and how trusting Jesus helped, and Daddy gives Mary two verses to memorize: Mark 5:36 and 1 John 4:18, perfect love drives out fear.

faq.q: Does it teach obedience to parents?
faq.a: Yes. After Rabbit in the Woods, Daddy tells the children that one of the Ten Commandments says to obey your father and your mother, and that obedience is a sign of honor and respect.

faq.q: Can we use it as a family devotional?
faq.a: Yes. Each story ends with the family talking it over, reading verses together and praying, and a parent can follow the same pattern at home.

faq.q: Do I need to read the books in order?
faq.a: No. Each story stands alone. This is Book 1; The Blessing Trail 2 and The Blessing Trail 3 tell new stories about the same family.

content_note.title: Content note
paras: One story includes a neighbor's house fire, with everyone safe, and another a scare when the children get lost in the woods. A boy is nearly bitten by a snake. All end well.

hero.tagline: One snowy night in an Iraqi guard tower, a woman humming The Twelve Days of Christmas decided to find out where the song came from. This big, funny book is what she found: one section for each day, with history, a Biblical interpretation, another culture's winter celebration, stories, recipes and puzzles.

audience.headline: A guard at Camp Bucca in Iraq started researching a Christmas song on the night it snowed in southern Iraq for the first time in sixty years.
audience.body: For families who want to celebrate all twelve days of Christmas, home cooks and holiday bakers, readers curious about the history of the song and the winter celebrations of other cultures, homeschool families, and anyone who loves puzzles and holiday crafts. Tammy Haurilick spent a year as a guard in Iraq, working the zero-to-four watch in a tower over a detainee yard. On a cold February night, with snow in her gloved hand, she started humming The Twelve Days of Christmas, and after her shift she began to research it. That research grew into a 342-page book that walks through the twelve days from Christmas Day to the Eve of Epiphany. Each day has the history of the gift and the feast days that fall on it, a Biblical interpretation, a winter celebration from another culture, stories from friends, family and soldiers, recipes, a puzzle, and cross stitch and red work designs. A note on the book: the tone is informal and joking, with some salty language. The foreword gives the author's own view that Christmas customs grew out of older winter festivals, and some readers will disagree with parts of her history. She says plainly that she is not trying to make a definitive statement, and she invites readers to agree or disagree. The book also describes celebrations of other faiths, such as Diwali, Ramadan and Eid, and Hanukkah, as cultural history.

quote.text: “The world is so much smaller than we can possibly imagine and yet at the same time so wonderfully immense and diverse.”
quote.cite: 12 Days of Crazy, Foreword

what_makes.title: What makes this book for families who want a fuller Christmas season
paras: Most holiday books give you one day. This one gives you twelve, and it is built to be used, not only read. Day 1 is A Partridge in a Pear Tree and Day 12 is Twelve Drummers Drumming, so you can read, cook and make along with the season.
Five things set it apart:
list: Each gift gets a Biblical interpretation. The partridge in a pear tree stands for Jesus Christ, the four colly birds for the four Gospels and the ten lords a-leaping for the Ten Commandments.
Each day visits another culture. The winter celebrations run from Dong Zhi in China and Shab-e Yalda in Iran to Saint Lucia Day, Hanukkah and Three Kings Day.
Each day has Remembrances: favorite holiday memories the author collected from family, friends and the Coalition Forces at Camp Bucca.
It is a cookbook too. Each day has recipes, traditional and from other countries, from Irish Boxty and Banoffee Pie to Groundnut Stew, Latkes and Wassail.
It is full of things to do: twelve puzzles with answers at the back, cross stitch designs, coloring and red work pages, and instructions for making your own Twelve Days of Christmas blocks.

sections.h2: For families who want to make the twelve days a season
paras: The book explains that the twelve days begin on Christmas Day and end on the Eve of Epiphany, January 5. If your family's Christmas is over by noon on the 25th, this gives you something to read, cook and make every day after, all the way to Three Kings Day.

sections.h2: For home cooks and holiday bakers
paras: Every day ends in the kitchen. The recipes are written in the same chatty voice as the rest of the book, with family favorites, simplified versions of traditional dishes and food from other countries' winter celebrations. The author's hope is simple: try a few and make them part of your own family traditions.

sections.h2: For readers curious about winter celebrations around the world
paras: Her year in Iraq changed how she saw the world, and she wanted the book to be as multicultural as she could make it. Each day spends a section on another culture's winter celebration, and she says she interviewed more than two hundred people, including religious leaders, along the way.

sections.h2: For homeschool families and anyone who loves puzzles and crafts

Short sidebars called Word Knerd explain where words and phrases come from.

details.Title: 12 Days of Crazy
details.Subtitle: Holiday Stories and Kitchen Adventures
details.Author: Tammy Haurilick

paras: It is two in the morning in February, in the rainy season, and so cold that for thirty minutes it snows in southern Iraq for the first time in sixty years. The author is in her tower at Camp Bucca, staring at the snow on her glove and keeping an eye on the empty yard below. She starts humming The Twelve Days of Christmas, and the song will not leave her head:
“I want to learn more about this song and where it came from.”
After her shift, she went to the computer lab and started looking. This book is where that search led.

The American guards ate cold, greasy food trucked in from the chow hall. The Iraqi guards they worked with ate boiled eggs wrapped in buttered flatbread and drank hot sweet chai. Before long, the Iraqi guards invited them to come sit on their porch and share it.
“Better food, interesting people, tentative friendships and some really, really cool stories all came together those cool mornings”
Those breakfasts made her want to know whether her new friends had a winter celebration too, and that question is why every day of the book visits another culture.

The first Remembrance comes from her father. In rural Vermont in 1959, his dad sent him into the woods to cut the family tree. After hours of finding nothing, he spotted a perfect blue spruce, climbed forty feet with a hand saw and took off the top seven feet. His father took one look and knew. Money was tight, so the tree stayed, and he ends the story this way:
“I am pretty sure that’s the best Christmas Tree we ever had.”

author.bio: Tammy Haurilick spent a year in Iraq as a guard inside the wire at Camp Bucca, a Theatre Internment Facility, where she worked the zero-to-four watch in a tower over the detainee yard. She calls that year both the worst of her life and the greatest blessing God ever gave her. It was there, on the night snow fell in southern Iraq for the first time in sixty years, that she began researching The Twelve Days of Christmas. Her friendships with the Iraqi guards shaped the book's multicultural approach, and she says her research drew on more than two hundred interviews. She describes herself as a first-generation immigrant, born to a Scottish mother and a Russian father, and says she grew up in several European countries thanks to her Army father.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author says she wrote it to tell the story of the song and to bring back old winter traditions:
“Which is why I really wanted to write this book, to put the history out there about the song”
Underneath the history is a simple belief about why people celebrate at all:
“People will find a way and a reason to get together to eat, talk, and just be with one another for human companionship.”
Her recipe pages put it in one line:
“I hope that you will try a few of these recipes and perhaps incorporate them into your family traditions.”

faq.q: What is 12 Days of Crazy about?
faq.a: It is a book about the twelve days of Christmas by Tammy Haurilick. For each day it gives the history of the gift in the song and the feast days that fall on it, a Biblical interpretation, a winter celebration from another culture, holiday memories, recipes and a puzzle. It began as research she started while serving as a guard in Iraq.

faq.q: What do the gifts in The Twelve Days of Christmas mean?
faq.a: The book gives a Biblical interpretation for each gift. They are, in order: Jesus Christ; the Old and New Testaments; Faith, Hope and Charity; the four Gospels; the first five books of the Bible; the six days of Creation; the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit; the Eight Beatitudes; the nine Fruits of the Holy Spirit; the Ten Commandments; the eleven faithful disciples; and the twelve points of belief in the Apostles Creed.

faq.q: When do the twelve days of Christmas start and end?
faq.a: The book says they begin on Christmas Day and end on the Eve of Epiphany, January 5, with the Feast of Epiphany on January 6. Day 1 is December 26, also known as Boxing Day, St. Stephen's Day and Wren's Day.

faq.q: Where did the song come from?
faq.a: The book says historians are divided. Some say it is English, from the early 1500s, and others say it is French. What is certain, it says, is that it first appeared in print in 1780 in a book called Mirth Without Mischief. The author adds that most of her sources disprove the idea that it was a hidden way to teach the catechism.

faq.q: Which winter celebrations from other cultures are in the book?
faq.a: They are, in order: Santa Claus in the United States and Christmas in Australia; Dong Zhi in China; Shab-e Yalda in Iran; Saturnalia in Rome; Diwali; Native American solstice rites; Kwanzaa; Saint Lucia Day; Ramadan and Eid ul Fitr; Hanukkah; Twelfth Night; and Three Kings Day.

faq.q: Does it include Christmas recipes?
faq.a: Yes. Every day has a recipes section, with traditional holiday dishes and food from other countries. Examples include Boxty, Shepherd's Pie, Banoffee Pie, Tong Yuan, Chicken and Dumplings, Bread Pudding, Groundnut Stew, cream puffs, Shortbread, Lefse, Latkes, Wassail, Eggnog and Churritos.

faq.q: Is it a Christian book?
faq.a: It is published by a Christian publisher, every day includes a Biblical interpretation of the gift, and the author calls her year in Iraq a blessing from God. It is also a history book with a light, joking tone. The foreword argues that Christmas customs grew out of older winter festivals, and it describes the holidays of other faiths as cultural history. The author says she is not making a final statement on the religions involved.

faq.q: Does it have activities for kids and families?
faq.a: Yes. There are twelve puzzles with answers at the back, cross stitch designs, coloring and red work pages, and instructions for making paper or cloth Twelve Days of Christmas blocks. Many recipes are simple enough to make together.

audience.headline: Every miracle of Jesus in the four Gospels, in order, with the passages printed in full.
audience.body: For Bible readers and teachers who want the miracles gathered in one place, small groups working through the Gospels and Acts, and believers who want to trust God more. Pastor Alfred Cherubim lists the thirty-seven miracles the Gospels record, sets out the passages for each one, then turns to the miracles of the apostles, from Peter walking on water to Paul on Malta. The book is mostly Scripture, quoted from the NIV, ESV, NLT and NET, with the author's teaching at the start and the end. A note on content: the closing teaching speaks plainly about judgment and says that denying God's miracles is denying God himself. It is a Bible reference and devotional book, not a scholarly commentary.

quote.text: None were performed randomly, for amusement, or for show.
quote.cite: The Miracles of Jesus Christ and His Apostles, opening teaching: Divine Miracles with a Divine Purpose

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers who want to see Jesus' miracles together
paras: The book begins with Jesus reading from the scroll of Isaiah in Nazareth, and then makes a simple case. The miracles were written down by eyewitnesses, and each one "was accompanied by a message and either met a serious human need or confirmed Christ’s identity and authority as the Son of God."
Five things set it apart:
list: It gathers all thirty-seven miracles. The book notes that the four Gospels record thirty-seven miracles of Jesus, with Mark's Gospel recording the highest number.
It keeps them in order. A chart lists every miracle with its references in Matthew, Mark, Luke and John, as far as possible in chronological order.
It prints the Scripture. Each miracle has its own numbered pages with the passage quoted in full, often from more than one Gospel and more than one translation.
It continues into Acts. A second part lists nineteen miracles of the apostles, from Peter walking on water to Paul healing the sick on Malta, with the passages for each.
It explains the three New Testament words for miracles, power (dynamis), sign (sēmeion) and wonder (teras), and ends with the reasons for the apostles' miracles and a short miracle prayer.

sections.h2: For Bible study groups and teachers
paras: The chart and the numbered pages make the book easy to use in a group. A meeting can take one miracle, read every Gospel account of it side by side, and talk about what it shows about Jesus. The author calls these Bible lessons on "the principles, purposes, and great powers of God Almighty."

sections.h2: For readers who want their faith strengthened
paras: The author asks a direct question: after a thorough study of the miracles, will you trust in God like never before? He adds, "isn’t it easy to believe in miracles if the Lord already created the universe by His word?"

sections.h2: For those studying the Book of Acts
paras: The second part starts with the reminder that the apostles were ordinary men: fishermen, a despised tax collector and a zealot among them. It lists their miracles, from Peter and John healing a lame man to Peter raising Tabitha and Paul raising Eutychus, and then asks why God worked through them. The book's answer is to glorify God and His Son and to confirm the gospel message.

sections.h2: For anyone seeking salvation
paras: The book closes on what it calls the greatest miracle: "the salvation of a spiritually dead sinner by God’s grace is His greatest miracle." It then calls those who have received God's forgiveness to proclaim the same gospel to the rest of the world.
