details.Author: Alfred Cherubim

paras: The book calls the wedding at Cana Jesus' first miraculous sign, as John's Gospel names it. It says this miracle showed Jesus' supernatural control over physical elements like water, and that it "revealed His glory as the Son of God and marked the beginning of His public ministry."

Miracle 2 prints John 4:43-54 in the NLT. A government official whose son is dying in Capernaum begs Jesus to come. Jesus tells him to go back home, that his son will live, and the man believes and starts home. His servants meet him on the way:
"Yesterday afternoon at one o’clock his fever suddenly disappeared!"
The father realizes it was the very hour Jesus had spoken, and his entire household believes in Jesus.

Among the apostles' miracles, the book prints Acts 28:1-6. After reaching the shore of Malta safely, Paul gathers brushwood for a fire and a viper fastens itself on his hand. The islanders expect him to swell up or drop dead:
"However, Paul shook the creature off into the fire and suffered no harm."
When nothing happened, they changed their minds about him. The book's reminder for every miracle is the same: "ALL miracles are God’s miracles."

author.bio: Pastor S. Alfred Cherubim is Senior Pastor of Redeemer Christ Assembly in Brampton, Canada, as he signs the book's closing miracle prayer. The book's last pages introduce him as pastor, servant and author, and point readers to his book Sharing Your Faith and Testimony.

They are, in order: Jesus Turned Water into Wine at the Wedding Feast at Cana; Jesus Heals an Official’s Son at Capernaum in Galilee; Jesus Drives Out an Evil Spirit from a Man in Capernaum; Jesus Heals Peter’s Mother-in-Law Who Was Sick with Fever; Jesus Heals Many Sick and Oppressed by Evening; First Miraculous Catch of Fish on the Lake of Gennesaret; Jesus Cleanses a Man With Leprosy; Jesus Heals a Centurion’s Paralyzed Servant in Capernaum; Jesus Heals a Paralytic Who Was Let Down from the Roof; Jesus Heals a Man’s Withered Hand on the Sabbath; Jesus Raises a Widow’s Son from the Dead in Nain; Jesus Calms a Raging Storm on the Sea; Jesus Casts Demons into a Herd of Pigs; Jesus Heals a Woman in the Crowd with an Issue of Blood; Jesus Raises Jairus’ Daughter Back to Life; Jesus Heals Two Blind Men; Jesus Heals a Man Who Was Unable to Speak; Jesus Heals an Invalid at Bethesda; Jesus Feeds 5,000-Plus Women and Children; Jesus Walks on Water; Jesus Heals Many Sick in Gennesaret as They Touch His Garment; Jesus Heals a Gentile Woman’s Demon-Possessed Daughter; Jesus Heals a Deaf and Dumb Man; Jesus Feeds 4,000-Plus Women and Children; Jesus Heals a Blind Man at Bethsaida; Jesus Heals a Man Born Blind by Spitting in His Eyes; Jesus Heals a Boy with an Unclean Spirit; Miraculous Temple Tax in a Fish’s Mouth; Jesus Heals a Blind, Mute Demoniac; Jesus Heals a Woman Who Had Been Crippled for Eighteen Years; Jesus Heals a Man with Dropsy on the Sabbath; Jesus Cleanses Ten Lepers on the Way to Jerusalem; Jesus Raises Lazarus from the Dead in Bethany; Jesus Restores Sight to Bartimaeus in Jericho; Jesus Withers the Fig Tree on the Road from Bethany; Jesus Heals a Servant’s Severed Ear while He is Being Arrested; and The Second Miraculous Catch of Fish at the Sea of Tiberias.

faq.q: How many miracles did Jesus perform?
faq.a: The four Gospels record thirty-seven, the book says, with Mark's Gospel recording the highest number. It adds John's note that Jesus did many other things as well, more than the whole world could hold in books if every one were written down.

faq.q: Does it include Jesus feeding the 5,000?
faq.a: Yes. Miracle 19, Jesus Feeds 5,000-Plus Women and Children, has its own pages with the Gospel passages, and Miracle 24 covers the feeding of the 4,000.

faq.q: Does it cover Jesus calming the storm?
faq.a: Yes. Miracle 12, Jesus Calms a Raging Storm on the Sea, is recorded in Matthew, Mark and Luke, and the chart lists all three references. Miracle 20, Jesus Walks on Water, comes later in the book.

faq.q: What miracles did the apostles perform?
faq.a: The book lists nineteen from the Gospels and Acts. They are, in order: Peter walked on water; all believers spoke in foreign languages; many signs and wonders were performed; Peter and John healed the lame man; Peter's shadow fell on the sick, healing them; Stephen performed amazing miracles and signs; Philip cast out demons and healed the lame; Peter and John laid hands on believers who then received the Holy Spirit; Peter healed Aeneas in Lydda; Peter raised Tabitha from the dead; Paul blinded Elymas the sorcerer; Paul and Barnabas performed signs and wonders in Iconium; Paul and Barnabas healed a crippled man who had faith; Paul and Silas cast a demon out of a fortune-telling slave girl; God did unusual miracles through Paul, even through handkerchiefs and aprons; Paul raised Eutychus from the dead; Paul was unharmed by a snake bite on Malta; Paul healed Publius' father of fever and dysentery; and Paul healed all the sick on Malta.

faq.q: What are the three New Testament words for miracles?
faq.a: They are, in order: power (dynamis), which means mighty deed; sign (sēmeion), a miracle that figuratively represents something else, such as the kingdom of God; and wonder (teras), which indicates something extraordinary.

faq.q: Why did Jesus perform miracles?
faq.a: The book says none were done randomly, for amusement or for show. Each met a serious human need or confirmed Christ's identity and authority as the Son of God, and at times Jesus refused to perform one, as when Herod hoped to see a sign.

faq.q: Does the book include a miracle prayer?
faq.a: Yes. It closes with a short Miracle Prayer by the author, asking God's forgiveness and healing from "the disease You call sin." It is a prayer of repentance, not a prayer for a particular healing.

audience.headline: In 2022, with tourniquets gone from markets around the world, a doctor suggested men's neckties. Joeth Strickland looked up at her warehouse crawl space and understood why God had sent her thirteen pallets of them.
audience.body: For readers who love true stories of answered prayer, for church members who give, sew, pack or volunteer, for supporters of missionaries, and for anyone living with disability or loss. Joeth Strickland tells how a girl who was legally blind in one eye and could not read until third grade came to run a ministry that ships donated goods to Christian workers around the world. The first section is her story: a family led to Christ by missionaries in Japan, lunch breaks learning customs forms, a crash with a tractor-trailer, nineteen surgeries and the death of her husband. The second section explains what the ministry does, why, and how readers can help. The voice is warm and conversational, like a friend telling stories at the kitchen table. A note on subjects: the book describes her injuries in the crash in some detail, and it touches on infertility and miscarriage, depression, bankruptcy, a death from COVID and, briefly, abortion. It is a memoir and a ministry story, not a how-to guide for starting a nonprofit.

quote.text: “If He can trust you with something small, He will continue to give more and more and more and more.”
quote.cite: Faithful in Small Things, Birth of a Ministry: When God Can Trust You in the Small Things

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who serve in small ways
paras: The ministry began with copy paper boxes covered in contact paper and lined up in a Sunday school room, so the women of the church would remember to bring things for missionaries. Joeth took the donations home and packed them in her breezeway, a room six by ten feet that also held her laundry and a table where her children played. She writes that they did not know they were starting a ministry. They were just being obedient.
Five things set it apart:
list: It shows how God prepared one person for one job: a mother who helped missionaries on furlough, an office job with a shipping department, and a memory that lets her see where everything sits in a 17,000 square foot warehouse.

It is full of specific answered prayers: thirteen pallets of neckties that became tourniquets, two bags of deep-sea fishing line that turned out to be exactly what a mission team needed, an ultrasound machine saved for three years for a hospital in Haiti, and a forklift that arrived in less than a week.

It is honest about hard things. The author writes about a lacerated spleen and a crushed foot, years of surgeries, two and a half years of depression, losing a business and a home in 2008, and walking in grace after her husband's death in 2021.

It explains how the ministry actually works: why some countries are hard to ship into, why sending goods can cost less than sending money, and how discarded prison uniforms became the fabric for more than 46,000 Bible bags.
It ends with practical ways to help: volunteer, give durable goods you no longer need, ask what is needed before you give, and remember people in need all year, not just in November and December.

sections.h2: For readers who love true stories of answered prayer
paras: Story follows story: an orphanage in South India praying through the night while the author's spleen healed, a blind girl in a clinic whose first sight was a salvation doll, message cards in Swahili already stamped and waiting when the request came. She sums it up in a line she repeats: God still does miracles.

sections.h2: For volunteers, givers and church mission committees
paras: The second section is a working guide to giving well. It explains why missionaries really do need what they ask for, why a $3.35 bottle of lotion can cost $45 in Honduras, and why a church could adopt one nursing home. It welcomes volunteers of every age, from a four-month-old who slept in a shopping cart to high school football teams.

sections.h2: For anyone living with disability
paras: The author was born pigeon-toed and legally blind in one eye, wore an eye patch until she was twelve and, after the crash, needed nineteen surgeries over fifteen years to walk. She still spends about three months a year in a wheelchair. She writes plainly about it and about the gifts God gave her for the work, including emotional self-control that helped her stay calm while she was pinned in the truck.

sections.h2: For widows and anyone walking through loss
paras: Walking in Grace, Not Grief tells the love story of two teenage pen pals who became prayer partners and then co-laborers for 42 years, and of his death from COVID in 2021. The author describes what God put in place before he died, from a paid-off house to a women's Bible study with exactly the five friends she would need.

details.Title: Faithful in Small Things
details.Subtitle: How God Grew a Ministry from One Home to Serve 104 Nations
details.Author: Joeth Strickland

paras: When war came to Ukraine in 2022, the ministry teamed with a Ukrainian pastor in Greensboro to fill shipping containers, and a friend with a medical background suggested trauma kits. Tourniquets had vanished from markets everywhere. A doctor said that if they could not send tourniquets, they should send men's neckties. Three years earlier, someone had donated thirteen pallets of them, and they had sat in the crawl space ever since. Some carried Bible verses. The ministry went on to ship thirty-six containers to Ukraine in about a year. The lesson the author draws:
“God knows what is needed and where it’s needed. We just send it along.”

On August 22, 2002, the author was driving a borrowed box truck to pick up a donation for an orphanage in South India, with two of her children aboard and a third on the way. A tractor-trailer turned right across her lane. She was pinned for an hour and twenty-eight minutes, twenty-three weeks pregnant, with a crushed foot, a broken femur, a severe burn and a lacerated spleen. That night, about 350 people at the orphanage prayed from 11 p.m. to 7 a.m. The morning ultrasound showed her spleen healed. Her son was born healthy. Before the helicopter took her to Duke, she asked when she could go home. An attendant told her:
“Ma’am, you’re not going home today,”
She had surgery every year for fifteen years after, and the ministry kept running.

For three years an ultrasound machine sat in the warehouse. Every attempt to send it to Honduras failed, and the team kept moving it out of the way. Then a retired Navy submarine captain who carries containers to Haiti on a converted training ship listed what a new NICU there needed:
“They’ve never seen a baby before it’s born in Haiti.”
She had the machine. Later she received a video of doctors and mothers in Haiti seeing a child's heartbeat before birth for the first time.

author.bio: Joeth Strickland is the founder of Crossing All Borders Ministries, which began almost forty years ago with a few boxes of donations in a breezeway in North Carolina. Raised partly on a US Air Force installation in Japan, she came to faith at age four through the work of American missionaries. She survived a crash with a tractor-trailer in 2002 and nineteen surgeries that followed, and she lives with disabilities from that accident. Today the ministry's all-volunteer team operates from a 17,000 square foot warehouse and has shipped essential hard goods to Christian workers in 104 countries.

publisher.about: Spirit Media Publishing is a Christian publishing and marketing company with a vision to reveal our Father's heart to all nations. It offers full-service book creation and publishing in paperback, hardback, digital and audiobook formats, along with children's titles, compact Express Books, website design and SEO, and podcast and video production. We are glad to publish the story of a ministry that grew from one breezeway to serve Christian workers in 104 countries.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author writes that God has taught her two things in almost forty years of shipping donated goods: His plans are better than hers, and the journey He planned for her life is better than anything she would have chosen. She tells her story so readers will ask God about the journey He has given them.
She is clear about whose story it is:
“This is God’s ministry. He gives me the privilege to oversee it.”

faq.q: What is Faithful in Small Things about?
faq.a: It is the true story of Crossing All Borders Ministries, told by its founder. It grew from a few boxes of donations in a breezeway to a 17,000 square foot warehouse whose all-volunteer team ships essential goods to Christian workers in 104 countries. The first section tells the author's life story; the second explains what the ministry does and how to help.

faq.q: Is it a memoir or a missionary biography?
faq.a: It is a Christian memoir. The author never became a career missionary. She and her husband once offered to join Operation Mobilization, and a leader there asked what would happen to every other ministry they supplied if they left. She writes that every believer is a missionary, and that God sent her to serve many nations from home.

faq.q: What is the necktie story about Ukraine?
faq.a: In early 2022, tourniquets disappeared from markets as war spread in Ukraine. A doctor suggested men's neckties, and the author realized why God had sent thirteen pallets of them three years earlier. The ministry and a Ukrainian pastor in Greensboro went on to ship thirty-six containers of supplies in about a year. The book says the ministry does not do plain humanitarian aid; everything it sends goes out to make Jesus known.

faq.q: Does the book cover the author's car accident?
faq.a: Yes. In 2002 a tractor-trailer turned across her lane while she drove a box truck to pick up a donation. She was pinned for nearly ninety minutes while twenty-three weeks pregnant. The chapter The Wreck: Miracles in the Midst of Tragedy tells of her healed spleen, her son born healthy, and nineteen surgeries over the next fifteen years.

faq.q: How did the author learn to read while legally blind in one eye?
faq.a: She was born with a turned-in eye that left her legally blind on that side, and she reached third grade without reading. Her third-grade teacher ordered large bold-print materials and told the two students who could not read that they would not leave her class until they could read at a fourth-grade level with confidence. By fourteen, she writes, she could see and she could read.

faq.q: Does the book talk about losing a husband?
faq.a: Yes. The chapter Walking in Grace, Not Grief tells their love story, from teenage pen pals and prayer partners to 42 years as co-laborers, and his death from COVID in 2021. She writes about what God put in place beforehand and about learning to walk in grace while challenges still fly around her.

faq.q: How can I help or volunteer?
faq.a: The book names the two most important ways: volunteering and giving durable goods you no longer need. It also asks readers to find out what is needed before they give, to trust missionaries when they say they need something, and to serve people in need all year. The ministry welcomes volunteers of any age, and you do not have to be a Christian to help.

faq.q: What miracles and answered prayers does the book describe?
faq.a: Many. They include a lacerated spleen found healed after a night of prayer, neckties that became tourniquets, fishing line that a team in Suriname needed, an ultrasound machine for Haiti, a blind girl who received her sight while holding a salvation doll, and a forklift donated within a week after a worker at a neighboring business mocked the ministry's prayers.

faq.q: How did missionaries in Japan shape the author's life?
faq.a: Her family moved to a US Air Force installation in Japan when she was two. There, one missionary played handball with her father every week for two years before leading him to Christ, and a missionary woman paired military wives with Japanese women to learn from each other. Her parents came to faith, and she did at age four. They came home with a fire for missions that became the root of her ministry.

hero.audience_line: For people facing cancer or another hard diagnosis, people going through chemotherapy, caregivers and spouses, friends who want to help, church care teams, and Christians wrestling with suffering.
hero.tagline: A permanent makeup artist and painter is told cancer is not a pretty way to die. She writes from the middle of treatment about chemo, grief, the things people say, and how to live beautifully on the inside.

audience.headline: A woman who spent her life making other women beautiful wrote this book while cancer was taking her own beauty away.
audience.body: For people facing cancer or another hard diagnosis, people going through chemotherapy, caregivers and spouses, friends who want to help, church care teams, and Christians wrestling with suffering. Lynn Soles was diagnosed with colon cancer on October 7, 2022, less than two weeks after her father-in-law died and a little over a year after her stepson died. She started writing on June 13, 2023, after three months of chemo and 22 days of radiation, and she was still writing when she learned she would need a colostomy. The book is part journal, part encouragement and part practical help. She tells the hard parts plainly, she is often funny, and she keeps coming back to one hope: that God sees. A note on subjects: the book describes chemotherapy, radiation, a hospital stay, a colostomy, grief and end-of-life planning in plain terms. It uses some strong language, including in one section title. In one chapter she tells how she tried THC edibles for nausea, which she notes are illegal where she lives. It is one woman's account, not medical advice.

quote.text: “God knows. God is there. God sees.”
quote.cite: Don't Die Ugly, Chapter 1, Facing the Great Divide

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people facing cancer and the people beside them
paras: Three days after her diagnosis, Lynn told her doctors she would not accept any treatment. She wanted to drink organic tea. They disagreed in the strongest terms, and their words became the title of the book. She took them as both a warning and a calling: if she could not control her body, she could still choose how to live.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is written during treatment, not after. Dated entries run from the day of diagnosis to August 2023, and the book ends before she knows how her story turns out.
It says out loud what not to say. One chapter lists terrible things to tell a cancer patient, from “Do you think you'll die?” to “Girl, you got this,” and explains why each one hurts.
It tells friends exactly how to help. Two chapters list the help that mattered most, from laundry and clean bathrooms to walking the dogs, and how to offer it so a tired patient can just say yes.
It is honest with God. She writes about feeling betrayed that God had not healed her, about feeling like Job, and about how speaking honestly with God opened her to emotional healing.

It comes from a life spent creating beauty. An artist who paints murals and restores brows and scars for women after surgery asks what it means to be beautiful when cancer takes your hair, your strength and your plans.

sections.h2: For people who have just heard the word cancer
paras: Lynn describes coming home from the doctor, holding her husband and crying for a long time, and then deciding they would face it together. She describes wanting to do nothing at all. If you are in that place now, her pages tell you that the fear, the anger and the mourning for the life you had are real, and that you are not alone.

sections.h2: For people going through chemotherapy
paras: She writes about the port under her collarbone, the three-day infusions, the nausea and the fog of chemo brain, the day the word tomatoes would only come out as “red.” She also gives a list of ways to manage chemo brain that worked for her: make lists, use sticky notes and a paper calendar, rest, reduce stress, move when you can and enlist helpers.

sections.h2: For caregivers, friends and church care teams
paras: If you love someone with cancer and do not know what to do, this book tells you. Ask specific questions that make it easy to say yes. Bring food, take the trash out, sit with them between appointments. Listen instead of advising. She writes that the people who give this kind of help are also blessed by the chance to do a little piece of God's work in this world.

sections.h2: For anyone who has felt like Job
paras: Her diagnosis was the third blow in just over fifteen months. Then the story of Job came to her three times: in her daily devotional, in a couples Bible study and in a radiation waiting room. She is honest that Job was not a book she ever wanted to study, and honest about what finally comforted her in it: Job's words, “I know that my redeemer lives.”

blocks.text: The book opens with a dedication to her treatment and support team and a preface that begins:

paras: Try to imagine writing a book about the hardest experience of your life … while you’re in the middle of it.

blocks.text: Chapter 1 tells how a self-described ugly duckling, the last of seven kids, grew into an artist and a beauty professional. Then comes the diagnosis:

paras: The day I got the cancer diagnosis divided my life into before and after.

blocks.text: Chapter 2 opens three days later, when she tells her doctors she will not accept treatment:

paras: “Cancer isn’t a pretty way to die,” they told me. “You don’t want to die ugly.”

blocks.text: The self-care chapter starts with perspective:

paras: When it seems like life is just going up in flames, it’s good to remember that you can’t paint roses on a burning canvas.

blocks.text: The chapters are:

items: People Can Be So Ignorant (No Words)
The Positive Value of Learning a New Way of Life
Five Practical Self-Care Tips for the Superhuman Woman

A Bible verse opening most chapters, from the NIV, NLT, RSV and NKJV

details.Title: Don't Die Ugly
details.Subtitle: Live Beautifully
details.Author: Lynn Soles

paras: When the doctors suggested chemotherapy, Lynn protested that she and her husband had already booked their anniversary trip to Aruba, and they were flying out that Saturday. The doctor's answer surprised her:
“Go to Aruba,” the doctor said. “Have way too much fun. We’ll start this after.”

She did exactly that. She jumped off a boat to snorkel, caught the biggest triggerfish and ate it on the beach, rode her first party boat and paddled a glass bottom kayak. Chemo began after they came home.
Of all the things people told her, one phrase bothered her most. She says she wanted to smack anyone who said it, and she explains why:
“I don’t ‘got this’ I’ve got cancer, and you’re just glad it’s not you.”
In the Cancer Friends chapter she says what she needed instead: not to have the moment rushed, but for a friend to stay in it with her.
In the last chapter, waiting for surgery, she finds a picture for what cancer has done to her life:
“Cancer has become something of a cocoon for me.”

She remembers raising butterflies indoors and learning that you cannot rush the process. When she goes to her room and lies down on her bed, she writes, it feels safe, and she prays there. She does not know what is on the other side, but she knows it will still be her, and it will be okay.

author.bio: Lynn Soles is a painter, a portrait artist and a permanent makeup professional in North Carolina. The last of seven children, she moved to Raleigh as a girl, won a Scholastic Presidential Gold Key award and art scholarships, and went on to paint commissioned murals across Eastern North Carolina and teach private art classes. She opened her first permanent makeup clinic in 2000. Her work includes brows, scar revisions and areola reconstruction for women after mastectomy, often by referral from their surgeons. She was diagnosed with colon cancer in October 2022 and wrote Don't Die Ugly during her treatment.

publisher.name: Spirit Media Publishing
publisher.about: Spirit Media Publishing is a Christian publishing and marketing company with a vision to reveal our Father's heart to all nations. It offers full-service book creation and publishing in paperback, hardback, digital and audiobook formats, along with children's titles, compact Express Books, website design and SEO, and podcast and video production. We are glad to publish a book that tells the hard truth about cancer and still points to hope.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: Lynn says in her preface that her life has always been about creating beauty:
“I want to create beauty with you, even in these difficult moments.”
Near the end she adds a second reason. Writing the book is part of leaving a legacy, not just stuff:
“Maybe it will help you as you walk your own journey.”
And she says what she hopes for herself:
“I hope when I get to my end, I’m Holy Spirit beautiful, not Hollywood good-looking.”

faq.q: What is Don't Die Ugly about?
faq.a: It is Lynn Soles's account of life as a cancer patient, written while she was in treatment for colon cancer. It covers her diagnosis, chemotherapy and chemo brain, the hurtful things people say, the friends and church who helped, grief, five self-care tips and the hope she holds onto. Its message is that you can live beautifully on the inside even when you cannot control your body or your future.

faq.q: Is it a cancer survivor story?
faq.a: Not in the usual sense. It is written from the middle of treatment, not from the other side. When she finished writing, the latest tests showed the treatment had not reduced the cancer enough, and she was scheduled for colostomy surgery. The book is about how to live while you do not yet know the outcome.

faq.q: Does it help with trusting God in hard times?
faq.a: Yes. She writes that she is trusting God and the doctors He has given her, that God is in the waiting, and that God knows, God is there and God sees. She is also honest that trust did not come easily, and that she had to talk with God about everything.

faq.q: Does it explain why God allows suffering?
faq.a: It does not offer a theory. It offers honesty. She writes, “I believe that God heals people; I also know that God decides who to heal and when.” She describes feeling betrayed that God had not healed her, finds herself in the story of Job, and is comforted by Job's hope of seeing God face to face.

faq.q: What Bible verses for hard times are in the book?
faq.a: They are, in order: Proverbs 31:30; Romans 12:15; Ephesians 3:20-21; 2 Corinthians 12:9-10; Proverbs 18:24; Job 19:23; Psalm 42:7; Psalm 88:7 and 16-17; Job 19:25-27; 1 Peter 3:3-4; Proverbs 24:26; Proverbs 8:14; Isaiah 3:18-24; Jeremiah 29:11; Revelation 21:4; and Romans 8:23.

faq.q: Does it have help for caregivers?
faq.a: Yes. She describes how her husband cared for her, from giving her at-home chemo to learning to put on her wigs and lashes, and she says that friends who look after the caregiver are precious. The Cancer Friends and Keeping the House Up chapters list the specific help that mattered most.

faq.q: Is it a good gift for someone going through chemo?
faq.a: It was written for them. She says she hopes it helps readers walk their own journey and helps their loved ones help them. It is short, at 95 pages, and many sections can be read on their own. Its tone is honest rather than cheerful, and it includes some strong language.

faq.q: Does it talk about grief?
faq.a: Yes. Her stepson died in July 2021 at 24, her father-in-law died in September 2022, and her diagnosis came less than two weeks later. She writes about grieving them, grieving the life she expected, and the day she went to buy their headstones. She says grief came in waves.

faq.q: How should I pray for someone with cancer?
faq.a: The book gives one patient's view. She is thankful for every person who prays for her, and some of her clients became her best pray-ers. She also says it can feel hard to give a sad update to people who have been praying, and that being told she was not choosing to be healed was a slap in the face. What helped most was people who prayed and also listened.

hero.eyebrow: By Nora L. Fozard · Foreword by Dr. Frank Summerfield
hero.audience_line: For Christian husbands, wives and parents who want to build a family of faith, and for any believer who needs strength to hold on to the dream God has put in their heart.

audience.headline: A young wife who once prayed "Lord, save him or send him on" was furious when God saved her husband. Decades and eight children later, she writes about the strength it takes to conceive a family of faith.
audience.body: For married couples and couples thinking about marriage, parents raising children in the faith, women looking for a spiritual mother or ready to become one, and believers going through tests and trials. Nora Fozard writes with humor and plain honesty about her own family, and builds each chapter around Bible people such as Sarah and Abraham, Elijah, Jonah and Paul. Scripture is quoted from the Amplified Bible, and every chapter ends with a prayer built from the verses listed beneath it. The title has two meanings. To conceive is to have a child, and it is also to grasp a vision God gives you. A note on subjects: the book is written for adults and is modest in tone. The author's story includes a pregnancy before marriage, a husband who drank and argued before he was saved, and her own season of anger and nightclubs. It teaches prayer for healing from a faith point of view. It is not a medical or fertility guide.

quote.text: “I saw myself through the eyes of faith.”
quote.cite: Strength to Conceive, Chapter 1: I Had A Dream

what_makes.title: What makes this book about faith a family story
paras: The book is about Sarah, who had been barren all her life and received strength to conceive because she judged God faithful. It is also about a girl from New Jersey and Philadelphia who danced around the house talking about her dreams, and grew up to lead a church and a large family with her husband in Durham, North Carolina.
Five things set it apart:
list: It uses one word two ways. The last chapter explains that to conceive means to get pregnant with, and also to fathom or understand. You have to grasp God's vision before you can carry it.
Every lesson starts at home. A plastic sword, a family with the flu, a yellow car bought with a sister's signature. The stories are funny and real.
It gives you a test with the answers. Chapter 3 says every faith test asks three questions, and the answers are praise, honor and glory.
It ends each chapter with a conception confession. A prayer in plain words, built from the Bible verses listed beneath it, under the line "may it be done to me according to your word."
It takes faith one step at a time. Chapters move from the faith gift to nurturing, disciplined and mountain-moving faith, and warn against phony and shipwrecked faith.

sections.h2: For husbands and wives
paras: Nora does not pretend her marriage started well. She writes about anger, arguments and a season of trying to drive her husband away after he was saved. The Love Test chapter shows how they learned to walk in love, and why she now calls him the man she envisioned and prayed for.

sections.h2: For parents raising children in the faith
paras: Two chapters speak straight to parents. Parents Are Teachers is about setting a standard from God's Word and not lowering it. Shipwrecked Faith is about the years between training a child and old age, and how to keep children from wrecking their faith.

sections.h2: For anyone in a season of testing
paras: The book says faith must be tested, and that even giants of faith like Elijah ran and hid. The chapters on the love test and the joy test give a simple way through: don't stop, keep going and look for joy in God's promises.

sections.h2: For women who need a spiritual mother
paras: Nora credits a prayer warrior she had known since childhood with keeping her marriage together. That woman prayed for her family for years and lived by faith to the age of 103. The book asks you to find spiritual parents like her, and then to become one.

details.Title: Strength to Conceive
details.Subtitle: Seeing God-Sized Vision for Your Family
details.Author: Nora L. Fozard

stories.h2: Save him or send him on
paras: Early in her marriage, Nora's husband drank, and when he drank, he argued. One night she ended up crying on the doorstep of the prayer warrior who had helped her mother years before, and she began to pray:
"Lord, save him or send him on."

Three years later she had forgotten that prayer. She got a job, bought a car and started going to nightclubs. Then her husband quit drinking, said he was saved and enrolled in Bible college. She was furious. In time she saw what he had that she did not: peace and joy.

The introduction to the first edition remembers a Sunday night at the old Mount Zion. The pastor thanked God for his wife, pregnant with their seventh child, and said with a smile that he was pushing for ten. Some in the church wondered if the Fozards were taking faith too far. Then Nora leaned forward and spoke up:
"Push on brother."
The writer says that sealed her place in his heart as a woman of faith. The family grew to eight children.

In Parents Are Teachers, the two youngest boys are playing downstairs. The family rule is that no one hits the baby, and the baby, almost six, knows it. He whacks his brother with a toy sword and runs upstairs crying for his dad. His father, with a guest watching, answers:
"Son, if you live by the sword, you’ll die by the sword. Now surrender your sword."
Then he tells the boy to pray for his brother. Nora uses the story to show how God, too, deals with sibling rivalry in His big family.

author.bio: Nora L. Fozard and her husband are the pastors of Mount Zion Christian Church in Durham, North Carolina, and have led a church family together for more than forty years. Under their leadership the church built a multipurpose development that houses a Christian academy, a Second Chance Facility, a Hispanic church and community programs and classes. She is a Bible teacher, prayer leader and Christian counselor, has had a national television program on the MBC Network, and is a songwriter who studied composition at the CBN Songwriting School. Above all, she loves being a wife and the mother of eight children.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: Nora believes that some people find it hard even to picture themselves in a strong family, especially if they grew up in a hard home. She wrote to help them see it. The author's introduction begins with the problem:
"Not everyone can imagine that!"
And at the close of the book she says what she wants for you:
"Your dream will come to pass by the word of faith."

faq.q: What is Strength to Conceive about?
faq.a: It is a Christian book on faith and family by Nora L. Fozard, a pastor's wife and mother of eight. Through her own story and the story of Sarah and Abraham, it teaches how faith is tested, grown and used, and how a couple can build what she calls a family of faith. Each chapter ends with a prayer.

faq.q: Is it a book about infertility?
faq.a: Not mainly. The title comes from Hebrews 11:11, where Sarah received strength to conceive though she was past age and had been barren all her life, and the book returns to her story often. But it is a book about faith, marriage and family, not a medical or fertility guide. Its view of conception is spiritual as well as physical: to conceive is also to grasp God's vision.

faq.q: What does it say about tests and trials?
faq.a: It says faith must be tested, and that God tests us to prove to us that all we have is in Him. Chapter 3 uses Abraham and Isaac to show that every faith test asks three questions. They are, in order: Will you praise God?; Will you honor God?; and Will you glorify God?

faq.q: What is faith, according to the book?
faq.a: The book names two kinds. Human faith is the ability every person has to believe. The God kind of faith is a gift from God. It pictures the difference with bubble gum: you may know how to blow bubbles, but you still need the gum. Later chapters teach that faith starts small, like a mustard seed, and grows.

faq.q: Does it help with Christian marriage?
faq.a: Yes, through example more than rules. The author tells how her marriage began before either of them was serving God, how her husband's salvation made her angry at first, and how the love test taught her to walk in love. The book also teaches honor between husband and wife from 1 Peter 3:7.

faq.q: Is it a book on godly parenting?
faq.a: In part. Parents Are Teachers is about setting a standard from God's Word and keeping it, and Shipwrecked Faith is about helping children through the years when faith is tested. Stories from raising eight children run through the whole book.

faq.q: Does it talk about faith over fear?
faq.a: Yes. The last chapter says that when you decide to receive more from God, fear and doubt will come, often in the words of people close to you. The author writes that she and her husband welcomed eight children without fear of how they would provide for them, and that no one in the family ever missed a meal.

faq.q: Is it about leaving a legacy of faith?
faq.a: Yes. The introduction to the first edition says the book is for those who want to leave a godly inheritance to their children's children. The author's own story begins with a spiritual mother who prayed for her family, and it ends with a call to stand for your family, your children and your church.

faq.q: What does it say about spiritual mentoring?
faq.a: Chapter 2, A Spiritual Mother Cared for Me, tells how an older prayer warrior took in a young mother on her doorstep and kept praying for the family for years. The author prays that every reader will find good spiritual parents and become a spiritual parent to others.

hero.audience_line: For Christian singles, married couples, the divorced and the widowed who want to understand God's plan for sex, and for parents and church leaders who know someone needs to talk about it.
hero.tagline: A pastor's wife and Christian counselor talks plainly about what the church often leaves unsaid: God made us with desire, He gave sex a home in marriage, and there is mercy and a way out for anyone who has gone wrong.

audience.headline: A pastor's wife who has counseled couples for years says the church usually stops at "It's wrong." This book says the rest.
audience.body: For single adults, dating and engaged couples, husbands and wives, the divorced and widowed, parents of teenagers, and pastors and church leaders. Nora Fozard writes as a Bible teacher and Christian counselor, in a direct, motherly voice, with Scripture mostly from the Amplified Bible and a reference list for the figures she cites. She speaks to readers whatever their situation, whether sexually active or waiting. A note on subjects: the book is written for adults and speaks frankly, though not graphically, about sex outside marriage, adultery, pornography, sexually transmitted diseases and abortion. It holds a traditional Christian view of marriage and sexuality, including on same-sex relationships, and it mentions public scandals. Its health figures are the author's sources and her view, not medical advice.

quote.text: “Read this book with the confidence that somebody knows and understands what you are going through.”
quote.cite: Sex Without Regrets, Introduction: Why This Book Is for You

what_makes.title: What makes this book honest and kind at once
paras: Most people who are living in sexual sin already know it is wrong, the introduction says. What they don't know is what life would look like without it, or how they would cope. The book is written for that person, and for the people who love them.
Five things set it apart:
list: It begins with God's design, not shame. The first chapter says desire comes from God, who made us for relationship, and that sex is good under His lordship.
It speaks to everyone. Single, married, divorced or widowed, active or abstaining, the introduction says God knows your needs, desires and longings.
It is plain about consequences. Broken homes, years of rebuilt trust after an affair, disease and children left without fathers are all named, with sources in a reference list.
It gives each reader a clear word. The Adultery chapter ends with separate calls to the church, to Christian women and to Christian men.
It ends with mercy. The last chapter, Go and Sin No More, says the message must be simple and true, but most of all merciful.

sections.h2: For single adults
paras: The book says sex belongs in marriage, and it does not pretend waiting is easy. Nora tells how she saved herself for her wedding night as a young woman, and Flee Youthful Lust speaks to anyone, young or old, who is tempted to rush. If you have already made choices you regret, the book points you to forgiveness and a new start.

sections.h2: For married couples
paras: Three chapters are for husbands and wives. They teach that intimacy is a gift and a shared duty in marriage, that couples should not hold back from each other, and that problems should be talked through honestly between the two of you instead of with outsiders.

sections.h2: For parents
paras: Teach Your Children asks parents a direct question: what are you teaching your children? Nora urges parents to reach their children before the world does, to know their friends, to raise sons as protectors and not predators, and to show their children what a loving marriage looks like.

sections.h2: For pastors and church leaders
paras: Where Is the Church? argues that nearly everyone talks about sex except the church. The book asks leaders to preach and teach God's plan, to counsel wisely those who are tempted or have strayed, and to speak the truth in love.

details.Title: Sex Without Regrets
details.Subtitle: Learning God's Idea of Sex with Zero Curses
details.Author: Nora L. Fozard

paras: In Teach Your Children, Nora remembers being a young woman determined to wait until marriage. Her mother warned her that many young men wanted only one thing, and would move on once they had it. So she was ready. If a date got out of line, she told him:
"I am not going to sleep with you because I am saving that for my wedding night."
If he could not respect that, she said goodbye.
One day her son asked what he should do if a girl hit him, and later, what he should do if his wife ever did. Her answer was the same both times:
"Walk away. You don’t hit a woman."
She tells how he opened doors for her and would not let her carry the bags, and how he learned it by watching his father treat her well. Her point for parents: sons learn how to treat women at home.

stories.h2: An old wound in a marriage
paras: As a pastor's wife, Nora has counseled many couples. In the Adultery chapter she describes one kind she has seen: a wife says her husband has grown cold, and in counseling it comes out that he never got past an affair she had put behind her years before. Rebuilding trust after infidelity can take a long time, she writes, and sometimes it cannot be fixed, because of what adultery does:
"You bring that someone else into your home and he or she corrupts your marriage."

author.bio: Nora L. Fozard is a Bible teacher, prayer leader and Christian counselor who has been in ministry for more than forty years. She and her husband are the senior pastors of Mount Zion Christian Church, with locations in Durham, Henderson, Rocky Mount and Burlington, North Carolina, and Capital City Church in Raleigh. She holds a Bachelor of Science in Christian counseling from Oral Roberts University and a Master of Arts in human service from Liberty University. Above all, she loves being a wife, the mother of eight children, and a grandmother and great-grandmother.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: Nora believes the church has said too little about sex, beyond telling people it is wrong. She writes in the introduction:
"I wrote this book because God told me to write about the repercussions of sexual sins."

She also wants readers to know there is a way out. The introduction promises that God has already made a way for you to be free, and the book ends with the words of Jesus to a woman who had been caught in adultery: neither do I condemn you, go and sin no more.

faq.q: What does the Bible say about sex, according to Sex Without Regrets?
faq.a: The book teaches that God created sexual desire and called it good, and that He ordained sex for marriage. Sex before marriage and outside of marriage is sin with real consequences. Within marriage, husbands and wives are not to deprive each other. And for anyone who has gone wrong, God offers forgiveness and a new start.

faq.q: Is the book for singles as well as married couples?
faq.a: Yes. The introduction speaks to readers who are single, married, divorced or widowed, sexually active or abstaining. Flee Youthful Lust is written for anyone tempted to rush into sex, young or old, and three chapters are written for husbands and wives.

faq.q: Does it help with intimacy in marriage?
faq.a: Yes, in plain and modest terms. Don't Deprive Your Spouse! and The Joy of (Married) Sex teach from 1 Corinthians 7 that intimacy is a shared gift and duty in marriage. When Conflict Is Dividing You urges couples to keep their problems between the two of them and to talk honestly.

faq.q: Can God forgive adultery or other sexual sin?
faq.a: The book says yes. It ends with Jesus telling the woman caught in adultery that He does not condemn her, and to go and sin no more. It is honest that rebuilding trust in a marriage after an affair can take a long time, and it advises seeking wise Christian counsel and, if you choose forgiveness, learning to forgive well.

faq.q: Does it give help for overcoming temptation?
faq.a: Yes. The introduction quotes 1 Corinthians 10:13, that God will not let you be tempted beyond your ability and will provide a way out. Flee Youthful Lust, built on 2 Timothy 2:22, teaches readers to run from youthful lusts and pursue righteousness, faith, love and peace, The Lust chapter says anyone driven by lust should seek help, and that anyone who acknowledges this sin will be forgiven by God.

faq.q: How does it help parents talk to their children about sex?
faq.a: Teach Your Children urges parents to start early, before the world teaches them first. It asks parents to know who their children spend time with, to teach sons to respect and protect women, and to model a loving marriage at home.

faq.q: What does it say about the body as a temple of the Holy Spirit?
faq.a: The introduction opens with 1 Corinthians 6:19: your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit and you are not your own. The book builds on that idea, saying our bodies belong to God and should be used for righteousness.

faq.q: Does it address domestic violence?
faq.a: Briefly. In a section on raising good men, the author tells sons never to strike a woman and to walk away instead, and she cites figures on how often women are hurt by someone they know. It is a short part of a chapter on parenting, not a guide for people in danger.

faq.q: What does it teach about holiness and sanctification?
faq.a: Flee Youthful Lust quotes 1 Thessalonians 4:3, that it is God's will for believers to be sanctified, set apart from sin, and to control their bodies in holiness and honor. The book presents sexual purity as part of a holy life, with mercy for those who have fallen.

hero.audience_line: For parents and grandparents who read with little ones, preschool and kindergarten teachers, Sunday school and children's ministry leaders, caregivers and daycare providers, and anyone who loves a little one.
hero.tagline: Say it. Hear it. Believe it. A call-and-response picture book in which a grown-up and a child trade words worth repeating, from I love you to You matter.

audience.headline: A teacher wrote a picture book where the child does not just hear the words. The child says them back.
audience.body: For parents and grandparents who read with little ones, preschool and kindergarten teachers, Sunday school and children's ministry leaders, caregivers and daycare providers, and anyone who loves a little one. I Say, You Say is built on one simple rhythm. On one page the grown-up says an affirmation. On the next page the child says it back. Then both of them say it again. Twelve affirmations go back and forth this way, from I love you and I believe in you to You are wonderfully and beautifully made and You matter. In the last pages the two voices become one, and everyone says We matter. Every line is short enough for a toddler to echo, so even a child who cannot read yet can join in.

quote.text: “To all my littles, You Matter!”
quote.cite: I Say, You Say, dedication

what_makes.title: What makes this book for little ones who are learning that they matter
paras: Many picture books tell a child a message. This one gives the child the words to say. The first spread sets the pattern: I say, “I love you!” on the left page and You say, “I love you!” on the right. By the second affirmation, a child knows what comes next.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is read together. Each affirmation is said by the grown-up and then by the child, so the child is not only listening but speaking.
Every line is short. Phrases like Don't give up! and You are seen! are easy for the youngest readers to repeat by ear.
It builds to one message. The words move from love and belief to purpose and worth, and arrive at You Matter.
It ends with everyone together. In the closing pages the I and the you become we: We say, “We Matter!”
It closes with Scripture and a plan. The last pages print Psalm 139:4 from the NIV and a short list of Ways to use this book at home and at school.

sections.h2: For parents and grandparents
paras: The book takes only a few minutes to read, and it is meant to be read more than once. You say the line, your child says it back, and the pictures give you both something to point at: a classroom, a playground, a school bus, a bedroom. It is a simple way to make sure the most encouraging words get said out loud, and often.

sections.h2: For preschool and kindergarten teachers
paras: The author is a teacher, and the book's last page of ideas speaks to the classroom. Teachers can add the affirmations to a Morning Meeting, and during a Stand up, Pair up routine students echo the teacher's words. The book says that with time, children feel more comfortable using the affirmations in other classroom situations too.

sections.h2: For Sunday school and children's ministry leaders
paras: The call-and-response pattern works with a whole group as well as with one child. The book closes with Psalm 139:4, a reminder that the Lord knows every word before it is spoken, which gives a leader a natural way to talk about the words we say to each other.

sections.h2: For toddlers who are learning to talk
paras: A child does not need to read to take part. The lines are two to six words long and come back again and again, so a little one can answer by ear. The pictures show a whole group of children, so many kids can find a face that looks like a friend.

details.Title: I Say, You Say
details.Author: Lola Brooks
details.Ages: 2–7 (read aloud at home and in class)
details.Binding: Paperback (perfect bound, matte) and hardback (case laminate)

paras: Two girls work at craft tables. On the first page the grown-up's line stands alone at the top: I say, “Don't give up!” On the next page the child takes her turn, and the line is said twice over, once in each speech bubble:
“Don't give up! Don't give up!”

Two girls walk hand in hand past the flowers. It is one of a run of affirmations about being noticed and belonging: You are wanted, You are seen and You are loved. Each one is short enough for a child to carry into a hard day.
For most of the book there are two voices, I and you. Then the roles change. A whole group of children stands together, and the words come from everyone at once:
“We say, ‘We Matter!’ We matter! We matter!”

author.bio: Lola Brooks is a teacher and the author of I Say, You Say. The book's closing page names her Teacher of the Year for 2021–2022 and invites readers to follow her website, lrbrooks.com. The classroom ideas in the book come from her own practice, and she keeps her own affirmation cards on her bathroom mirror and fireplace mantle.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: Lola Brooks wrote it for her “littles,” the children in her care, and she dedicates it to them with the same two words the whole book is built to say: You Matter.
Her page of ways to use the book shows that the words are meant to leave the page. She suggests affirmation cards around the home, car, job or school:
“As reminders that You Matter!”
And she ends with an open invitation to readers:
“The sky's the limit!”

faq.q: What is I Say, You Say about?
faq.a: It is a call-and-response picture book by Lola Brooks. A grown-up says an affirmation, a child says it back, and both say it again. Twelve affirmations build to the central message, You Matter, and the book ends with everyone saying We matter together.

faq.q: What age is I Say, You Say for?
faq.a: Ages 2 to 7: toddlers, preschoolers and children in kindergarten and the early grades. Each line is only a few words long, so a child who cannot read yet can still echo it by ear, and an early reader can read the child's part alone.

faq.q: What affirmations are in the book?
faq.a: They are, in order: I love you; I believe in you; You are destined for great things; Don't give up; I'm so proud of you; You are purposed; You are wanted; You are seen; You are loved; You are important; You are wonderfully and beautifully made; and You Matter. The closing chorus is We matter.

faq.q: Can it help build a child's self-esteem?
faq.a: That is what the book is for. Every page tells a child they are loved, wanted, seen and important, and the call-and-response pattern has the child say those words out loud, not only hear them. The book is a read-aloud, not a self-help program.

faq.q: Is it a good read-aloud for preschool and kindergarten?
faq.a: Yes. It is short, the pattern is easy to follow, and a whole class can answer together. The book's own page of ideas suggests adding the affirmations to a classroom Morning Meeting.

faq.q: Can teachers use it for social emotional learning?
faq.a: Yes. The author, a teacher, suggests a Stand up, Pair up routine in which students echo the teacher's affirmations. The book says that with time, children feel more comfortable using the words in other classroom situations.

faq.q: Is it a Christian book with Bible affirmations?
faq.a: It is published by a Christian publisher and closes with Psalm 139:4 from the New International Version: “Before a word is on my tongue you, LORD, know it completely.” The affirmations themselves are simple words of love and worth, and they are not each tied to a verse.

faq.q: Does it tell a child they are wonderfully made?
faq.a: Yes. One of the twelve affirmations is You are wonderfully and beautifully made. The grown-up says it, the child says it back, and then both say it again.

faq.q: Is it a good bedtime book?
faq.a: It works well at bedtime. It is not a story with a plot. It is a short back-and-forth of loving words, and one of its later pages shows a child tucked in under the covers, so it is easy to read as the last thing before lights out.

audience.headline: A journal that talks to a young reader like a friend: it asks questions, shares its own story and promises to listen.
audience.body: For tweens and young teens discovering who they are, adopted and foster children, kids from hard family situations, young readers learning to name anger and fear, and the parents, youth leaders, counselors and orphan care ministries who want something to work through with them. The narrator, Tanya, introduces herself on the first page and talks to the reader throughout. Most pages are questions with space to write or draw, plus coloring pages, a family tree, birthday and gratitude lists, daily plans and mood trackers. A note on subjects: Tanya tells the reader that her father became cruel when she was eight, and the journal invites readers to write about what is hard at home and about people who treat them badly. Several pages can be torn out to keep them private. The book prints no age range.

quote.text: “Don't be ashamed even if your emotions are not good because we are here to deal with them.”
quote.cite: Who Am I?, the opening letter from Tanya

what_makes.title: What makes this journal a friend on paper
paras: The journal opens with a letter: "Hi, let me introduce myself." Tanya says she needs a friend too, that she is dealing with some stuff in her own life, and that she will share it in these pages. Then she promises that everything you talk about will stay between you.
Five things set it apart:
list: It talks with the reader, not at them. Questions run from what you like to eat to the scariest moment you remember, and Tanya answers some of them about herself.
It teaches feelings in plain steps. Pages name emotions, track your mood, and give rules like using words instead of yelling, taking three deep breaths and asking for help.
It is honest about family. There is a family tree, but also a page to choose what is hard at home, a letter to someone in your family and Tanya's own story of a father who became cruel.
It protects privacy. Pages about anger, fear and people who hurt you carry a note that you can rip the page out if you are afraid someone will see it.
It keeps pointing to God. Short prayers and verses from Genesis, Lamentations, Matthew, Ephesians and 1 John tell the reader they were created in God's image and that Jesus will never leave them.

sections.h2: For young people who want to know themselves
paras: The first section asks for three good qualities and three bad ones, what people say about you and what you think God will say. Later sections cover what you like to do, your friends, your dreams for this year and for age twenty, and your biggest fears.

sections.h2: For kids from hard places
paras: Tanya does not pretend every family is safe. She asks, "Is your family safe?" and "Is your father protecting you?" and tells how long it took her to believe God is a good Father when her own dad was cruel. She also tells the reader that only strong people can truly say they are sorry.

sections.h2: For parents, foster parents and mentors
paras: The journal works well with a trusted adult nearby. Pages invite the reader to seek advice from parents, talk to someone they trust and pray together. The back pages add yearly goal sheets, daily planners, anger button worksheets and extra mood trackers to keep the conversation going.

sections.h2: For kids who love to write and draw
paras: There are coloring pages, places to draw your family and your friend, a list of movies you like, a chore rating from one to ten and a page of easy ideas: invent a new milkshake, plant a vegetable garden, make a playlist, learn to skateboard.

details.Author: Tetiana Kurylo

paras: In the Friends section, Tanya tells the reader about her own childhood. She had a lot of friends and a lot of fun, and problems at home because her dad was not a kind man. Her friends helped. When she was sad, they made her laugh. Then she asks the reader what they feel when they think about their own friends, and adds that Jesus is a best friend who will never leave.

My Fears starts honestly. Tanya admits that when she is scared she can yell, get mad, say bad words and hurt people, and that she is learning to control her fear. The page asks the reader to circle what they do: yell, fight, run away, get silent, cry. Then come steps to stop, name what is wrong and tell the other person how you feel. She ends with good news:
"The most important thing I want to tell you is that we are all afraid and adults are afraid, too."

stories.h2: A prayer for when you are not sure
paras: Twice the journal offers a short prayer for a reader who does not yet trust God. It does not ask them to pretend:
"God, I do not know if you are kind, but I want to believe that you are. I want to know what plans you have for my life."

author.bio: Tetiana Kurylo writes to young readers as Tanya, a friend who shares her own story. In the journal she tells of a childhood full of friends who made her laugh when she was sad, a father who became cruel when she was eight, a sister she often fought with, and the many years it took her to believe God is a good Father. Who Am I? is the fourth of her journals.

why.title: Why this journal exists
paras: Tanya says she has learned from her friendships with young people that everyone's past shapes their present. She wrote the journal to be the friend she needed. Her opening letter says:
"Like you, I am in need of a friend."
And the last section ends with a promise:
"We will share more stories together because this is only the beginning!"

faq.q: What is Who Am I? by Tetiana Kurylo?
faq.a: It is a guided Christian journal for young readers, written as a conversation with a friendly narrator named Tanya. It has eight sections of questions, drawing and coloring pages, mood trackers and tools for handling emotions. It is not the children's picture book of the same title by another author.

faq.q: Does it help kids with self-esteem?
faq.a: Yes. It tells readers they were created in God's image and are valuable, asks them to write one positive thing about themselves and to say they are awesome out loud in the mirror each morning, and teaches that words that do not line up with God's thoughts are lies.

faq.q: Does it help kids understand their feelings?
faq.a: Yes. What I Feel names emotions with pictures, gives mood trackers and offers ways to understand anger, such as going outside, counting to ten, asking yourself why you feel that way and talking to someone you trust.

faq.q: What does it say about fear?
faq.a: It lists types of fear, such as fear of rejection and fear of the unknown, explains three responses to fear (fight, run away or freeze) and gives rules to calm down. It quotes 1 John 4:18 and tells readers God's love is bigger than any fear.

faq.q: Is it good for adopted or foster children?
faq.a: It can be. The author writes for children from hard family situations and is honest about her own. Pages ask whether home is safe, give space to name what is hard and allow private pages to be torn out. A trusted adult nearby is a good idea.

faq.q: Does it teach kids who they are in Christ?
faq.a: Yes. Me and God uses Genesis 1:26 and Ephesians 1:4 to tell readers they were made in God's image and chosen in love, and earlier pages call Jesus a friend who will never leave them.

faq.q: Is it part of a series?
faq.a: Yes. It is the fourth of Tetiana Kurylo's journals. The others are My Way to Adoption and Becoming a Family, for adoptive parents, and Finding Yourself, a journal in English and Russian for adopted children that uses the same friendly narrator.

audience.headline: A journal for a child who has a past before this family, from a narrator who knows what it is to be told you are a nobody.
audience.body: For adopted and foster children, tweens working out who they are, Russian-speaking children still learning English, and the adoptive and foster parents, counselors, children's ministry leaders and grandparents who care for them. Every prompt is printed in English with a Russian translation beside it. The narrator, Tanya, introduces herself, promises to listen and keep everything confidential, and tells her own story along the way. Pages ask where the child lived before and where they live now, what they felt when they joined their new family and who they like most there. A note on subjects: Tanya says her father beat her and told her she was a nobody, and the journal invites children to write to the parents they had before adoption about being left and hurt. Those pages can be torn out to keep them private. The book prints no age range.

quote.text: “I want you to understand that it is not your fault your family chose to leave you.”
quote.cite: Finding Yourself, Family

what_makes.title: What makes this journal for adopted children
paras: It is written for a child whose story did not start with this family. Questions ask about life before, the happiest and scariest moments of childhood, and what it felt like to arrive. Then the journal says what many adopted children need to hear, more than once: it is not your fault.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is in two languages. Each prompt appears in English with the Russian beside it, so a child still learning English and the family who loves them can both use it.
It talks like a friend. Tanya shares her own story, admits her own fears and promises that everything the reader writes will stay between them.
It makes room for the first family. A letter page invites the child to write to a friend or to the parents they had before adoption about what they felt when they were left.
It teaches feelings in plain steps. Rules like use words, ask for help and say thank you sit beside steps for anger and fear and a chart showing how a conflict grows.
It ends with who you are. Me and God tells the reader they were made in God's image, have a purpose for their life and will find the answers when they search.

sections.h2: For adopted and foster children
paras: Family asks the hardest questions gently. Who is your family? What is hard for you: they don't understand me, I think I am bad, life in America, I don't feel like I belong? The journal answers with encouragement to stay: building relationships is hard, but you can do it.

sections.h2: For Russian-speaking children and bilingual families
paras: Because every prompt is printed in both English and Russian, a child can answer in the language that comes easiest, and a parent can read along. It was clearly made with Russian-speaking children in mind.

sections.h2: For adoptive parents
paras: The journal gives a child words for things that are hard to say out loud. Pages on emotions, fears and the first family open conversations, and the private pages can be torn out, so a child can write freely. Parents should know the book offers the child that choice.

sections.h2: For counselors and children's ministries
paras: The structure is simple and repeatable: questions, a short word from Tanya, a fun break after the hard parts, and a verse or prayer. The back pages add goals for the year, daily plans and mood trackers.

details.Title: Finding Yourself
details.Subtitle: I'm God's Kid, and Like Nobody Else
details.Author: Tetiana Kurylo

stories.h2: The answer that took ten years
paras: Early in the journal, Tanya tells the reader that her dad said she was a nobody and that he did not love her, and that she believed him for a long time. Everyone told her God loved her, but she asked why a kind God would give her such a father. She looked for the answer for ten years. Then, she writes, God told her that her dad chose the way he lived, that He could not force him, that it hurt Him to see it, and that He is not the same kind of father. She writes what happened next:
"I believed him and then everything began to change in my life."

The Family section asks the reader to do something out loud. After explaining that God designed us to grow in a family, Tanya writes that it is not the child's fault their family chose to leave, and asks them to say it now: "It is not my fault." Then she explains why it matters for the new family too: without facing the past, it is hard to build a good relationship with the people who are here now.

stories.h2: A friend who was broken too
paras: In Friends, Tanya admits she was not always a good friend, because people had hurt her and she could not trust anyone. Then she found someone who helped her and healed her broken heart. She hopes the reader finds Him too, and invites them along:
"Let's journey together! I promise, it will be fun!"

author.bio: Tetiana Kurylo writes to young readers as Tanya, a friend who shares her own story. In the journal she tells of a childhood full of friends, a father who hurt her and told her she was a nobody, and the ten years it took to hear God say He is a different kind of father. Finding Yourself is the third of her journals and the one written for adopted children, in English and Russian.

why.title: Why this journal exists
paras: Tanya says she looked for herself for a long time, thinking she was what her past and other people said about her. She wrote this journal so a child in the same place would not search alone. She tells them:
"I can tell you one thing: you have a purpose for your life!"
The journal opens with the question "Looking for yourself?" Its last pages answer it:
"Now I know who I am."

faq.q: What is Finding Yourself?
faq.a: It is a guided Christian journal for adopted children by Tetiana Kurylo, printed in English with a Russian translation of every prompt. A friendly narrator named Tanya asks questions, shares her own story and helps the reader understand their past, their feelings and their new family.

faq.q: Is it written for adopted children?
faq.a: Yes. It asks where the child lived before and where they live now, what they felt when they joined their new family and what is hard about it, and it gives a letter page for the parents they had before adoption. It repeats that what happened is not their fault.

faq.q: Is the journal in Russian?
faq.a: It is in English and Russian. Every prompt and most of Tanya's notes appear in English with a Russian translation, so it works for Russian-speaking children who are still learning English.

faq.q: Does it help with self-esteem?
faq.a: Yes. It asks the reader to draw or write positive things about themselves, tells them they are awesome and were created in God's image, and says that what God thinks of them is the truth, not the bad things people said.

faq.q: Does it help a child deal with fear of rejection?
faq.a: It names fear of rejection among the fears a child might feel, explains that we fight, run away or freeze when we are scared, and gives steps to calm down, use words and ask for help. The Family section speaks directly to a child who does not feel they belong.

faq.q: Does it teach kids who they are in God?
faq.a: Yes. Me and God uses Genesis 1:26 to tell the reader they were made in God's image, tells them they have a purpose for their life, and uses Matthew 7:8 to promise that those who search will find.

faq.q: Is it part of a series?
faq.a: Yes. It is the third of Tetiana Kurylo's journals. Who Am I? is a similar journal for young readers in English only, and My Way to Adoption and Becoming a Family are written for adoptive parents.

hero.audience_line: For Telugu readers in India and around the world who want to rest in God instead of working for Him, and for pastors, leaders and churches serving Telugu-speaking believers.
hero.tagline: The Telugu edition of Only God Works, printed as దేవుడు మాత్రమే పనిచేస్తాడు. A minister of nearly forty years shows from Scripture that God calls you to Himself, and to rest while He works through you.

audience.headline: Only God Works in Telugu: the same ten short chapters, from Called to Finished, for readers who think and pray in Telugu.
audience.body: This is the Telugu translation of Only God Works by Kevin White. Its message is the one he says set him free after ten years as a workaholic for God: God has called you to Himself, not to do His work for Him. The book walks through ten words, with Scripture throughout, and shows how rest leads to more fruit, not less. The whole book, including the Scripture passages, is printed in Telugu script. A note on subjects: the author is frank about burnout, illness from overwork and being voted out as a pastor, and one chapter uses the intimacy of a bride and groom as a picture of closeness with God. It is written for adults.

quote.text: దేవుడు మాత్రమే పనిచేస్తాడు !
quote.cite: Only God Works (Telugu edition), Introduction

what_makes.title: What makes this edition for Telugu readers
paras: The Telugu edition keeps the book's opening scene. It asks you to imagine the day after you die, in a heaven where nothing was made by human hands, and where people from many nations thank you because God worked through your giving, your mission trips and your prayers. Then it asks who is really doing the work.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is the whole book in Telugu, with the same ten chapters, the conclusion and the author's personal letter.
Its chapter titles still read as one sentence. In Telugu they begin పిలువబడుట (Called), కేవలం (Only), దేవుడు (God) and పని (Work).
It names a half-truth. God has called you, the author writes, and the enemy adds two words: to work.
It comes from a hard story. The author tells of overwork, being dismissed by his church, and a trip to India in 1998 that changed how he lived.
It looks to the finish line. The last chapter is about the 10/40 window and the people who still have little or no access to know about Jesus.

sections.h2: For Telugu-speaking believers who are worn out
paras: Chapter 5, స్వేచ్ఛ (Freedom), reads God's promise of rest in Hebrews 4 and Psalm 23 and says that freedom from work means freedom to rest. Resting, the author adds, does not mean being lazy or useless.

sections.h2: For pastors and church leaders
paras: The author writes that many pastors and leaders have left the ministry because of the lie that God called them to work for Him. A pastor or leader who serves in Telugu can hand this edition to the people in their care.

sections.h2: For families and churches who read in more than one language
paras: The Telugu edition follows the English book chapter for chapter, so a family or a small group can read Only God Works side by side in English and in Telugu.

sections.h2: For anyone who wants their life to count in eternity
paras: The subtitle is Investing Now What Matters Then. The closing chapter talks about the Great Commission and the people who have never held a Bible, and the book ends with a personal letter and a prayer from the author for the reader.

details.Title: Only God Works
details.Subtitle: (Telugu) Investing Now What Matters Then
details.Author: Kevin White

paras: The introduction asks you to imagine heaven. Nothing there was made by human hands. Your yard and the work on your house are not there. Instead, people you have never met, many from other nations, tell you how God worked through your tithes, offerings, mission trips and prayers to bring them to Jesus.
మీరు చనిపోయిన మరుసటి రోజు అని ఊహించుకోండి.

In Chapter 4 the author tells how, in 1998, God took him to India and showed him Christ followers without basic necessities, most without Bibles, who still passionately pursued God's presence. On the plane home he committed to pursue the presence of God every day for the rest of his life. Chapter 9 tells the harder story around it: a church he built while working up to ninety hours a week, a vote that dismissed him, and a stranger who told him he had not been fired but set free.

Chapter 10, Finished, describes the 10/40 window, the region of North Africa, the Middle East and Asia where most people with little or no access to know about Jesus live, including many in India. It reads Matthew 24:14 as God's finish line and Revelation 7 as a picture of every nation worshiping together, and says only God can finish the work.

author.bio: Kevin White experienced God's call into full-time vocational ministry at seventeen and has served in full-time Christian ministry for nearly forty years. After a decade as what he calls a workaholic for God, he found freedom in Christ and started With Love From Jesus Ministries and Global Hope India. He has been to India more than fifty times, taking 1,000 people on mission trips. He is CEO of Spirit Media and the author of Audacious Generosity, Get to the Point and What's Your Word?
