publisher.about: Spirit Media Publishing is a Christian publishing and marketing company with a vision to reveal our Father's heart to all nations. It offers full-service book creation and publishing in paperback, hardback, digital and audiobook formats, along with children's titles, compact Express Books, website design and SEO, and podcast and video production. We are glad to publish Only God Works in Telugu, as part of carrying its message to the nations.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: Only God Works was the first book the author wrote, twenty-five years before it was published, and he says it was written more for himself than for the world. His personal letter at the end calls the message a matter of life or death for billions of people far from God, and says the revelation that only God works saved his life.
The book's own pages say Spirit Media is committed to sharing the Good News of Jesus in all 195 nations of the world. The Telugu edition carries that message to readers in their own language.

faq.q: What is this book?
faq.a: It is the Telugu edition of Only God Works by Kevin White, printed under the title దేవుడు మాత్రమే పనిచేస్తాడు. It teaches that God has never called us to work for Him, but to intimacy with Him, and to let Him work in and through us.

faq.q: What are the chapters?
faq.a: They are, in order: Called; Only; God; Work; Freedom; Intimacy; Humility; Gratitude; Fruit; and Finished. An introduction comes first, and a conclusion and a letter from the author close the book.

faq.q: Is it a Telugu Christian book?
faq.a: Yes. It is a Christian teaching book printed entirely in Telugu script, for Telugu-speaking believers, pastors and churches.

faq.q: Does it quote the Bible in Telugu?
faq.a: Yes. The Scripture passages are given in Telugu. It is a book about the Bible's teaching, not a Bible itself.

faq.q: Does it tell the story of the prodigal son?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 4 quotes Luke 15 in full and turns to the older brother, who stayed home working for something that was already his. The author says many of us are like him.

faq.q: What does it say about God's love?
faq.a: It says God wants you, not your work, and that from Genesis to Revelation the Bible shows a loving Heavenly Father pursuing His children. The author writes that God would love him the same if he did not do one more thing for Him.

faq.q: Is it a book about resting in God?

paras: In Time-Management, the author points to Daniel, who took time to pray every day even with threats of being cast into a den of lions. He imagines a reader objecting that people did throw Daniel among hungry lions, and answers that no harm came to him and that he prospered in the kingdom.
His conclusion is short: "There are always rewards attached to prioritizing properly."

Near the end of Proper Investment of Time, the author admits the chapter may feel a bit harsh, since choosing where to invest time can change some relationships. Then he points to Jesus, who was sent to die for sinners and yet spent the majority of His ministry with twelve men. There were others with them, the author notes, but the secrets of the Kingdom were shared with the twelve.
Just before that, he tells readers to look for the people they may have overlooked, and to write them in:
"Pencil these people into your calendar. Be intentional with these relationships. They could represent your legacy."

In the first chapter the author points to Isaiah 38, where God turned the shadow on the sundial of Ahaz backward ten degrees because Hezekiah asked. He notes that there are several theories about how it happened, and warns that attempting to explain it can lead some to doubt God. He puts it simply, that faith requires no explanation, and then asks the reader whether they have faith that God can help with their time, even in supernatural ways.

After the chapter on idioms, he says why he wrote it at all:

faq.q: Is the book written about military service?

faq.q: Is it a good Veterans Day gift?

faq.q: Does it address PTSD?

faq.q: Does it include a prayer for soldiers?
faq.a: No. It includes one prayer, in Setting Your Time Straight, and it is about time: it asks the Father to forgive wasted time and to help you invest as much of it as possible in Him and in others.

faq.q: Can a veterans' group or men's Bible study use it?

paras: The author's stated hope is simple. He wants you to see that your time is precious, that no one can replace it, and that God belongs at the top of the list. He puts it as a prayer:
“My prayer is that this booklet will help you recognize and realize that you are a potential success.”
After the chapter on idioms, he says why he wrote it at all:
“My prayer is that we will not neglect what is so valuable and be better stewards of our precious time.”

faq.q: Is it written specifically for volunteers?
faq.a: Not only. The Special Edition for Volunteers has its own cover, edition name and ISBN, but the words inside are the same as in the other Your Time editions. It is written for any Christian, though two chapters, Gifts of Time and Time Management Misconceptions, speak directly to people who give their time.

faq.q: What does it say about volunteering at church?
faq.a: That it is good, and that it is not enough on its own. The author counted the volunteers in his home church and found that 36 percent give their time. He says many churchgoers think church is the best or only place to give time, and he urges readers to give it outside the church as well.

faq.q: Does it encourage serving others outside the church?
faq.a: Yes. The author says there may be a whole world out there that is not getting the time investment it needs from people in the church. He suggests visits, help and phone calls, and points to Cornelius, who made time to visit his family and friends.

faq.q: Is it about mission trips?
faq.a: No. It does not discuss mission trips. It does note that most of us may not be able to travel on short notice as Peter did in Acts 10, but that we may be able to visit someone as Cornelius did, with a little planning and time.

faq.q: Is it a good Christian gift to thank volunteers?
faq.a: It is made to be given. It is short, 60 pages in a 4 x 6 inch size, and its subtitle calls time the greatest gift you receive and give. It is a short Christian reflection on time, not a volunteer handbook.

faq.q: Is it a book on biblical stewardship of time?
faq.a: Yes. The closing prayer asks God for help to be a better steward of your time, and the last Take a Moment to Focus question asks what changes you can make to be one. The book draws on Isaiah 38, Daniel 6, Luke 18, Acts 10 and Psalm 39.

faq.q: Does it help with work-life balance?
faq.a: Some of it. It does not use that phrase. It says we tend to fit God, family and others in at the end of the day, and asks you to plan everything else around those three. For volunteers it also says plainly that a yes to one person or situation is a no to someone or something else.

faq.q: Does it have questions for discussion?
faq.a: Yes. Each of the nine chapters ends with a Take a Moment to Focus question and space to write. One asks: Are you spending your time for the right reasons, instead of just following the crowd? A volunteer team could take one question per meeting.

hero.audience_line: For believers who sometimes struggle to trust God in hard situations, seekers who sense there is a God and want to reach Him, and anyone who wants a daily devotional that ends in action.
hero.tagline: Sixty short devotions with true stories from a pastor's wife, a month of daily faith steps, Scripture to build your faith and a log book to record how God answers.

audience.headline: A pastor's wife who learned faith through a car chase, a long wait and a coworker who would not stop talking about God hands you sixty devotions and a month of steps to take.
audience.body: For church members and believers growing in faith, new Christians, seekers who are not sure how to reach God, believers facing trials, and small groups, Bible classes and women's and men's ministries that want something practical. Nora Fozard writes plainly and warmly. Each devotion opens with a short saying about faith and a Bible verse, most often from the Amplified Bible, then a page or two of teaching and, often, a story from her own life. A short glossary explains words like confess, faith, Savior and sin, so readers from any church background can follow. A note on subjects: the stories include a miscarriage, a hard early marriage and prayer for the sick. The book teaches confessing God's promises out loud and expecting healing, and it is written from a Spirit-filled point of view that expects miracles today.

quote.text: “Faith is like breathing. You can’t live without it.”
quote.cite: Faith in Action, Faith: A Daily Journey

what_makes.title: What makes this book a devotional you act on
paras: The introduction names two readers: the believer who knows God is with them but lacks the faith to believe Him, and the seeker who realizes there is a God and wants relief from trying situations. The book is built to move both from reading to doing.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is five books in one. Sixty daily reflections, a month of faith steps, a collection of Scripture, a personal log book and a closing list of things to remember.
Every devotion starts with a saying you can carry. "Faith never walks without leaving landmarks." "Faith never tries, it does." Each is paired with a Bible verse printed in full.
The stories are true and close to home. A night chase on the road to Pittsboro, stolen coats returned to a church bus, a man with gout who handed over his cane.
It explains its words. A Few Words About Words defines confess, faith, Savior and sin, and pictures human faith and the God kind of faith with a piece of bubble gum.
It asks you to write. The log book gives nine lists of ten lines each, from what you are believing God for to your answered prayers, so you can look back and see what God has done.

sections.h2: For believers who want a daily devotional
paras: The first section gives sixty different messages, which the author says is enough for two months of devotions. Each one fits on two or three pages: a saying, a verse, a short teaching and often a story. It works with a cup of coffee in the morning or at the end of the day.

sections.h2: For anyone whose faith is being tested
paras: Many of the devotions are about waiting. Nora writes about holding on to a promise through a miscarriage, two years of waiting and voices at church that said the answer would be different. Her point is simple: faith is never shaken by circumstances or delays, and God is always on time.

sections.h2: For new Christians and seekers
paras: Because churches use words differently, the book stops to explain them. Confess means saying out loud what you believe. Savior is the one who rescues us from sin. The tone is kind, not churchy, and the introduction speaks directly to the person who is still looking for God.

sections.h2: For small groups and ministries
paras: The Faith in Action section can be used as a month-long faith challenge, one page a day. Each page ends with a step headed Your Faith in Action: tell a friend about God's goodness, make someone smile, read the Bible through in a year, take time to dance before the Lord. Those steps make easy discussion starters for a class or women's or men's group.

details.Title: Faith in Action
details.Subtitle: Expanded and Updated for the 21st Century Church
details.Author: Nora Fozard

paras: About twenty people took a bus to an all-night prayer meeting. They carried their Bibles inside and left their coats and pocketbooks locked on the bus. In the morning everything was gone: wallets, credit cards, coats. They went back into the church and prayed that the person would put it all back. The next day, every bit of it was back on the bus. Nora writes:
"God didn’t overlook or forget our love for Him and our service toward all His saints."

stories.h2: The cane on the church wall
paras: Going house to house to pray for people, Nora and a friend met a man leaning on a cane who said he did not need God right then. He thought again and asked for prayer for his gout. They laid hands on him and anointed him with oil, and she writes that the swelling went down and he ran around the house. He gave them the cane, and the church hung it on the wall with other medical aids that healed people no longer needed. They called them their "hanging trophies."

stories.h2: The prayer she forgot she prayed
paras: Nora married young, had children back to back and drifted from church. She told God out loud that she would not stay in a marriage like the one she had. A few months later her husband enrolled in Bible college and began treating her with kindness, which made her angry. Then God reminded her of what she had prayed. She writes:
"God’s faith was bigger than mine."

author.bio: Nora Fozard was a young bride struggling to help support her family when a coworker pointed her to deeper faith in Jesus, and her husband, a contractor, went to Bible college. Today the Fozards lead Mt. Zion Christian Church in Durham, North Carolina. She has degrees from Oral Roberts and Liberty universities. She and her husband have eight children and numerous grandchildren and great-grandchildren who join them in serving God.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: Nora says her own life changed because one man at work kept speaking faith to her, day after day. She wants to do the same for you. The introduction says it plainly:
"May you find the strength that you need by putting your Faith in action!"
The conclusion gives the reason underneath it:
"Let us as Christians, learn to trust God more, and watch Him bring things to pass in our lives."

faq.q: What is Faith in Action about?
faq.a: It is a Christian devotional and faith-building workbook by Nora Fozard. It moves from reading about faith to living it: sixty short devotions with true stories, a month of daily faith steps, Scripture to build your faith, a log book to record how God answers and a list of short encouragements.

faq.q: Is Faith in Action a daily devotional?
faq.a: Yes. The first section has sixty daily reflections, which the author says is enough for two months of devotions. The second section adds a month of daily faith steps you can use as a thirty-day challenge or one at a time.

faq.q: What is faith, according to the book?
faq.a: The book names two kinds. Human faith is the confidence we have in the outcome of our actions. The God kind of faith is a gift from God. In the bubble gum picture, human faith chews and blows, and the God kind of faith is the gum itself. Without it, there are no bubbles.

faq.q: What does the book say about faith without works?
faq.a: It quotes James 2:20, "faith without works is dead," and gives examples of what the author calls dead works: praying but not acting, asking for prayer but refusing to change. Her answer is that faith is a way of life, and that God sets the same choice before us every day.

faq.q: Does it help with trusting God in hard times?
faq.a: Yes. Many devotions are about waiting and trouble: faith that is never shaken by circumstances or delays, faith that can stand the storms of life. The stories include a miscarriage and a long wait, a night chase and stolen belongings returned after prayer.

faq.q: Does the book include prayer journal pages?
faq.a: Some. Your Personal Faith in Action Log Book has nine lists with ten lines each. They are, in order: My Own Faith in Action List; My What I'm Believing God For List; My What I Need to Pray About List; My Answered Prayer List; My Who I Won to Christ List; My Never to Forget List; My Confession List; My Giving List; and My Alleluia List. The author suggests keeping a separate notebook as the answered prayers grow.

faq.q: Is it a devotional for women?
faq.a: The back cover calls it a prayer journal for women, and a few devotions speak to women directly. Most of the book is written for any believer, and its stories and steps work just as well for men.

faq.q: What does the book teach about walking by faith?
faq.a: One devotion is titled with it: doubt and unbelief are contagious, so stay away and walk by faith. The book's last encouragement says walking by faith is an everyday journey, and asks you not to let fear stop you from reaching your destiny.

hero.audience_line: For police officers, deputies, troopers, dispatchers and corrections officers, for the families and chaplains who stand behind them, and for any Christian working long shifts.
hero.tagline: A pocket-size Christian book on time for people whose days rarely go to plan: God first, then family and others, in nine brief chapters with a question after each and a prayer to pray aloud.

audience.headline: No shift goes exactly to schedule. This short book starts from that fact, and asks who still gets your time when the day is taken by things you did not plan.
audience.body: For people in law enforcement and the families who wait up for them. Daniel W. Evans writes about time from a biblical point of view in nine short chapters: God as the One who controls it, the calendars and clocks we use to monitor it, and how to put God, family and others ahead of everything else on the list. Each chapter ends with an honest question to write about. A note on this edition: the words inside are the same in every special edition of Your Time. This one carries a cover and edition name for law enforcement, but the book does not describe police work. It is a short Christian reflection on time, not a peer-support or counseling guide.

quote.text: “While family, friends, and circumstances may force themselves upon us, God will not.”
quote.cite: Your Time, Time-Management

what_makes.title: What makes this edition for law enforcement
paras: This is the law enforcement edition of a book about time. The text is the same as in every other Your Time edition, and it does not mention officers or policing. What it does offer is a plain look at unplanned days, at time owed to family, and at giving your time to people who need help, all things an officer knows well.
Five things set it apart:
list: It fits a uniform pocket or a duty bag. At 60 pages in a 4 x 6 inch size, each chapter is a few pages long.
It admits the day will not go to plan. The author writes that unforeseen situations can bombard us on any given day, at work, at home, traveling, or with an emergency involving family or a friend.
It keeps family on the list. God, family and others, the author says, are the things to plan everything else around, not to tack on at the end.
It takes waiting seriously. In the chapter on idioms he notes that some people wait to be courteous, but others wait because they really need the help.
It closes with a prayer. Setting Your Time Straight is a short prayer to pray aloud, asking for help to invest your time in God and others.

sections.h2: For officers whose shifts run long
paras: The Time-Management chapter says we are the best managers of our own time, and that each of us still has trouble managing it. It names the interruptions that take a day apart, and says the answer is to put the most important things first rather than fit them in at the end.

sections.h2: For spouses and families at home
paras: The author notes that not even our own family members know every little detail of our day. One of his Take a Moment to Focus questions asks whether you are spending enough time with family, friends and others. A family could read that chapter together.

sections.h2: For police chaplains and men's and women's Bible studies
paras: Each of the nine chapters ends with a question and space to write, and the book closes with a prayer. That makes it easy to use as a short study, one chapter a week, without any special training.

paras: The book's subtitle calls time the greatest gift you receive and give. A short book with a prayer in it is easy to hand to an officer. It is a reflection on time and priorities, and it does not claim to replace counseling or peer support.

paras: In Time-Management, the author points to Daniel, who took time to pray every day even with threats of being cast into a den of lions. He imagines a reader objecting that people did throw Daniel among hungry lions, and answers that no harm came to him and that he prospered in the kingdom.
His conclusion is short: "There are always rewards attached to prioritizing properly."

In Time Idioms, the author picks one phrase we say without thinking and asks what it means to the person who asked for help. When we say give me a second, he writes, we are asking them to wait until we are able or ready to respond.
"Most wait to be courteous, but others wait because they really need the help."
He lists six more sayings, from killing time to it's about time, and says the point is not to find fault but to see how often we waste time without noticing.

In Gifts of Time, the author looks at Jesus stopping on the way to Jerusalem to bless children, and at Cornelius, who did not check his schedule or put off sending for Peter. He says God speaks for one of two reasons, to make us a blessing to someone or to give us a blessing, and he wonders whether our schedules are so tight that we would miss it.

author.bio: Daniel W. Evans is a Christian author who says that he has traveled through the states as an evangelist and listened to many pastors talk about church growth. In Your Time he writes from that experience and from his home church in Durham, North Carolina, where he counted how many members give their time as volunteers and found the figure to be 36 percent. He uses Scripture and personal observation to urge readers to put God first and to steward every hour well. The back of the book describes two other offerings from him: a one-day process in five steps, and A Commitment to Unleash Your Leader Potential, a program for the leader in each of us.

paras: In Gifts of Time, the author notices something easy to skip in Acts 10. Cornelius not only sent for Peter at once. He also made the time to visit his family and friends, and invited them to his house to hear what Peter would say. Peter, for his part, invited the men Cornelius sent to stay overnight, and went with them the next day, both against the customs he was raised in.
The author says most of us may not be able to travel on short notice as Peter did, but we may be able to visit as Cornelius did, with a little planning and time.

In Gifts of Time, the author looks at Jesus stopping on the way to Jerusalem to bless children, and at Cornelius, who did not check his schedule or put off sending for Peter. He says God speaks for one of two reasons, to make us a blessing to someone or to give us a blessing, and he wonders whether our schedules are so tight that we would miss it.
In Proper Investment of Time, he asks whether you are investing your time in the right people, and gives three steps. The first is to acknowledge that time is limited:
"Acknowledge that not only your money and energy, but also your time is a finite resource."

The second is to become aware of where it goes, since, as he puts it, your calendar will reveal the truth. The third is to change what needs to change, including activities that are unproductive or unhealthy.

faq.q: Is it a good gift for coworkers?
faq.a: Yes, for most offices. The book is general and short. A few pages speak to work, such as the unplanned day and business owners who spend most of their time on under-performing employees. It does not assume anything about the reader's job.

faq.q: Does it help with work-life balance?

hero.audience_line: For Nagamese readers in Nagaland and Northeast India who want to rest in God instead of working for Him, and for pastors, leaders and churches serving Nagamese-speaking believers.

audience.headline: Only God Works in Nagamese: the same ten short chapters, from Called to Finished, for readers who think and pray in Nagamese.
audience.body: This is the Nagamese translation of Only God Works by Kevin White. Its message is the one he says set him free after ten years as a workaholic for God: God has called you to Himself, not to do His work for Him. The book walks through ten words, with Scripture throughout, and shows how rest leads to more fruit, not less. Most of the book is in Nagamese, written in Latin letters. A few passages, the closing prayer and some notes from Spirit Media are printed in English, as they are in the original. A note on subjects: the author is frank about burnout, illness from overwork and being voted out as a pastor, and one chapter uses the intimacy of a bride and groom as a picture of closeness with God. It is written for adults.

quote.text: Khali Esor hi kaam kurae!
quote.cite: Only God Works (Nagamese edition), Introduction

what_makes.title: What makes this edition for Nagamese readers
paras: The Nagamese edition keeps the book's opening scene. It asks you to imagine the day after you die, in a heaven where nothing was made by human hands, and where people from many nations thank you because God worked through your giving, your mission trips and your prayers. Then it asks who is really doing the work.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is the whole book in Nagamese, with the same ten chapters, the conclusion and the author's personal letter.
Its chapter titles still read as one sentence. In Nagamese they begin Called, Khali (Only), Esor (God) and Kaam (Work).
It names a half-truth. God has called you, the author writes, and the enemy adds two words: to work.
It comes from a hard story. The author tells of overwork, being dismissed by his church, and a trip to India in 1998 that changed how he lived.
It looks to the finish line. The last chapter is about the 10/40 window and the people who still have little or no access to know about Jesus.

sections.h2: For Nagamese-speaking believers who are worn out
paras: Chapter 5, Ajad (Freedom), reads God's promise of rest in Hebrews 4 and Psalm 23 and says that freedom from work means freedom to rest. Resting, the author adds, does not mean being lazy or useless.

sections.h2: For pastors and church leaders
paras: The author writes that many pastors and leaders have left the ministry because of the lie that God called them to work for Him. A pastor or leader who serves in Nagamese can hand this edition to the people in their care.

sections.h2: For families and churches who read in more than one language
paras: The Nagamese edition follows the English book chapter for chapter, so a family or a small group can read Only God Works side by side in English and in Nagamese.

paras: The introduction asks you to imagine heaven. Nothing there was made by human hands. Your yard and the work on your house are not there. Instead, people you have never met, many from other nations, tell you how God worked through your tithes, offerings, mission trips and prayers to bring them to Jesus.
Apni bhabna kuribi, ki aji toh apni muri jaa la dusra din ase.

In Chapter 4 the author tells how, in 1998, God took him to India and showed him Christ followers without basic necessities, most without Bibles, who still passionately pursued God's presence. On the plane home he committed to pursue the presence of God every day for the rest of his life. Chapter 9 tells the harder story around it: a church he built while working up to ninety hours a week, a vote that dismissed him, and a stranger who told him he had not been fired but set free.

Chapter 10, Finished, describes the 10/40 window, the region of North Africa, the Middle East and Asia where most people with little or no access to know about Jesus live, including many in India. It reads Matthew 24:14 as God's finish line and Revelation 7 as a picture of every nation worshiping together, and says only God can finish the work.

author.bio: Kevin White experienced God's call into full-time vocational ministry at seventeen and has served in full-time Christian ministry for nearly forty years. After a decade as what he calls a workaholic for God, he found freedom in Christ and started With Love From Jesus Ministries and Global Hope India. He has been to India more than fifty times, taking 1,000 people on mission trips. He is CEO of Spirit Media and the author of Audacious Generosity, Get to the Point and What's Your Word?

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: Only God Works was the first book the author wrote, twenty-five years before it was published, and he says it was written more for himself than for the world. His personal letter at the end calls the message a matter of life or death for billions of people far from God, and says the revelation that only God works saved his life.
The book's own pages say Spirit Media is committed to sharing the Good News of Jesus in all 195 nations of the world. The Nagamese edition carries that message to readers in their own language.

faq.q: What is this book?
faq.a: It is the Nagamese edition of Only God Works by Kevin White, printed under the title Khali Esor Hi Kaam Kurae. It teaches that God has never called us to work for Him, but to intimacy with Him, and to let Him work in and through us.

faq.q: What are the chapters?
faq.a: They are, in order: Called; Khali (Only); Esor (God); Kaam (Work); Ajad (Freedom); Intimacy; Humility; Gratitude; Fruit; and Finished. An introduction comes first, and a conclusion and a personal letter from the author close the book.

faq.q: Is the Bible quoted in Nagamese?
faq.a: Yes, for the most part. The Scripture passages are given in Nagamese with their NIV or NLT references. A few passages are printed in English, as in the original.

faq.q: Is it a book about resting in God?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 5, Ajad (Freedom), reads God's promise of rest in Hebrews 4 and says freedom from work means freedom to rest. The author says rest does not mean being useless or lazy.

faq.q: Does it teach intimacy with God?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 6 is about intimacy with God, and the book names intimacy, humility and gratitude as the three things God gives us to focus on.

faq.q: What does it say about faith and work?
faq.a: It says the work God wants done is a work only He can do, and that our part is to pursue His presence and follow His instructions. It does not tell readers to stop working or to become lazy.

faq.q: What does it say about bearing fruit?
faq.a: Chapter 9, Fruit, says only God produces fruit, and that fruit comes from intimacy with God, not from our own striving.

faq.q: Does it talk about the Great Commission?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 10, Finished, looks at the 10/40 window and the people with little or no access to know about Jesus, and the author's letter invites readers to be part of fulfilling the Great Commission.

hero.audience_line: For parents who are in the middle of an adoption and need a place to be honest about what they feel, and for the spouses, children and friends who share that home.
hero.tagline: A guided Christian journal for the hard and happy seasons after a child comes home, with eight parts of prompts, short teaching pages and the author's own story of mistakes and turnaround.

audience.headline: After sixteen years of serving orphans, the author packed up and walked away. This journal is what she learned when God turned her around.
audience.body: For adoptive and foster parents, newly formed and blended families, couples raising adopted children together, and the grandparents, pastors, counselors and church ministries who support them. Tetiana Kurylo writes from many years of work with orphans and from her own family, where she is a mother to four children and to her husband's two. The journal moves through eight parts, from naming where you are right now to your marriage, your other children, the days you feel done and your foundation in God. Short teaching pages sit between generous writing space. A note on subjects: the book speaks frankly about trauma, anger, rejection, guilt and marriages strained by adoption, and the author describes a father who drank and beat her family. It is a journal for parents, not a clinical guide.

quote.text: “Why do you carry a burden that is not yours?”
quote.cite: Becoming a Family, Part 1: My Turnaround Moment

what_makes.title: What makes this journal different
paras: It opens with an admission. Tetiana writes that she has worked with orphans for many years and made a lot of mistakes along the way, and still does sometimes. She asks you to be honest with what you feel, because accepting and loving others and ourselves is the hardest thing in life.
Five things set it apart:
list: It starts with you. Part 1 asks how you are feeling, what you are struggling with, where your spouse is emotionally and what you feel toward your child, before it says anything about the child.
It makes room for joy. My Happy Moments has pages for photos and small victories, like a child who said thank you after lunch.
It explains why children push back. When a traumatized child feels close to a parent, the book says, they feel vulnerable and shut down, and the closer you get the more they defend themselves.
It protects the marriage. Me and My Spouse warns that adoption brings pressure on a marriage and asks couples to keep their relationship a priority over any problem with the kids.
It is honest about guilt. I Am Done speaks to adoptive moms who feel they are not doing enough, and says plainly that you do more than a lot.

sections.h2: For parents in the middle of the process
paras: The opening letter says it: if you have this journal in your hands, you are in the adoption process. Each part gives prompts and lined space, so you can write through the hard days and look back on how far you have come.

sections.h2: For couples raising adopted children together
paras: The author writes that she has seen marriages destroyed because of adoption. Me and My Spouse asks you to list your partner's good qualities, write down what offends you, plan a romantic evening and keep talking before big decisions. She calls her own husband her biggest partner in her healing.

sections.h2: For families with biological children
paras: Me and My Kids is about the children who were already home. Their world gets turned upside down too. The book suggests asking them to write a letter about what they feel, explaining their new siblings' stories and planning time just with them: a walk, ice cream, a movie, cooking together.

sections.h2: For any parent who feels done
paras: Part 7 begins: we can feel that we can't do this, and that is okay. The author says it is normal, that it is a time to get help and take a break, and that you will be here many times because you are doing the hardest thing: choosing love.

paras: This is just to remind you that you are not dealing with ordinary kids, but kids with trauma, pain, anger, and sin.

paras: How did I receive healing? It was through people who loved me even when I did something wrong.

blocks.text: My Expectations reframes what success means:

paras: Success has different meanings in the language of adoption because here, it isn't measured by what our kids achieve, but what we have done for them.

This is just to remind you that you are not dealing with ordinary kids, but kids with trauma, pain, anger, and sin.
How did I receive healing? It was through people who loved me even when I did something wrong.
Success has different meanings in the language of adoption because here, it isn't measured by what our kids achieve, but what we have done for them.

details.Title: Becoming a Family
details.Subtitle: Keeping God As Your Co-Parent
details.Author: Tetiana Kurylo

paras: For a while, Tetiana writes, her story did not look like it would have a happy ending. Her children came to her traumatized, and she had so much pain inside that she was partly using them to find her own healing. In 2017, after sixteen years of serving orphans, she was done. She packed up, moved to New York and found a great job with a great family. In six months there, God changed her thinking. Her part was to love, help, teach and support, not to choose for the children. She writes:
"You can't imagine what a huge weight fell from my shoulders when I realized I'm only responsible for my part, and the way they choose to live is not my burden."

stories.h2: The boy with the bigger walls
paras: Working with some aged-out orphans, she had problems with one boy and was so mad at him. Then he told her his story. She writes that God spoke to her in that moment about his walls, and she gives what He said:
"His walls are much bigger than some other walls that you've seen, and you can either help me to tear down these walls or just stay away from them."

Children raised in emotional isolation, she explains, learned that crying and kindness were weakness. Still, they can surprise you. One of her boys received a Christmas present while she was away from Ukraine and kept the bags of candy for a month so he could share them with her. Once they feel safe, she says, they open.

author.bio: Tetiana Kurylo has worked with orphans for many years, including sixteen years of service before 2017, and writes from her own adoption story as well as that work. She is honest that the journey included many mistakes and a season of walking away, and that God changed the way she thought about love, responsibility and burdens. She now describes great relationships with her four children and her husband's two, and calls her husband her biggest partner in healing. She also writes from her own experience of Ukrainian culture. Becoming a Family is the second of her journals for adoptive families.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: Tetiana learned the hard way that parents cannot carry an adopted child's healing alone. She wrote this journal so they would not try. The opening letter says:
"Through it all, I've learned we have a Heavenly Father who knows what we need, and He has all the answers."
And it ends with the line the whole book keeps coming back to:
"Spend time seeking Him and His answers. You are not alone."

faq.q: What is Becoming a Family?
faq.a: It is a guided Christian journal for parents in the middle of the adoption process, by Tetiana Kurylo. It has eight parts of prompts and writing space, with short teaching pages and Bible verses, and it is the second journal in her series after My Way to Adoption.

faq.q: Who is it for?
faq.a: Adoptive parents first, and couples raising adopted children together. Foster parents, blended families and the people who support them will find much of it fits. The author's own experience is with older children who grew up in orphanages.

faq.q: What are the eight parts?
faq.a: They are, in order: Where Am I?; My Happy Moments; My Difficult Moments; My Expectations; Me and My Spouse; Me and My Kids; I Am Done; and Me and God.

faq.q: Does it help with a child's trauma?
faq.a: It helps parents understand it. The book explains that traumatized children shut down when they feel close and vulnerable, that people with trauma may reject you before you hurt them, and that this is not your fault. It points parents to consistent love, boundaries and prayer, and lists eight books on trauma and attachment.

faq.q: Does it cover marriage during adoption?
faq.a: Yes. Me and My Spouse warns that adoption brings pressure on a marriage and asks couples to stand as one, talk before big decisions and keep their relationship a priority. It has pages for your spouse's good qualities and for planning time together.

faq.q: Does it help blended families and stepparents?
faq.a: In part. The author is a mother to her husband's two children and writes honestly about feeling vulnerable with them. The book is written for adoption, but many pages fit a blended home.

faq.q: What does it say to adoptive moms who feel guilty?
faq.a: Feelings of Guilt, in Part 7, says adoptive moms often feel they are not doing enough because they did not carry the child. Its answer is that you do a lot, more than their biological parents did, and that it is okay not to do everything right. It gives steps: think about what you do well, ask God for His way of seeing and bring those thoughts to light.

faq.q: Is it about adoption from Ukraine?
faq.a: Partly. The author writes from her own experience of Ukrainian culture and orphanages, and some pages explain how children raised there learned to handle emotions. The journal prompts work for any adoption.

audience.headline: A woman who has worked with orphans and adopted her husband's two children asks the questions most families do not ask themselves before they adopt.
audience.body: For prospective adoptive parents, couples considering adoption, families waiting for a match, foster parents, and the friends, pastors, caseworkers and church orphan care ministries who walk beside them. Tetiana Kurylo draws on her work with orphans in Ukraine, on the stories of many families who have adopted and on her own experience as a stepmother. Most of the book is lined journal space under short prompts: why do you want to adopt, what are you afraid of, what does your spouse say, how will your biological children be affected, what is God saying. Between the prompts are short, frank teaching pages. A note on subjects: the book speaks openly about trauma, children who reject their new parents, not feeling love right away, and the author's own abusive father. It is a journal and a guide, not a legal or agency handbook.

quote.text: “You will learn to love this kid (it is not like with a newborn,) but in this case, the love will be a choice for you every day!”
quote.cite: My Way to Adoption, Part 3: On the Way to My New Life

what_makes.title: What makes this journal different
paras: The opening page says it plainly: Tetiana wants you to make a conscious decision about the child or children you are adding to your family. She warns that you might change your mind after considering questions you normally would not ask yourself, and says that is the point.
Five things set it apart:
list: It follows the real order of an adoption. Your story and why you want to adopt, your expectations, the trip to meet your child, and the first weeks at home.
It brings the whole family in. There are pages on your spouse, on being one team and on your biological children, who will have new siblings with a very different past.
It is honest about love. The author writes that you may not like or love your child right away, and that it was a process for her to grow to love her husband's two children.
It explains where these children come from. Part 4 describes six differences in mentality she has seen in children raised in Ukrainian orphanages and boarding schools, and how parents can help.
It keeps sending you to God. Prompts ask what God is saying, and you are told to write down your revelations and come back to read them in difficult times.

sections.h2: For couples deciding whether to adopt
paras: Part 1 starts with why. When did you start to think about adoption, what fears did you have, and are you and your spouse on the same page? The book asks you to be honest with each other because you are building a foundation for your future.

sections.h2: For families adopting an older child
paras: The author writes about children who have learned to protect themselves first, who test your love relentlessly and who may need to be taught gratitude, respect and caring for others "like a little child in a big body." Her advice is to stay consistent, keep boundaries and let them experience what love is.

sections.h2: For parents with biological children at home
paras: Adoption affects your children too. The book warns that adopted children often fight with their siblings and can act out in anger, and it gives pages to ask your kids what they feel and what they expect. Prepare them beforehand, it says, because this will be a difficult process for them as well.

sections.h2: For anyone who supports adoptive families
paras: Pastors, caseworkers, grandparents and friends will find the same honest picture. The last pages add a reading list of eight books on trauma, attachment and adoption, and the book urges parents to meet with friends who have adopted and not to do it alone.

details.Subtitle: Preparation for the Adventure Ahead
details.Author: Tetiana Kurylo

stories.h2: When does the child become my child?
paras: Tetiana writes that she thought it was easy: her decision, the paperwork, and that was it. It was not. With biological children, she says, you care about them for nine months before birth. With adopted children you see things you would never see in your own, and it can push you away emotionally. Her answer is not to push them away, and to go to God for the love she does not have. She adds:
"This is a process and a good process when kids become our kids!"

stories.h2: I'd rather attack, before you hurt me
paras: Part 4 explains why children from boarding schools may push away the people who love them most. The system, she writes, taught them that you are either weak or you attack first. She tells of learning the same thing in childhood, when her father hurt her, until God showed her she could trust Him with every fear. Her conclusion for parents:
"They will reject you before you hurt them."

stories.h2: The question that does not help
paras: At the end of Part 4 the author asks parents not to ask themselves what life would look like if they had not adopted. She admits that for seven years she let her boys make her crazy, until she realized she could lead. She tells parents to deal with their own trauma, find people who can help and pray every time, and promises that children given love and acceptance will want to follow.

author.bio: Tetiana Kurylo has worked with orphans and gathered the stories of many families who have adopted. Drawing on years of living in Ukraine and travels to the United States, she writes about how children shaped by orphanages and boarding schools learn to survive and what they need in order to trust. She became a parent by adopting her husband's two children, and writes honestly about how long it took to grow to love them. My Way to Adoption is the first of her journals for adoptive families.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: Tetiana has seen what happens when families adopt with high hopes and no preparation. She wrote this journal so that you would ask the hard questions first, and have something to come back to later. The opening letter says:
"I truly pray that God will lead you and your family in the way He wants, because when you have struggles, you will need to have something to stand on!"
Part 1 ends with the same promise:
"And in times of difficulty, you may find comfort in returning to read the pages of this journal."

faq.q: What is My Way to Adoption?
faq.a: It is a guided Christian journal for families preparing to adopt, by Tetiana Kurylo. Most of its pages are for writing, under prompts that follow the adoption from the first decision to the first days at home, with short teaching pages and Bible verses between them.

faq.q: Does it help with adopting a child?
faq.a: It helps you prepare your heart and your family. It does not cover agencies, paperwork or law. It asks why you want to adopt, what you expect and fear, what your spouse and children think, and what God is saying, and it gives space to record the trip, the first meeting and the first weeks.

faq.q: Is it for adoptive parents of older children?
faq.a: Yes. Much of the teaching is about children who grew up in orphanages and boarding schools, who may not know what love and trust are and who may test your love relentlessly. The author's own experience is with older children.

faq.q: Does it talk about trauma?
faq.a: Yes, plainly. Part 4 says where there is trauma there is defense, and that children may reject you before you can hurt them. The book advises consistency, boundaries and love, and points parents to God for healing. It also lists eight books on trauma and attachment.

faq.q: Is it about international adoption from Ukraine?
faq.a: Partly. The author lived and worked with orphans in Ukraine, and Part 4 describes six differences in mentality she has seen in those children. They are, in order: fear of making mistakes; everyone owes me something; not knowing how to show feelings or emotions; religion; I can't change anything; and food. The journal prompts work for any adoption.

faq.q: Is it useful for foster parents?
faq.a: Much of it is. The prompts on expectations, biological children, trauma and not doing it alone fit foster care as well, and the reading list includes books written for foster and adoptive families. The book itself speaks of adoption.

faq.q: Does it cover stepchildren and blended families?
faq.a: In part. The author became a mother to her husband's two children and writes that it was a process to grow to love them. The book is written for adoption, but her story will be familiar to stepparents.

faq.q: Is there a next journal?
faq.a: Yes. My Way to Adoption is Journal 1. Becoming a Family: Keeping God as Your Co-Parent, by the same author, is for parents who are already in the middle of the adoption process.

audience.headline: Family, friends and circumstances will always find their way onto a mom's list. This short book points to the One who never forces His way on, and asks whether He is getting any of the day.
audience.body: For mothers who give their time away from the moment they wake up. Daniel W. Evans looks at time from a biblical point of view in nine short chapters: God as the One who controls it, the calendars that run a household, how to put God, family and others first, and how to invest the hours we have. Each chapter ends with an honest question to write about. A note on this edition: the words inside are the same in every special edition of Your Time. This one carries a cover and edition name for moms, but the book does not describe a mother's life specifically. Mothers appear in one passage, as an example of how the loudest need can crowd out a quieter one.

quote.text: “While family, friends, and circumstances may force themselves upon us, God will not.”
quote.cite: Your Time, Time-Management

what_makes.title: What makes this edition for moms
paras: This is the Special Edition for Moms of a book about time. The pages are the same as in every other Your Time edition, and the book is written for any Christian. It suits a mother because it is short, it can be read one chapter at a time between everything else, and its central list, God, family and others, is the list a mom already lives by.
Five things set it apart:
list: It can be read in snatches. At 60 pages in a 4 x 6 inch size, each chapter is a few pages and ends with one question.
It speaks to the day that falls apart. The author lists a cavity at the dentist, a flat tire, a health issue and an emergency with a family member as the kinds of things that take over a day.
It keeps family near the top. God, family and others, he writes, are what everything else should be planned around.
It has a picture every parent will recognize. A mother caring for a difficult child while the well-behaved one gets less attention is the book's own example of how time gets misplaced.
It starts with time for God. The top priority, the author says, is to give Him time each day, because we need time with Him.

sections.h2: For moms whose time is never their own
paras: The Time-Management chapter says each of us has trouble managing our own time, and that unforeseen situations can bombard us on any given day, at home, at school, at work or at church. The author's answer is to adjust our priorities instead of tacking God on at the end of the to-do list.

sections.h2: For moms raising more than one child
paras: In Proper Investment of Time, the author pictures a mother caring for a difficult child while neglecting a child who behaves well, and asks what can happen to the well-behaved child as a result. He uses it to show that the investments that demand the most attention are not always the ones that need it most.

sections.h2: For moms' groups and Bible studies
paras: Each of the nine chapters closes with a Take a Moment to Focus question and room to write. One asks whether, considering how much time Jesus spent with people, you are spending enough time with family, friends and others. A group can take one chapter at a time.

details.Title: Your Time
details.Subtitle: The Greatest Gift You Receive and Give
details.Author: Daniel W. Evans
details.Scripture: NIV and the Amplified Bible (AMP, AMPC)

paras: To show that some investments demand more attention than others on the surface, the author asks the reader to picture a home:
"Think of a mother caring for a difficult child while neglecting a child who behaves well."

He asks what can happen to the well-behaved child as a result, and then carries the same picture into the workplace and the church: business owners who pour time into under-performing employees instead of their best workers, and pastors who burn out ministering to the broken instead of training leaders to share the load.

In Gifts of Time, the author looks at Jesus stopping on the way to Jerusalem to bless children, and at Cornelius, who did not check his schedule or put off sending for Peter. He says God speaks for one of two reasons, to make us a blessing to someone or to give us a blessing, and he wonders whether our schedules are so tight that we would miss it.
In Proper Investment of Time, he asks whether you are investing your time in the right people, and gives three steps. The first is to acknowledge that time is limited:
"Acknowledge that not only your money and energy, but also your time is a finite resource."

The second is to become aware of where it goes, since, as he puts it, your calendar will reveal the truth. The third is to change what needs to change, including activities that are unproductive or unhealthy.

author.bio: Daniel W. Evans is a Christian author who says that he has traveled through the states as an evangelist and listened to many pastors talk about church growth. In Your Time he writes from that experience and from his home church in Durham, North Carolina, where he counted how many members give their time as volunteers and found the figure to be 36 percent. He uses Scripture and personal observation to urge readers to put God first and to steward every hour well. The back of the book describes two other offerings from him: a one-day process in five steps, and A Commitment to Unleash Your Leader Potential, a program for the leader in each of us.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author's stated hope is simple. He wants you to see that your time is precious, that no one can replace it, and that God belongs at the top of the list. He puts it as a prayer:
“My prayer is that this booklet will help you recognize and realize that you are a potential success.”
After the chapter on idioms, he says why he wrote it at all:
“My prayer is that we will not neglect what is so valuable and be better stewards of our precious time.”

faq.q: Is it written specifically for moms?
faq.a: No. The Special Edition for Moms has its own cover, edition name and ISBN, but the words inside are the same as in the other Your Time editions. It is written for any Christian. Mothers appear in one passage, the picture of a mother caring for a difficult child while a well-behaved child is neglected.

faq.q: Is it a good Mother's Day gift?
faq.a: It was made to be given to moms. It is short, 60 pages in a 4 x 6 inch size, plainly Christian, and ends with a prayer to pray aloud. The book itself does not mention Mother's Day.

faq.q: Is it a devotional for busy moms?
faq.a: Some of it. It is not a dated daily devotional. It has nine short chapters, each a few pages, and each closes with one question to write about, so it can be read a chapter at a time on a busy day.

faq.q: Does it help working moms with work-life balance?
faq.a: Some of it. The book does not use that phrase. It says we work hard at managing our time and then try to fit God, family and others into it, and it asks you to plan everything else around those three instead.

faq.q: Does it encourage a daily quiet time with God?
faq.a: Yes. The author says the top priority in our time management must be to give God time each day, and adds that it is not that He needs time with us: we need time with Him.

faq.q: Is it a book on time management skills?
faq.a: Partly. It is a short Christian book about time, not a manual of techniques. It gives plain steps, ending with the ABC's of investing time. They are, in order: Acknowledge that time is a finite resource; Become aware of where you are investing it; and Change what is unproductive or unhealthy.

faq.q: Is it a book on biblical stewardship of time?
faq.a: Yes. The closing prayer asks God for help to be a better steward of your time, and the last question asks what changes you can make to be one. The book draws on Isaiah 38, Daniel 6, Luke 18, Acts 10 and Psalm 39.

faq.q: Can a moms' group use it for discussion?
faq.a: Yes. Each of the nine chapters ends with a Take a Moment to Focus question and space to write. One asks: Is God included in your daily routines of managing your schedules?

audience.headline: Most dads plan the week around work and fit the family in after. This short book asks you to turn that around, and to put God at the top of the list instead of tacking Him on at the end.
audience.body: For fathers who want their time to go where it matters. Daniel W. Evans looks at time from a biblical point of view in nine short chapters: God as the One who controls it, the calendars and clocks that run the week, how to put God, family and others ahead of everything else, and how to invest the years you are given. Each chapter ends with an honest question to write about. A note on this edition: the words inside are the same in every special edition of Your Time. This one carries a cover and edition name for dads, but the book does not describe fatherhood specifically. Its pages on priorities, investing time and mentoring are where a father will find himself.

quote.text: “We would be well served to plan everything else around the most important things: God, family, and others.”
quote.cite: Your Time, Time-Management

what_makes.title: What makes this edition for dads
paras: This is the Special Edition for Dads of a book about time. The text is the same as in every other Your Time edition and is written for any Christian. What fits a father is its direction: plan the week around God, family and others, invest time on purpose, and think about who you are mentoring, because they could represent your legacy.
Five things set it apart:
list: It puts family in the plan, not the leftovers. The author says we tend to manage our time and then fit God, family and others into it, and that it should be the other way around.
It talks about legacy. Pencil people into your calendar, he writes, and be intentional with them, because they could represent your legacy.
It asks about mentoring. One question asks whether you are being mentored and whether you are investing time in mentoring others.
It shows faith under pressure. Daniel kept praying daily even with threats of the lions' den, and the author says there are always rewards attached to prioritizing properly.
It fits a jacket pocket. At 60 pages in a 4 x 6 inch size, each chapter is a few pages.

sections.h2: For dads who feel the job takes the best hours
paras: The Time-Management chapter says we work hard at managing our time every day and then attempt to fit God, family and others into it. The author asks for a change of order: put the most important things first and plan everything else around them.

sections.h2: For fathers thinking about the kind of man they are raising
paras: Proper Investment of Time asks whether you are investing in the right people, and says the people you choose could represent your legacy. It points to Jesus, who spent most of His ministry with twelve men. For a dad, the nearest of those people are at home.

sections.h2: For men's groups and Bible studies
paras: Each of the nine chapters ends with a Take a Moment to Focus question and room to write, and the book closes with a prayer to pray aloud. A men's group can work through it in nine short sessions.

details.Title: Your Time
details.Subtitle: The Greatest Gift You Receive and Give
details.Author: Daniel W. Evans
details.Scripture: NIV and the Amplified Bible (AMP, AMPC)

paras: In Time-Management, the author points to Daniel, who took time to pray every day even with threats of being cast into a den of lions. He imagines a reader objecting that people did throw Daniel among hungry lions, and answers that no harm came to him and that he prospered in the kingdom.
His conclusion is short: "There are always rewards attached to prioritizing properly."

Near the end of Proper Investment of Time, the author admits the chapter may feel a bit harsh, since choosing where to invest time can change some relationships. Then he points to Jesus, who was sent to die for sinners and yet spent the majority of His ministry with twelve men. There were others with them, the author notes, but the secrets of the Kingdom were shared with the twelve.
Just before that, he tells readers to look for the people they may have overlooked, and to write them in:
"Pencil these people into your calendar. Be intentional with these relationships. They could represent your legacy."
In Proper Investment of Time, he asks whether you are investing your time in the right people, and gives three steps. The first is to acknowledge that time is limited:
"Acknowledge that not only your money and energy, but also your time is a finite resource."

The second is to become aware of where it goes, since, as he puts it, your calendar will reveal the truth. The third is to change what needs to change, including activities that are unproductive or unhealthy.

author.bio: Daniel W. Evans is a Christian author who says that he has traveled through the states as an evangelist and listened to many pastors talk about church growth. In Your Time he writes from that experience and from his home church in Durham, North Carolina, where he counted how many members give their time as volunteers and found the figure to be 36 percent. He uses Scripture and personal observation to urge readers to put God first and to steward every hour well. The back of the book describes two other offerings from him: a one-day process in five steps, and A Commitment to Unleash Your Leader Potential, a program for the leader in each of us.

It offers full-service book creation and publishing in paperback, hardback, digital and audiobook formats, along with children's titles, compact Express Books, website design and SEO, and podcast and video production. We are glad to publish a short book that asks fathers, and everyone else, to give God, family and others the first of their time.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author's stated hope is simple. He wants you to see that your time is precious, that no one can replace it, and that God belongs at the top of the list. He puts it as a prayer:
“My prayer is that this booklet will help you recognize and realize that you are a potential success.”
After the chapter on idioms, he says why he wrote it at all:
“My prayer is that we will not neglect what is so valuable and be better stewards of our precious time.”

faq.q: Is it written specifically for dads?
faq.a: No. The Special Edition for Dads has its own cover, edition name and ISBN, but the words inside are the same as in the other Your Time editions. It is written for any Christian and does not describe fatherhood specifically. Its pages on family priorities, legacy and mentoring fit a father well.

faq.q: Is it a good Father's Day gift?
faq.a: It was made to be given to dads. It is short, 60 pages in a 4 x 6 inch size, plainly Christian, and ends with a prayer to pray aloud. The book itself does not mention Father's Day.

faq.q: Is it a daily devotional for men?
faq.a: No. It is not dated or daily. It is nine short chapters, each a few pages with one question to write about, that a man can read one at a time.

faq.q: Can a men's Bible study use it?
faq.a: Yes. Each of the nine chapters ends with a Take a Moment to Focus question and space to write. One asks: Do you acknowledge how much you need God and then realize how much more time you need with Him?

faq.q: What does it say about mentoring?
faq.a: It asks you to find mentors and to be one. The author says to identify people who would be valuable to your success and you to theirs, and to ask whether they are someone you would like to have as a mentor or someone you need to mentor. Jesus, he notes, spent most of His ministry with twelve men.

faq.q: Does it help with work-life balance?
faq.a: Some of it. The book does not use that phrase. It says we fit God, family and others in around our own planning, and asks you to plan everything else around those three instead.

faq.q: Is it a book on biblical stewardship of time?
faq.a: Yes. The closing prayer asks God for help to be a better steward of your time, and the last question asks what changes you can make to be one. The book draws on Isaiah 38, Daniel 6, Luke 18, Acts 10 and Psalm 39.

faq.q: Is it a book on time management skills?
faq.a: Partly. It is not a manual of techniques. It gives plain steps, ending with the ABC's of investing time. They are, in order: Acknowledge that time is a finite resource; Become aware of where you are investing it; and Change what is unproductive or unhealthy.

hero.audience_line: For Tamil readers in India, Sri Lanka and around the world who want to rest in God instead of working for Him, and for pastors, leaders and churches serving Tamil-speaking believers.

audience.headline: Only God Works in Tamil: the same ten short chapters, from Called to Finished, for readers who think and pray in Tamil.
audience.body: This is the Tamil translation of Only God Works by Kevin White. Its message is the one he says set him free after ten years as a workaholic for God: God has called you to Himself, not to do His work for Him. The book walks through ten words, with Scripture throughout, and shows how rest leads to more fruit, not less. The whole book, including the Scripture passages, is printed in Tamil script. A note on subjects: the author is frank about burnout, illness from overwork and being voted out as a pastor, and one chapter uses the intimacy of a bride and groom as a picture of closeness with God. It is written for adults.

quote.cite: Only God Works (Tamil edition), Introduction

what_makes.title: What makes this edition for Tamil readers
paras: The Tamil edition keeps the book's opening scene. It asks you to imagine the day after you die, in a heaven where nothing was made by human hands, and where people from many nations thank you because God worked through your giving, your mission trips and your prayers. Then it asks who is really doing the work.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is the whole book in Tamil, with the same ten chapters, the conclusion and the author's personal letter.
Its chapter titles still read as one sentence. In Tamil they begin அழைக்கப்படுதல் (Called), முற்றிலும் (Only), தேவன் (God) and கிரியை (Work).
It names a half-truth. God has called you, the author writes, and the enemy adds two words: to work.
It comes from a hard story. The author tells of overwork, being dismissed by his church, and a trip to India in 1998 that changed how he lived.
It looks to the finish line. The last chapter is about the 10/40 window and the people who still have little or no access to know about Jesus.

sections.h2: For Tamil-speaking believers who are worn out
paras: Chapter 5, சுதந்திரம் (Freedom), reads God's promise of rest in Hebrews 4 and Psalm 23 and says that freedom from work means freedom to rest. Resting, the author adds, does not mean being lazy or useless.

sections.h2: For pastors and church leaders
paras: The author writes that many pastors and leaders have left the ministry because of the lie that God called them to work for Him. A pastor or leader who serves in Tamil can hand this edition to the people in their care.

sections.h2: For families and churches who read in more than one language
paras: The Tamil edition follows the English book chapter for chapter, so a family or a small group can read Only God Works side by side in English and in Tamil.

details.Title: Only God Works
details.Subtitle: (Tamil) Investing Now What Matters Then
details.Author: Kevin White

paras: The introduction asks you to imagine heaven. Nothing there was made by human hands. Your yard and the work on your house are not there. Instead, people you have never met, many from other nations, tell you how God worked through your tithes, offerings, mission trips and prayers to bring them to Jesus.
இன்று நீங்கள் இறந்த மறுநாள் என்று கற்பனை செய்து பாருங்கள்.

In Chapter 4 the author tells how, in 1998, God took him to India and showed him Christ followers without basic necessities, most without Bibles, who still passionately pursued God's presence. On the plane home he committed to pursue the presence of God every day for the rest of his life. Chapter 9 tells the harder story around it: a church he built while working up to ninety hours a week, a vote that dismissed him, and a stranger who told him he had not been fired but set free.

Chapter 10, Finished, describes the 10/40 window, the region of North Africa, the Middle East and Asia where most people with little or no access to know about Jesus live, including many in India. It reads Matthew 24:14 as God's finish line and Revelation 7 as a picture of every nation worshiping together, and says only God can finish the work.

author.bio: Kevin White experienced God's call into full-time vocational ministry at seventeen and has served in full-time Christian ministry for nearly forty years. After a decade as what he calls a workaholic for God, he found freedom in Christ and started With Love From Jesus Ministries and Global Hope India. He has been to India more than fifty times, taking 1,000 people on mission trips. He is CEO of Spirit Media and the author of Audacious Generosity, Get to the Point and What's Your Word?

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: Only God Works was the first book the author wrote, twenty-five years before it was published, and he says it was written more for himself than for the world. His personal letter at the end calls the message a matter of life or death for billions of people far from God, and says the revelation that only God works saved his life.
The book's own pages say Spirit Media is committed to sharing the Good News of Jesus in all 195 nations of the world. The Tamil edition carries that message to readers in their own language.

faq.q: What is this book?
faq.a: It is the Tamil edition of Only God Works by Kevin White, printed under the title தேவன் மாத்திரமே கிரியை செய்கிறார். It teaches that God has never called us to work for Him, but to intimacy with Him, and to let Him work in and through us.

faq.q: What are the chapters?
faq.a: They are, in order: Called; Only; God; Work; Freedom; Intimacy; Humility; Gratitude; Fruit; and Finished. An introduction comes first, and a conclusion, a letter from the author and a few more words from him close the book.

faq.q: Is it a Tamil Christian book?
faq.a: Yes. It is a Christian teaching book printed entirely in Tamil script, for Tamil-speaking believers, pastors and churches.

faq.q: Does it quote the Bible in Tamil?
faq.a: Yes. The copyright page says the Scripture passages are taken from a Tamil Bible. It is a book about the Bible's teaching, not a Bible itself.

faq.q: What does it say about the Garden of Eden?
faq.a: Chapter 4 goes back to Genesis 2 and 3. It says God placed the man in the garden in partnership with Him, that there was no assignment to work for God before the fall, and that the curse after the fall was labor.

faq.q: Does it use the verse that with God all things are possible?
faq.a: Yes. Matthew 19:26 is quoted in the chapter on God and again in the chapter on intimacy, where the author says trusting God to do the impossible draws us close to Him.

faq.q: Does it speak of prayer with thanksgiving?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 8, Gratitude, reads Philippians 4:6 and says gratitude comes before provision, so that we give thanks for what God has promised before we see it.

faq.q: Is it a book about resting in God?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 5, Freedom, reads God's promise of rest in Hebrews 4 and says freedom from work means freedom to rest. The author says rest does not mean being useless or lazy.

audience.headline: The Heart Journey book teaches. This journal is where you do the work, one prompt, one prayer and one encounter with Jesus at a time.
audience.body: For women using Heart Journey: Healing through Encounters with Jesus & Psychology, women's small groups and ministries running the study, and the leaders and counselors who facilitate them. The journal follows the book chapter by chapter, from Restoring My Heart to Restoring My Life. It does not repeat the book's teaching. Each chapter lists the supplies you need, then gives Individual Heartwork prompts with space to write, guided activities with QR codes for audio versions, a Heart Group Discussion, a closing prayer and Keystone Scriptures to memorize. A note on subjects: the exercises ask you to revisit childhood memories, unmet needs and trauma, and to work on forgiveness and boundaries. Like the book, the journal says it is not a substitute for therapy, and it recommends a trusted friend and, where needed, a licensed psychotherapist for support.

quote.text: “Ask the Lord how He wants to soothe your soul, then sit and listen.”
quote.cite: Heart Journey Accompanying Journal, Heart Journey Self-Assessment

what_makes.title: What makes this journal the other half of the study
paras: The author calls the journal a required complement to the book, because it holds all the Heartwork exercises and activities that facilitate the healing the book describes. Reading alone, she writes, is not enough.
Five things set it apart:
list: It starts with an honest look. The Self-Assessment asks you to describe a whole heart, rate how whole yours feels from one to ten, and name the rooms of your heart that need renovation.
It is hands-on. You build a timeline of your life with colored pencils and photos, label each trauma and unmet need, draw, write letters and make a vision board.

It guides you into encounters with Jesus. Scripted activities such as Restored Childhood with Jesus, Beautiful Place Prayer and Oscillation with Jesus are written out in full, with QR codes for audio versions.
It is ready for a group. Every chapter has a Heart Group Discussion called Time to Share, and the journal gives prayers you can pray together.
It helps you hold on to what changed. Keystone Scriptures close each chapter, and the last pages ask you to write your purpose statement and twelve chapter titles of your own for what you learned.

sections.h2: For women going through Heart Journey
paras: Keep the book open beside the journal. The book's chapters point you to the matching Heartwork, and the journal carries the questions, the space to answer and the guided activities. The author suggests a second journal for women who want to go through the study again.

sections.h2: For small group members and facilitators
paras: The journal repeats the notes for small group facilitators: one chapter every two weeks, at least two meetings per chapter, safety first, sharing kept balanced and the focus kept on Jesus. Each Time to Share page gives a short list of questions to discuss, and one ends with a reminder that fits the whole study: "Progress, not perfection!"

sections.h2: For women who process by writing
paras: Most pages are prompts and lines. Some ask simple questions about your upbringing and needs. Others go deeper, like writing a letter to your younger self and letting Jesus speak words of comfort and hope to her.

sections.h2: For women ready to look ahead
paras: The last chapters turn from healing to purpose. You make a vision board, trace God's purpose through your life, list your spiritual gifts and finish ten sentences that become your purpose statement, ending with when you feel His pleasure.

details.Title: Heart Journey Accompanying Journal
details.Subtitle: Healing through Encounters with Jesus & Psychology
details.Author: Dr. Barbara Lowe

paras: Chapter Five asks you to gather photos from childhood and early adult life and draw a timeline. Good memories go above the line at the age they happened; painful ones go below. Then you label each trauma with a T and each unmet need with UN, in different colors. The journal is gentle about it:
"Remember, perception is key in trauma work, so do not judge whether or not something should be listed on the bottom of your timeline."

Restored Childhood with Jesus is one of the guided activities, written out in full. You get comfortable and use your holy imagination to picture your parents, years before you were born, receiving what they needed to parent you well. The activity begins:
"To begin this activity, find somewhere comfortable."

The final Heartwork borrows an exercise the author uses after a momentous season. You write twelve chapter titles for a book about what you learned on your Heart Journey, each with a short summary. Two examples are given from the woman whose story runs through the study, such as "I Deserve to Be Pursued." Then the pages are yours.

author.bio: Dr. Barbara Lowe is an ordained minister, licensed psychologist, Master ART therapist, board certified life coach and Somatic Experiencing practitioner. She wrote Heart Journey and this companion journal as a ministry project, writing as a Christian minister and drawing on Scripture, encounters with Jesus and standard psychological principles and tools to guide women through healing from trauma.
