why.title: Why this journal exists
paras: The study tools introduction explains it with the man at the pool of Bethesda: Jesus asked him if he wanted to be well, and then he had to pick up his mat and walk. The journal says the Heartwork is our part:
"It is through this intentional engagement that the flow of healing can reach and transform your heart home."
And the first page of Heartwork begins simply:
"To get an idea of where your heart is now, journal below on how you are feeling."

faq.q: What is the Heart Journey Accompanying Journal?
faq.a: It is the companion workbook to Heart Journey by Dr. Barbara Lowe. It holds the Heartwork for each of the book's twelve chapters: writing prompts, guided encounters with Jesus, group discussion questions, prayers and Scriptures to memorize.

faq.q: Do I need the Heart Journey book too?
faq.a: Yes. The journal does not repeat the book's teaching; it gives the exercises that go with it. The author describes the two as a pair and calls the journal a required complement to the book.

faq.q: Is it a prayer journal for women?
faq.a: It is a guided journal for women that includes prayer. Written prayers appear throughout, many prompts ask you to sit before the Lord and write what He says, and the scripted activities are prayerful encounters with Jesus. Most of the pages are healing exercises rather than a daily prayer log.

faq.q: Does it include guided Christian meditations?
faq.a: Yes. Scripted activities such as Restored Childhood with Jesus, Beautiful Place Prayer and Oscillation with Jesus are written out in full, and QR codes on the page give audio versions.

faq.q: Can a women's Bible study group use it?
faq.a: Yes. Every chapter has a Heart Group Discussion called Time to Share, with questions to discuss, and the journal includes the same facilitator notes as the book, with a suggested pace of one chapter every two weeks.

faq.q: Does it help with childhood trauma?
faq.a: It is where the book's trauma work is done. You build a timeline, label traumas and unmet needs, and work through them in later chapters with guided activities. It reminds you to move at a safe pace and to seek a licensed psychotherapist when needed.

faq.q: What does the journal ask about forgiveness?
faq.a: Chapter Nine includes Unburdening from Resentment activities, a page on making amends and a page on what it calls sticky resentments, alongside the group discussion for that chapter.

hero.audience_line: For Christian women ready to heal from childhood wounds and trauma, and for the small groups, ministry leaders and counselors who walk with them.
hero.tagline: A twelve-chapter study for women ready for wholeness, joining Scripture, encounters with Jesus and standard psychological tools to restore the heart from soul pain to God-given purpose.

audience.headline: An ordained minister who is also a licensed psychologist invites you to restore your heart the way you would restore a neglected house, room by room, with Jesus as the master restorer.
audience.body: For women healing from trauma and unmet childhood needs, Christian women in recovery, women's small groups and Bible study leaders, women's ministry leaders, church care teams, and counselors and coaches who want a resource that holds faith and psychology together. Dr. Barbara Lowe writes as a Christian minister, from a Christian perspective, while drawing on standard psychological principles, neuroscience and body-based tools. The book teaches; the companion Heart Journey Journal holds the exercises, and the author calls the journal a required complement. A note on subjects: the book discusses childhood abuse, abandonment, addiction, trauma responses in the body and forgiveness. It says plainly that it is not a substitute for therapy, asks readers to self-monitor and move at the pace of grace, and points anyone who feels unsafe to professional help.

quote.text: “Dear one, your heart's home is akin to that house, brimming with immense potential and inherent value.”
quote.cite: Heart Journey, Your Heart Journey

what_makes.title: What makes this study different
paras: The book opens with a picture. You inherit a worn, moldy house, and an appraiser arrives, tells you it is a national treasure, offers to guide the restoration and has already paid for it. Your heart, the author writes, is that house, and the Lord has already paid the cost.
Five things set it apart:
list: It joins two fields on purpose. The author is an ordained minister, licensed psychologist, Master ART therapist, board certified life coach and Somatic Experiencing practitioner, and she writes as a minister using Scripture alongside psychological tools.

It moves in three stages. Safety and stability come first, then deconstruction and restoration of unmet needs and trauma, then integration and stepping into purpose. You master the stability tools before the deeper work.
It has a map. The fourteen letters of RECONSTRUCTION name each step, from Resource to Navigate Relationships Anew.
It invites encounters with Jesus. Guided, scripted activities ask you to bring Jesus into painful memories, and audio versions are offered by QR code.
It is built for groups. Notes for small group facilitators suggest one chapter every two weeks, with teaching, activities, Scripture, prayer and discussion questions in every chapter.

sections.h2: For women carrying childhood wounds
paras: Chapter One follows three women going home for the holidays: one to a family where she always belonged, one to an absent father and an unsafe house, and one to a mother who could not hug her. The book asks which story looks like yours, and then shows how unmet needs and trauma shape the rooms of the heart.

sections.h2: For women's small groups and Bible studies
paras: Each chapter includes teaching, activities, supporting Scriptures, prayer and questions for individual reflection and group discussion. The facilitator notes are careful: keep the group safe, keep sharing balanced, keep the focus on Jesus, and refer anyone who needs more to a licensed professional.

sections.h2: For counselors and ministry leaders
paras: The acknowledgements credit a long list of researchers and clinicians, and the chapters draw on ideas such as the window of tolerance, attachment, the body's fight-or-flight response and memory. Endorsers include a professor of Christian psychology and psychiatrists from Duke University Medical Center.

sections.h2: For anyone stuck on forgiveness
paras: Chapter Nine, Restoring My Peace, comes after the trauma work, not before it. The author writes that most people in a room raise their hand when asked about unforgiveness, and she walks through forgiving others and yourself at each age and stage of life, and making amends.

details.Title: Heart Journey
details.Subtitle: Healing through Encounters with Jesus & Psychology
details.Author: Dr. Barbara Lowe

stories.h2: Three women go home for the holidays
paras: Chapter One opens with three drives home. The first woman walks into the smell of turkey and sweet potato casserole and a family that has always had her back. The second drives home with memories of a father who left when she was eight and dread of what waits inside. The third, whose story is real and shared with her consent, reaches to hug her mother and feels her stiffen. The book asks you which story is closest to yours, and says healing begins by telling it.

The study tools chapter turns to the healing at Bethesda, where a man had waited thirty-eight years and Jesus asked whether he truly longed to be well. The author's point is that Jesus meets us, and we have a part to play. Reading alone is not enough; the healing comes through doing the Heartwork. She writes:
"In our own lives, faith is not merely a passive belief, but an active force that requires us to step out in obedience and engage in the work that leads to transformation."

Many readers did not get the nurture they needed as children. The book's answer is a tool it calls Self-Momming, practiced daily. The woman whose story runs through the book used the example of a kind neighbor from her childhood to learn it. The author sums it up:
"It helps us replace the harsh inner critic with a nurturing and wise parent who is governed by the love and wisdom of God."

author.bio: Dr. Barbara Lowe is an ordained minister, licensed psychologist, Master ART therapist, board certified life coach and Somatic Experiencing practitioner. In Heart Journey she writes as a Christian minister, drawing on Scripture, encounters with Jesus and standard psychological principles and tools to guide women through healing from trauma. One endorser writes that she has watched Dr. Barbara bring whole heart healing to hundreds of women over five years. Heart Journey is a ministry project and comes with the Heart Journey Journal.

publisher.about: Spirit Media Publishing is a Christian publishing and marketing company with a vision to reveal our Father's heart to all nations. It offers full-service book creation and publishing in paperback, hardback, digital and audiobook formats, along with children's titles, compact Express Books, website design and SEO, and podcast and video production. We are glad to publish a study that invites women to let our Father restore the home of the heart.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author writes that women often pour their energy into others while neglecting their own hearts, and that everyone has experienced traumatic events, unmet needs and the lies of the enemy. She believes those wounds can heal. The introduction says:
"Yet, we were MADE for freedom!"
And it tells the reader why she is holding this book:
"I wholeheartedly believe that you have been led to this book to receive healing in the innermost places of your pain."

faq.q: What is Heart Journey?
faq.a: It is a twelve-chapter Christian study for women healing from trauma and unmet needs, by Dr. Barbara Lowe. It brings together Scripture, guided encounters with Jesus and standard psychological tools, and it is meant to be used with the Heart Journey Journal, which holds the exercises.

faq.q: Is it Christian counseling?
faq.a: No. The author is a licensed psychologist but writes as a Christian minister, and the book says it is not a substitute for therapy. It is offered for education and Christian edification, and it urges readers to see a licensed provider for any mental health concern.

faq.q: Does it help with healing from childhood trauma?
faq.a: That is its main subject. It starts with stability skills, then works through unmet childhood needs, trauma held in the body, boundary ruptures and forgiveness, and ends with purpose. It asks you to master the stability tools first and move at the pace of grace.

faq.q: Can it be used as a women's Bible study?
faq.a: Yes. It is written for women, with notes for small group facilitators, Scripture in every chapter and questions for group discussion. The suggested pace is one chapter every two weeks, with at least two meetings per chapter.

faq.q: What are the steps of the RECONSTRUCTION method?
faq.a: They are, in order: Resource; Eliminate Unhelpful Behaviors; Consecrate the Healing Process to the Lord; Orient to Restoration; Narrate Your Story; Satisfy Unmet Needs; Time Reverse Trauma; Repair Boundary Ruptures; Unburdening from Resentment; Cede to a New Way of Living; Taste Goodness Daily; Inventory Purpose; Operate from Purpose; and Navigate Relationships Anew.

faq.q: What does the book teach about forgiveness?
faq.a: Chapter Nine, Restoring My Peace, covers it after the trauma work. It explores the themes under your resentments, uses your holy imagination to forgive yourself at each age and stage of life, and considers where to make amends.

faq.q: Does it cover healthy boundaries?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter Eight, Restoring My Boundaries, defines boundaries, looks at how God works through them, finds where yours were ruptured and teaches how to set them without false guilt.

faq.q: Do I need the journal?
faq.a: The author says yes. She calls the Heart Journey Journal a required complement to the book, because it holds all the Heartwork exercises, the scripted encounters with Jesus and the group discussion pages. The journal is sold separately.

hero.audience_line: For teachers, school staff and administrators, for Sunday school teachers and homeschool parents, and for parents and principals looking for a teacher appreciation gift.
hero.tagline: A short Christian book for people who spend their days giving time to others: God first, then family and others, in nine brief chapters with a question after each and a prayer to pray aloud.

audience.headline: A teacher's day is spent on other people's children. This short book asks where God and your own family fit, and how to invest the hours wisely when every student needs some.
audience.body: For teachers who give their time away all day and still bring work home. Daniel W. Evans looks at time from a biblical point of view in nine short chapters: God as the One who controls it, the calendars and clocks that measure it, how to put God, family and others first, and how to invest time in the right people. Each chapter ends with an honest question to write about. A note on this edition: the words inside are the same in every special edition of Your Time. This one carries a cover and edition name for teachers, but the book does not describe classroom life. Its pages on giving time, mentoring and investing in people are where a teacher will see their own work.

quote.text: “Helping people by giving them your time is the best gift you can give.”
quote.cite: Your Time, Setting Your Time Straight

what_makes.title: What makes this edition for teachers
paras: This is the Special Edition for Teachers of a book about time. The pages are the same as in every other Your Time edition, written for any Christian. A teacher will recognize a good deal of it anyway: a chapter on giving time to others, a passage about the child who acts up drawing attention away from the child who behaves, and a steady case for mentoring.
Five things set it apart:
list: It knows the attention problem. The author's example of a mother caring for a difficult child while neglecting a child who behaves well will be familiar to anyone with a class.
It argues for investing in your best people too. He writes that continued training for the best workers would likely make them even better, and asks the same of leaders everywhere.
It treats mentoring as a calling. One question asks whether you are being mentored and whether you are investing time in mentoring others.
It honors time given away. Helping people by giving them your time, the closing chapter says, is the best gift you can give.
It fits a desk drawer or a tote bag. At 60 pages in a 4 x 6 inch size, a chapter fits a planning period.

sections.h2: For classroom teachers who give their time all day
paras: Gifts of Time says we must give some of our time to others, just as Jesus fit people into His schedule everywhere He went, and that one of the greatest ways to please God is by helping others. For a teacher, that describes the job. The chapter asks that God and family not be the ones left out.

sections.h2: For teachers balancing many students' needs
paras: Proper Investment of Time says some investments require more attention than others on the surface. Its picture of a well-behaved child neglected while a difficult one takes all the attention, and its warning about leaders who burn out instead of training others, are worth a teacher's reflection.

sections.h2: For Sunday school teachers and homeschool parents
paras: The book is plainly Christian and short. Each chapter ends with a Take a Moment to Focus question, and the book closes with a prayer. A teacher can use one question a week for personal reflection or with a staff devotion.

sections.h2: For parents and principals saying thank you
paras: The subtitle calls time the greatest gift you receive and give. A teacher gives a year of it to every class. A small book on that subject, with a prayer at the end, is a fitting teacher appreciation gift.

details.Title: Your Time
details.Subtitle: The Greatest Gift You Receive and Give
details.Author: Daniel W. Evans
details.Scripture: NIV and the Amplified Bible (AMP, AMPC)

paras: To show that some investments demand more attention than others on the surface, the author asks the reader to picture a home:
"Think of a mother caring for a difficult child while neglecting a child who behaves well."

He asks what can happen to the well-behaved child as a result, and then carries the same picture into the workplace and the church: business owners who pour time into under-performing employees instead of their best workers, and pastors who burn out ministering to the broken instead of training leaders to share the load.

Near the end of Proper Investment of Time, the author admits the chapter may feel a bit harsh, since choosing where to invest time can change some relationships. Then he points to Jesus, who was sent to die for sinners and yet spent the majority of His ministry with twelve men. There were others with them, the author notes, but the secrets of the Kingdom were shared with the twelve.
Just before that, he tells readers to look for the people they may have overlooked, and to write them in:
"Pencil these people into your calendar. Be intentional with these relationships. They could represent your legacy."

In Time Idioms, the author picks one phrase we say without thinking and asks what it means to the person who asked for help. When we say give me a second, he writes, we are asking them to wait until we are able or ready to respond.
"Most wait to be courteous, but others wait because they really need the help."
He lists six more sayings, from killing time to it's about time, and says the point is not to find fault but to see how often we waste time without noticing.

author.bio: Daniel W. Evans is a Christian author who says that he has traveled through the states as an evangelist and listened to many pastors talk about church growth. In Your Time he writes from that experience and from his home church in Durham, North Carolina, where he counted how many members give their time as volunteers and found the figure to be 36 percent. He uses Scripture and personal observation to urge readers to put God first and to steward every hour well. The back of the book describes two other offerings from him: a one-day process in five steps, and A Commitment to Unleash Your Leader Potential, a program for the leader in each of us.

We are glad to publish a short book that honors teachers and asks them, and every reader, to give God, family and others the first of their time.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author's stated hope is simple. He wants you to see that your time is precious, that no one can replace it, and that God belongs at the top of the list. He puts it as a prayer:
“My prayer is that this booklet will help you recognize and realize that you are a potential success.”
After the chapter on idioms, he says why he wrote it at all:
“My prayer is that we will not neglect what is so valuable and be better stewards of our precious time.”

faq.q: Is it written specifically for teachers?
faq.a: No. The Special Edition for Teachers has its own cover, edition name and ISBN, but the words inside are the same as in the other Your Time editions. It is written for any Christian and does not describe teaching. Its chapters on giving time and investing in people fit a teacher's work closely.

faq.q: Is it a good teacher appreciation gift?
faq.a: It was made to be one. It is short, 60 pages in a 4 x 6 inch size, plainly Christian, and its subtitle calls time the greatest gift you receive and give. The book itself does not mention Teacher Appreciation Week.

faq.q: Is it a book on time management for teachers?
faq.a: Partly. It is a short Christian book about time for every reader, not a classroom planning guide. It gives plain steps, ending with the ABC's of investing time. They are, in order: Acknowledge that time is a finite resource; Become aware of where you are investing it; and Change what is unproductive or unhealthy.

faq.q: Does it speak to teacher burnout?
faq.a: Not by name. It does warn that many pastors burn themselves out ministering to the broken instead of training leaders to help shoulder the load, and says this is true in many other areas of leadership too. It also says you may need to end activities that are unproductive or unhealthy.

faq.q: Does it include a prayer for teachers?
faq.a: It includes one prayer, in Setting Your Time Straight, written for every reader rather than for teachers. It asks the Father to forgive wasted time and to help you invest as much of it as possible in Him and in others.

faq.q: What does it say about mentoring?
faq.a: It asks you to find mentors and to be one. One question asks whether you are being mentored and whether you are investing time in mentoring others, and the author points out that Jesus spent most of His ministry with twelve men.

faq.q: Does it encourage a daily quiet time with God?
faq.a: Yes. The author says the top priority in our time management must be to give God time each day, and adds that it is not that He needs time with us: we need time with Him.

faq.q: Is it a book on biblical stewardship of time?
faq.a: Yes. The closing prayer asks God for help to be a better steward of your time, and the last question asks what changes you can make to be one. The book draws on Isaiah 38, Daniel 6, Luke 18, Acts 10 and Psalm 39.

hero.eyebrow: By Kaylee Stavlas · Illustrated by Maria Vangi O'Brien
hero.audience_line: For children ages 4 to 8 with big dreams, the parents and grandparents who read to them, and the teachers, homeschool families and children's ministry leaders who want to show kids that no one is too young to help.
hero.tagline: An eight-year-old girl sees children in Haiti eating cookies made of mud, starts a cookie business of her own and gives over 1,000 dollars to help. A read-aloud picture book that shows miracles can be made out of the mud.

audience.headline: One video, one warm kitchen and one question: what if I can change the world?
audience.body: For children ages 4 to 8, the parents and grandparents who read aloud with them, and the teachers, homeschool families and Sunday school leaders who want to start a conversation about helping others. Kaylee Stavlas tells the story of an eight-year-old girl who watches a video of children in Haiti eating sun-dried mud to quiet their hunger, and decides to do something about it. She bakes rainbow-sprinkled cookies, sells them in her neighborhood, at church, at conferences and at business fairs, and gives over 1,000 dollars to children in Haiti. Her grandmother, Maria Vangi O'Brien, painted the pictures. A note on subjects: the story names hunger plainly, and some children may ask why kids would eat mud. It is told gently, it moves quickly from sadness to action, and it ends with hope and a recipe to bake together.

quote.text: “Can only one person change the world?”
quote.cite: You Can Change the World, the story

what_makes.title: What makes this book for kids who want to help
paras: The story starts in a fluffy, vanilla-cream-colored chair and a video on a computer screen. Children in Haiti are crouched on a dusty dirt road, eating something gray, round and crumbling. The girl wonders what kind of cookies they are, and then she learns the truth. Everything after that is about what one child does next.
Five things set it apart:
list: It turns a big problem into a child-sized step. The girl does not solve world hunger. She bakes what she loves to bake and sells it to the people around her.
It is built around one question. The girl asks herself, “What if I can use my talents to somehow make a difference?” and keeps reminding herself of it when the work is hard.
It is honest that it takes time. The money comes after many long months of baking, selling and repeating.
It gives children their own turn. Eight Questions for Reflection ask what they are good at, who they would like to help and what business they would start.
It ends in the kitchen. A Mud Cookies recipe, with sprinkles, chocolate chips and a gummy worm on top, lets a family bake the story together.

sections.h2: For parents and grandparents reading aloud
paras: The words are made to be read out loud: a scratchy, prickly, itchy, dusty dirt road, and a sadness that is eye-widening, jaw-tightening and tear-drenching. The story is short enough for one sitting, and the turn from sadness to a crazy good idea gives a child something to cheer for.

sections.h2: For teachers, homeschool families and Sunday school leaders
paras: The Questions for Reflection at the back make it easy to use with a group. Children list three things they are really good at, name someone they would like to help, and think about how they would change the world. It fits a lesson on compassion, giving or service.

sections.h2: For kids with big dreams
paras: The girl in the story is eight. She does not wait to grow up, get permission or have a lot of money. She uses something she already loves to do. The last page says it plainly: “no matter your age, YOU can CHANGE the WORLD.”

sections.h2: For families who bake together
paras: The book closes with a simple Mud Cookies recipe made from a box of cake mix, eggs, oil, chocolate chips and rainbow sprinkles, topped with a gummy worm. It is a fun way to talk about the story while the cookies are in the oven.

details.Title: You Can Change the World
details.Subtitle: Miracles Can Be Made Out of Mud
details.Author: Kaylee Stavlas

paras: Children in Haiti look back at the girl from a computer screen. They have big, sweet eyes and warm smiles, and they are eating something that looks like cookies. Then she learns what it is:
“Sun-dried, cookie-shaped, bitter, sour mud!”
Her eyes fill with tears. She knows she has to help, but how?

She walks into her warm kitchen thinking and praying for an idea. She loves to bake cookies. What if she started her own cookie business and sold cookies to raise money to help? She spends hours baking rainbow-sprinkled cookies. It is hard at first, but she keeps reminding herself of one line:
“What if you can change the world.”

She sells cookies in her neighborhood, at church, at conferences and at local business fairs, and takes orders from everyone. After many long months, she is able to give over 1,000 dollars to children in Haiti, which provides over a year's worth of food, water, education and a teacher's salary. The book says this was “only the start of her big adventure in entrepreneurship.”

author.bio: Kaylee Stavlas is from Raleigh, North Carolina, and is the founder of NEX GEN CEO, where she teaches business, financial literacy and servant leadership to young entrepreneurs. Her About the Author page names her Miss North Carolina Teen USA 2024 and describes her as a homeschooled student dually enrolled at Liberty University, a podcast host, an opera singer and a teen attorney in Durham Teen Court. Her work includes NEX GEN CEO Clubs, student business fairs and a mayor-sanctioned Next Generation Entrepreneurship Day. The book is illustrated by her grandmother, Maria Vangi O'Brien, a graduate of Parsons School of Design who has spent decades working with young children and making art.

We are glad to publish a picture book that tells children they are never too young to help.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The book is dedicated “to all children who have a dream to change the world.” Its last page puts the whole message in one line:
“Always remember, no matter your age, YOU can CHANGE the WORLD.”
The closing page about NEX GEN CEO, the student business group the author co-founded, says the same thing for older kids: “We all were built to problem-solve and give back.”

faq.q: What is You Can Change the World about?
faq.a: It is a picture book about an eight-year-old girl who sees children in Haiti eating cookies made of sun-dried mud. She starts a cookie business, sells cookies for many months and gives over 1,000 dollars to help. It ends with Questions for Reflection and a Mud Cookies recipe.

faq.q: Is it a good read-aloud picture book?
faq.a: Yes. It is written to be read out loud, with playful strings of words like scratchy, prickly, itchy and dusty. It is short enough for one sitting and is full colour on every page.

faq.q: Does it teach children about entrepreneurship?
faq.a: Yes, at a child's level. The girl turns something she loves, baking, into a business, sells at fairs, at church and in her neighborhood, and gives the money away. The book calls it the start of her adventure in entrepreneurship, and two reflection questions ask children what business they would start.

faq.q: Does it teach kindness and compassion?
faq.a: Yes. The girl cries when she sees the children in Haiti, and her sadness turns into action. One reflection question asks, Is there someone you would like to help?

faq.q: Can it be used for social emotional learning or character education?
faq.a: It works well as a discussion book. The Questions for Reflection ask children to name their strengths, think about others and imagine how they would change the world. It is a story, not a curriculum, and has no lesson plans.

faq.q: Is it a book about giving back?
faq.a: Yes. The whole story is about giving: the girl gives what she earns to children in Haiti, which provides over a year's worth of food, water, education and a teacher's salary. The NEX GEN CEO page at the back says the group values serving and giving back to its local and global community.

faq.q: Does it talk about servant leadership?
faq.a: Not in the story itself. The author's page says she teaches servant leadership to young entrepreneurs, and the NEX GEN CEO page says students learn and grow in servant leadership.

faq.q: Is it a Christian picture book?
faq.a: Some of it. The girl prays for an idea and sells cookies at church. It does not quote Scripture or preach, so it suits church, school and home alike.

faq.q: What age is it for?
faq.a: Ages 4 to 8, as a read-aloud with a parent, grandparent or teacher. The reflection questions also suit older children who want to start a small business of their own.

hero.audience_line: For kidney patients, dialysis patients and their caregivers, living donors, and the families and friends who stand beside someone on the road to a transplant.
hero.tagline: A caregiver's honest, practical and often funny account of one couple's road from kidney failure through dialysis to a living-donor transplant, written in everyday words by someone who has been through it.

audience.headline: She met her husband on a church stage. Barely a year into their marriage, they were told to put him on the national transplant list.
audience.body: For kidney transplant patients, people on dialysis, living donors, spouses and caregivers, people waiting for a donor, transplant support groups, church care teams and the nurses and chaplains who serve them. Laila Williams says it plainly on the first pages: this is not a medical book. Your medical team will tell you everything medical. What she offers is what she needed and did not always have, someone who has been through it and will tell you what to expect, what was hard and what turned out better than hoped. The transplant was her husband's; the journey, she writes, was theirs. A note on subjects: the book describes kidney failure, dialysis at home, a surgery that went badly wrong before it went right, and the strain of illness on a marriage. It speaks of God's care and prayer, and it is written for any reader.

quote.text: “It is a harbor of hope for the ones who are tired and don’t think anyone understands.”
quote.cite: Transplanted, Introduction

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people on the transplant road
paras: The introduction names what the author was missing when the journey began: a practical idea of how they were going to do things, from someone who would talk to her in normal everyday words. She wrote the book to be that person for the next family.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is a caregiver's view. The transplant was her husband's, and Laila writes as the wife beside him through dialysis at home, a long surgery day and recovery, and she gives caregivers a chapter of their own.
It is practical. Chapters cover types of dialysis and where it happens, juggling a job with treatment, joining the waiting list, insurance, Medicare and fundraising.
It shows how to ask for a kidney. Chapter 7 describes what they tried, from a Facebook album to T-shirts with the donation details, and how their donor found them through social media.
It tells the hard day honestly. Transplant day brought five bumps, from a fallen tree to a surgery stopped halfway, and the author does not smooth them over.

It goes past the surgery. Part 3 covers recovery and four breakthroughs for life after transplant: medications, exercise, sleep and food. Part 4 covers counseling, peer support and care for the caregiver.

details.Title: Transplanted
details.Subtitle: A Tale of Three Kidneys
details.Author: Laila Williams

paras: The day began at 4 a.m. A storm dropped a tree across the donor's road minutes after she left. The lead surgeon was stuck in traffic. Then, an hour into surgery, the author's husband reacted to a drug, his blood pressure fell and the transplant was stopped, with the new kidney put on ice. Toxins built up, so he needed five hours of emergency dialysis. Just before 3 a.m. the next day, both surgeons came out to say it had worked. The author writes:
"Our transplant was not smooth. It had not gone according to plan. We still had a long road of recovery ahead of us."

stories.h2: The donor who would not give up her kidney to anyone else
paras: Their donor found them by scrolling through Facebook and saw one of the author's posts. Before she finished reading, she commented that she would start the process of getting tested. On transplant day she woke from her own surgery and asked how the recipient was doing. Told that his part had not started yet, she let the staff know in no uncertain terms that the kidney was meant for him. The author writes of her:
"I also love our beautiful, wonderful, feisty donor for how she showed up during this time."

The last chapter explains the title. Three kidneys played the central roles: her husband's original two that were failing, and the transplanted one the couple calls Billy the Kid(ney). She adds a second reason she found by accident, the opening of A Tale of Two Cities, and says that is exactly what a transplant journey can feel like:
"It was the best of times, it was the worst of times."

author.bio: Laila Williams is a wife, caregiver and one half of what she calls Team Williams. She and her husband met on stage at their church during a midweek band rehearsal, where she played keys, and they married on that same stage fourteen months later. Both are degreed in engineering. She walked beside her husband through kidney failure, dialysis and a living-donor kidney transplant, and wrote Transplanted to be the encouragement she needed and did not have.

paras: When the journey started, the author was overwhelmed with medical talk and short on encouragement. She wanted to hear from someone who had already come through it. The introduction says:
"I needed to see someone who had made it through and to believe that it really could be okay."
And then the reason for the book in one line:
"I'm hoping I can be that person for you."

faq.q: What is Transplanted about?
faq.a: It is a memoir and practical guide by Laila Williams about her husband's kidney failure, dialysis and living-donor kidney transplant, told from the caregiver's side. It covers the whole road, from the first crisis to life after transplant, in four parts.

faq.q: Is it a medical book?
faq.a: No. The author says so in the introduction. Your medical team gives the medical guidance. This book shares what one couple learned, what they wished they had known sooner and what helped, in everyday words.

faq.q: Is it a good memoir for caregivers?
faq.a: Yes. The author was her husband's caregiver through home dialysis and transplant, and she writes openly about exhaustion, frustration and guilt. Chapter 21, Don't Forget to Care for the Caregivers, gives small, practical ways to look after yourself.

faq.q: Does it cover dialysis?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 2 covers types of dialysis, where it happens, training and supplies, and Chapter 3 covers juggling a job with dialysis. The couple did peritoneal dialysis at home, and transplant day brought an emergency round of hemodialysis.

faq.q: Does it explain how to find a living kidney donor?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 6 covers who can donate and signing up for the waiting list, and Chapter 7, Finding Your Donor: Promote and Ask, shares what they tried, including social media, T-shirts and decals. Their own donor found them through Facebook.

faq.q: Does it talk about counseling during a health crisis?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 19 tells how the couple chose a Christian counselor with experience in chronic illness and shares three take-aways. They are, in order: sometimes roles in a marriage need to shift for a time, and that's okay; sometimes even things you like are going to take a toll, and that's when you get to let go of them; and communication is key.

faq.q: What is life like after a kidney transplant, according to the book?
faq.a: Part 3 calls it And Then There's Life! It describes four breakthroughs. They are, in order: living with lifelong medications; you get to focus on exercise; get enough sleep and rest; and food, which is not all doom and gloom. The food chapter gives four guidelines, including avoiding buffets and controlling sodium.

faq.q: Is Transplanted a Christian book?
faq.a: It is written by a Christian and speaks of prayer and of God taking care of the couple, and they chose a counselor who shared their faith. Most of the book is practical and fits any reader on a transplant journey.

Evans looks at time from a biblical point of view in nine short chapters: God as the One who controls it, the limit of our days, how to put God, family and others first, and how to invest the time that is left. details.Author: Daniel W. Evans
details.Scripture: NIV and the Amplified Bible (AMP, AMPC)

paras: In Time and Priorities, the author reminds readers that the Bible says we all have an appointment with death (Hebrews 9:27), and that David asked the Lord to help him know his end and the measure of his days (Psalm 39:4). His bottom line is that our time on earth is limited and only God knows how much we have, so He must be the priority.
He comes back to the same psalm later, adds that God has promised our days shall be lengthened when we obey His word, and ends the chapter plainly:
"Our time here has a limit. Invest well, my friends!"

In Time-Management, the author points to Daniel, who took time to pray every day even with threats of being cast into a den of lions. He imagines a reader objecting that people did throw Daniel among hungry lions, and answers that no harm came to him and that he prospered in the kingdom.
His conclusion is short: "There are always rewards attached to prioritizing properly."
In Proper Investment of Time, he asks whether you are investing your time in the right people, and gives three steps. The first is to acknowledge that time is limited:
"Acknowledge that not only your money and energy, but also your time is a finite resource."

The second is to become aware of where it goes, since, as he puts it, your calendar will reveal the truth. The third is to change what needs to change, including activities that are unproductive or unhealthy.

author.bio: Daniel W. Evans is a Christian author who says that he has traveled through the states as an evangelist and listened to many pastors talk about church growth. In Your Time he writes from that experience and from his home church in Durham, North Carolina, where he counted how many members give their time as volunteers and found the figure to be 36 percent. He uses Scripture and personal observation to urge readers to put God first and to steward every hour well. The back of the book describes two other offerings from him: a one-day process in five steps, and A Commitment to Unleash Your Leader Potential, a program for the leader in each of us.

faq.a: Partly. It is not a manual of techniques. It gives plain steps, ending with the ABC's of investing time. They are, in order: Acknowledge that time is a finite resource; Become aware of where you are investing it; and Change what is unproductive or unhealthy.

Evans looks at time from a biblical point of view in nine short chapters: God as the One who controls it, the calendars we share, how to put God, family and others first, and how to invest time in the right people. Each chapter ends with an honest question to write about. A note on this edition: the words inside are the same in every special edition of Your Time. This one carries a cover and edition name for an anniversary, but the book is not about marriage and does not mention anniversaries. It is a short Christian reflection on time that a couple can read together.

what_makes.title: What makes this edition for an anniversary
paras: This is the Special Edition for Anniversary of a book about time. Its pages are the same as in every other Your Time edition, and it does not discuss marriage. What fits an anniversary is its main idea: time is the gift you can never take back once it is given, and the people you give it to are your legacy.
Five things set it apart:
list: It names what a couple gives each other. Time once given, the author says, can never be gotten back, and that is why its rewards are eternal.
It keeps God first. The top priority, he writes, is to give God time each day.
It puts family next. God, family and others are what everything else should be planned around.
It speaks of legacy. Be intentional with the relationships that matter, he says; they could represent your legacy.
It is easy to share. At 60 pages in a 4 x 6 inch size, a couple can read a chapter together and talk through its one question.

sections.h2: For newlyweds starting out
paras: The book's order of priorities, God first, then family and others, gives a young marriage a simple frame. The ABC's of investing time, acknowledge, become aware and change, help a couple look at where their hours really go. The author notes that your calendar will reveal the truth.

paras: In Time and Priorities, the author reminds readers that the Bible says we all have an appointment with death (Hebrews 9:27), and that David asked the Lord to help him know his end and the measure of his days (Psalm 39:4). His bottom line is that our time on earth is limited and only God knows how much we have, so He must be the priority.
He comes back to the same psalm later, adds that God has promised our days shall be lengthened when we obey His word, and ends the chapter plainly:
"Our time here has a limit. Invest well, my friends!"

In Gifts of Time, the author notices something easy to skip in Acts 10. Cornelius not only sent for Peter at once. He also made the time to visit his family and friends, and invited them to his house to hear what Peter would say. Peter, for his part, invited the men Cornelius sent to stay overnight, and went with them the next day, both against the customs he was raised in.
The author says most of us may not be able to travel on short notice as Peter did, but we may be able to visit as Cornelius did, with a little planning and time.
In Proper Investment of Time, he asks whether you are investing your time in the right people, and gives three steps. The first is to acknowledge that time is limited:
"Acknowledge that not only your money and energy, but also your time is a finite resource."

The second is to become aware of where it goes, since, as he puts it, your calendar will reveal the truth. The third is to change what needs to change, including activities that are unproductive or unhealthy.

author.bio: Daniel W. Evans is a Christian author who says that he has traveled through the states as an evangelist and listened to many pastors talk about church growth. In Your Time he writes from that experience and from his home church in Durham, North Carolina, where he counted how many members give their time as volunteers and found the figure to be 36 percent. He uses Scripture and personal observation to urge readers to put God first and to steward every hour well. The back of the book describes two other offerings from him: a one-day process in five steps, and A Commitment to Unleash Your Leader Potential, a program for the leader in each of us.

faq.q: Is it a good anniversary gift?
faq.a: It was made to be given as one. It is short, 60 pages in a 4 x 6 inch size, plainly Christian, and its subtitle calls time the greatest gift you receive and give. It suits a first anniversary or a fiftieth.

faq.q: Is it a devotional for couples?
faq.a: Not as written. It is written to one reader at a time. A couple can still read a chapter together and talk through its Take a Moment to Focus question, such as: Is God included in your daily routines of managing your schedules?

faq.q: Can a couples' Bible study use it?
faq.a: Yes, with that in mind. Each of the nine chapters ends with a question and space to write, and the book closes with a prayer. A group can take one chapter at a time.

faq.q: Does it help a couple with work-life balance?
faq.a: Some of it. It does not use that phrase. It says we work hard at managing our time and then try to fit God, family and others into it, and it asks you to plan everything else around those three instead.

faq.q: Does it encourage a daily quiet time with God?

paras: The subtitle calls time the greatest gift you receive and give. For a graduate about to have far more say over their own hours, a short book on spending them well, with a prayer at the end, is a lasting gift.

Then he points to Jesus, who was sent to die for sinners and yet spent the majority of His ministry with twelve men. There were others with them, the author notes, but the secrets of the Kingdom were shared with the twelve.

"Pencil these people into your calendar. Be intentional with these relationships. They could represent your legacy."

hero.audience_line: For busy people overwhelmed by clutter at home or at work, families downsizing or clearing a parent's home, and anyone who has cleaned up before and watched the clutter come right back.
hero.tagline: Two organizing professionals share a five-step Clutter Campaign built on one idea, Clutter is Postponed Decisions®, and one simple test: if you do not know it to be useful, believe it to be beautiful or love it, let it go.

audience.headline: Everything around you either nourishes you or drains you. This book shows you how to keep the first and lose the second.
audience.body: For busy people who feel a pang of guilt every time they open a closet, professionals whose desks slow them down, families moving, downsizing or clearing out a parent's home, and anyone who has organized before only to see the clutter return. Barbara Hemphill and Maggie Bedrosian bring more than twenty-five years of professional organizing and executive coaching to a plain process: decide what you want your setting to be, drop the excuses, make the time, pick tools that fit you and keep it going. Peter Walsh wrote the foreword. A note on subjects: several stories involve a parent's death and the work of clearing a home afterward, and one touches on a marriage under strain. The book is practical and warm, not clinical, and it is not about forcing one perfect look on your home.

quote.text: “Everything—everything—you have in your life either nourishes you or drains you.”
quote.cite: Love It or Lose It, Part I: Escaping the Clutter Trap

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who are tired of clutter coming back
paras: Most organizing books give tips. This one starts with why the mess keeps returning. The authors call it the Clutter Trap, “a state of cumulative disorder,” and they trace it to a single cause: decisions we keep putting off. Fix the decisions, and the tips finally stick.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is built on one idea. Clutter is Postponed Decisions®, and every step helps you make the daily decisions that keep a setting clear.
It gives you one test for every object. Is it useful? Is it beautiful? Do you love it? Unless an item meets one of those standards, the book says to let it go.
It is flexible. Each of the five steps has six options, so you can do a quick cleanup before a holiday dinner or a full campaign for your home or office.
It starts with a measure. The Love It or Lose It Inventory has fourteen statements to score, and the gap between where you are and where you want to be shows how much your setting is costing you.
It is full of real stories, from a United States Ambassador who wished he had done this twenty-five years sooner to a couple who emptied and rebuilt their kitchen in one long weekend.

sections.h2: For anyone overwhelmed by clutter at home
paras: The book knows the feeling: the closet you hate to open, the garage you avoid, the guests you do not invite. It does not scold. It asks you to picture the setting you want, then walks you through getting there one option at a time, with a three-question test you can carry in your head.

sections.h2: For busy professionals and business owners
paras: Many of the stories happen at work: an office makeover photographed for a national magazine, a business saved when an assistant quit without warning, and a whole office that took the Inventory together and cleared its space within a week. Step Four, Select Your Tools, starts with a simple rule: keep closest what you use most often.

sections.h2: For families downsizing or clearing a parent's home
paras: Part III calls this the toughest clutter trap of all, because it comes when you are grieving. One story describes more than fifty dressers in a house of eighteen rooms. The book gives three questions to ask now, so your own family never has to make every decision you put off.

sections.h2: For organizers, coaches and groups
paras: The Five-Step Clutter Campaign can be run alone or together. Part III explains how to set up a Clutter Campaign group, and Step Three lists the questions to ask before hiring a professional organizer.

paras: The clutter did not arrive in one single day. It will not be gone in one single day!

details.Title: Love It or Lose It
details.Subtitle: Living Clutter-Free Forever

paras: At the end of a seminar and book signing, a woman tells Barbara privately, “You may have just saved my marriage.” Her husband had filled the attic, the garage and a storage shed, and she had begun to think about divorce. Then Barbara said that people who cannot let go of things have often had a significant unresolved loss. The woman remembered that her husband's mother died when he was four, and for the first time she linked that loss to his need to hold on. She went home hoping he would get help, and no longer ready to give up.

A client calls to say her mother has died and asks what is involved in clearing the house. Her mother had stacked her papers, and when the stacks grew she put them in a dresser drawer. When a dresser filled, she bought another one. There were more than fifty dressers in a house of eighteen rooms, and it took three people eleven days to sort through it all. At one point the daughter looks up in tears:
“I hope I don't do this to my family.”

stories.h2: A royal mess in one weekend
paras: A couple decides the kitchen has to be done all at once. They start on the Saturday of a three-day weekend, empty the pantry onto every counter and the dining room table, sort as they go, send out for Chinese food and eat off paper plates. They finish late Monday morning and take themselves out to lunch. She says it sure feels good to go in and make a royal mess, “and get everything better-than-new in two days.”

author.bio: Barbara Hemphill grew up in Nebraska and started her organizing business in 1978 with a $7 ad in a New York City newspaper. She is the author of Taming the Paper Tiger, Less Clutter More Life and Walking with Barbara: 30 Emails from God, the founder of Productive Environment Institute and a past president of the National Association of Productivity & Organizing Professionals. She has appeared on NBC's Today Show, CBS This Morning, CNN and Good Morning America, and she is based in Raleigh, North Carolina. Maggie Bedrosian calls herself a reforming classic clutterer. She is the author of Life Is More Than Your To-Do List, a former host of television's Spotlight on Business, a past president of the Washington DC chapters of the American Society for Training and Development and the National Speakers Association, and a co-founder of the Washington Writers Workshop.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: Barbara writes that the book was born from clients who still had challenges after getting organized. They said things like “I can clean up the clutter, but it seems to come right back.” So she turned to a long-term friend and colleague:
“I worked with Maggie, a long-term friend and colleague, to create the book they were asking for.”

Maggie's turn came in 1996, when her office was chosen for a before-and-after makeover for a national magazine and she felt, for the first time, the liberating joy of a clutter-free space. She closes her note with the authors' hope for every reader:
“We hope it helps you feel your own liberating joy of living and working in a place you love.”

faq.q: What is Love It or Lose It about?
faq.a: It is a practical guide to getting organized and staying that way. Barbara Hemphill and Maggie Bedrosian explain the Clutter Trap, give a simple three-question test for every object and lay out a five-step Clutter Campaign so clutter does not come back.

faq.q: What are the five steps of the Clutter Campaign?
faq.a: They are, in order: Design your vision; Eliminate your excuses; Commit your time; Select your tools; and Maintain your success. Each step has six options, and you do not need to do every option every time.

faq.q: What does Clutter is Postponed Decisions mean?
faq.a: It is the cornerstone idea of the book. Clutter builds up when we put off deciding where something belongs, whether we need it or what our setting should be. The campaign helps you make those daily decisions so the clutter has nowhere to collect.

faq.q: Will it help if I feel overwhelmed by clutter?
faq.a: Yes. Part I describes that feeling closely, from the closet you fear to open to the guests you do not invite. Even a Setting Satisfaction Gap of 60 or more on the Inventory is met with “NOT TO WORRY!” and the note that you are now poised for change.

faq.q: Should I hire a professional organizer?
faq.a: The book says it can help. Step Three, Option 5, Hire a Professional, lists three benefits of working with one and eight questions to ask before you choose, from references to a not-to-exceed estimate. Option 6 offers another route: exchange services with someone whose skills differ from yours.

faq.q: Does it help with a cluttered home office?
faq.a: Yes. Many of the stories take place in offices, and Step Four starts with keeping closest what you use most often. One reader's whole office took the Inventory together and cleared its area within a week.

faq.q: How do I let go of guilt about getting rid of things?
faq.a: Step Two, Option 4, Banish Fear and Guilt, says the antidote to fear is knowledge and the antidote to guilt is wisdom. One story tells how a family's inherited dishes went to a great-granddaughter who wanted them, packed with old photos and written memories.

faq.q: Is it a minimalism book that tells me how to simplify my life?
faq.a: Not exactly. The authors say it is not about one sleek look, anyone else's taste or even simplicity, though many people find it leads that way. The test is what is useful, beautiful or loved to you.

faq.q: Is this a new book?
faq.a: It is a new edition, published in 2023. The copyright page also prints the book's original Library of Congress catalog number from 2002.

hero.audience_line: For families who want to plan ahead, adult children of aging parents, caregivers and anyone who wants their loved ones to find what they need in an emergency or after a death.
hero.tagline: A fill-in workbook that puts your will, accounts, insurance, passwords, health care wishes and funeral preferences in one place, written by a professional organizer who learned through loss why it matters.

audience.headline: If something happened to you in the next hour, would your family know where to find your will?
audience.body: For families planning ahead, adult children helping aging parents, caregivers, executors, and anyone recovering from an illness or accident who wants their affairs in order. Ann Cueva has worked as a professional organizer for twenty-five years. After losing her son, her mother and her mother-in-law, and after her family spent thousands of dollars searching for a will that turned up months later in a hatbox, she made the checklist and forms she wished every family had. The book is a large-format workbook: a short story of why it matters, six key tips, then page after page of forms to fill in and keep. A note on subjects: the opening chapter tells of the sudden death of the author's 17-year-old son, with no cause ever found, and of two family deaths in 2014. It is told simply and with faith, and the rest of the book is practical forms. It is not legal advice and does not replace a will or an attorney.

quote.text: “It is not a morbid task to complete. It will actually bring you peace.”
quote.cite: Grief Without Chaos, Chapter One: Peace of Mind

what_makes.title: What makes this workbook for families who want to be ready
paras: Ann has watched clients buy organizing books, read thirty pages, feel overwhelmed and say they will do it later. Her answer is printed in capital letters: LATER NEVER COMES! So this book is short on reading and long on blanks to fill in, one subject at a time.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is a workbook, not a lecture. After three short chapters, the rest of the book is checklists and fill-in forms.
It covers what families actually get asked: will, advance directives, safe deposit box, banking, investments, insurance, bills, physicians, digital accounts, social media and passwords.
It starts where you are. The first key tip is to fill in what you already know, which shows you what you still need.
It tells you when to update it. Ann suggests using your birthday each year to review your vital documents.
It has a sense of humor. A real memo of one man's funeral instructions asks for no neckties and a service no longer than 45 minutes.

sections.h2: For families who want to plan ahead
paras: Ann asks one question of her clients: if something were to happen to you in the next hour, would your family know where to find your important documents or know your last wishes? Most cannot answer with confidence. The Document Checklist and forms give you a single place to put the answers.

sections.h2: For adult children of aging parents
paras: The book compares two losses three months apart. With her mother, there was time to prepare and ask questions. With her mother-in-law, everyone knew there was a will, but no one could find it. Doing this workbook with a parent is a way to have the conversation before you need it.

sections.h2: For people recovering from surgery, illness or an accident
paras: Ann notes that most of the same information would be needed if you were incapacitated. One reader filled it in before a life-threatening surgery, and another wrote that after a car accident his family did not have a clue where to find important information.

sections.h2: For caregivers, executors and those who help them
paras: The forms collect contacts for physicians, bankers and insurance, with spaces to tuck in business cards. The checklist even reminds you to arrange compensation for a family member who serves as executor. Ann suggests working through the book with someone, because it makes the process easier.

stories.h2: A packet in the emergency room
paras: In July 2003, Ann was celebrating her sister's birthday in Orlando when her husband called: they thought her 17-year-old son had had a heart attack. That night in the emergency room, a woman handed her a packet and said she would need to begin making funeral arrangements the next day. Because Ann's paperwork was in order, it did not take long to gather. The funeral director said he had never seen anyone have all of the information he needed on the first request. After two autopsies, the cause of death is still unknown. Ann writes that this book may be her son's legacy:
“Until then, maybe this book, created to help others remove the chaos from grief, will be his legacy.”

In 2014, three months after her mother died, Ann's mother-in-law fell, was in a coma within twenty-four hours and passed away. Everyone knew she had a will. It was not in the desk where she said it was, and the family had no access to her safe deposit box. They hired an attorney, spent thousands of dollars, and finally found a copy at another law firm. Four months later, a copy turned up in a hatbox at the top of her closet.
“Knowing where her will was stored could have saved us time, money, and a lot of frustration.”

Chapter Two includes, with permission and for the laughs, one man's written instructions for his own funeral. He wants a closed casket, no neckties, a pastor who reflects on his life rather than using the occasion to pontificate, and an agenda with time limits. The whole celebration should last no longer than 45 minutes, and he ends on a hope:
“It is my desire that the ratio of laughter and levity when compared to sadness and carrying fall significantly in the camp of the former.”

author.bio: Ann Cueva is the president and owner of Custom Organizing, Inc., a professional home and office consulting business she began in 1994. Paperwork became her niche when she saw that most people struggle with it. She is a Certified Productive Environment Specialist, a Certified Before I Go Solutions Facilitator and a Core member of the Productive Environment Institute in Raleigh, North Carolina. She is a Golden Circle member of the National Association of Productivity and Organizing Professionals and has served on the Board of Faithful Organizers. She lives in Clearwater, Florida, and wrote this book from her own experience with emergencies and losing loved ones.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: After the search for her mother-in-law's will, Ann realized she needed a checklist and a conversation with at least two other family members about where everything was kept. She began asking her clients the same question, and most could not answer it:
“And so I knew something had to be done!”
She dedicates the book to Jesus Christ, who she says supplies love, wisdom, great grace and comfort every day, and she sends readers off with her own blessing:
“God bless you on your path of taking ‘PIECES of paper to PEACE of mind.’”

faq.q: What is Grief Without Chaos about?
faq.a: It is an end of life planning workbook. Ann Cueva shares why she made it, gives six key tips, and then provides a checklist and fill-in forms so your family can find your documents, accounts and wishes in an emergency or after a death.

faq.q: Is it an important documents organizer?
faq.a: Yes. Most of the book is forms, starting with a Document Checklist of items like a will, living will, health care power of attorney, insurance policies, deeds, tax returns and military documents, and space to record where each one is kept.

faq.q: Is it a grief book?
faq.a: Not in the usual sense. It is a practical workbook meant to keep grieving families from having to gather information in a crisis. The first chapters include the author's own story of loss, told briefly and with faith.

faq.q: Does it help with funeral planning?
faq.a: Yes. There is a Funeral Preferences form, a personal history section and a humorous real memo of one man's funeral instructions as an example. The personal information form also asks about a military burial.

faq.q: Is it useful when caring for an aging parent?
faq.a: Yes. Ann contrasts losing her mother, when there was time to prepare, with losing her mother-in-law, whose will could not be found. Filling in the forms with a parent is a way to ask the questions while you still can.

faq.q: Does the author write about the death of her son?
faq.a: Yes, in Chapter One. Her 17-year-old son died suddenly in 2003, and after two autopsies the cause is still unknown. She writes that this book may be his legacy.

faq.q: Is it a way of leaving a legacy for my family?
faq.a: That is how the book describes it. A page near the front reads, This book belongs to, and calls it a gift to your loved ones. One reader wrote that following the guide helped her create a gift and financial legacy for her family.

faq.q: Does it cover end of life care decisions?
faq.a: It gives you places to record them, not advice about them. The checklist and Health Care pages include a living will, a health care power of attorney, a do-not-resuscitate order and your physicians. It is not medical or legal advice.

faq.q: How often should I update it?
faq.a: Once a year. Ann suggests using your birthday as a reminder to review your vital documents and update the book.

hero.audience_line: For weary believers, pastors and ministry leaders running on empty, and every Christian who wants to know that their life truly matters in eternity.
hero.tagline: God never called you to work for Him. A minister of nearly forty years shows from Scripture that He calls you to Himself, and to rest while He works through you.

audience.headline: A pastor who nearly killed himself working for God tells what changed when he learned that only God works.
audience.body: For believers who feel worn out, for pastors and leaders who measure themselves by what they produce, and for every Christian who wants to invest now in what will matter in heaven. Kevin White was called into full-time ministry at seventeen. For his first ten years he lived, he writes, as a workaholic for God, and it nearly cost him his health, his marriage and his family. Only God Works is the message that set him free: God has called you to Himself, not to do His work for Him. In ten short chapters, with Scripture on almost every page, he shows how rest leads to more fruit, not less. A note on subjects: the author is frank about burnout, illness from overwork and being voted out as a pastor. One chapter uses the intimacy of a bride and groom as a picture of closeness with God. The book is written for adults. It is a teaching book, not a study guide with lessons and answers.

quote.text: God wants you, not your work.
quote.cite: Only God Works, Chapter 6: Intimacy

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people tired of working for God
paras: The book opens on the day after you die. In heaven, you notice that everything you see was made by God. The yard you worked on is gone. The hours spent on your house are gone. What remains is a crowd of people from many nations, thanking you because God worked through your giving, your mission trips and your prayers. That scene sets the question the whole book asks: who is really doing the work?
Five things set it apart:
list: It names a half-truth. God has called you, the author writes, and the enemy adds two little words: to work. Chapter 1 sets the truth and the lie side by side.
Its chapter titles read as one sentence. Chapters 1 through 4 are Called, Only, God and Work. The next six are Freedom, Intimacy, Humility, Gratitude, Fruit and Finished.
It asks you to answer. Simple blanks ask, after a verse, who does the work, and Chapter 5 gives you a page to write your own resignation letter from the work only God can do.
It comes from a hard story. The author tells of sleeping three hours a night for two years, being dismissed by his church, and a trip to India in 1998 that changed how he lived.

It looks to the finish line. The last chapter is about the 10/40 window, the people who still have little or no access to know about Jesus, and what it will look like when God's work on earth is finished.

sections.h2: For pastors and ministry leaders
paras: As a young pastor, the author went to leadership conferences that taught, "If it is to be, it is up to me." He believed it and, he says, failed miserably. If you lead a church or a ministry and feel that everything rests on you, this book is written with you in mind. He says countless pastors, teachers, evangelists and leaders have left the ministry because of the lie that God called them to work for Him.

sections.h2: For believers who are worn out
paras: Chapter 5 says it plainly: "Freedom from work means freedom to rest." The author reads Hebrews 4, Psalm 23 and Matthew 11 and argues that God's rest is not only waiting in heaven. Resting, he adds, does not mean being lazy or useless.

sections.h2: For people who measure themselves by their work
paras: When we meet someone, we ask what they do. The author says we take our identity from our work, and he shows a diagram of who we were in creation, after the fall, and in Christ. He retells the story of the older brother in Luke 15, who stayed home but was not happy. "You stayed home working for something that is already yours."

sections.h2: For anyone who wants their life to count in eternity
paras: The subtitle is Investing Now What Matters Then. The closing chapters talk about the Great Commission, giving and the billions of people who have never held a Bible, and the book ends with a personal letter and a prayer from the author for the reader.

paras: The introduction asks you to imagine heaven. Nothing there was made by human hands. Your yard is not there, and neither is the work on your house. Instead, people you have never met, many from other nations, tell you one by one how God worked through your tithes, offerings, mission trips and prayers to bring them to Jesus. Then it sinks in that the time you spent on work does not show up anywhere.
"In heaven, only the work done by God matters."

In Chapter 9, the author tells how he planted a church while working up to ninety hours a week. The church grew fast. Within a year of a big celebration, the new leaders were in conflict, and a vote dismissed him as pastor. A month later, at a gathering of pastors, a man he had never met followed him to his car.
"Kevin, perhaps you haven't been fired. Perhaps you've been set free."

Later, the author was asked to speak to several hundred pastors about finding freedom in Christ. He felt unqualified, since he had been fired. He led them through Steps to Freedom in Christ by Dr. Neil T. Anderson, sharing his own story at each step, and watched pastors repent, cry, worship and even dance. He writes that God showed him one thing that day:
"Real fruit depends on God, not us."

author.bio: Kevin White experienced God's call into full-time vocational ministry at seventeen and has served in full-time Christian ministry for nearly forty years. After a decade as what he calls a workaholic for God, he found freedom in Christ, joined the staff of a counseling ministry for pastors, and started With Love From Jesus Ministries, which distributes food, clothing and household items to people in need. He also started Global Hope India and has been to India more than fifty times, taking 1,000 people on mission trips. He is CEO of Spirit Media and the author of Audacious Generosity, Get to the Point and What's Your Word?

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: Only God Works was the first book the author wrote, twenty-five years before it was published. He held on to it all that time. In Chapter 6 he writes:
"What I wrote then was more for me than for the world."
His personal letter at the end says why he has now shared it:
"The revelation that only God works saved my life!"

faq.q: What is Only God Works about?
faq.a: It is a short teaching book by Kevin White. It says God has never called us to work for Him, but to intimacy with Him, and to let Him work in and through us. The book walks through ten words, from Called to Finished, with Scripture throughout.

faq.q: What are the ten chapters?
faq.a: They are, in order: Called; Only; God; Work; Freedom; Intimacy; Humility; Gratitude; Fruit; and Finished. An introduction comes first, and a conclusion and a personal letter from the author close the book.

faq.q: Is it a book about resting in God?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 5 is built on the line "Freedom from work means freedom to rest," and reads God's promise of rest in Hebrews 4, Psalm 95 and Psalm 23. The author says rest does not mean being useless or lazy.

faq.q: Is that rest the same as a Sabbath day?
faq.a: Not only. The author reads Exodus 34:21 and Hebrews 4 and writes, "This rest is a place and not a date." He says it is a provision from God that has already started and does not end.

faq.q: What does it say about faith and work?
faq.a: It says God is honored when we work hard to provide for our families, and that the work God wants done is a work only He can do. Our part, the author writes, is to pursue His presence and follow His instructions. A chapter says your focus is the same whether you are a teacher, a truck driver, a doctor or a pastor.

faq.q: Does it teach intimacy with God?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 6 is called Intimacy and begins, "You were created in the image of God for intimacy with God." The book names intimacy, humility and gratitude as the three things God gives us to focus on.

faq.q: What does it say about bearing fruit and the fruit of the Spirit?
faq.a: Chapter 9, Fruit, says only God produces fruit, and quotes Galatians 5:22-23. The author contrasts what he calls the plastic fruit of his years of overwork with the real fruit he saw once he stopped. He writes, "Fruit is a natural byproduct of intimacy with God."

faq.q: Is it for pastors facing burnout?
faq.a: It speaks to them directly. The author describes his own years as a workaholic pastor, sleeping between 3:00 a.m. and 6:00 a.m., and says the lie of working for God has driven countless pastors and leaders out of ministry. It is a book of teaching and testimony, not a clinical guide to burnout.

faq.q: Does it cover identity in Christ?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 4 includes a diagram showing our identity in creation as significant, secure and accepted, in corruption after the fall, and restored in Christ. The author writes, "Our identity is IN Christ."

faq.q: Does it talk about the Great Commission?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 10, Finished, looks at the 10/40 window and the more than 3 billion people the book says have limited or no access to know about Jesus, and at Matthew 24:14 as the finish line. The author writes that only God can finish the work.

hero.audience_line: For Christian moms and dads raising children in today's culture, from the baby dedication to the empty nest, and for the pastors, small groups and grandparents who stand beside them.
hero.tagline: A pastor and father of four writes from experience, not theory: twenty-nine short chapters on raising healthy, godly children who grow up to be properly independent adults.
chips: Break their will, not their spirit

audience.headline: Kids have not changed, says this pastor and father of four. What has changed is what parents expect of them.
audience.body: For Christian parents of toddlers, teens and grown children, couples planning a family, blended families, church parenting classes and the pastors and grandparents who help. Roger Loomis has watched many parents in his church struggle, and he and his wife raised two sons and two daughters of their own. He takes one subject per chapter, from leading your children to Jesus and dedicating a baby, to table talk, phones and social media, discipline, chores, dating, the empty nest and relating to adult children. Each chapter opens with a quotation or a verse and closes with a My Thoughts page for your own notes. A note on subjects: the book takes a firm, conservative biblical position throughout. Chapters 12 and 13, on cultural relativism, speak frankly about teen sexual behavior, pornography, profanity, same-sex attraction, transgender identity, premarital sex and cohabitation, and the author asks parents to discuss them with children in an age-appropriate manner. Chapter 18 describes how his family used spanking and where he draws the limits. It is a pastor's counsel, not a clinical or psychological guide.

quote.text: “Raising Parents Is Tough speaks from experience, not theory.”
quote.cite: Raising Parents Is Tough, Introduction

what_makes.title: What makes this book for parents who want a pastor's plain counsel
paras: The book begins in Eden, with Cain and Abel. The author wonders whether Adam and Eve saw the anger building between their sons, and what they did or did not do about it. That question runs through every chapter: what are you seeing in your home, and what will you do?
Five things set it apart:
list: It covers the whole span of parenting, from baby dedication and the first five years to dating, the empty nest and adult children.
It is honest about the author's own family. He admits he and his wife were less than perfect parents, and he tells what worked and what did not.
It names today's pressures directly: social media, cell phones and other devices, entitlement, horror movies and a culture he calls relativistic.
It separates discipline from punishment. Discipline, he writes, is instruction, and he gives three methods besides spanking: time out, grounding and taking away privileges.
It is built for reflection. Twenty-nine short chapters, each closing with a My Thoughts page, suit a small group or a couple reading together.

sections.h2: For parents of young children
paras: The author believes a child's personality, worldview and view of God are shaped from birth to age five. Early chapters cover dedicating a baby, recognizing each child's God-given bent, and setting boundaries before a child can reason. His summary is short: “Children do not raise themselves.”

sections.h2: For parents of teenagers
paras: Chapters on social media, cell phones, healthy boundaries, entitlement, dating and work ethic speak to the teen years. He recommends curfews, no technology at the dinner table and a part-time job in high school, so children learn that bills, rent and groceries are coming.

sections.h2: For empty nesters and parents of adult children
paras: The goal, he writes, is to create an empty nest, and to raise children who do not have to spend their adult years getting over it. The last chapters talk honestly about grown children who live far away, and about how to keep relating to them as adults.

sections.h2: For pastors, small groups and church parenting classes
paras: The author writes as a pastor who says pastoring is parenting. The short chapters, Scripture throughout and a My Thoughts page after each chapter make the book easy to use for a class or study group.
