paras: Some of the author's most memorable childhood moments happened at the family dinner table, where he and his six siblings learned to listen, share their day and pray over meals. He remembers sitting alone at the table late one evening because he refused to eat brussels sprouts. His mother told him to at least try them, and she won.
“In the end, she triumphed over my stubbornness. I now love brussels sprouts!”

Growing up with six siblings, the author's family took one long trip, to see his great-grandparents in Tennessee in the summer of 1969, where a great uncle led them through a cave with Civil War relics inside. Most summers were stay-cations. Once his dad set up a tent in the backyard, and the kids cooked hotdogs over an open fire with their cousins. His point is simple:
“You don't have to spend a lot of money, not when you're with people you love.”

The author writes that the goal of parenting is an empty nest. Three of his four grown children live in North Carolina and Tennessee, and he and his wife see them once or twice a year. He misses them, and he is glad they are following God's plan for their lives:
“We taught our kids to fly, but they flew too far!”

author.bio: Roger Loomis is a pastor at Hope Community Church in Jefferson, Ohio, and writes that pastoring is parenting. He and his wife raised two sons and two daughters, whom she homeschooled, and they are now empty nesters with grandchildren. He grew up in northeast Ohio, one of seven children, with summer weekends on his grandparents' farm. He wrote this book, he says, to bring instruction and hope to the parents in his church and beyond.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author writes that one hour a week in the pulpit does not give him much time to help a parent:
“If I can help you in either a large or small way to avoid some of the pitfalls parents face today, it will be worth the hours I put into this work of love.”
He does not claim to have every answer, and he invites readers who disagree with some of his opinions to give the book an honest chance anyway. He closes with what he has said for years:
“If we don't have two things in our lives—Jesus and a family—we are robbed of all that matters.”

faq.q: What is Raising Parents Is Tough about?
faq.a: It is a Christian parenting book by pastor Roger Loomis. In twenty-nine short chapters he covers faith in the home, discipline, technology, boundaries, chores, dating, the empty nest and relating to adult children, each with Scripture and a My Thoughts page.

faq.q: Is it a godly parenting book based on the Bible?
faq.a: Yes. The author states plainly that he accepts the Bible as God's word and the source for faith and daily conduct, and every chapter draws on Scripture. He calls parents to make the home the place where children come to know Jesus.

faq.q: Does it cover baby dedication?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 3, Baby (Child) Dedication, explains it from Hannah and Samuel and from Jesus being presented in the Temple. The author says a dedication does not save a child; it is more of a parental dedication to raise the child in the ways of the Lord.

faq.q: Does it address blended families?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 6, His, Hers, and Theirs, discusses the challenges of blended families, including a stepparent's role, and shares twelve common problems as described by a licensed clinical social worker.

faq.q: Does it help with family devotions?
faq.a: Yes, in Chapter 16, The Family Altar. The author admits his family did not keep a set daily Bible time, and encourages parents to do what works: use mealtimes, everyday events and good Christian films to talk about God's Word.

faq.q: Does it talk about becoming empty nesters?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 27, Empty Nest, says the goal of parenting is to raise children who can leave well, and Chapter 28 covers relating to children in their adult years. The author shares his own experience of grown children living far away.

faq.q: Does it teach life skills for teens?
faq.a: Yes. The Work Ethic chapter stresses chores from preschool on, and the Empty Nest chapter recommends a part-time job in high school and teaching children that bills, rent and groceries will be theirs to pay. Other chapters cover problem-solving and keeping your word.

faq.q: What does the book say about spanking?
faq.a: Chapter 18 says the author's family did spank, as the exception and not the rule, never in anger, never after age twelve and never on the face, legs, arms or head. Chapter 19 offers three other methods: time out, grounding and taking away privileges.

faq.q: Does it address social media and cell phones?
faq.a: Yes. Chapters 8 and 9 are about social media and devices, and Chapter 7 recommends no technology at the dinner table. Chapters 12 and 13 discuss the sexual content children can meet online and recommend porn blockers and close monitoring.

hero.audience_line: For Christians who want to hide God's Word in their hearts but have always said they cannot memorize, and for the pastors, teachers and small groups who want to help them.
hero.tagline: A Scripture performer and Bible memory teacher shows why memorizing God's Word still matters and teaches the POWER System, a simple step-by-step way to do it in five to ten minutes a day.

audience.headline: A pastor's kid who memorized the whole book of James wrote this for everyone who has ever said, "I don't have a good memory."
audience.body: For Christians of all ages and backgrounds who know Scripture memory is good for them but feel stuck: new believers, longtime church members, busy parents, students and seniors. It also serves Sunday school teachers, small group leaders and pastors who want a plan they can hand to others. Jeremy Kluth founded Scripture Alive, a ministry through which he presents whole chapters and stories of the Bible from memory, and he studied communications at Moody Bible Institute. The book is short and practical: five chapters, a closing section on living out what you memorize, and verse lists and resources at the back. Each chapter ends with a set of questions called FIVE Take. A note on subjects: Chapter 2 tells of the death of the author's mother from cancer when he was thirteen. Scripture quotations are from the English Standard Version unless marked NIV.

quote.text: “The power to remember is central to our lives as believers.”
quote.cite: Power to Remember, Introduction: Our Power to Remember

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who think they cannot memorize
paras: The book opens with a man who spent less than a day in a jail in China. He had no phone, no book and no Bible, only what he could recite, and he found it was very little. Jeremy asks the reader to imagine the same thing, and then shows a way to change it.
Five things set it apart:
list: It starts with why. Before any method, Chapter 3 gives eight biblical reasons to memorize Scripture, from overcoming temptation to renewing your mind.
It names the excuses out loud. Chapter 4 takes eight obstacles one at a time, from I don't have a good memory to I think it sounds legalistic, and answers each.
It gives a method you can follow. The POWER System walks through picking a passage, making a plan with a pace, place, time and partner, and praying before you start.
It fits different learners. Under See it, Say it and Do it, readers can write, type, draw, sing, recite, act out or add hand motions to a verse.
It ends with tools. The back of the book lists 200 memory verses on 30 topics, 40 Bible stories, 30 chapters and 10 short books to memorize, plus organizations, performers and books.

sections.h2: For believers who say they cannot memorize
paras: Jeremy hears the same two answers again and again: I don't have a good memory, and I don't have time. He argues that memory grows with practice, like a muscle, and that Scripture memorization does not require a lot of time. Five to ten minutes a day is the plan he lays out.

sections.h2: For busy parents and caregivers
paras: The time chapter speaks to a mom of young children and to someone caring for aging parents. It suggests pairing memory work with things you already do, giving the Lord the first five minutes you have, and trimming the extras that eat away at your day.

sections.h2: For small groups, classes and accountability partners
paras: The book says plainly that going it alone is a major reason people quit. It asks every reader to choose an accountability partner, meet weekly or every other week and recite to each other. It also suggests memorizing as a church small group, and each chapter's FIVE Take questions give a group something to discuss.

sections.h2: For older readers wondering if it is too late
paras: Jeremy tells of a pastor in California who was sixty-eight when he started memorizing whole books of the Bible and performing them. His point is that desire, practice and consistency matter more than age, and that memorizing can help keep the mind engaged as we grow older.

stories.h2: Two hours on a mission trip
paras: At twelve, Jeremy went with his church on a weeklong mission to Costa Rica. Too young to build, he became the gofer kid who fetched nails and paintbrushes. One of the repairmen, who also served as a translator, asked him whether he did daily devotions, then invited him outside for his own morning time with God. After two hours of reading, prayer and creation, Jeremy was hooked. He writes that during that week he truly gave his life to Christ.

His mother had lived with breast cancer for seven years when it moved into her lungs. She died in August of 2010, when he was thirteen. He turned to Scripture, and James 1:2-4 became his greatest comfort. He memorized it to keep it with him at all times. Years later he memorized the whole first chapter of James, all 27 verses, and later still the entire book.
"I turned to Scripture for hope and help."

As a Scripture performer, Jeremy plans by the calendar. If a performance is eight weeks away and the passage is 50 verses, he gives himself six weeks to memorize and keeps two weeks to review. That works out to about eight verses a week, a little over one a day. He writes down each day's verse and works on it every day. He uses it to show that a big goal broken into small tasks can be reached.

author.bio: Jeremy Kluth is the founder of Scripture Alive, a ministry dedicated to engaging people with the Word of Truth. He combines over a decade of acting experience with biblical training from Moody Bible Institute (BA, Communications), and his dramatic Scripture presentations include whole chapters and stories from fifteen books of the Bible. He leads Bible Memory Workshops, does guest preaching, and has presented God's Word live at camps, chapels, conferences and churches, nationally and internationally. He has traveled to twenty-five countries. He grew up in Colorado and now lives in Illinois.

publisher.about: Spirit Media Publishing is a Christian publishing and marketing company with a vision to reveal our Father's heart to all nations. It offers full-service book creation and publishing in paperback, hardback, digital and audiobook formats, along with children's titles, compact Express Books, website design and SEO, and podcast and video production. We are glad to publish a practical guide that helps believers carry God's Word with them wherever they go.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: In the acknowledgments, Jeremy credits his dad with the idea of launching a Bible memory and performance ministry and teaching others how to memorize Scripture, and says he might never have written the book without it. In Chapter 2 he says he wrote it for fellow believers who want to memorize Scripture but feel they cannot:
"You feel stuck and don’t think you can actually accomplish it for one reason or another."
The introduction states his hope for the reader:
"My prayer and hope is that my book is simply the vehicle for you to recognize and embrace the power that God has given you to remember His Word."

faq.q: What is Power to Remember about?
faq.a: It is a practical guide to Scripture memory by Jeremy Kluth, founder of the Scripture Alive ministry. It explains why memorizing God's Word still matters when the Bible is on every phone, answers the excuses that keep believers from trying, and teaches a step-by-step method called the POWER System.

faq.q: What is the POWER System for Scripture memory?
faq.a: It is the five-step method in Chapter 5. The steps are, in order: Pick, Plan, and Pray; Overcome Excuses; Work On It Daily; Express It; and Review It. The review step has two parts, Reinforce and Retain, and then you repeat the process with a new passage.

faq.q: What are the eight reasons to memorize Scripture in the book?
faq.a: They are, in order: it is God's will for you; it brings you healing and comfort; it brings godly success to your life; it helps you to overcome sin and temptation; it equips you to refute the enemy's lies and affirm truth; it equips you to teach and encourage other Christians; it renews your mind (and strengthens your brain); and it helps you know what you believe.

faq.q: Is Scripture memory one of the spiritual disciplines?
faq.a: Yes. The book says there is a reason Scripture memorization is considered one of the spiritual disciplines: it takes discipline and it nurtures our spiritual growth. Jeremy places it beside reading and studying the Word, prayer, sharing your faith and being part of a church.

faq.q: Does memorizing Scripture help with renewing your mind?
faq.a: That is one of the book's eight reasons. Chapter 3 ties memory work to Romans 12:2 and being transformed by the renewal of your mind, and to replacing negative self-talk with what God says. The closing section adds that praying memorized Scripture lets the author be transformed by the renewal of his mind.

faq.q: What does the book say about the sword of the Spirit and spiritual warfare?
faq.a: It says our real battle is against spiritual forces of evil (Ephesians 6:12) and points to Jesus, who answered Satan in the wilderness by quoting Scripture He carried in His heart. The Do it section uses the armor of God passage in Ephesians 6, including the sword of the Spirit, to show how hand motions help a verse stick.

faq.q: Is it a good book for beginners and new believers?
faq.a: Yes. It is written for people of all ages and backgrounds, including those who have never memorized a verse. Jeremy says to choose a pace that is comfortable, even one verse a month, and the resource lists suggest where to start.

faq.q: Can it be used for discipleship or small groups?
faq.a: Yes. The book asks every reader to find an accountability partner and suggests memorizing a passage together as a church small group. Each chapter ends with FIVE Take questions, and the closing section is about sharing the Word, praying it and living it out.

faq.q: What obstacles does the book answer?
faq.a: They are, in order: I don't have a good memory; I don't have time; I tried before, but it didn't work; I don't know how to do it; I don't know which Scriptures to memorize; I don't feel like it; I don't think it matters; and I think it sounds legalistic.

audience.body: This is the Hindi translation of Only God Works by Kevin White. Its message is the one he says set him free after ten years as a workaholic for God: God has called you to Himself, not to do His work for Him. The book walks through ten words, with Scripture throughout, and shows how rest leads to more fruit, not less. The whole book, including the Scripture passages, is printed in Hindi in Devanagari script. A note on subjects: the author is frank about burnout, illness from overwork and being voted out as a pastor, and one chapter uses the intimacy of a bride and groom as a picture of closeness with God. It is written for adults.

what_makes.title: What makes this edition for Hindi readers
paras: The Hindi edition keeps the book's opening scene. It asks you to imagine the day after you die, in a heaven where nothing was made by human hands, and where people from many nations thank you because God worked through your giving, your mission trips and your prayers. Then it asks who is really doing the work.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is the whole book in Hindi, with the same ten chapters, the conclusion and the author's personal letter.
Its chapter titles still read as one sentence. In Hindi they begin कॉल किया गया (Called), केवल (Only), भगवान (God) and कार्य (Work).
It names a half-truth. God has called you, the author writes, and the enemy adds two words: to work.
It comes from a hard story. The author tells of overwork, being dismissed by his church, and a trip to India in 1998 that changed how he lived.
It looks to the finish line. The last chapter is about the 10/40 window and the people who still have little or no access to know about Jesus.

sections.h2: For Hindi-speaking believers who are worn out

sections.h2: For pastors and church leaders

paras: The introduction asks you to imagine heaven. Nothing there was made by human hands. Your yard and the work on your house are not there. कल्पना कीजिए कि यह आपके मरने के अगले दिन है।

In Chapter 4 the author tells how, in 1998, God took him to India and showed him Christ followers without basic necessities, most without Bibles, who still passionately pursued God's presence. On the plane home he committed to pursue the presence of God every day for the rest of his life. Chapter 9 tells the harder story around it: a church he built while working up to ninety hours a week, a vote that dismissed him, and a stranger who told him he had not been fired but set free.

Chapter 10, Finished, describes the 10/40 window, the region of North Africa, the Middle East and Asia where most people with little or no access to know about Jesus live, including many in India. It reads Matthew 24:14 as God's finish line and Revelation 7 as a picture of every nation worshiping together, and says only God can finish the work.

He has been to India more than fifty times, taking 1,000 people on mission trips. He is CEO of Spirit Media and the author of Audacious Generosity, Get to the Point and What's Your Word?

paras: Only God Works was the first book the author wrote, twenty-five years before it was published, and he says it was written more for himself than for the world. His personal letter at the end calls the message a matter of life or death for billions of people far from God, and says the revelation that only God works saved his life.

faq.q: What is this book?
faq.a: It is the Hindi edition of Only God Works by Kevin White, printed under the title केवल ईश्वर काम करता है. It teaches that God has never called us to work for Him, but to intimacy with Him, and to let Him work in and through us.

faq.q: Is it a Hindi Christian book?
faq.a: Yes. It is a Christian teaching book printed entirely in Hindi, for Hindi-speaking believers, pastors and churches.

faq.a: Yes. The Scripture passages are given in Hindi, and the copyright page carries the NIV and NLT notices. It is a book about the Bible's teaching, not a Bible itself.

faq.q: What does it say about worry?
faq.a: It quotes Philippians 4:6-7, which tells us not to be anxious about anything but to pray with thanksgiving. The book says freedom from anxiety is fruit only God can produce.

faq.q: Does it use the prayer Jesus taught?
faq.a: Yes. The introduction and later chapters quote Jesus' prayer, Your Kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven, and the author says this rest and this work of God are for now, not only for heaven.

hero.eyebrow: By Barbara Hemphill · Foreword by Kevin White
hero.audience_line: For Christians who want short, honest readings about hearing God, for busy professionals and business owners who want order and peace, and for anyone who would like to take a walk with a wise friend.
hero.tagline: Thirty emails, written one a day without planning ahead, by a woman who started an organizing business in part to hear from God. Stories, practical wisdom and faith, a few minutes at a time.

audience.headline: As a child she begged God to speak and heard only silence. More than forty years of clearing clutter later, she wrote down what she heard, one email a day.
audience.body: For Christians who want brief, honest readings about faith and everyday life, women and men who long to hear God more clearly, and busy professionals and business owners who want to accomplish their work and enjoy their lives. Barbara Hemphill accepted a challenge to publish 30 emails in 30 days without writing them ahead of time. She writes about the pianos that followed her from a Nebraska farm to Grenada and India, the hat she finally let go, the Garden of Eden as the beginning of clutter, how to tame your email, and the seven principles behind her organizing work. Each email takes a few minutes to read. A note on subjects: Barbara writes openly about a long history of depression, including a time in Grenada when she had thoughts of driving off a mountain road, and about the end of her first marriage. These passages are brief and hopeful, and the book is warm and encouraging throughout.

quote.text: “I started an organizing business clearing the clutter from closets in an attempt to hear from God.”
quote.cite: Walking with Barbara, Email 1: Tell Me More

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who want faith and order in the same life
paras: Most of these emails start with a story from Barbara's own life and end with something you can do today. The first one sets the pattern: the next time someone says something that upsets you, try saying “Tell me more,” and see what happens.
Five things set it apart:
list: It was not planned. Barbara wrote each email on the day it went out, and her team later gathered them as a surprise for her 75th birthday.
It is short. Thirty emails, each a few pages, that can be read one a day for a month or all at once.
It mixes the practical and the spiritual. One email gives the Seven Bedrock Principles of Productive Environment Institute; another says clutter began in the Garden of Eden.
It is honest. Barbara writes about a one-room school where she was bullied, about depression and about a marriage that ended.
It closes with her heart. The conclusion tells of a man in India she came to help, and of the Shepherd's House Ministry that grew from it.

sections.h2: For readers who long to hear God
paras: Barbara grew up with a grandfather who said “God told me...” while she heard nothing. She writes that she has since learned God speaks to her in many ways, none of them out loud, and she begins each day in a chair set aside for listening. Readers who have felt the same silence will find a companion here.

sections.h2: For busy professionals and business owners
paras: Several emails are straight business wisdom from more than forty years of helping people clear clutter: a Finding SYSTEM instead of a filing system, File-Act-Toss, the Art of Wastebasketry and a plan for taming your email. One company story tells of an executive who went from 24,000 emails to 4,000 in a single day.

sections.h2: For anyone trying to let go
paras: Barbara's rule is to have nothing in your home you do not know to be useful, think to be beautiful, or love. She tells how hard it was to follow her own rule with a straw hat that belonged to a mother-in-law she loved, and how it felt to finally give it away with a prayer of thanksgiving.

sections.h2: For women's groups and friends who read together
paras: Each email is short and personal, which makes it an easy reading to share over coffee or at the start of a meeting. Topics like encouragement, mentoring, patience, anger and gratitude open good conversations.

details.Title: Walking with Barbara
details.Subtitle: 30 Emails from God
details.Author: Barbara Hemphill

paras: Barbara's grandparents, who managed a county poor farm in Kansas, scraped together $800 for her mother's piano. Barbara began lessons at about five and later accompanied 13 college ensembles. In Grenada, during a dark season of depression, an out-of-tune upright left by the last renter held a piece of music in its bench that she played over and over. In India, a grandmother's gift of $600 bought a hand-made Pleyel, and she remembers it lumbering on an oxcart toward the ship. She opens the email with a line she loves:
“But as you go through life's journey, remember that the black keys also create music.”

For months a straw hat that belonged to her mother-in-law hung over the dresser where Barbara begins each morning. She loved it because she loved her. But when someone asked what she would like to have, she realized that most of what surrounded her were things she had accepted, not chosen. She moved the hat to a closet shelf, and later donated it with a prayer of thanksgiving.
“There are several places in my home that are bare now. It felt scary at first, but it's beginning to feel very exciting.”

Barbara wanted to write a book for her 75th birthday. Then a horseback riding accident broke her collarbone, the pain stopped her writing and the 30-email project halted after Day 28. On her birthday, her team held a virtual party and showed her a beautifully designed book of the emails she had already written. She lists the lessons they taught her, starting with one of her favorite sayings:
“Yesterday's mess can become tomorrow's message.”

author.bio: Barbara Hemphill started her career in the organizing industry in 1978 with a $7 ad in a New York City newspaper. Her first best-selling book, Taming the Paper Tiger, helped her launch and grow the organizing industry. She founded Productive Environment Institute in 2008 and has taught hundreds of Certified Productive Environment Specialists worldwide. She calls herself the Vision Accelerator, working with leaders who want God to work through them to create healthier cultures and more productive workplaces, and she was chosen in 2022 for Women to Know in America. In 2020 she launched the Shepherd's House Ministry in India. She lived in India for nearly five years in the 1970s and has three adopted children from India.

publisher.about: Spirit Media Publishing is a Christian publishing and marketing company with a vision to reveal our Father's heart to all nations. It offers full-service book creation and publishing in paperback, hardback, digital and audiobook formats, along with children's titles, compact Express Books, website design and SEO, and podcast and video production. We are glad to publish these emails from a friend whose work has helped so many make room for what matters.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: Barbara writes in the conclusion that her other books were written for the sake of her business:
“I have written this book for the sake of my heart.”
The introduction says the book is the fruit of one of her team's guiding principles, Together We Are Better, and the last email ends with her own saying:
“It will all turn out in the end. Otherwise, it isn't the end yet.”

faq.q: What is Walking with Barbara about?
faq.a: It is a Christian book of thirty short emails that Barbara Hemphill wrote one a day, without planning them ahead. They mix stories from her life, practical wisdom from more than forty years of organizing, and what she has learned about listening to God.

faq.q: Can it be used as a daily devotional?
faq.a: Yes. The thirty emails can be read one a day for a month, and each takes only a few minutes. It is not a formal devotional with a verse and prayer for every day, though Scripture appears through the book.

faq.q: Is it a devotional for women?
faq.a: It is written by a woman in a warm, personal voice, and many of its stories come from her life as a wife, mother and business owner. Nothing in it is limited to women, and its business emails suit any reader.

faq.q: Does it talk about how to hear God's voice?
faq.a: Yes, especially in Email 1. Barbara begged God to speak as a child and heard only silence. She writes that she has since learned God speaks to her in many ways, none of them out loud, and that she begins each day listening for what God would like her to hear.

faq.q: Is it about walking with God?
faq.a: In a way. The title invites you to walk alongside Barbara, and the foreword asks readers to come take a walk with her and hear God speak through her emails. The dedication thanks Jesus Christ for guiding her through 75 years, even when she did not feel Him.

faq.q: Does it include tips to get organized?
faq.a: Yes. Email 7 gives the Seven Bedrock Principles of Productive Environment Institute, including Today's mail is tomorrow's pile, the Art of Wastebasketry and File-Act-Toss. Other emails cover filing systems, closets, margin and other people's clutter.

faq.q: Does it help with an overflowing email inbox?
faq.a: Yes. Email 26, Taming the (Your) Email Tiger, applies her organizing principles to email, including the question of what is the worst thing that would happen if you deleted or unsubscribed.

faq.q: Does the book talk about depression?
faq.a: Some of it. Barbara writes briefly and honestly that depression haunted her life, including a dark season in Grenada, and that after years of prayer she found peace from it most of the time. It is a personal story, not a guide to treatment.

faq.q: Does it talk about mentoring?
faq.a: Yes. Email 5, Mentoring: Sharing Your Gifts, explains where the word mentor comes from and answers a reader's questions about how to start, how to find mentees and how to approach them.

faq.q: Who is Barbara Hemphill?
faq.a: She is a professional organizer who started her business in 1978, the author of Taming the Paper Tiger and the founder of Productive Environment Institute, which trains Certified Productive Environment Specialists.

hero.audience_line: For Christians who want to know what the Bible says about Heaven, readers grieving a believing loved one, and the pastors, teachers and small groups who study it together.
hero.tagline: A Texas pastor draws on more than 35 years of study to answer, question by question, what the Bible teaches about two Heavens: the place believers go when they die, and the New Heaven and New Earth where they will live forever.

audience.headline: Many Christians know more about Hawaii than Heaven. A pastor sets out to change that, one question at a time.
audience.body: For Christians who have questions about Heaven and want the answers from Scripture: what happens the moment a believer dies, whether we will know each other, what we will do there and what the New Jerusalem will be like. It also serves people grieving a believing loved one, pastors and teachers preparing a series, youth groups and Bible study classes. Dr. Neale B. Oliver is the pastor of Henderson Street Baptist Church in Cleburne, Texas, and this is his second book, after All About The Second Coming of Christ. The book is written as questions and answers, and every chapter ends with a seven-point review, five big questions and a group discussion guide. A note on subjects: the book speaks openly about death, including the death of the author's parents and the death of infants and children, and its last chapter is about Hell. Scripture quotations are from the Holman Christian Standard Bible unless marked.

quote.text: “Heaven is the best gift you will ever receive, and I’m excited to tell you about it.”
quote.cite: What's Up in Heaven?, Introduction

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people with questions about Heaven
paras: The idea came from a woman in the author's church. At the end of a teaching series, she said the one thing she learned was that there are two Heavens. The book is built on that: Part One is Immediate Heaven, the place you go when you die, and Part Two is Eternal Heaven, the New Heaven and New Earth.
Five things set it apart:
list: It answers real questions in plain words. Chapters are organized around questions people ask a pastor, such as Will you be married to your spouse in Heaven?, Do Christians have a personal guardian angel? and Do you become an angel after you die?
It answers the question nobody asks. Chapter 1 asks what we will not do in Heaven: we will not be bored and we will not sin. Then it says what we will do: worship and work.

It follows the Bible's own description of the city. The New Jerusalem chapters walk through Revelation 21 and 22: the size of the city, its walls and gates, the River of Living Water and the Tree of Life.
It is ready for a group. Every chapter closes with a seven-point review, five big questions and a discussion guide in three parts: Motivation, Examination and Application.

It is honest about the hard parts. A chapter answers whether God promises young children go to Heaven, and the final chapter says that since Heaven is real, so is Hell. The book closes with the ABC's of Salvation.

sections.h2: For anyone grieving a believing loved one
paras: The book returns again and again to one comfort: when a believer takes their last breath on Earth, they take their first breath in Heaven. The author writes as a pastor who consoles families, and as a son whose parents died ten days apart while he was writing. He also answers whether our family and friends in Heaven miss us as we miss them.

sections.h2: For pastors, teachers and Bible study leaders
paras: Each chapter can stand alone as a lesson. The seven-point review sums it up, the five big questions check what was learned, and the discussion guide gives a group something to brainstorm, study and put into practice during the week. One pastor quoted at the front used the book for a six-week sermon series, and a youth pastor studied the first two chapters with his students.

sections.h2: For readers who want Scripture, not speculation
paras: The preface says plainly that the aim is not to repeat other books on Heaven but to help you discover what the Bible teaches. Nearly every answer quotes the passage it rests on, and the author says where the Bible is inconclusive, as with guardian angels.

sections.h2: For anyone not sure where they will spend eternity
paras: The book does not assume every reader is ready. It asks directly whether you will be in Heaven, explains how to get there, and ends with three simple steps: admit, believe and confess, followed by a prayer.

stories.h2: A new pair of Converse All Stars
paras: The introduction opens with an eight-year-old boy who could not wait. His dad said he could have a pair of Chuck Taylor All Stars, and every day he asked his mom how many more days until payday. Two days early, she took him to the store. He wore the shoes out, raced every boy in the neighborhood and cleaned them each night with a wet washcloth.
"In those new shoes, I ran faster, jumped higher, and climbed quicker."
He tells the story because Heaven is a better gift than anything he ever waited for.

stories.h2: Two hospital rooms in one hour
paras: Chapter 3 begins with a day of pastoral visits. First he prayed with a couple who had just had their first child, and the room was full of joy. Then he walked to the other end of the hospital, to the Alzheimer's unit, where a church member's mother was dying. Afterward he sat in his car for several minutes, drained.
"In a matter of one hour, I experienced the joy of new life and the sadness of life fading away."
The chapter goes on to show why, for a Christian, there can be joy at death as well as at birth.

In Chapter 2, a grieving relative tells the author that every time they walk into the church, they see the casket from a funeral held there years before. They cannot focus on the service and have stopped coming. He prays with them that God would help them see their loved one rejoicing in Heaven. It takes a few years and many conversations, but one Sunday he looks out at the congregation and sees his friend there, worshipping God.

author.bio: Dr. Neale B. Oliver is the pastor of Henderson Street Baptist Church in Cleburne, Texas. What's Up in Heaven? grows out of more than 35 years of study, research and teaching about Heaven, and it follows his first book, All About The Second Coming of Christ. As a pastor he consoles families who have lost loved ones, uses Scripture in pre-marital counseling, and joins his church's men's prayer ministry for early Monday morning prayer. Each Monday he posts a short video called Monday Minute with Pastor Neale. He believes every pastor can and should write a book.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The book began with one answer. As the author closed a teaching series at his church, he asked what people had learned, and a woman answered:
"I learned there are two Heavens. I thought there was just one!"
In the preface he says what he wants to do with the question:
"I do not intend to repeat what other authors have written, but to help you discover what the Bible teaches about Heaven."

faq.q: What is What's Up in Heaven about?
faq.a: It is a question-and-answer guide to what the Bible teaches about Heaven, by Dr. Neale B. Oliver, a pastor in Cleburne, Texas. It explains that there are two Heavens: Immediate Heaven, where believers go the moment they die, and Eternal Heaven, the New Heaven and New Earth where they will live forever.

faq.q: Is Heaven real?
faq.a: The book says yes and spends a chapter on it, A Real Place Called Heaven. The author points out that the word Heaven appears over 600 times in the Bible and that Jesus, who came from Heaven, spoke about it. He writes that he believes Heaven is an actual place.

faq.q: What happens when we die, and where do we go?
faq.a: For the believer, the book says the move is immediate: their last breath on Earth is their first breath in Heaven. Chapter 3, Dying Is Not Dying, It's Living, explains why a Christian leaves the earthly body behind, and Chapter 4 explains how Heaven connects to the resurrection and the new body.

faq.q: What is Heaven like?
faq.a: The book says Heaven will not be boring and there will be no sin there. Believers will worship and work, in a job that fits their gifts. Part Two describes the New Jerusalem from Revelation 21 and 22: a city of 12,000 stadia, a wall of jasper, gates of pearl, a street of gold, the River of Living Water and the Tree of Life.

faq.q: Do people become angels when they die?
faq.a: No. The book says you are a person created in God's image and that does not change in Heaven. It points to Moses and Elijah at the Transfiguration, who appeared as themselves. A whole chapter, Angels, God's Heavenly Agents, covers when God created angels, whether they appear today and what they do for Christians.

faq.q: Will we be married in Heaven, and will we know each other?
faq.a: The book answers both. On marriage it says no, based on Matthew 22, but believes husbands and wives will still be together: Married? No! Together? Yes! It also says you will be the same person in Heaven that you are on Earth, yet without sin.

faq.q: Does the book cover the Garden of Eden?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 11, The Garden of Eden, Restored, shows how the River of Living Water and the Tree of Life in Revelation 22 bring back what was lost in Eden, and asks whether God had a redemptive plan from the beginning.

faq.q: Is it a good book for someone dealing with grief and loss?
faq.a: It was written by a pastor who consoles grieving families, and much of it speaks to them. It answers whether loved ones in Heaven miss us, and whether God promises young children go to Heaven when they die. It is a Bible study more than a grief guide, so it teaches as it comforts.

faq.q: Does it explain salvation?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 5 asks how you get to Heaven, and the book closes with the ABC's of Salvation. They are, in order: admit that you are a sinner; believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God who died for your sins; and confess your sins and commit your life to Him. A short prayer follows.

faq.q: Is it a book about end times prophecy?
faq.a: Partly. It follows the Book of Revelation from Heaven now to the New Jerusalem and refers to the Rapture and the Second Coming along the way. Its focus is Heaven itself. The author's first book, All About The Second Coming of Christ, covers the events of Christ's return.

faq.q: Can it be used as a small group study guide?
faq.a: Yes. Every chapter ends with a seven-point review, five big questions and a discussion guide for large groups, small groups or one-on-one settings. A pastor quoted at the front used it for a six-week sermon series.

hero.eyebrow: By Angela Cunningham Simms · Foreword by JoHanna Gilyard James
hero.audience_line: For inmates and former inmates, single mothers, survivors of abuse, people fighting addiction, and the families and church mothers who keep praying for them.
hero.tagline: Angela Cunningham Simms tells how God carried her through abuse, prison, homelessness, addiction and heart surgery, in short, candid chapters written so that God gets the glory and you know you can too.

audience.headline: She has been knocked down, locked up and counted out, and she tells all of it so that someone else will see their own story and turn to Jesus.
audience.body: For every inmate, single mother, drug addict and abused person, which is how the author dedicates the book, and for anyone who loves someone in those places. It also speaks to praying parents and grandparents, church mothers and pastors who stay with people for years. Angela grew up in a segregated neighborhood of Fredericksburg, Virginia, singing in a holiness church's junior choir. She lost her mother at thirteen and was in an abusive relationship and pregnant by twelfth grade. She went on to serve time in prison, raise four children through homelessness and addiction, and survive heart surgery. Through it all, she writes, God kept placing earthly angels in her life. A note on subjects: this is a frank adult testimony. It describes domestic violence, molestation, prison, giving birth under guard, crack addiction, suicidal feelings and a shooting into the family's home. Scripture quotations are from the New Living Translation.

quote.text: “God kept me when I didn’t have the right mind to keep myself.”
quote.cite: You Can Too, Conclusion: Your Story Is for God's Glory

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who need to rise again
paras: Chapter 1 opens with a list most people would hide. Angela writes that she has been knocked down and knocked out, set out and set up, picked on and picked over. Then she adds the line that sets the tone for the whole book:
"I have been locked out and locked up. Yet, in every circumstance, God has been right there every single day of my fifty-six years."
Five things set it apart:
list: It hides nothing. She writes that God forgives our sins but doesn't always remove the consequences, and she says she does not make excuses.
It is short. Eleven chapters and a conclusion, most only a few pages, each a single testimony with its own title, from Lost in a Faraway Land to Forgiven to Forgive.
It honors the people God sent. Pastors, a first lady, church mothers who pray at 5 a.m. and noon, and an uncle who found her in a hospital hallway all appear as what she calls earthly angels.

It keeps going past the hard years. Later chapters tell of near-blindness, blood clots, quadruple bypass surgery, a daughter's surgery and a son's heart attack, and of serving as a Go Red for Women ambassador for the American Heart Association.
It ends with a charge. Get back up, forgive yourself, straighten your crown and reign. A final word from her brother, a pastor, and family and church photographs close the book.

sections.h2: For inmates, former inmates and their families
paras: Angela describes prison plainly: GED classes half the day, an industrial laundry that paid fifty cents a day, and the jailhouse noodles she still cooks. Years later, two of her sons and a bonus son were incarcerated in three different places at once. In her final word she points others toward the steps to get their voting rights restored and says there is a better way.

sections.h2: For single mothers and survivors of abuse
paras: She was a teenage mother of two with black eyes and bruises, and later homeless with four children. She does not soften the lesson:
"Abuse, be it verbal, mental, or physical is not love. If you're in it, get out!"

sections.h2: For anyone fighting addiction
paras: At one of her lowest points she had been smoking crack all day and night and had blown $700 in a single day. In shame she called her pastor and first lady, who came at once and took her to a church mother. That woman put her to bed, asked no questions and cared for her for days. Later, Angela poured herself into organizing gospel events for neighborhood children, and she writes that as long as she was in church, she was not doing drugs.

sections.h2: For praying parents and grandparents
paras: A church mother taught her that there is no distance in prayer. Angela leaned on it when her sons were in three separate prisons and when her daughter and son were in two hospitals in two states at the same time. She writes that both sons later became GED teachers and came home to their children.

details.Author: Angela Cunningham Simms

stories.h2: Her name in a hospital hallway
paras: In Chapter 2, Angela is far from home and alone, in labor for more than forty-two hours during a snowstorm, under guard. Then she hears her name. An uncle from Petersburg, Virginia, who worked at that hospital without her knowing it, walks down the hall, looks around and shouts it. He is not allowed in her room, but he lets her family know where she is.
"God used this to remind me that I'm never alone."

One Sunday in 2019 she and her grandchildren heard a sermon called The Devil Is a Liar. That night, sitting with her daughter in the living room, they heard gunshots and dropped to the floor. Bullets shattered her granddaughter's bedroom window and passed through to the shower where her grandson had just been. Police later counted thirteen bullets, fired in a gang retaliation aimed at a former resident of the house.
"I believe God sheltered us with His angels."

Angela had quit the outward sins, but she writes that when it came to forgiving her abuser, she failed the test. So one day she called him and asked whether he was saved. He said yes. She asked whether he owed her an apology, and he gave one.
"No longer bound, no more chains holding me literally or figuratively."

author.bio: Angela Cunningham Simms was born and raised in Fredericksburg, Virginia. Having fought through drug addiction, physical and sexual abuse, imprisonment, homelessness and despair, she believes God allowed her to triumph so she can share how He saved and redeemed her, and how He can do the same for others. She is a mother and grandmother, a YouTube personality, and the author of My Story Is for God's Glory and You Can Too. She has shared her journey at the University of Mary Washington and at Howard University's Cramton Auditorium. A heart attack survivor, she serves as a lifetime ambassador for Guilford County Go Red for Women in North Carolina, a signature movement of the American Heart Association.

We are glad to publish a testimony that shows no one is too far gone for our Father to reach.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: In Chapter 4, Angela writes that she should have been dead, and that she feels grateful, honored and called to write. Her dedication says what she hopes for each reader:
"I pray you will see your story and submit your life to Christ. Then I will know my life has not been in vain."
Her final word explains why she tells even the worst of it:
"I want others to know my story so they too can be strengthened to make a change."

faq.q: What is You Can Too about?
faq.a: It is a Christian memoir and testimony by Angela Cunningham Simms. In short chapters she tells how God carried her through the death of her mother, an abusive relationship, prison, homelessness with four children, crack addiction and serious illness, and how people from her church kept pointing her back to Jesus.

faq.q: Who is it written for?
faq.a: She dedicates it to every inmate, single mother, drug addict and abused person. It also speaks to anyone facing life after incarceration and to families with a loved one in prison: she writes about her own time inside and about praying for her sons while they were incarcerated.

faq.q: Does the book speak to domestic violence survivors?
faq.a: Yes. Angela was in an abusive relationship as a teenager and writes about black eyes, bruises and losing everything. She tells readers plainly that abuse is not love and urges anyone in it to love themselves enough to leave.

faq.q: What does it say about the power of prayer and prayer warriors?
faq.a: Prayer runs through the whole book. Chapter 10, There Is No Distance in Prayer, is named for something a church mother always said, and Angela gives a shout-out to her circle of prayer warriors, quoting James 5:16 on the prayer of a righteous person.

faq.q: What part do praying mothers play in the book?
faq.a: A large one. Her own mother died when she was thirteen, and church mothers stepped in. One took her under her wing and never gave up on her, another nursed her for days after a crack binge, and a group of sisters prays at 5 a.m. and noon every day.

faq.q: Does it talk about forgiving yourself and others?
faq.a: Yes. Angela tells readers who see themselves in her story to repent, get back up and forgive themselves. The chapter Forgiven to Forgive tells how she called her abuser decades later, received an apology and was set free.

faq.q: Where does grace and mercy come in?
faq.a: Her prayer at the front of the book begins by thanking God that His grace and mercy follow her all her days. Throughout, she credits God's unmerited favor, grace and mercy for keeping her, even when she was out of control.

faq.q: Does it tell of divine protection?
faq.a: It does, more than once. She survives a pulmonary embolism and quadruple bypass surgery, and in 13 Bullets she tells how gunfire tore through her home without hitting anyone. She writes that she believes God sheltered them with His angels.

faq.q: Is the book graphic?
faq.a: It is frank but not detailed for shock. It names abuse, molestation, prison, addiction and suicidal feelings in plain words, and one scene describes being chained while in labor. It is written for adults.

hero.audience_line: For home cooks who keep dehydrated, freeze-dried and powdered foods on hand, whether for long-term food storage, emergencies or simply fewer trips to the store.
hero.tagline: A quick-reference chart book that answers one question for hundreds of shelf-stable ingredients: how much dry product and how much water to add.

audience.headline: A grandmother with a passion for preparedness wrote down the answer she kept needing: how much product, and how much water.
audience.body: For home cooks building a pantry of shelf-stable food, families who keep supplies for emergencies, and anyone who would rather reach for dried vegetables than make a last-minute run to the grocery store. Wanda Bailey Clark started cooking with dehydrated, freeze-dried and powdered ingredients several years ago. She now packages mixes for convenience and disaster support and keeps her pantry stuffed. This book is the tool she made for herself. It opens with a short explanation of how each drying process works and what happens to nutrition, then gives chart after chart, one entry per product. It is a reference, not a cookbook of recipes, and not a guide to building a storage plan. The U.S. charts are rounded to the nearest 1/4 teaspoon.

quote.text: “The amount of water needed to reconstitute products is based on how much water was removed during the dehydration, freeze-drying, or powder process.”
quote.cite: Pantry Stuffers Rehydration Calculations Made Easy, Reconstitution

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who cook from the pantry
paras: Every product dries differently, so every product needs a different amount of water. Wanda writes that reconstitution is different product to product, and the book is built around that fact: you look up the item, and the chart tells you how much dry product, how much water and how much ready-to-use food you will get.
Five things set it apart:
list: Each entry is one simple formula. For example, dehydrated carrots: 1 cup carrots plus 2 cups water makes 4 cups carrots.

It covers the whole pantry. Vegetables from asparagus to zucchini, freeze-dried fruits and berries, dehydrated and dried beans, textured vegetable protein, freeze-dried meats, cheeses, eggs and dairy, fruit juice powders, sauces, syrups and wine powders.
It separates dehydrated from freeze-dried. The same vegetable often appears twice, because the two processes take different amounts of water and give different yields.
It starts with the basics. A short opening section explains dehydration, freeze-drying and powdering, and what happens to vitamins and minerals in each.
It includes the small helps. A list of garlic substitutions for one clove, egg and cream cheese conversions, and soaking directions for dried beans with a list of forty varieties.

sections.h2: For home cooks building long-term food storage
paras: If you keep a shelf of dried and freeze-dried products, the hard part is often using them in everyday cooking. The charts turn each product into an amount you can measure, so dried and freeze-dried foods can go into regular meals instead of waiting on a shelf.

sections.h2: For families preparing for emergencies
paras: Wanda packages mixes for disaster support. When the power is out or the stores are empty, there is no time to search for the right ratio. This book keeps the answer in one place for vegetables, proteins, dairy and staples like milk and eggs.

sections.h2: For anyone who wants fewer trips to the store
paras: Out of milk, eggs or sour cream halfway through a recipe? The book was written to meet that exact need. Wanda says its purpose is the last-minute substitution: how much product and how much water to add.

sections.h2: For cooks who want vegetables out of season
paras: She keeps a supply as a nutritious alternative to out-of-season vegetables. The opening section explains that most vitamins and minerals stay intact during dehydration, except vitamin C, and that dehydration keeps more of them than canning or freezing.

paras: The Eggs & Dairy section gives the amounts as a single egg, the way most recipes call for them:
"1 egg = 2 TBS whole egg powder with 3 TBS of water"
Egg whites take equal parts powder and water. The same section shows how to make 3 ounces or 8 ounces of cream cheese from powder.

Dehydrated beans go straight to water. Dried beans are different, and the book explains the steps: cover them with two inches of water, soak at least two hours, pour off the soaking water, add fresh water and cook. It adds a rule of thumb:
"As a general rule, one cup of dried beans will produce three cups of cooked beans."

stories.h2: When the recipe calls for a clove of garlic
paras: Tucked into the vegetable charts is a short list of what equals one clove of garlic. They are, in order: 1 tsp chopped garlic; 1/2 tsp minced garlic; 1/8 tsp garlic powder; 1/2 tsp garlic flakes; 1/4 tsp granulated garlic; and 1/2 tsp garlic juice. It is the kind of answer you need in the middle of cooking, and the reason the book exists.

author.bio: Wanda Bailey Clark is a busy suburban wife, mother and grandmother with a passion for preparedness. Although she had long known that dehydrated, freeze-dried and powdered ingredients existed, she began using them only several years ago. Today she packages mixes for convenience and disaster support, keeps her pantry stuffed to avoid last-minute trips to the grocery store, and keeps a supply as a nutritious alternative to out-of-season vegetables. She dedicates her work first to Jesus Christ, her Lord and Savior.

paras: Wanda kept running into the same problem in her own kitchen, especially when she needed a substitution in a hurry. faq.q: What does Pantry Stuffers Rehydration Calculations Made Easy cover?
faq.a: It is a chart reference for shelf-stable dehydrated, freeze-dried and powdered foods. Each entry gives the amount of dry product and water and the amount of ready-to-use food it makes. It covers vegetables, fruits, beans and legumes, textured vegetable protein, freeze-dried meats, cheeses, eggs and dairy, juice powders, sauces, syrups and wine powders.

faq.q: How much water do you add to powdered milk?
faq.a: The book's chart says 1/4 cup milk powder plus 1 cup water makes 1 cup milk. It also charts buttermilk, heavy cream, sour cream, butter, margarine and cream cheese powders.

faq.q: Does it cover textured vegetable protein (TVP)?
faq.a: Yes. TVP has its own section with eleven kinds, from plain to bacon bits, beef chunks, chicken, ham, pepperoni, sausage, sloppy joe mix and taco bits. Plain TVP is 1 cup TVP plus 2 cups water for 2 1/4 cups.

faq.q: How do you use egg powder?
faq.a: For one egg, the book says to use 2 tablespoons of whole egg powder with 3 tablespoons of water. For egg whites, it is 2 tablespoons of egg white powder with 2 tablespoons of water.

faq.q: Does it include peanut butter powder?
faq.a: Yes. It lists 3 tablespoons of peanut butter powder plus 2 teaspoons of water for 1 tablespoon of peanut butter, with sugar and oil added to taste. Peanut butter is one entry in a section of pantry powders that also includes honey, shortening, soy sauce, teriyaki, vinegar, Worcestershire and maple syrup.

faq.q: Is it an emergency food and food storage book?
faq.a: It is written by someone who packages mixes for disaster support and keeps a stocked pantry, and it helps you cook with the dried foods you store. It does not tell you what to store or how much. It is a calculation companion, not a storage plan.

faq.q: Does it explain how to cook dried beans?
faq.a: Yes. It separates dehydrated beans and legumes, which do not need pre-soaking, from dried beans, which need to be pre-soaked. For dried beans it says to cover them with two inches of water, soak at least two hours, drain, add fresh water and cook, and that one cup of dried beans makes about three cups cooked.

faq.q: Is it a kitchen conversion chart?
faq.a: Not a general one. It does not convert cups to ounces or Fahrenheit to Celsius. It answers how much water to add to each dried, freeze-dried or powdered product, with the U.S. amounts rounded to the nearest 1/4 teaspoon.

faq.q: Does it explain food preservation methods?
faq.a: Briefly. The Basics section explains dehydration, the oldest form of food preservation, along with freeze-drying and the powder process, and what each does to vitamins and minerals. The rest of the book is charts.
